entry_json.upgrade_note: Use for adding value to something already acceptable. For fixing something faulty, 'improve' or 'remedy' is more accurate.

entry_json.definition: to make an existing problem worse
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Building new roads often exacerbates the congestion it was meant to relieve.
example_sentences: Cutting benefits exacerbated child poverty in the poorest districts.
Remote working may exacerbate inequality between office and manual staff.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Its object must already be a problem. You exacerbate poverty or tension, never a neutral thing.

entry_json.definition: the set of reasons behind a decision or belief
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rationale behind the curfew was never explained to residents.
example_sentences: The rationale for the reform was to reduce administrative cost.
Critics accepted the rationale but questioned the timing.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Refers to a whole line of reasoning, so it is usually singular. Do not write 'many rationales' where you mean 'several reasons'.

entry_json.definition: a disadvantage of something that is otherwise useful
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main drawback of remote working is weaker informal contact.
example_sentences: Every proposed solution carries a drawback of some kind.
The obvious drawback is the cost of maintaining two systems.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use when weighing advantages against disadvantages. For something harmful rather than merely inconvenient, use 'risk' or 'danger'.

entry_json.definition: the money available to a person, organisation or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools with limited financial resources cannot replace ageing equipment.
example_sentences: Financial resources should follow need rather than political influence.
Charities compete for the same shrinking financial resources.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Suits institutional contexts. For a household, 'income' or 'savings' is clearer than 'financial resources'.

entry_json.definition: as a result of what has just been mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fewer trains were running; consequently, roads became heavily congested.
example_sentences: The harvest failed and, consequently, prices rose across the region.
Consequently, the policy achieved the opposite of its stated aim.
entry_json.upgrade_note: A linking adverb, not a conjunction: use a full stop or semicolon before it, never a bare comma splice.

entry_json.definition: used to contrast two facts directly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Exports rose steadily, whereas imports fell for three consecutive years.
example_sentences: Older workers valued security, whereas graduates prioritised flexibility.
Reading scores improved, whereas writing scores remained unchanged.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Ideal for Task 1 comparisons of two data points. Both halves need a full clause with its own subject and verb.

entry_json.definition: in addition, and reinforcing what has just been said
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Furthermore, the scheme cost less than the campaign it replaced.
example_sentences: Furthermore, evening opening would benefit shift workers.
The plan is expensive; furthermore, it addresses only the symptoms.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Begins a new sentence adding a second supporting point. One per paragraph is plenty; a chain of them reads mechanically.

entry_json.definition: because of; as a result of
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Owing to poor weather, the harvest was delayed by a month.
example_sentences: Owing to rising costs, several projects were postponed indefinitely.
Attendance fell owing to the closure of the branch line.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Followed by a noun phrase, never a clause. Write 'owing to the delay', not 'owing to the train was late'.

lemma: a significant proportion of the population

entry_json.headword: a significant proportion of the population
entry_json.ipa: ə sɪɡˈnɪfɪkənt prəˈpɔːʃn əv ðə ˌpɒpjuˈleɪʃn
entry_json.definition: a notably large share of the people in a country or group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A significant proportion of the population lives within reach of a station.
example_sentences: A significant proportion of the population has no savings at all.
Digital services exclude a significant proportion of the population.
A significant proportion of the population remains unaware of the scheme.
collocations: a significant proportion of the population
entry_json.upgrade_note: Takes a singular verb ('a proportion ... has'). Only use 'significant' where the share really is large; otherwise 'a small proportion'.

entry_json.definition: during the last twenty or thirty years
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In recent decades, family size has fallen across most of Europe.
example_sentences: In recent decades, manufacturing has given way to services.
Air travel has become far cheaper in recent decades.
collocations: in recent decades there has been
entry_json.upgrade_note: Pairs naturally with the present perfect for change over time. For the present situation only, use 'at present' or 'currently'.

entry_json.definition: young people in the years between childhood and adulthood
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Adolescents need considerably more sleep than school timetables allow.
example_sentences: Adolescents are particularly sensitive to comparison with their peers.
Screen use among adolescents has been studied intensively but inconclusively.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Suits academic and health contexts. In a friendly Speaking answer, 'teenagers' sounds more natural than 'adolescents'.

entry_json.definition: people who have reached retirement age
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Free travel for senior citizens reduces isolation as well as cost.
example_sentences: Senior citizens make up a growing share of the electorate.
Housing designed for senior citizens keeps them independent for longer.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Respectful and neutral. 'The elderly' is also accepted, but avoid 'old people' in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: to deal with a problem or subject in a serious way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report addresses overcrowding but ignores its causes.
example_sentences: Any credible plan must address the shortage of trained staff.
The government has yet to address the underlying cause of the deficit.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means to tackle a problem, not merely mention it. For simply discussing a topic, use 'discuss' or 'examine'.

entry_json.definition: to find out something definite by checking carefully
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Inspectors could not ascertain how long the fault had existed.
example_sentences: The survey sought to ascertain why patients missed appointments.
It is difficult to ascertain the true cost of the programme.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Formal and investigative, usually with 'whether' or a fact as its object. Not used for casually learning news.

entry_json.definition: to increase suddenly and sharply
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Demand for bicycles surged when fuel prices rose.
example_sentences: Applications surged after the fees were abolished.
Energy prices surged within a single quarter.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Only for sudden, steep rises in Task 1. For a gentle rise use 'climbed steadily' or 'rose gradually'.

entry_json.definition: to fall very quickly and by a large amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Passenger numbers plummeted when the service was reduced.
example_sentences: Sales plummeted in the final quarter of the year.
Confidence plummeted following the announcement.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Reserve it for dramatic falls; a small decrease should be 'dipped' or 'declined slightly'.

entry_json.definition: to discourage someone from doing something, usually by making it costly or difficult
entry_json.own_context_sentence: High fees deter capable students from applying at all.
example_sentences: Visible patrols deter opportunistic theft more effectively than cameras.
Complicated forms deter exactly the people the scheme should reach.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Followed by a person plus 'from' plus an -ing form. It means discourage, not physically prevent — for that use 'prevent'.

entry_json.definition: needing a lot of effort, skill or attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nursing is physically and emotionally demanding work.
example_sentences: The course is intellectually demanding but well supported.
Caring for a relative is more demanding than most employers realise.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use for work, roles and courses. For a problem that is hard to solve, use 'complex' or 'intractable'.

entry_json.definition: simple to understand or do, with no complications
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The application process is straightforward once the documents are gathered.
example_sentences: The solution is technically straightforward but politically difficult.
Registering online is relatively straightforward for confident users.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Best for processes and explanations. Its negative, 'far from straightforward', is a useful hedge in essays.

entry_json.definition: giving good value because it does not waste money or resources
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rail freight is far more economical than road haulage over long distances.
example_sentences: Smaller engines are more economical without being noticeably slower.
Buying in bulk is economical only if the food is actually eaten.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means efficient value, not low price. For a low price alone, use 'inexpensive' — 'cheap' can imply poor quality.

entry_json.definition: far too high in price to be reasonable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tenants are charged exorbitant fees simply to renew a contract.
example_sentences: Exorbitant childcare costs push parents out of the workforce.
The exorbitant price of insulin has been widely criticised.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Carries clear criticism of unfairness. For something merely costly, use 'costly' or 'prohibitively expensive'.

entry_json.definition: existing widely in a particular place or among a particular group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Short-term contracts are especially prevalent in hospitality.
example_sentences: Obesity is more prevalent in areas with fewer sports facilities.
The practice remains prevalent despite repeated official warnings.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Used with 'in' or 'among' plus a group or place, typically for problems and conditions rather than pleasant things.

entry_json.definition: to correct something that is wrong or unsatisfactory
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Additional funding alone will not remedy the shortage of teachers.
example_sentences: The regulator ordered the company to remedy the safety failures.
Training can remedy weak literacy far later than was once assumed.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use for situations, shortcomings and imbalances. For machines and objects, 'repair' is the natural verb.

entry_json.definition: to bring something under control and use its power usefully
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coastal countries are beginning to harness tidal energy.
example_sentences: Schools could harness pupils' curiosity instead of suppressing it.
The scheme harnesses private investment for public infrastructure.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Its object should be a force or potential — energy, enthusiasm, data. Do not write 'harness a pen'.

entry_json.definition: to state something firmly as true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Campaigners assert that the consultation was never genuine.
example_sentences: The authors assert that the effect persists into adulthood.
It is often asserted, though rarely shown, that competition raises standards.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Implies a claim made without full proof, so it works well when you then challenge it. For neutral reporting use 'state'.

entry_json.definition: to become gradually worse in quality or condition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air quality deteriorated steadily as traffic volumes grew.
example_sentences: The building deteriorated rapidly once repairs were postponed.
Relations between the two authorities deteriorated over the funding dispute.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Intransitive — something deteriorates by itself. To say what caused it, use 'exacerbate' or 'worsen' with an object.

entry_json.definition: a harmful or unwanted result
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Night shifts have a well-documented adverse effect on health.
example_sentences: The charge had no adverse effect on trade in the city centre.
Researchers found an adverse effect on sleep but not on attainment.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Always with 'on' plus what is harmed. 'Adverse' collocates with effect, impact, consequences and conditions.

entry_json.definition: new and unlike anything done before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city trialled a novel approach to collecting food waste.
example_sentences: A novel solution is not automatically a better one.
The team developed a novel method for measuring the effect.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Means innovative, and is used before a noun. Do not use it for something merely recent — a novel car is not a new car.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is clearly noticeable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Attendance improved markedly after the free breakfast scheme began.
example_sentences: Results differ markedly between the two age groups.
The two cities differ markedly in how they fund transport.
entry_json.upgrade_note: Use where a difference or change is visible in the data. It modifies verbs and comparatives, not plain adjectives.

entry_json.definition: suitable for growing crops, rather than only for grazing animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once the topsoil washes away, arable land takes decades to recover.
example_sentences: Countries with little arable land have to import most of what their people eat.
Building on arable farmland is a decision that cannot be undone.

contexts.text: Once the topsoil washes away, arable land takes decades to recover.
My uncle farms about forty hectares, and only half of it is really arable.
The chart shows a steady fall in the share of arable land between 1990 and 2020.

confusables.difference: Arable says what the land is used for: crops rather than pasture. Fertile says how rich it is. Poor soil can still be arable, and fertile grassland is not.
minimal_pair: The valley floor is arable.
The valley floor is fertile.

entry_json.avoid: Not "arable animals". The word describes land and farming, never livestock.

entry_json.definition: the whole area of land whose rainfall drains into one river or reservoir
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rainfall across the whole catchment feeds a single reservoir north of Verdon.
example_sentences: Tree planting in the upper catchment slows the water down before it reaches the town.
Flood defences work best when the entire catchment is managed as one system.

contexts.text: Rainfall across the whole catchment feeds a single reservoir north of Verdon.
If you pollute anywhere in the catchment, it ends up in the drinking water eventually.
Planning decisions taken upstream affect every household in the catchment below.

entry_json.avoid: In schools and hospitals "catchment area" means the area served, not drainage.

entry_json.definition: the slow process by which land, soil or an ecosystem loses its quality
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Soil degradation is harder to reverse than most people assume.
example_sentences: Decades of overgrazing caused visible degradation along the eastern ridge.
The report links degradation of the coastline to the removal of the dunes.

contexts.text: Soil degradation is harder to reverse than most people assume.
You can see the degradation just by looking at the colour of the fields.
Intensive farming raises yields in the short term and accelerates degradation in the long term.

confusables.difference: Degradation is the standard word for land, soil and ecosystems. Deterioration is the general word for anything getting worse, including health and buildings.
minimal_pair: Land degradation is now measurable.
His health showed a steady deterioration.

entry_json.avoid: Degradation of X, never degradation to X.

entry_json.definition: limited in amount, so it will eventually run out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fresh water is a finite resource, even in countries that never think about it.
example_sentences: Oil is finite, and every government knows roughly when its own fields will empty.
Treating farmland as finite would change how quickly councils approve new estates.

contexts.text: Fresh water is a finite resource, even in countries that never think about it.
My time is finite, so I have to choose what actually matters.
An economy built on finite reserves has to plan for the year they stop paying.

confusables.difference: Finite means there is an end. Infinite means there is none. Learners often want "unfinite", which does not exist.
minimal_pair: Coal supplies are finite.
The possibilities felt infinite.

entry_json.avoid: Not "finited" or "unfinite". The opposite is infinite.

entry_json.definition: to destroy waste completely by burning it at very high temperature
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Roughly a third of the city's rubbish is incinerated rather than buried.
example_sentences: Incinerating plastic releases substances that filters cannot fully capture.
The plant incinerates waste and sells the heat back to the housing estate beside it.

contexts.text: Roughly a third of the city's rubbish is incinerated rather than buried.
They want to incinerate the waste locally, and nobody living nearby is happy about it.
Waste that cannot be recycled is sorted, dried and then incinerated for heat.

confusables.difference: Incinerate is the technical word for controlled disposal in a furnace. Burn is the everyday word and covers accidental fire too.
minimal_pair: The plant incinerates medical waste.
The barn burned for six hours.

entry_json.avoid: Incinerate takes an object. Rubbish does not "incinerate" by itself.

entry_json.definition: impossible to undo or return to how it was
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once a species disappears, the loss is irreversible, however much money arrives afterwards.
example_sentences: Clearing ancient woodland does irreversible harm that replanting cannot repair.
Governments hesitate because the decision is expensive and irreversible.

contexts.text: Once a species disappears, the loss is irreversible, however much money arrives afterwards.
The damage to his hearing was irreversible, which is why he wears protection now.
Scientists disagree about the point at which warming becomes irreversible.

entry_json.avoid: Not "unreversible". The prefix is ir- before r.

entry_json.definition: a chemical used to kill insects and other pests that damage crops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heavy pesticide use protects the harvest and quietly kills the insects that pollinate it.
example_sentences: Some pesticides stay in the soil long after the crop has been harvested.
Farmers who cut pesticide use often accept a smaller but more reliable yield.

contexts.text: Heavy pesticide use protects the harvest and quietly kills the insects that pollinate it.
I buy organic vegetables when I can afford them, mainly because of the pesticides.
Pesticide sales rose sharply in the first decade and then levelled off.

confusables.difference: A pesticide kills things that eat the crop. A fertiliser feeds the crop. Both are sprayed on fields, which is why learners swap them.
minimal_pair: They sprayed pesticide to stop the beetles.
They spread fertiliser to raise the yield.

entry_json.avoid: Countable: one pesticide, several pesticides.

entry_json.definition: to make damaged or flooded land usable again
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The docks were reclaimed and turned into flats within a decade.
example_sentences: Reclaimed industrial land is cheaper to build on than farmland, and less controversial.
It takes years to reclaim a site where heavy metals have soaked into the soil.

contexts.text: The docks were reclaimed and turned into flats within a decade.
They want to reclaim the old quarry and plant it as woodland.
Land reclaimed from the estuary now carries a third of the city's housing.

confusables.difference: Reclaim means make the land usable, often for something new. Restore means put it back the way it was.
minimal_pair: The quarry was reclaimed as a business park.
The marsh was restored to its original state.

entry_json.avoid: Reclaim also means "get back" — reclaim your luggage. Context decides.

entry_json.definition: the ability of a system, place or person to recover after a shock
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flood resilience is cheaper to design in than to add afterwards.
example_sentences: Building resilience means accepting that some floods will happen anyway.
Diverse crops give a farm more resilience than a single high-yield variety.

contexts.text: Flood resilience is cheaper to design in than to add afterwards.
What surprised me was the resilience of the people, not the scale of the damage.
A town with one employer has very little economic resilience.

confusables.difference: Resilience is recovering after the shock lands. Resistance is stopping it landing at all. A wall resists water; a town recovers.
minimal_pair: The coast is building resilience.
The coast is building resistance.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "a resilience" or "resiliences".

entry_json.definition: a situation in which there is not enough of something people need
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Water scarcity already shapes farming decisions across the drier south.
example_sentences: Scarcity of housing pushes rents up faster than any other single factor.
A drought creates scarcity within weeks, and rebuilding supplies takes years.

contexts.text: Water scarcity already shapes farming decisions across the drier south.
We never think about scarcity here, because the shelves are always full.
Price rises are usually the first visible sign of scarcity.

confusables.difference: Scarcity is the abstract condition and suits academic writing. A shortage is a specific gap in a specific place at a specific time.
minimal_pair: Water scarcity is a structural problem.
There was a shortage of bottled water on Tuesday.

entry_json.avoid: Scarcity of X, never scarcity in X.

entry_json.definition: waste water and human waste carried away from homes in pipes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Untreated sewage entering rivers is a public health problem before it is an environmental one.
example_sentences: Older cities carry sewage and rainwater in the same pipe, which is why storms cause spills.
Investing in sewage treatment is unglamorous and saves more lives than most projects.

contexts.text: Untreated sewage entering rivers is a public health problem before it is an environmental one.
After heavy rain the sewage just overflows straight into the river.
Sewage is screened, settled and treated biologically before the water is released.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "a sewage" or "sewages".

entry_json.definition: the responsible care of something you look after for others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farmers are increasingly paid for stewardship rather than for output alone.
example_sentences: Stewardship schemes reward hedgerows and wetlands instead of extra hectares of wheat.
The idea behind stewardship is simple: you are holding the land for whoever comes next.

contexts.text: Farmers are increasingly paid for stewardship rather than for output alone.
My grandparents talked about stewardship, though they never used that word.
Good stewardship of a coastline means accepting that some of it will be given up.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable, and it takes of: stewardship of the land.

entry_json.definition: poisonous, and harmful to living things even in small amounts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Toxic waste from the old plating works is still sealed beneath the car park.
example_sentences: Some cleaning products are toxic enough that the label tells you not to mix them.
Social media can turn toxic within hours when a story goes wrong.

contexts.text: Toxic waste from the old plating works is still sealed beneath the car park.
The atmosphere in that office was completely toxic, so I left after a year.
The compound is toxic to fish at concentrations too low to taste.

entry_json.avoid: Toxic to something, never toxic for something.

entry_json.definition: an area of land that is permanently or seasonally covered by shallow water
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coastal wetlands absorb storm surges that would otherwise reach the houses behind them.
example_sentences: Draining wetlands for farmland removed the flood protection the villages relied on.
A restored wetland stores carbon and cleans water at the same time.

contexts.text: Coastal wetlands absorb storm surges that would otherwise reach the houses behind them.
We spent a morning walking round a wetland reserve, and I saw birds I'd never seen before.
The area of protected wetland doubled over the twenty-year period.

entry_json.avoid: Usually plural when general: wetlands are, not wetland is.

entry_json.definition: plant or animal material burned or processed as a source of energy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Biomass accounted for a small but rising share of the country's heat supply.
example_sentences: Burning biomass releases carbon that the next crop is supposed to absorb again.
Biomass suits rural heating far better than it suits city electricity.

contexts.text: Biomass accounted for a small but rising share of the country's heat supply.
The whole village is heated by a biomass boiler, which sounds odd until you see it.
Whether biomass counts as clean energy depends entirely on where the wood came from.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "biomasses".

entry_json.definition: a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and warms the planet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Transport is now the largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries.
example_sentences: Methane is a greenhouse gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide does.
Cutting greenhouse gases means changing how we heat buildings, not just how we drive.

contexts.text: Transport is now the largest single source of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries.
Flying is the one thing I do that really adds to greenhouse gas emissions.
Greenhouse gas concentrations rose steadily throughout the period shown.

entry_json.avoid: Before a noun it stays singular: greenhouse gas emissions, not greenhouse gases emissions.

entry_json.definition: releasing no more carbon than is removed again, so the net effect is zero
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council has promised to be carbon neutral within fifteen years.
example_sentences: A carbon neutral building still uses energy; it just balances what it uses.
Claiming to be carbon neutral is easy, and proving it is not.

contexts.text: The council has promised to be carbon neutral within fifteen years.
My company says it's carbon neutral, but most of that is offsetting.
Becoming carbon neutral is far cheaper for a service business than for a steelworks.

confusables.difference: Carbon neutral balances to zero. Carbon negative removes more than it releases, so the balance goes below zero.
minimal_pair: The plant is carbon neutral.
The forest scheme is carbon negative.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate only before a noun: a carbon-neutral campus, but the campus is carbon neutral.

entry_json.definition: an economic model in which products are reused and recycled instead of thrown away
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A circular economy treats waste as a design fault rather than an inevitable by-product.
example_sentences: In a circular economy, the company that sells you a washing machine also takes it back.
Recycling alone is not a circular economy; it is the last step of a linear one.

contexts.text: A circular economy treats waste as a design fault rather than an inevitable by-product.
The circular economy idea makes sense to me, but repairs still cost more than replacing.
Moving towards a circular economy requires manufacturers to design for repair from the start.

entry_json.avoid: Takes an article: a circular economy, the circular economy.

entry_json.definition: coal, oil or gas, formed underground over millions of years and burned for energy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that export fossil fuels have the least incentive to stop selling them.
example_sentences: Burning fossil fuels is the single largest reason the atmosphere is warming.
Subsidies keep fossil fuels artificially cheap and slow every alternative down.

contexts.text: Countries that export fossil fuels have the least incentive to stop selling them.
We're still paying for fossil fuels every time we fill the car up.
Fossil fuel imports fell by roughly a quarter after the new plants opened.

entry_json.avoid: Plural for the group: fossil fuels are cheap. Singular before a noun: fossil fuel subsidies.

entry_json.definition: plastic designed to be used once and then thrown away
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several countries have banned single-use plastic cutlery outright.
example_sentences: A charge of a few pence cut single-use plastic bags dramatically within months.
Single-use plastic is convenient, cheap, and almost impossible to recycle profitably.

contexts.text: Several countries have banned single-use plastic cutlery outright.
I try to avoid single-use plastic, though it's hard with fresh food.
Consumption of single-use plastic fell in the two years after the charge was introduced.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated before the noun. The plastic is single use, but a single-use bag.

entry_json.definition: how clean or polluted the air in a place is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Poor air quality costs cities more in hospital admissions than in lost working days.
example_sentences: Schools near busy roads record the worst air quality in the whole borough.
Air quality is one of the few environmental problems residents can smell.

chunk.shape: air quality + NOUN / ADJ + air quality

contexts.text: Poor air quality costs cities more in hospital admissions than in lost working days.
The air quality near the ring road is noticeably worse in summer.
Air quality improved most sharply in the year the low-emission zone opened.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "air qualities".

entry_json.definition: the gradual increase in the height of the sea caused by a warming climate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rising sea levels will reach the low-lying farmland long before they reach the town.
example_sentences: Rising sea levels do not arrive as a flood; they arrive as a slightly worse storm each decade.
Adapting to rising sea levels may mean abandoning some places entirely.

contexts.text: Rising sea levels will reach the low-lying farmland long before they reach the town.
Whole islands are being written off because of rising sea levels, which frightens me.
Coastal defences at Sandmouth were rebuilt in response to rising sea levels.

entry_json.avoid: Normally plural: rising sea levels are, not rising sea level is.

entry_json.definition: a storm, flood, heatwave or drought that is far outside the normal range
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Insurers were the first to notice that extreme weather events had stopped being rare.
example_sentences: One extreme weather event is chance; a pattern of them is something else.
Rural areas recover from extreme weather more slowly because repairs arrive last.

contexts.text: Insurers were the first to notice that extreme weather events had stopped being rare.
We changed our holiday plans twice last year because of extreme weather.
The graph records eleven extreme weather events in the final decade alone.

entry_json.avoid: "Weather" is uncountable, so count the events: three extreme weather events, not three extreme weathers.

entry_json.definition: to stop using or providing something gradually, over a planned period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The plan is to phase out coal power over eight years rather than close the plants at once.
example_sentences: Governments phase things out when banning them overnight would cost too many jobs.
Phasing out a subsidy is politically harder than never introducing it.

chunk.shape: phase + OBJECT + out / phase out + OBJECT

contexts.text: The plan is to phase out coal power over eight years rather than close the plants at once.
They're going to phase out the old buses, so the fumes should get better.
Diesel vehicles were phased out between 2028 and 2034.

confusables.difference: Phase out is gradual and planned, with a date at the end. Ban is immediate and total. Choose phase out when the sentence mentions a timescale.
minimal_pair: Coal will be phased out by 2035.
Coal was banned last April.

entry_json.avoid: Separable: phase it out, never "phase out it".

entry_json.definition: to use or consume less of something, without stopping completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I've been trying to cut down on meat, mostly for health reasons.
example_sentences: Cutting down on short car journeys is the easiest change most families can make.
She cut down on flying without ever deciding to stop completely.

contexts.text: I've been trying to cut down on meat, mostly for health reasons.
Households that cut down on food waste save money before they save anything else.
Advice to cut down on sugar works better than advice to give it up.

confusables.difference: Cut down on means less. Cut out means none at all. The difference matters when a sentence promises a result.
minimal_pair: I've cut down on sugar.
I've cut out sugar entirely.

entry_json.definition: the amount of data a connection can carry at one time

entry_json.definition: made specially for one customer rather than sold ready-made

entry_json.definition: to put a system, resource or group of people into action where they are needed

entry_json.definition: a small, usually temporary fault in a system

entry_json.definition: easy to understand and use without being taught

entry_json.definition: describing old technology that is still in use because replacing it is difficult

entry_json.definition: the first working version of something, built to test the idea

entry_json.definition: no longer needed, because something else now does the job

entry_json.definition: able to grow much larger without breaking or costing much more

entry_json.avoid: Scalable to a size. Not "scalable for".

entry_json.definition: working smoothly with no visible breaks or difficulties between the parts

Seamless integration is the promise; two systems arguing quietly is the reality.

entry_json.definition: a weakness that can be attacked or exploited

Most successful attacks exploit a known vulnerability that was never patched.

entry_json.definition: unfairness built into an automated system by the data it learned from

contexts.text: Algorithmic bias is not a bug in the code; it is the past reproduced at speed.

Courts using automated risk scores have been criticised for algorithmic bias.

entry_json.definition: to make a copy of data so it is not lost

contexts.text: I only started to back up my photos after I lost four years of them.
Organisations that back up daily still discover they cannot restore anything.
Data should be backed up to a second location, not merely to a second folder.

entry_json.avoid: Two words as a verb, one word as a noun: make a backup, back up your files.

entry_json.definition: keeping files on remote servers reached over the internet rather than on your own device

example_sentences: Cloud storage is cheap to start with and expensive to leave.

contexts.text: All my work is in cloud storage now, which is convenient until the connection drops.

Spending on cloud storage overtook spending on local servers in 2021.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not "a cloud storage".

entry_json.definition: the trail of information a person leaves behind through their online activity

contexts.text: Teenagers build a digital footprint years before they understand what it is.
Employers check a candidate's digital footprint long before the interview.
A digital footprint can convict someone as easily as it can clear them.

entry_json.avoid: Countable and singular per person: your digital footprint.

entry_json.definition: to change or develop as fast as something else is changing

example_sentences: Training budgets rarely keep pace with the systems they are meant to support.

collocations: struggle to keep pace with demand

contexts.text: Regulation has never kept pace with the technology it is supposed to govern.
I find it hard to keep pace with how quickly the tools change.
Wages failed to keep pace with housing costs throughout the period.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. Keep pace with is more formal and suits writing about trends; keep up with suits speech and people.
minimal_pair: Supply kept pace with demand.
I can't keep up with the news.

entry_json.avoid: With is obligatory: keep pace with something, never "keep pace to".

entry_json.definition: over a long period of time, when the final result becomes clear

example_sentences: The whole thing has been commercialised beyond recognition.
The ceremony was commercialised after the site was listed and visitor numbers rose.

contexts.text: Festivals are commercialised in the same decade they become popular enough to defend.
The whole thing has been commercialised beyond recognition.
The ceremony was commercialised after the site was listed and visitor numbers rose.

confusables.difference: Monetise is neutral and technical, finding a way to earn from something. Commercialise carries a complaint that the thing was changed for the worse.
minimal_pair: The festival has been commercialised.
The site monetised its archive through subscriptions.

entry_json.avoid: Usually passive and usually critical. Note the spelling with s in British English.

entry_json.definition: the whole pattern of how a group lives, not just one activity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fishing was a way of life on that coast before it became a job people commuted to.
example_sentences: For my grandparents farming was a way of life, not a business.
The reservoir ended a way of life that had continued in the valley for centuries.

chunk.shape: X is a way of life

contexts.text: Fishing was a way of life on that coast before it became a job people commuted to.
For my grandparents farming was a way of life, not a business.
The reservoir ended a way of life that had continued in the valley for centuries.

confusables.difference: Lifestyle is chosen by an individual and can be changed next year. A way of life is inherited by a whole community and changing it is a loss.
minimal_pair: Herding is a way of life here.
She adopted a healthier lifestyle.

entry_json.avoid: Singular life. Not "ways of lives".

entry_json.definition: matching or suitable for the style or spirit of something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The extension was designed in keeping with a terrace that had stood for two centuries.
example_sentences: The décor was in keeping with the age of the building, which I liked.
The policy was in keeping with commitments the department had already published.
collocations: in keeping with the character of

chunk.shape: X is in keeping with Y

contexts.text: The extension was designed in keeping with a terrace that had stood for two centuries.
The décor was in keeping with the age of the building, which I liked.
The policy was in keeping with commitments the department had already published.

confusables.difference: Similar to compares two things directly. In keeping with says one fits the standard or spirit set by the other, which is a judgement.
minimal_pair: The new wing is in keeping with the original.
The new wing is similar to the original.

entry_json.avoid: Formal. The opposite is out of keeping with.

entry_json.definition: belonging to the ordinary people of a region and passed on informally
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Folk remedies survive because they are cheap, available and occasionally right.

contexts.text: Folk remedies survive because they are cheap, available and occasionally right.
My uncle plays in a folk band at the weekends.
Folk music of the region was recorded systematically only after 1950.

confusables.difference: Traditional describes anything long established, including things made by elites. Folk specifically means it came from ordinary people rather than from a court or academy.
minimal_pair: Folk songs were never written down.
The traditional ceremony involves the mayor.

entry_json.avoid: Attributive only in this sense. Folks meaning people is a separate informal word.

entry_json.definition: involving or comparing two or more different cultures
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cross-cultural misunderstanding is usually about timing and directness rather than about vocabulary.

Cross-cultural comparison requires that the same question means the same thing in both languages.

contexts.text: Cross-cultural misunderstanding is usually about timing and directness rather than about vocabulary.
We had some cross-cultural training before the posting, which helped.
Cross-cultural comparison requires that the same question means the same thing in both languages.

confusables.difference: Multicultural describes a place where several cultures live together. Cross-cultural describes an interaction or comparison between them.
minimal_pair: Cross-cultural training prepares staff for the posting.
The city is genuinely multicultural.

entry_json.avoid: Attributive and hyphenated. Not "the team is cross-cultural".

entry_json.definition: to gradually accept a difficult truth or change that cannot be undone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities that lost their industry are still come to terms with what replaced it.
example_sentences: It took me years to come to terms with moving away.
The community come to terms with the closure over a much longer period than planners assumed.
collocations: come to terms with a loss
come to terms with the change

contexts.text: Cities that lost their industry are still come to terms with what replaced it.
It took me years to come to terms with moving away.
The community come to terms with the closure over a much longer period than planners assumed.

confusables.difference: Accept can be immediate and easy. Come to terms with says it took time and that the thing was painful.
minimal_pair: She is coming to terms with the diagnosis.
She accepted the invitation.

entry_json.avoid: Plural terms. Not "come to term with".

entry_json.definition: respected because it has been done the same way for a very long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The time-honoured method takes three days and produces a result nobody has improved on.
example_sentences: They still do it the time-honoured way, by hand.
The time-honoured procedure was retained after the review found no faster alternative.

contexts.text: The time-honoured method takes three days and produces a result nobody has improved on.
They still do it the time-honoured way, by hand.
The time-honoured procedure was retained after the review found no faster alternative.

confusables.difference: Old-fashioned suggests the method should have been replaced. Time-honoured suggests it has earned the right to continue. Same age, opposite judgement.
minimal_pair: The time-honoured recipe uses no shortcuts.
The old-fashioned till slowed every transaction.

entry_json.avoid: Attributive and hyphenated. Slightly formal and can sound ironic if overused.

entry_json.definition: to do something special to show that a particular day or event matters
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Communities mark an occasion in ways that reveal what they think worth remembering.
example_sentences: We usually mark an occasion with a meal rather than presents.
The anniversary was mark an occasion with a public exhibition rather than a ceremony.

contexts.text: Communities mark an occasion in ways that reveal what they think worth remembering.
We usually mark an occasion with a meal rather than presents.
The anniversary was mark an occasion with a public exhibition rather than a ceremony.

confusables.difference: Celebrate implies happiness. Mark an occasion works equally for sad anniversaries, where celebrating would be wrong.
minimal_pair: They marked the occasion with a minute of silence.
They celebrated the win all evening.

entry_json.avoid: Mark the occasion with a thing, not by a thing.

entry_json.definition: a change in how people travel, from one type of transport to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Achieving modal shift requires the alternative to be faster, not merely available.
example_sentences: The whole point of the scheme was modal shift, getting people off the roads.
Modal shift from car to rail was measured over the four years after the line opened.
collocations: modal shift from car to rail

contexts.text: Achieving modal shift requires the alternative to be faster, not merely available.
The whole point of the scheme was modal shift, getting people off the roads.
Modal shift from car to rail was measured over the four years after the line opened.

confusables.difference: Traffic reduction just means fewer vehicles, which could mean fewer journeys. Modal shift means the same journeys happen by a different means.
minimal_pair: Modal shift moved commuters onto the tram.
Traffic reduction followed the factory closure.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Technical term, so define it on first use in an essay.

entry_json.definition: a place where passengers can change easily from one transport line to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A well-designed interchange saves more journey time than a faster train does.
example_sentences: You change at the big interchange and it is about five minutes.
Passenger flows through the interchange were modelled before the platform was widened.

word_family.note: able to be swapped without difference

contexts.text: A well-designed interchange saves more journey time than a faster train does.
You change at the big interchange and it is about five minutes.
Passenger flows through the interchange were modelled before the platform was widened.

confusables.difference: A station is where you board one service. An interchange is specifically where several services meet and you can move between them.
minimal_pair: The interchange links four bus routes and the tram.
The station has one platform.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Stress falls on the first syllable for the noun.

entry_json.definition: the amount of traffic or people a system can handle in a given time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Widening the road raised throughput and left journey times exactly where they were.
example_sentences: The bottleneck is the junction, so throughput never improves.
Passenger throughput at the terminal exceeded its design figure within two years.

contexts.text: Widening the road raised throughput and left journey times exactly where they were.
The bottleneck is the junction, so throughput never improves.
Passenger throughput at the terminal exceeded its design figure within two years.

confusables.difference: Capacity is the maximum the system could handle. Throughput is what it actually handles, which is usually lower.
minimal_pair: Throughput fell during the works.
Capacity is nine trains an hour.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. One word.

entry_json.definition: goods carried in bulk by lorry, train, ship or aircraft
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving freight by rail cuts emissions per tonne and requires terminals nobody wants nearby.
example_sentences: Most of what comes into this port is freight, not passengers.
Rail freight volumes rose after the new terminal opened in the eastern corridor.

contexts.text: Moving freight by rail cuts emissions per tonne and requires terminals nobody wants nearby.
Most of what comes into this port is freight, not passengers.
Rail freight volumes rose after the new terminal opened in the eastern corridor.

confusables.difference: Cargo is what is inside one specific ship or aircraft on one journey. Freight is the general category and the industry that moves it.
minimal_pair: Rail freight grew by a fifth.
The cargo was unloaded overnight.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not freights.

entry_json.definition: to reduce the amount of traffic crowding a road or area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Charging drivers to enter the centre decongested it faster than any road scheme had.
example_sentences: Nothing they have tried has actually decongested that junction.
The bypass was intended to decongest the market square and largely did.

contexts.text: Charging drivers to enter the centre decongested it faster than any road scheme had.
Nothing they have tried has actually decongested that junction.
The bypass was intended to decongest the market square and largely did.

confusables.difference: Divert sends traffic somewhere else and the total is unchanged. Decongest reduces the amount in one place, whether by diverting or by removing journeys.
minimal_pair: The charge decongested the centre.
Lorries were diverted along the ring road.

entry_json.avoid: Formal and mostly used in planning. Reduce congestion is safer in speaking.

entry_json.definition: a scheme where drivers leave their car outside a city and take a bus or tram in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Park and ride works only where the last stage is faster than driving would have been.
example_sentences: We use the park and ride whenever we go into town at the weekend.
Park and ride usage doubled after the parking charges in the centre were raised.

contexts.text: Park and ride works only where the last stage is faster than driving would have been.
We use the park and ride whenever we go into town at the weekend.
Park and ride usage doubled after the parking charges in the centre were raised.

confusables.difference: A car park is only somewhere to leave the car. Park and ride is the whole scheme, including the service that takes you the rest of the way.
minimal_pair: The park and ride runs every ten minutes.
The car park was full by eight.

entry_json.avoid: Treated as a singular noun phrase. Not park and rides.

entry_json.definition: the final short stage of a journey or delivery, which is often the most expensive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The last mile costs more per kilometre than the entire distance before it.
example_sentences: The last mile is the bit that always goes wrong with deliveries.
Last mile costs accounted for the largest share of total delivery expenditure.

contexts.text: The last mile costs more per kilometre than the entire distance before it.
The last mile is the bit that always goes wrong with deliveries.
Last mile costs accounted for the largest share of total delivery expenditure.

confusables.difference: Door to door describes the whole journey from start to finish. The last mile is only the final stretch of it.
minimal_pair: The last mile is done by bicycle.
The door to door time is ninety minutes.

entry_json.avoid: Usually with the. A fixed industry term, so keep it singular.

entry_json.definition: during the hours when demand is lowest and fares are usually cheaper
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Off-peak pricing spreads demand without adding a single vehicle to the fleet.
example_sentences: I always travel off-peak because it is nearly half the price.
Off-peak loadings rose while peak loadings remained unchanged.

contexts.text: Off-peak pricing spreads demand without adding a single vehicle to the fleet.
I always travel off-peak because it is nearly half the price.
Off-peak loadings rose while peak loadings remained unchanged.

confusables.difference: Cheap is about price alone. Off-peak is about time, and the lower price is a consequence of it.
minimal_pair: The off-peak ticket is valid after nine thirty.
The ticket was cheap because it was bought early.

entry_json.avoid: Works as adjective and adverb. Hyphenated in both uses.

entry_json.definition: to travel from place to place within an area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How easily people get around without a car decides who can take which jobs.
example_sentences: It is easy to get around here as long as you have a bike.
Older residents get around less once the local bus route is withdrawn.

contexts.text: How easily people get around without a car decides who can take which jobs.
It is easy to get around here as long as you have a bike.
Older residents get around less once the local bus route is withdrawn.

confusables.difference: Travel usually means longer journeys between places. Get around means moving within one town or area, day to day.
minimal_pair: I get around by bike.
She travels to Spain twice a year.

entry_json.avoid: Get about is the equally common British alternative.

entry_json.definition: to begin a journey
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Commuters who set off before seven avoid a queue that doubles their journey by eight.
example_sentences: We set off at five to beat the traffic.
Vehicles that set off outside the peak arrived in half the time.

contexts.text: Commuters who set off before seven avoid a queue that doubles their journey by eight.
We set off at five to beat the traffic.
Vehicles that set off outside the peak arrived in half the time.

confusables.difference: Leave focuses on the place you are going away from. Set off focuses on the journey beginning.
minimal_pair: We set off for the coast at six.
We left the house at six.

entry_json.avoid: Set off for a destination, not set off to a destination.

entry_json.definition: to be delayed by something outside your control
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Freight that is held up at the border loses value in ways the shipping cost never shows.
example_sentences: Sorry I am late, I was held up on the ring road.
Services were held up for over an hour following a signal failure.

chunk.shape: X is held up by Y

contexts.text: Freight that is held up at the border loses value in ways the shipping cost never shows.
Sorry I am late, I was held up on the ring road.
Services were held up for over an hour following a signal failure.

confusables.difference: Be late is the result. Be held up is the cause, and it says the delay was not your fault.
minimal_pair: The train was held up outside the station.
The train was late by twelve minutes.

entry_json.avoid: Passive in this sense. The active hold up means to rob.

entry_json.definition: with vehicles packed so closely together that they can barely move
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic sat bumper to bumper along a road that had been widened to prevent exactly this.
example_sentences: It was bumper to bumper the whole way in this morning.
Vehicles were recorded bumper to bumper for four kilometres at the eastern approach.

contexts.text: Traffic sat bumper to bumper along a road that had been widened to prevent exactly this.
It was bumper to bumper the whole way in this morning.
Vehicles were recorded bumper to bumper for four kilometres at the eastern approach.

confusables.difference: Congested is the formal word and works in a report. Bumper to bumper is vivid, spoken and paints the picture.
minimal_pair: The road was bumper to bumper.
The route is congested at peak times.

entry_json.avoid: No hyphens after a verb, hyphenate before a noun as bumper-to-bumper traffic.

entry_json.definition: a further result caused indirectly by something that happened earlier
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A single closed lane has a knock-on effect across a network that has no spare capacity.
example_sentences: One late train has a knock-on effect on everything after it.

chunk.shape: X has a knock-on effect on Y

contexts.text: A single closed lane has a knock-on effect across a network that has no spare capacity.
One late train has a knock-on effect on everything after it.
Port delays had a knock-on effect on manufacturing output the following quarter.

confusables.difference: A side effect happens alongside the main effect, at the same time. A knock-on effect happens afterwards, because of the first one.
minimal_pair: The closure had a knock-on effect on later services.
The drug has a side effect of drowsiness.

entry_json.avoid: Effect on, not effect to. Hyphenate knock-on before the noun.

entry_json.definition: a central point where many transport routes meet and connect

contexts.text: A city becomes a transport hub because of geography and then keeps the role through investment.
The town grew up as a transport hub because of the canal.
The transport hub handled connections for four regional lines and the airport.

The interchange is under the shopping centre.

entry_json.avoid: Countable. Say a hub for a region, not a hub of a region.

entry_json.definition: the part of a road on which vehicles travel in one direction
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Closing one carriageway for repairs halves capacity and more than doubles the queue.

contexts.text: Closing one carriageway for repairs halves capacity and more than doubles the queue.
The northbound carriageway was shut all weekend.
Both carriageways were resurfaced during the twelve-week programme.

confusables.difference: A lane is one marked strip. A carriageway is all the lanes going the same way.

The inside lane was coned off.

entry_json.avoid: British term. A dual carriageway is a road with two separated carriageways.

entry_json.definition: travelling on public transport without paying the required fare
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fare evasion costs less to tolerate than the barriers built to prevent it, on some routes.

contexts.text: Fare evasion costs less to tolerate than the barriers built to prevent it, on some routes.
They have brought in inspectors because of fare evasion.
Fare evasion rates were highest on routes without barriers at either end.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not fare evasions.

entry_json.definition: measured or provided from the exact start of a journey to its exact end

contexts.text: Door-to-door time is the only measure a traveller experiences, and timetables never show it.
Door-to-door it takes me about an hour and ten.
Door-to-door journey times were compared for car, bus and cycle across the same route.

confusables.difference: Point to point measures between two named stations or stops. Door to door includes getting to the station and from it, which is where the time hides.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenated before a noun, open as an adverb.

entry_json.definition: all the trains, carriages and wagons that a railway operates

The rolling stock on that line is older than I am.
Investment in rolling stock lagged behind track renewal throughout the period.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Not rolling stocks.

entry_json.definition: to reduce the pressure on something that is overloaded

The new line has really take the strain off the old one.
Additional evening services take the strain off the last two trains of the day.

entry_json.avoid: Off the thing under pressure. Not "take the strain of".

entry_json.definition: physical measures such as humps and narrowings that force drivers to slow down
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic calming changes driver behaviour where signs and limits alone had not.
example_sentences: They put in traffic calming on our road after the accident.

contexts.text: Traffic calming changes driver behaviour where signs and limits alone had not.
They put in traffic calming on our road after the accident.
Traffic calming measures reduced average speeds by nine kilometres per hour.

The speed limit was cut to twenty.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. Usually appears as traffic calming measures.

entry_json.definition: currently being built and not yet in use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two of the four crossings are under construction and neither will open this decade.

contexts.text: Two of the four crossings are under construction and neither will open this decade.
The new bridge is still under construction, it has been ages.
The extension remained under construction throughout the survey period.

confusables.difference: Being built is the plain passive and works anywhere. Under construction is the fixed phrase used on signs and in reports, and it needs no auxiliary chain.

entry_json.avoid: No article. Not "under a construction".

entry_json.definition: a transport service that runs back and forth frequently over a short fixed route

There is a shuttle service from the car park every ten minutes.
The shuttle service carried more passengers than the mainline connection it fed.

entry_json.definition: when a train or bus arrives at a station or stop

The train pulled in just as I got to the platform.
The last service to pull in before midnight carried the highest evening load.

entry_json.definition: charging drivers directly for using particular roads at particular times
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Road pricing is the only measure that reliably reduces traffic and the hardest one to introduce.

People hate the idea of road pricing until they see what it does to journey times.
Road pricing schemes reduced peak vehicle numbers in every city that adopted them.

entry_json.definition: to be unable to move because of the volume of vehicles
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Drivers who get stuck in traffic daily lose more hours a year than most annual leave allows.

I get stuck in traffic every single morning on that stretch.
Respondents who get stuck in traffic regularly reported lower satisfaction with their commute.

entry_json.definition: a system where different services connect with one ticket and one timetable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Integrated transport is a matter of timetables and ticketing rather than of new vehicles.

What we lack is integrated transport, the bus never meets the train.
Integrated transport policy was adopted in three of the six regions reviewed.

Public transport carries most commuters here.

entry_json.definition: the total distance travelled, measured in miles

contexts.text: Average annual mileage per household fell for the first time in three decades.
My mileage dropped massively when I started working from home.
Vehicle mileage was recorded from the odometer at each service.

confusables.difference: Distance is the general measure between two points. Mileage is the accumulated total that a vehicle or person has covered.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable. British writing still uses miles for road distance despite metric elsewhere.

entry_json.definition: to slow down gradually until stopping completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The network grind to a halt whenever snow arrives before the gritters do.

Production grind to a halt within days of the port dispute beginning.

contexts.text: The network grind to a halt whenever snow arrives before the gritters do.
Everything just grind to a halt when the tunnel closed.
Production grind to a halt within days of the port dispute beginning.

The driver stopped at the lights.

entry_json.avoid: Past tense is ground. Not grinded.

entry_json.definition: having good transport links to other places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Districts that are well connected attract employers regardless of what the rents are.
