entry_json.avoid: Double the l: controlled, controlling.

entry_json.definition: a talk between two or more people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A five-minute conversation with a neighbour taught me more than an hour of revision.
example_sentences: We had a long conversation about her plans.
I overheard a conversation on the bus in three languages.
entry_json.avoid: We HAVE a conversation, not 'do' or 'make' one.

entry_json.definition: to prepare food by heating it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cook at home most evenings because eating out is expensive.
example_sentences: He cooked dinner for six people.
Learning to cook saved me a lot of money.

confusables.difference: A cook is a person; a cooker is the machine you cook on. "My mother is a good cooker" is a well-known mistake.

entry_json.definition: the kitchen machine you cook food on, with rings on top and an oven below
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flat came with a cooker but no fridge.
example_sentences: Turn the cooker off when you leave.
The gas cooker is older than I am.

confusables.difference: A cooker is the appliance. The person who cooks is a cook.

entry_json.avoid: 'Cooker' is British. Americans call it a 'stove' or a 'range'.

entry_json.definition: the activity of preparing food, or the food someone makes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cooking is the one part of the week I never rush.
example_sentences: I miss my mother's cooking.
Cooking for yourself is cheaper and usually healthier.
entry_json.avoid: We DO the cooking. Uncountable: not "cookings".

entry_json.definition: a little cold, in a way that feels nice
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The evenings stay cool here even in July.
example_sentences: Keep the milk in a cool place.
A cool breeze came off the sea.
entry_json.avoid: In speech 'cool' also means 'very good' or 'fine', but that use is informal and does not belong in writing.

entry_json.definition: a thing made to be exactly like another thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keep a copy of every document you send with your application.
example_sentences: I made two copies of the form.
She bought a second-hand copy of the textbook.
entry_json.avoid: We MAKE a copy, not 'do' one.

entry_json.definition: the place where two lines, walls or streets meet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a small shop on the corner of my street.
example_sentences: He waited for me on the corner by the bank.
There was a plant in the corner of the room.
entry_json.avoid: ON the corner of a street, but IN the corner of a room.

entry_json.definition: right; with no mistakes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only one of the four answers is correct.
example_sentences: Is this the correct spelling?
Please give the correct address on the form.

confusables.difference: They mean the same for answers and facts, but 'correct' is slightly more formal, and only 'right' is used for directions: turn right.

entry_json.definition: in a way that has no mistakes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I remember correctly, the deadline is the fifteenth.
example_sentences: The form was not filled in correctly.
She pronounced my name correctly the first time.

entry_json.definition: the amount of money you need to pay for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cost of renting a room here has risen faster than wages.
example_sentences: The cost of living has gone up sharply.
We shared the cost of the taxi.

confusables.difference: A price is what a seller asks for one item, and is written on a label. A cost is the total money something takes, including bills, time and effort.

entry_json.avoid: Say "the cost OF something", not "the cost for".

entry_json.definition: to say numbers in order, or to find out how many there are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I counted eleven people waiting at the stop before the bus came.
example_sentences: The children learned to count to twenty.
Every mark counts in the writing test.
entry_json.avoid: 'Count on someone' means depend on them, and has nothing to do with numbers.

entry_json.definition: an area of land with its own government and people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My country has changed a great deal in the last twenty years.
example_sentences: She has worked in five different countries.
The country imports most of its energy.

confusables.difference: 'The country' can also mean land away from towns, which is the 'countryside'. Context tells you which: "I grew up in the country" means the countryside.

entry_json.definition: two people who are married or in a relationship; also two of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A young couple moved into the flat below last month.
example_sentences: I will be back in a couple of minutes.
The couple have lived here for forty years.

confusables.difference: A 'pair' is two things that belong together: a pair of shoes. A 'couple' is two people together, or loosely 'about two'.

entry_json.avoid: In British English "a couple of" needs the 'of': a couple of days.

entry_json.definition: a set of lessons on a subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course runs for ten weeks and ends with a written test.
example_sentences: I am doing a course in graphic design.
The course fee includes all the materials.
entry_json.avoid: 'Of course' means 'obviously' and is one fixed phrase. Say "do" or "take" a course, not "make" one.

entry_json.definition: the child of your uncle or aunt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My cousin and I grew up in the same street and still talk every week.
example_sentences: I have eleven cousins on my father's side.
Her cousin studies medicine in Dublin.
entry_json.avoid: The 's' sounds like a 'z': KUZ-n.

entry_json.definition: to put something over something else; or to include a subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course covers both writing tasks in the first two weeks.
example_sentences: Snow covered the fields for a week.
Does the insurance cover a lost passport?

entry_json.definition: a large farm animal kept for its milk and meat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keeping cows produces far more greenhouse gas than growing wheat.
example_sentences: There were cows in the field behind the house.
The farm has two hundred dairy cows.

entry_json.definition: very strange or not thinking clearly; or loving something very much
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The traffic at rush hour is crazy, so I leave an hour early.
example_sentences: It would be crazy to drive when the train is faster.
He is crazy about football.
entry_json.avoid: Informal. In writing use 'unreasonable', 'extreme' or 'illogical'.

entry_json.definition: the thick white part that comes from the top of milk
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take my coffee black; my flatmate puts cream in everything.
example_sentences: She served the fruit with cream.
Add a little cream to the sauce at the end.
entry_json.avoid: Uncountable: not "creams".

entry_json.definition: to make something new that did not exist before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new factory will create around two hundred jobs.
example_sentences: She created a website for the club.
Tourism creates work but also raises rents.

confusables.difference: 'Make' is everyday and physical: make a cake. 'Create' suits ideas, jobs, art and problems, and is stronger in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Two syllables: kree-ATE.

entry_json.definition: good at thinking of new ideas, or involving new ideas
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools should leave more room for creative subjects, not fewer.
example_sentences: She has a very creative approach to teaching.
He works in a creative industry.

entry_json.definition: a way of buying something now and paying for it later
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Buying a phone on credit costs more in the end than saving for it.
example_sentences: She paid for the ticket with a credit card.
The shop offers interest-free credit for a year.

entry_json.definition: an action that is against the law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Crime in the area fell after the youth centre reopened.
example_sentences: Theft is the most common crime in the city.
He committed no crime, but he was questioned.
entry_json.avoid: We COMMIT a crime, never 'do' or 'make' one. 'Crime' in general is uncountable: "crime is falling".

entry_json.definition: a person who has broken the law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Prison should turn criminals into workers, not into better criminals.
example_sentences: The criminals were caught within a week.
She works with young criminals in the community.

entry_json.definition: to go from one side of something to the other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Crossing the main road on foot takes nerve at this time of day.
example_sentences: Look both ways before you cross the street.
The ferry crosses the channel twice a day.
entry_json.avoid: Cross the road with no preposition. Not "cross over the road" unless you mean going over a bridge.

entry_json.definition: a large number of people together in one place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A crowd had already formed outside the hall an hour before the doors opened.
example_sentences: The crowd cheered when the team came out.
She hates crowds, so she shops early.

entry_json.definition: full of people, with little space
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The train is so crowded at eight that I now leave at seven.
example_sentences: The beach was crowded all weekend.
Crowded housing makes it hard for children to study.

confusables.difference: 'Crowd' is the noun, the people themselves. 'Crowded' is the adjective describing the place: a crowd of people, a crowded room.

entry_json.definition: to produce tears from your eyes because you feel sad or hurt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I nearly cried when I opened the results, out of relief rather than sadness.
example_sentences: The baby cried all night.
She cried when she said goodbye at the airport.
entry_json.avoid: The past is 'cried'.

entry_json.definition: the way of life of a group of people, and the things they do and believe
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living abroad taught me more about my own culture than about the new one.
example_sentences: Food is an important part of any culture.
The museum celebrates local culture and history.

entry_json.definition: a small round thing that you drink tea or coffee from, with a part at the side to hold it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A cup of tea is how every difficult conversation starts in this country.
example_sentences: Would you like a cup of coffee?
She washed the cups and left them to dry.

confusables.difference: A cup is for hot drinks and has a handle. A glass is clear, has no handle and is for cold drinks.

entry_json.definition: a piece of furniture with doors and shelves, used for storing things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a cupboard in the hall where we keep everything we never use.
example_sentences: The plates are in the cupboard above the sink.
She keeps her books in a cupboard.
entry_json.avoid: The 'p' is silent and it has two syllables: KUB-əd.

entry_json.definition: with hair or lines that turn in rings, not straight
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister has curly hair and mine is completely straight.
example_sentences: He has short curly hair.
The photo shows a small child with curly brown hair.

entry_json.definition: a person who buys something from a shop or a business
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cafe keeps its regular customers because the staff never change.
example_sentences: The shop was full of customers on Saturday.
Good customer service costs money but keeps people coming back.

confusables.difference: A customer buys goods in a shop. A client pays for a professional service, from a lawyer, designer or accountant.

entry_json.definition: to use a knife to make something into pieces or to make a hole in it; or to make an amount smaller
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council plans to cut spending on street cleaning.
example_sentences: Cut the vegetables into small pieces.
The company cut prices by ten per cent.
entry_json.avoid: The past tense and past participle are also 'cut': I cut it yesterday.

entry_json.definition: to travel by bicycle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cycle to work whenever the weather allows.
example_sentences: She cycles ten kilometres each way.
More people would cycle if the lanes were separated from traffic.
entry_json.avoid: 'Cycle' is the normal British verb; Americans usually say 'ride a bike'.

entry_json.definition: an informal word for father
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My dad taught me to drive in an empty car park on Sunday mornings.
example_sentences: My dad works nights at the hospital.
I called my dad from the airport.

confusables.difference: 'Dad' is what you call him and what you say to friends. 'Father' is formal and belongs in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'dad' in an IELTS essay; use 'father' or 'parents'.

entry_json.definition: happening every day
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A short daily walk did more for my health than the gym membership I never used.
example_sentences: The daily commute takes over an hour.
She reads a daily newspaper on the train.

entry_json.definition: to move your body in time with music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the festival everyone danced in the street until well after midnight.
example_sentences: We danced for hours at the wedding.
She learned to dance as a child.

entry_json.definition: a person who dances, especially as a job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dancers had trained together since they were children.
example_sentences: She is a professional dancer with a small company.
He is a good dancer but says he is not.

entry_json.definition: the activity of moving to music
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Dancing is the cheapest exercise I know and the only one I enjoy.
example_sentences: We go dancing every Friday night.
Dancing lessons start at seven.
entry_json.avoid: We GO dancing, as with 'go swimming' and 'go shopping'.

entry_json.definition: the chance that something bad will happen and hurt you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The real danger of studying alone is that nobody corrects your mistakes.
example_sentences: There is a danger that the river will flood again.
Children were in danger from the traffic outside the school.
entry_json.avoid: Say "in danger", not 'in the danger'.

entry_json.definition: not safe, because it can hurt someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling here is only dangerous where the lanes stop suddenly.
example_sentences: It is dangerous to swim beyond the flags.
Working at night on the roads is dangerous.
entry_json.avoid: Say "it is dangerous TO do something".

entry_json.definition: with little or no light; or close to black in colour
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It gets dark here at four in the afternoon in December.
example_sentences: She was wearing a dark blue suit.
Do not walk home through the park after dark.
entry_json.avoid: Use 'it' for light: "it is dark", not "there is dark".

entry_json.definition: facts and numbers collected so they can be studied
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The data show a steady fall in car use among people under thirty.
example_sentences: We collected data from four hundred students.
The data is stored on a secure server.

confusables.difference: 'Information' is always uncountable. 'Data' is usually treated as uncountable too in everyday use, but scientific writing often takes a plural verb: the data show.

entry_json.avoid: Never "datas". Both "the data is" and "the data are" are accepted; be consistent.

entry_json.definition: a particular day of a month or year
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Write the date at the top of the form.
example_sentences: What is the date of your test?
The closing date for applications is 3 May.
entry_json.avoid: Say "on 3 May" or "on the third of May".

entry_json.definition: a person's female child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Their daughter has just started at the same school I went to.
example_sentences: She has a daughter and two sons.
His daughter is studying abroad.
entry_json.avoid: The 'gh' is silent: DAW-tə.

entry_json.definition: a period of twenty-four hours, or the time when it is light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I study best in the first two hours of the day.
example_sentences: It rained every day for a fortnight.
The museum is open six days a week.

confusables.difference: 'Every day' as two words means daily: I walk every day. 'Everyday' as one word is an adjective: everyday clothes.

entry_json.definition: no longer alive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The tree at the front of the house has been dead for two winters.
example_sentences: My grandfather has been dead for ten years.
The battery in the smoke alarm was dead.

confusables.difference: 'Dead' is an adjective describing a state: he is dead. 'Died' is the past of the verb: he died in 2010. "He is died" is wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Never "he is died" or "he has dead".

entry_json.definition: when two people or companies agree to do something together, especially in business; or a large amount when used with 'great'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We got a good deal on the flat because the last tenant left in a hurry.
example_sentences: The two companies signed a deal last week.
A great deal of money was spent on the road.
entry_json.avoid: 'A great deal of' is used with uncountable nouns: a great deal of time, not "a great deal of people".

entry_json.definition: used at the start of a letter or email before a person's name
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Dear Sir or Madam is still the safest opening when you do not have a name.
example_sentences: Dear Ms Ahmed, I am writing to ask about the course.
Dear Tom, thanks for sending the notes.
entry_json.avoid: In a formal letter, 'Dear Sir or Madam' pairs with 'Yours faithfully'; 'Dear Mr Smith' pairs with 'Yours sincerely'.

entry_json.definition: the end of life
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air pollution causes thousands of early deaths every year.
example_sentences: The number of deaths on the roads has fallen.
After his death the house was sold.

confusables.difference: 'Death' is the noun, the event. 'Dead' is the adjective, the state. "After his dead" is wrong — say "after his death".

entry_json.definition: to choose what you will do after thinking about it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I decided to take the test in June rather than wait until autumn.
example_sentences: We decided against buying a car.
She has not decided which course to apply for.
entry_json.avoid: Say "decide TO do something", never "decide doing".

entry_json.definition: a choice you make after thinking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving here was the best decision I have made.
example_sentences: The council made its decision last night.
It was a difficult decision to leave my job.
entry_json.avoid: We MAKE a decision, never 'take' one in the American sense and never 'do' one.

entry_json.definition: going a long way down from the top
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The river is deep enough for ships as far as the old bridge.
example_sentences: The water is too deep for children here.
She took a deep breath before she started.
entry_json.avoid: The measurement goes before the word: "two metres deep".

entry_json.definition: for sure; used when you are completely sure about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will definitely apply again if I do not get the score I need.
example_sentences: That is definitely the right answer.
She is definitely coming to the meeting.
entry_json.avoid: The spelling has no 'a': definitely, not "definately". This is one of the most common written errors in English.

entry_json.definition: the title you get when you finish a course at university; or a unit for how hot something is or how big a turn is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A degree opens the first door, but experience opens the rest.
example_sentences: She has a degree in economics.
The temperature reached thirty-five degrees.
entry_json.avoid: Say "a degree IN economics", not "a degree of economics".

entry_json.definition: tasting very good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The soup at the market stall is cheap and delicious.
example_sentences: That cake was delicious, thank you.
Street food here is delicious and safe.
entry_json.avoid: 'Delicious' is already strong, so avoid 'very delicious'. Use 'absolutely delicious' instead.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to look after people's teeth
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go to the dentist twice a year, whether anything hurts or not.
example_sentences: I have an appointment at the dentist on Thursday.
The dentist said I should use a softer brush.
entry_json.avoid: Use 'the': "go to the dentist".

entry_json.definition: one part of a large organisation such as a university, shop or government
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The engineering department has its own library on the top floor.
example_sentences: She works in the sales department.
The health department published new guidance.
entry_json.avoid: You work IN a department.

entry_json.definition: to be affected or decided by something else; or to need someone for help
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How long the journey takes depends on the traffic.
example_sentences: Whether I apply depends on the fee.
Many older people depend on the bus service.
entry_json.avoid: Always 'depend ON'. "It depends of the weather" and "depends to" are both wrong.

entry_json.definition: to say what someone or something is like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In Part 2 you are asked to describe a place that matters to you.
example_sentences: Describe the chart in your own words.
She described the flat as small but bright.
entry_json.avoid: Never "describe me the picture". Say "describe the picture to me".

entry_json.definition: words that say what someone or something is like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The description of the flat online left out the noise from the road.
example_sentences: Give a full description of what happened.
The job description lists eight main duties.
entry_json.avoid: Say "a description OF something".

entry_json.definition: a large dry area of land with very little rain, where few plants can grow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parts of the region are turning into desert as the rains fail.
example_sentences: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
Very few plants survive in the desert.

confusables.difference: One 's' and stress on the first syllable is the dry land: DEZ-ət. Two 's's and stress on the second is the sweet course after a meal: dih-ZERT.

entry_json.definition: the way something is planned and made, or a drawing showing this
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Good design makes a small flat feel twice the size.
example_sentences: The design of the new station won an award.
She studies graphic design.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to decide how something will look and work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The designer had clearly never carried a pram up those steps.
example_sentences: She works as a web designer.
The designer chose local wood for the whole building.

entry_json.definition: a table you sit at to write or work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cleared my desk completely before I started revising.
example_sentences: There is a lamp on my desk.
Ask at the information desk on the ground floor.
entry_json.avoid: We sit AT a desk.

entry_json.definition: to break something so badly that it is gone or cannot be fixed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fire destroyed three shops in the old market.
example_sentences: The forest was destroyed to make room for farmland.
War destroyed most of the city centre.

confusables.difference: 'Damage' means harmed but still there and possibly repairable. 'Destroy' means gone for good.

entry_json.definition: a small fact or piece of information about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The examiner wants detail, not just a general answer.
example_sentences: She explained the plan in detail.
Please check the details on your ticket.
entry_json.avoid: The fixed phrase is 'in detail', with no article and no plural.

entry_json.definition: a police officer or other person whose job is to find out who broke the law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Detective stories are good practice because you keep reading to find out what happened.
example_sentences: A detective interviewed all the neighbours.
She reads a detective novel a week.

entry_json.definition: to grow or change into something bigger or better, or to make something new over time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took a year of daily practice to develop any real confidence in speaking.
example_sentences: The company is developing a cheaper battery.
The town has developed quickly since the road was built.
entry_json.avoid: No double p in the base form: develop, but developed and developing.

entry_json.definition: a piece of equipment made for a particular purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most students now do their reading on a device rather than on paper.
example_sentences: The hospital uses a small device to measure blood sugar.
Turn off all electronic devices during the test.
entry_json.avoid: 'Device' is the noun; 'devise' is the verb meaning to invent, and sounds different at the end.

entry_json.definition: a conversation between two people, especially in a book, play or lesson
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We practised a short dialogue about booking a room.
example_sentences: Listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.
The two governments have begun a dialogue about trade.
entry_json.avoid: British spelling keeps the 'ue': dialogue. American English often writes 'dialog'.

entry_json.definition: a book where you write what you do each day, or plan what you will do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a diary in English, which forces me to write something every night.
example_sentences: Let me check my diary for Thursday.
She has kept a diary since she was twelve.

confusables.difference: These two look alike but are unrelated. A diary is a book; dairy means milk products, and the vowels are in the other order.

entry_json.definition: a book or app that lists words and explains what they mean
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Use a dictionary that explains words in English, not one that only translates.
example_sentences: Look the word up in a dictionary.
A learner's dictionary gives example sentences too.
entry_json.avoid: We look a word UP IN a dictionary.

entry_json.definition: to stop living
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother died at ninety-one, in the house she was born in.
example_sentences: Thousands of trees died in the drought.
He died two years before I was born.

confusables.difference: 'Die' is the verb: he died last year. 'Dead' is the adjective: he is dead. Do not mix them.

entry_json.avoid: The -ing form is 'dying', with a y. 'Dyeing' with an e means colouring cloth.

entry_json.definition: the food a person or group usually eats
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A diet with more vegetables and less meat is better for you and for the planet.
example_sentences: She is on a diet before the wedding.
A balanced diet matters more than any single food.
entry_json.avoid: 'Your diet' is what you normally eat; 'on a diet' means eating less to lose weight. The two senses are different.

entry_json.definition: the way in which two things are not the same
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main difference between the two courses is the number of contact hours.
example_sentences: There is a big difference between reading and speaking.
Ten minutes of planning makes a real difference to an essay.
entry_json.avoid: Say "the difference BETWEEN A and B", not "the difference of".

entry_json.definition: not the same as something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Life in a small town is completely different from life in the capital.
example_sentences: The two reports reach different conclusions.
She is very different from her sister.
entry_json.avoid: British English prefers 'different from'; 'different to' is also accepted, but 'different than' sounds American.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is not the same
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People learn differently, so one method will never suit everyone.
example_sentences: The word is pronounced differently in the north.
She sees the problem differently from me.

entry_json.definition: not easy to do or understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The listening test is difficult mainly because you hear it only once.
example_sentences: It is difficult to find a cheap flat near the centre.
She asked a difficult question.

confusables.difference: They mean the same here, but 'hard' also means solid, and 'difficult' can describe a person who is not easy to deal with.

entry_json.avoid: Say "it is difficult TO do something" or "I find it difficult to", not "I am difficult to".

entry_json.definition: using information stored as numbers in a computer
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Older people can be left behind as services move to digital only.
example_sentences: The library has a large digital collection.
Digital skills are now needed for almost every job.

entry_json.definition: the main meal of the day, usually eaten in the evening
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We usually have dinner at about seven, once everyone is home from work.
example_sentences: I cooked dinner for my flatmates on Sunday.
The hotel price includes breakfast but not dinner.
entry_json.avoid: We say "have dinner", not "eat dinner" in most situations, and never "take dinner".

entry_json.definition: going straight from one place to another, with nothing in between
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a direct train from the airport to the city centre, so I did not have to change.
example_sentences: A direct flight costs more, but it saves three hours.
The report shows a direct link between air quality and health.

confusables.difference: Direct describes a thing (a direct flight). Directly tells you how something happens (fly directly to Rome).

entry_json.definition: the way that someone or something is going, or is pointing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got lost because I walked in the wrong direction for twenty minutes.
example_sentences: The wind changed direction and the smoke blew towards the town.
She gave me clear directions to the exam centre.

confusables.difference: Directions tell you how to get somewhere. Instructions tell you how to do something, like build a shelf.

entry_json.definition: a person who is the head of a company, or who tells the actors what to do in a film
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The director of the college gave a short speech at the opening.
example_sentences: She is a director at a small engineering firm.
The film was made by a young Iranian director.

entry_json.definition: not clean; with marks on it that need washing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The windows were so dirty that I could hardly see the garden.
example_sentences: I put my dirty clothes in the washing machine.
The river near my home town is dirty because of the factories.

confusables.difference: Dirty is the everyday word for anything not clean. Polluted is used about air, water or land damaged by chemicals or waste, and is the better word in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: to have a different opinion from someone else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I disagree with the idea that money is the only reason people work.
example_sentences: My brother and I disagree about almost everything.
Some experts disagree with this conclusion.
entry_json.avoid: We disagree WITH a person or an idea, and disagree ABOUT a topic. Not "disagree to".

entry_json.definition: to stop being seen, or to stop existing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Small shops are slowly disappearing from our high street.
example_sentences: The sun disappeared behind the clouds.
Many languages will disappear within the next fifty years.

confusables.difference: Vanish means disappear suddenly and in a way that is hard to explain. Disappear is neutral and far more common.

entry_json.definition: something very bad that happens and hurts many people or destroys a lot of things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The floods last year were the worst natural disaster in the region's history.
example_sentences: My first driving lesson was a complete disaster.
Governments should spend more on preparing for natural disasters.

entry_json.definition: to find something, or to learn a fact, for the first time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Scientists have discovered that even short walks improve concentration.
example_sentences: I discovered a good quiet library near my flat.
Researchers discovered the drug almost by accident.

confusables.difference: You discover something that was already there but nobody knew about it. You invent something that did not exist until you made it. Fleming discovered penicillin; Bell invented the telephone.

entry_json.definition: the act of finding something for the first time, or the thing that is found
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The discovery of antibiotics changed medicine completely.
example_sentences: It was an important scientific discovery.
Space research often leads to useful discoveries here on Earth.

entry_json.definition: to talk about something with other people in order to decide or understand it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the seminar we discussed whether tourism helps small towns.
example_sentences: I need to discuss my results with my tutor.
The essay asks you to discuss both views.
entry_json.avoid: Never "discuss about". You discuss something. Only the noun takes about: a discussion about tourism.

entry_json.definition: a conversation about something in which people give their opinions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had a long discussion about the cost of university.
example_sentences: The topic is still under discussion.
Class discussions helped me more than reading alone.

entry_json.definition: an illness of the body, especially a serious one with a name
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heart disease is far more common in countries where people sit all day.
example_sentences: Clean water prevents many diseases.
The disease spreads quickly in crowded cities.

confusables.difference: A disease has a medical name and a cause, like malaria. An illness is the general experience of being unwell, and is the wider, softer word.

entry_json.definition: a flat container you serve food in; also, food cooked in a particular way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rice and curry is the dish I miss most when I am abroad.
example_sentences: I always do the dishes after dinner.
The restaurant serves several vegetarian dishes.

entry_json.definition: the amount of space between two places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The distance between my flat and the campus is about three kilometres.
example_sentences: I can walk that distance in half an hour.
Distance learning allows people in villages to study.

entry_json.definition: no longer married, because the two people have ended the marriage by law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My parents got divorced when I was ten, but I stayed close to both of them.
example_sentences: She is divorced and lives with her two children.
Divorced couples often share the care of their children.
entry_json.avoid: We say "get divorced", not "become divorced".

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to help people who are ill get better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I went to the doctor because the cough would not go away.
example_sentences: My sister is training to be a doctor.
In rural areas there are too few doctors.

entry_json.definition: a piece of paper, or something saved on a computer, with important information on it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You must bring your passport and two other documents to the test centre.
example_sentences: I saved the document before closing my laptop.
All the legal documents were signed that morning.

entry_json.definition: an animal with four legs that many people keep as a pet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I walk my dog before breakfast, which is how I get my exercise.
example_sentences: Their dog barks whenever the post arrives.
Some flats do not allow dogs.

entry_json.definition: the money used in the United States and some other countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course cost about two thousand dollars, which took me a year to save.
example_sentences: Prices are often given in dollars on international websites.
He earns a few dollars an hour.

entry_json.definition: the part of a building or room that you open to go in or out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Someone knocked on the door just as the lesson started.
example_sentences: Please close the door behind you.
The flat next door has been empty for months.

entry_json.definition: twice as big, twice as much, or made of two parts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rent in the capital is almost double what I paid at home.
example_sentences: We booked a double room for two nights.
The number of students has doubled since 2010.

entry_json.definition: towards or in a lower place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Prices came down slightly after the new supermarket opened.
example_sentences: Sit down and take a short break.
The chart shows unemployment going down after 2015.

confusables.difference: Down is the general direction. Downstairs is specific: to or on a lower floor of a building.

entry_json.definition: to copy something from the internet onto your own computer or phone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I download the lessons at the library because my home connection is slow.
example_sentences: You can download the form from the university website.
Millions of people download music every day.
entry_json.avoid: Download is the opposite of upload. You download FROM the internet and upload TO it.

entry_json.definition: to or on a lower floor of a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The kitchen is downstairs and the bedrooms are on the floor above.
example_sentences: I heard someone moving about downstairs.
She ran downstairs to answer the door.

entry_json.definition: plays and acting as an art form; also a serious play or film
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I joined a drama club to build my confidence in speaking.
example_sentences: She studied drama at university.
The series is a historical drama set in the 1920s.

entry_json.definition: to make a picture with a pen or pencil
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I used to draw a lot as a child, but I stopped when school got busy.
example_sentences: He drew a quick map so I could find the office.
Children should be encouraged to draw and paint.

confusables.difference: You draw with a pencil or pen, in lines. You paint with a brush and colour.

entry_json.definition: a picture made with a pen or pencil; the activity of making such pictures
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a child's drawing of a house stuck on the fridge.
example_sentences: Drawing helps me relax after a long day of studying.
The gallery is showing drawings by local artists.

entry_json.definition: the pictures and events in your mind while you sleep; also something you hope will happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Studying abroad was a dream of mine long before I could afford it.
example_sentences: I had a strange dream about missing my exam.
For many young people, owning a home is now an impossible dream.

entry_json.definition: a piece of clothing for a woman or girl, covering the body and part of the legs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She wore a simple blue dress to the interview.
example_sentences: I bought a dress for my cousin's wedding.
The school has a strict dress code.

entry_json.definition: to put water, tea or juice in your mouth and take it down into your body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I drink far too much coffee when I am revising for exams.
example_sentences: You should drink plenty of water in hot weather.
He does not drink alcohol at all.

entry_json.definition: to control a car, bus or other vehicle and make it move
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I learned to drive at eighteen, but I still prefer the train.
example_sentences: It takes about an hour to drive into the city.
Fewer young people are learning to drive than twenty years ago.

confusables.difference: You drive a car, a bus or a lorry. You ride a bicycle, a motorbike or a horse.

entry_json.definition: a person who drives a car, bus or other vehicle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bus driver waited while an elderly man got on.
example_sentences: My father was a taxi driver for thirty years.
Careless drivers cause most accidents in the city.

entry_json.definition: the activity of controlling a car or other vehicle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I passed my driving test on the second attempt.
example_sentences: Driving in heavy traffic makes me tense.
Dangerous driving should be punished more severely.

entry_json.definition: to let something fall; or to become lower in number or level
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Temperatures drop sharply at night in the desert.
example_sentences: I dropped my phone and cracked the screen.
Sales dropped by twelve per cent in the final quarter.

confusables.difference: In charts, drop and fall are almost the same, but drop suggests a quicker, sharper change. Fall is the safer general word.

entry_json.definition: a medicine; also something people take to change how they feel, that the law does not allow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: New drugs have made the illness much easier to live with.
example_sentences: The drug is only available on prescription.
Schools run programmes to keep young people away from drugs.
entry_json.avoid: Drug has two meanings. In writing, say "prescription drugs" or "medicine" if you mean treatment, so the reader does not think of illegal drugs.

entry_json.definition: with no water in it or on it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dry season lasts from June to September where I come from.
example_sentences: Hang the washing outside until it is dry.
Farmers struggle when the soil stays dry for months.

entry_json.definition: all through a period of time, or at some point inside it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I worked part-time during the summer holiday to pay for the course.
example_sentences: Please switch off your phone during the exam.
Air quality gets worse during the winter months.

confusables.difference: During answers "when": during the lesson. For answers "how long": for two hours. Not "during two hours".
During is followed by a noun (during the meeting). While is followed by a clause (while we were meeting).

entry_json.avoid: Never put a length of time after during. "I slept for eight hours", not "during eight hours".

entry_json.definition: one of the two parts of the body that you hear with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The music was so loud that my ears hurt afterwards.
example_sentences: He has an ear infection and cannot fly.
Workers near the machines wear ear protection.

entry_json.definition: before the usual or expected time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get up early because the house is quiet then and I can study.
example_sentences: We arrived early and had to wait outside.
Booking early is usually cheaper.

confusables.difference: Early means before the expected time. Soon means a short time from now. "He came early" and "he is coming soon" say different things.

entry_json.definition: to get money by working
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I earn just enough to cover my rent and my course fees.
example_sentences: Graduates tend to earn more over a lifetime.
She earns a good salary but works very long hours.

confusables.difference: You earn money by working. You win money or a prize in a competition or a game.

entry_json.definition: the world we live on; also the brown ground that plants grow in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The Earth is warming faster than most scientists predicted.
example_sentences: Plant the seeds in soft, damp earth.
It is the largest desert on Earth.

entry_json.definition: without difficulty
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You can easily reach the city centre by bus in fifteen minutes.
example_sentences: Young children learn a second language easily.
The information can easily be found online.

entry_json.definition: the direction you look towards to see the sun come up
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The airport is a few kilometres to the east of the city.
example_sentences: The map shows heavy rainfall in the east of the country.
Their windows face east, so the flat is bright in the morning.

entry_json.definition: not difficult; something you can do without trying hard
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first part of the listening test was easy, but the last section was not.
example_sentences: It is easy to get lost in a city you do not know.
Online banking makes it easy to send money home.
entry_json.avoid: Say "it is easy to do something", not "it is easy doing something".

entry_json.definition: to put food in your mouth and take it down into your body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to eat more vegetables now than I did as a student.
example_sentences: We ate at a small restaurant near the station.
Many people eat too much sugar without realising it.

confusables.difference: Eat out means eat in a restaurant rather than at home. It is not the same as simply eating outside.

entry_json.definition: the process of teaching and learning, usually at school or university
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Free education gave my parents chances their own parents never had.
example_sentences: She works in higher education.
Governments should spend more on primary education.
entry_json.avoid: Education is uncountable: "an education system", not "educations".

entry_json.definition: a change that happens because of something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Working night shifts had a serious effect on my health.
example_sentences: Tourism has had a positive effect on the local economy.
The new rules took effect in January.

confusables.difference: Effect is almost always the noun: it has an effect. Affect is the verb: it affects people. If you can put "an" or "the" in front, you want effect.

entry_json.avoid: Not "effect on health" as a verb. Write "affects health" or "has an effect on health".

entry_json.definition: the round thing with a hard outside that a bird makes and that we often eat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually have eggs and toast before an early class.
example_sentences: Add two eggs and mix well.
Egg prices have risen this year.

entry_json.definition: using or producing electricity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Electric cars are becoming cheaper, but charging points are still rare.
example_sentences: The flat has an electric cooker.
Sales of electric bikes have doubled.

confusables.difference: Electric goes with the individual thing that runs on electricity: an electric car. Electrical goes with the general field or system: electrical engineering, electrical equipment.

entry_json.definition: connected with electricity in general
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A fault in the electrical system caused the fire.
example_sentences: He studied electrical engineering in Manchester.
Do not use electrical equipment near water.

entry_json.definition: the power that comes into homes and makes lights and machines work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Our electricity bill doubled last winter.
example_sentences: Many villages still have no electricity at all.
Wind farms now generate a quarter of the country's electricity.

entry_json.definition: using very small parts that control electricity, like a computer or a phone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost all our reading is done on electronic devices now.
example_sentences: Please keep electronic devices switched off during the test.
Electronic payments have replaced cash in many shops.

entry_json.definition: a very large grey animal with a long nose called a trunk
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Seeing wild elephants for the first time is something I will never forget.
example_sentences: Elephants live in family groups.
The number of wild elephants is falling.

entry_json.definition: other, or different from the person or thing already mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If nothing else works, I will simply ask my tutor for help.
example_sentences: Is there anything else you would like to add?
Someone else had already taken the last seat.
entry_json.avoid: Else comes after the word it describes: "something else", never "else something".

entry_json.definition: a message sent from one computer or phone to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I send about twenty emails a day at work.
example_sentences: I have not had a reply to my email yet.
Please send your application by email.

entry_json.definition: to pay someone to work for you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory employs about four hundred people from the surrounding villages.
example_sentences: Small businesses employ most of the country's workers.
She was employed as a research assistant.

entry_json.definition: a person who is paid to work for a company or organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employees at my company can work from home two days a week.
example_sentences: The firm has three hundred employees.
Happy employees usually stay longer.

confusables.difference: The employee is the worker. The employer is the company or person who pays them. Employer holds the money.

entry_json.definition: a person or company that pays people to work for them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My employer paid for the training course, which I could not have afforded myself.
example_sentences: Employers now look for communication skills as much as degrees.
The hospital is the biggest employer in the town.

entry_json.definition: with nothing or nobody inside
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The train was almost empty at that time of the morning.
example_sentences: Please leave your empty cups on the tray.
Several shops on the street have been empty for a year.

entry_json.definition: the last part of something, or the point where it stops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will have saved enough by the end of the year.
example_sentences: The library is at the end of this road.
At the end of the film, nobody speaks.

confusables.difference: "At the end of" points to a place or time: at the end of the road. "In the end" means finally, after a lot of thought: in the end, I stayed.

entry_json.definition: the last part of a story, film or event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The film has a happy ending, which surprised me.
example_sentences: I did not expect that ending at all.
Some readers found the ending disappointing.

entry_json.definition: the power that makes machines work; also the strength you need to be active
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Solar energy now costs less than coal in many countries.
example_sentences: I have no energy at all after a night shift.
Households are being asked to use less energy.
entry_json.avoid: Energy is usually uncountable. Write "a lot of energy", not "many energies".

entry_json.definition: the part of a vehicle or machine that makes it move
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The car would not start because the engine had frozen overnight.
example_sentences: Modern engines use far less fuel.
There was a strange noise coming from the engine.

confusables.difference: An engine is the machine. An engineer is the person who designs or repairs machines.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to design or repair machines, roads or buildings
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My cousin is a civil engineer and works mainly on bridges.
example_sentences: The company is hiring three software engineers.
Engineers were called in to check the structure.

entry_json.definition: to like doing something and to feel happy while you do it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I really enjoy cooking at the weekend because it is the one thing I do slowly.
example_sentences: Did you enjoy the concert?
Most children enjoy learning through games.

entry_json.definition: extremely large

The company made an enormous profit that year.

entry_json.definition: as much or as many as you need
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I did not have enough time to check my answers at the end of the test.
example_sentences: The room is big enough for six people.
Not enough is being done about air pollution.
entry_json.avoid: Enough goes BEFORE a noun (enough money) but AFTER an adjective (big enough). Not "enough big".

entry_json.definition: to go into a place; also to type information into a computer
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please do not enter the exam room until you are called.
example_sentences: Enter your student number and password.
She entered the competition and came second.
entry_json.avoid: Enter takes no preposition when it means go in: "enter the building", not "enter into the building".

entry_json.definition: the natural world of land, water and air; also the conditions you live or work in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap flights are convenient, but they damage the environment.
example_sentences: Plastic waste is harmful to the environment.
I work best in a quiet environment.
entry_json.avoid: When it means the natural world, it takes THE: "protect the environment".

entry_json.definition: the things you need to do a particular job or activity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The school has good teachers but very old equipment.
example_sentences: Safety equipment must be worn in the workshop.
Hospitals need modern equipment as well as staff.
entry_json.avoid: Equipment is uncountable. Say "a piece of equipment" or "some equipment", never "an equipment" or "equipments".

entry_json.definition: a mistake
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One small error in the calculation changed the whole result.

The website keeps showing an error message.

entry_json.definition: more than usual, or more than others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public transport is expensive here, especially at peak times.
example_sentences: I like most sports, especially swimming.
The problem affects older people especially.

confusables.difference: Especially means above all, particularly. Specially means for one particular purpose: "a room specially designed for children".

entry_json.definition: a short piece of writing on one subject, usually done for school or university
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I write a practice essay every Sunday and mark it the next morning.
example_sentences: The essay has to be twelve hundred words.
Plan your essay before you start writing.

entry_json.definition: the money used in many European countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The trip cost me around three hundred euros in total.
example_sentences: Prices are shown in euros and pounds.
The euro has been in use since 2002.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is surprising or more than expected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is busy even at seven in the morning.
example_sentences: He did not even say goodbye.
Rents are rising, and prices in the capital are even higher.

confusables.difference: "Even" alone adds surprise to one idea. "Even though" joins two clauses and means although: even though it rained, we walked.

entry_json.definition: the part of the day between the afternoon and the time you go to bed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I study in the evening because I work during the day.
example_sentences: We are meeting on Friday evening.
The shop stays open until nine in the evening.
entry_json.avoid: We say "in the evening" but "on Friday evening". Never "in Friday evening".

entry_json.definition: something that happens, especially something planned and important
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The festival is the biggest event in our town's year.
example_sentences: Sporting events bring visitors and money to a city.
The company organises events for its staff.

entry_json.definition: at any time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Have you ever taken an international exam before?
example_sentences: It is the best film I have ever seen.
Nothing ever changes in that office.
entry_json.avoid: Ever is mainly for questions and negatives. In a positive sentence use "always": "I always walk", not "I ever walk".

entry_json.definition: each one of a group, with none left out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I check my vocabulary list every morning before breakfast.
example_sentences: Every student must bring identification.
The bus leaves every twenty minutes.
entry_json.avoid: Every is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb: "every student has", not "every students have".

entry_json.definition: every person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everybody in my class was nervous before the speaking test.
example_sentences: Everybody knows that smoking is harmful.
I would like to thank everybody who helped.

confusables.difference: Everybody and everyone mean exactly the same. Everyone is slightly more common in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Everybody takes a singular verb: "everybody was", not "everybody were".

entry_json.definition: ordinary; happening as a normal part of life
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Using English for everyday tasks helped me more than any textbook.
example_sentences: These are everyday problems that most families face.
The app is designed for everyday use.

confusables.difference: Everyday, one word, is an adjective before a noun: everyday life. Every day, two words, means each day: I study every day.

entry_json.avoid: Never write "I study everyday." That needs two words: every day.

entry_json.definition: every person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone I know is worried about the cost of housing.
example_sentences: Everyone has the right to an education.
Not everyone agrees with this view.
entry_json.avoid: Everyone is one word when it means all people. "Every one" as two words means each single thing: every one of the books.

entry_json.definition: all things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everything I needed for the exam was in one small bag.
example_sentences: Money is not everything.
She wrote down everything the lecturer said.
entry_json.avoid: Everything takes a singular verb: "everything is ready", not "everything are ready".

entry_json.definition: in or to all places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are cameras everywhere in the city centre now.
example_sentences: I looked everywhere for my keys.
Plastic waste is found almost everywhere, even in the deep ocean.

entry_json.definition: facts or information that show if something is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is strong evidence that sleep affects how well students learn.
example_sentences: The study provides clear evidence of a link.
We should not accept a claim without evidence.
entry_json.avoid: Evidence is uncountable: "a piece of evidence" or "much evidence", never "an evidence" or "evidences".

entry_json.definition: completely correct and with no mistake in the detail
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cannot remember the exact number, but it was around forty students.
example_sentences: Give the exact date of your arrival.
The exact cause of the fire is still unknown.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is completely correct, with nothing missing or added
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The journey takes exactly forty minutes if the traffic is light.
example_sentences: That is exactly what I meant.
Nobody knows exactly how many people were affected.

entry_json.definition: an important test at a school or college that shows what you know or can do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am taking the exam in April, so I practise every evening.
example_sentences: She passed all her exams first time.
The exam lasts two hours and forty minutes.
entry_json.avoid: You TAKE an exam when you sit it; you PASS it only if you succeed. "I passed the exam yesterday" means you got the result, not that you sat it.

entry_json.definition: a thing that shows what a larger group or idea is like
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Singapore is a good example of a city that solved its traffic problem.
example_sentences: Can you give me an example?
For example, many students now study online.
entry_json.avoid: Write "for example" or "such as", not "for example such as". After "such as" you do not need a comma-plus-example structure.

entry_json.definition: extremely good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The public transport in that city is excellent, and I never needed a car.
example_sentences: She has excellent communication skills.
The hotel was clean and the service was excellent.
entry_json.avoid: Excellent is already the top of the scale, so avoid "very excellent".

entry_json.definition: not including someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is open every day except Sunday.
example_sentences: Everyone passed except one student.
I like all kinds of music except heavy metal.

confusables.difference: Except means not including. Accept is a verb meaning to say yes or take something. They sound similar but do completely different jobs.

entry_json.definition: feeling very happy because something good is going to happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was excited about moving abroad, though I was nervous too.
example_sentences: The children were too excited to sleep.
I am excited about starting the new course.

confusables.difference: You are excited (that is how you feel). The thing is exciting (that is what it does to you). "I am exciting" says you are fun to be around.

entry_json.definition: making you feel happy and interested; full of things that happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving to a new city was the most exciting year of my life.
example_sentences: It was an exciting match right up to the end.
The job offers exciting opportunities to travel.

entry_json.definition: activity that you do to keep your body strong and healthy; also a task for practice
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get most of my exercise by cycling to work.
example_sentences: Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
Do the grammar exercises on page forty.
entry_json.avoid: When it means physical activity, exercise is uncountable: "do some exercise", not "do exercises" (that means practice tasks).

entry_json.definition: to be real, or to be present in the world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The problem existed long before anyone wrote about it.
example_sentences: Free universities still exist in a few countries.
No such rule exists here.

entry_json.definition: to think that something will probably happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I expect the results to arrive within two weeks.
example_sentences: We did not expect so many people to come.
Employers expect graduates to have some work experience.

confusables.difference: Expect is in your head: you think it will happen. Wait for is what your body does: you stay somewhere until it happens. "I am waiting for the bus", not "expecting the bus" at the bus stop.
Expect means you think it will happen. Hope means you want it to happen, whether or not it is likely.

entry_json.definition: costing a lot of money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Renting in the city centre is far too expensive for most students.
example_sentences: Organic food is expensive but better for the soil.
It was the most expensive mistake of my career.

confusables.difference: Things are expensive; prices and costs are high. Say "an expensive flat" but "a high price", never "an expensive price".

entry_json.definition: the knowledge and skill you get from doing something; also an event that affects you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two years of teaching gave me more experience than any course could.
example_sentences: The job requires at least three years' experience.
Living abroad was a difficult but valuable experience.
entry_json.avoid: Uncountable when it means knowledge (much experience), countable when it means an event (a strange experience). Not "many experiences" for skill.

entry_json.definition: a careful test done to find out if an idea is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the experiment, one group slept eight hours and the other only five.
example_sentences: The experiment was repeated three times.
Animal experiments remain controversial.

entry_json.definition: a person who knows a great deal about a particular subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Health experts agree that walking is the easiest exercise to keep up.
example_sentences: She is an expert on renewable energy.
You do not need to be an expert to use the software.
entry_json.avoid: An expert is expert ON or IN a subject, not "expert about".

entry_json.definition: to tell someone about something in a way that makes it easy to understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My teacher explained the difference to me twice before I understood it.
example_sentences: Can you explain how the system works?
The report explains why the costs rose.
entry_json.avoid: Never "explain me". You explain something TO someone: "explain it to me".

entry_json.definition: a statement that makes something clear or easy to understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a simple explanation for the drop in visitor numbers.
example_sentences: He offered no explanation for being late.
The book gives a clear explanation of the theory.

entry_json.definition: to say or show what you think or feel
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a year to express my ideas in English without hesitating.
example_sentences: Several residents expressed concern about the new road.
She finds it hard to express her feelings.

entry_json.definition: a word or phrase used in a particular way; also the look on your face
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a notebook of useful expressions for the speaking test.
example_sentences: "To cut a long story short" is a common English expression.
There was a worried expression on his face.

entry_json.definition: more than the usual or expected amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I took an extra hour each evening to review what I had learned.
example_sentences: There is an extra charge for luggage.
Staff were paid extra for working weekends.

entry_json.definition: very great in degree; much more than normal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Extreme weather is becoming more common in parts of the country.
example_sentences: The desert has extreme temperatures at night.
Some of the views expressed were quite extreme.

entry_json.definition: to a very great degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Finding a flat near the university was extremely difficult.
example_sentences: The test was extremely well organised.
Water is extremely scarce in that region.
entry_json.avoid: Extremely goes with normal adjectives (extremely cold), not with extreme ones. Not "extremely enormous".

entry_json.definition: one of the two parts of the body that you see with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Staring at a screen all day leaves my eyes tired.
example_sentences: She has dark brown eyes.
Close your eyes for a moment and rest.

entry_json.definition: the front part of your head, where your eyes and mouth are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You could see from her face that the news was good.
example_sentences: Wash your face in cold water to wake up.
I never forget a face, but I always forget names.

entry_json.definition: a thing that is known to be true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fact that so few people vote should worry the government.
example_sentences: Check your facts before you write the essay.
In fact, the opposite happened.

entry_json.definition: one of the things that helps to cause a result
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cost is the main factor stopping people from cycling to work.
example_sentences: Several factors explain the fall in sales.
Diet is an important factor in heart disease.

entry_json.definition: a building where things are made in large numbers by machines
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The car factory closed and two thousand people lost their jobs.
example_sentences: Most of the clothes are made in factories overseas.
The factory runs twenty-four hours a day.

entry_json.definition: to not succeed in something you are trying to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I failed my first driving test because I was too nervous.
example_sentences: The plan failed for a simple reason: nobody explained it.
Students who fail the exam can retake it in June.

confusables.difference: You fail a test you took and did badly in. You miss a class or a bus you did not get to at all.

entry_json.definition: right and the same for everyone; not helping one person more than another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is not fair that some students pay far more for the same degree.
example_sentences: The referee's decision seemed fair to both sides.
Workers are asking for a fair wage.

entry_json.definition: to move down towards the ground; also to become lower in number or level
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment fell steadily between 2015 and 2019.
example_sentences: Be careful on the steps; the ice makes people fall.
House prices fell sharply after the crisis.
entry_json.avoid: Fall is irregular: fall, fell, fallen. "Prices falled" is always wrong.

entry_json.definition: not true or not correct
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Decide whether each statement is true or false.
example_sentences: The article contained several false claims.
He gave a false name at the hotel.

entry_json.definition: a group of people who belong together, such as parents and children
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I come from a large family, so the house was never quiet.
example_sentences: My family live in a small town in the north.
Family size has fallen in most developed countries.

entry_json.definition: known about by very many people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city is famous for its old bridges and its food.
example_sentences: She is a famous scientist in her field.
It is one of the most famous buildings in the world.
entry_json.avoid: Famous FOR a thing, famous AS a role: "famous for its cheese", "famous as a writer".

entry_json.definition: a person who likes a sport, singer or team very much; also a machine that moves air
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have been a fan of that team since I was a child.
example_sentences: Thousands of fans waited outside the stadium.
The office fan is the only thing keeping us cool.

entry_json.definition: extremely good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The food at the festival was fantastic and surprisingly cheap.
example_sentences: We had a fantastic time in the mountains.
That is a fantastic idea.
entry_json.avoid: Fantastic is informal. In Task 2 writing, prefer "excellent" or "highly effective".

entry_json.definition: a long way from a place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The nearest hospital is quite far from the village.
example_sentences: How far is the station from here?
Rents are far higher than they were five years ago.
entry_json.avoid: In positive statements we usually say "a long way", not "far": "It is a long way from here." Far is natural in questions and negatives.

entry_json.definition: an area of land where people grow food or keep animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandparents ran a small farm and grew most of what they ate.
example_sentences: The farm has been in the family for a century.
Wind farms now cover part of the hillside.

entry_json.definition: a person who owns or works on a farm
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farmers in the region depend on one rainy season each year.
example_sentences: My uncle is a rice farmer.
Farmers are being paid to plant trees.

entry_json.definition: the work of growing food on land, or keeping animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farming employs fewer people than it did, but it still feeds us all.
example_sentences: Organic farming uses fewer chemicals.
Farming methods have changed enormously since 1950.

entry_json.definition: the style of clothes that is popular at a particular time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fast fashion is cheap for the shopper and expensive for the planet.
example_sentences: Long coats are back in fashion this winter.
She works in the fashion industry.

entry_json.definition: moving or happening at high speed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A fast train would cut the journey from four hours to two.
example_sentences: The internet connection here is not very fast.
She is a fast reader.

confusables.difference: Fast usually describes movement (a fast car). Quick usually describes a short time (a quick meeting). Both can mean speedy.
Fast is both adjective and adverb: "he runs fast". There is no word "fastly".

entry_json.definition: having too much flesh on the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Doctors avoid the word fat and say overweight instead.
example_sentences: The dog has got fat because nobody walks it.
Fatty foods should be eaten in small amounts.
entry_json.avoid: Calling a person fat is rude in English. Use "overweight" when writing or speaking politely.

entry_json.definition: a man who has a child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My father taught me to cook before I left home.
example_sentences: He became a father at twenty-five.
Fathers now take more time off work than they used to.

entry_json.definition: liked more than all the others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My favourite time of day is early morning, before anyone else is up.
example_sentences: What is your favourite subject at school?
This is my favourite café in the whole city.
entry_json.avoid: Favourite is already the top choice, so "most favourite" is wrong. British spelling keeps the u: favourite.

entry_json.definition: the bad feeling you have when you think something dangerous may happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fear of speaking in public stopped me applying for the job for years.
example_sentences: Many people have a fear of flying.
There are fears that prices will rise again.

entry_json.definition: an important or noticeable part of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main feature of the new library is that it never closes.
example_sentences: The app has several useful features.
Heavy rainfall is a feature of the region's climate.

entry_json.definition: to give food to a person or animal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme feeds around two hundred children every school day.
example_sentences: I feed the cat before I leave for work.
The country can no longer feed itself without imports.

entry_json.definition: to know something in your body or your mind, for example when you are happy, tired or cold
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I felt much calmer once I had practised the test under real conditions.
example_sentences: Do you feel tired in the afternoon?
Many workers feel that they are not listened to.
entry_json.avoid: After feel, use an adjective, not an adverb: "I feel bad", not "I feel badly".

entry_json.definition: what you feel in your mind or body, for example when you are happy, sad or worried
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a feeling that the interview had gone badly, and I was right.
example_sentences: It is not always easy to describe your feelings.
There were mixed feelings about the decision.

entry_json.definition: being a woman or a girl; in animals, being the one that can have babies or eggs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only a quarter of the engineering students were female.
example_sentences: The chart compares male and female employment rates.
Female doctors outnumber male doctors in some countries.

confusables.difference: Female is the technical or statistical word, used with nouns: female students. Woman is the ordinary word for a person: "a woman I know".

entry_json.definition: a special time when people celebrate something, often with music or food
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rice festival at home lasts three days and everyone stops working.
example_sentences: The city holds a film festival every autumn.
Music festivals bring thousands of visitors.

entry_json.definition: stories about people and events that are not real
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read fiction on the train and non-fiction at my desk.
example_sentences: The novel is a work of science fiction.
Children who read fiction develop wider vocabulary.

entry_json.definition: an area of land used for growing food or playing sport; also a subject you work or study in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She is one of the leading researchers in her field.
example_sentences: The children were playing football in the field behind the school.
Farmers plant these fields with wheat every spring.
collocations: a leading figure in the field

entry_json.definition: to hit or attack someone; also to try hard to stop something bad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments must fight air pollution, not just measure it.
example_sentences: The two boys were fighting in the playground.
She has spent years fighting for equal pay.

entry_json.definition: a number, especially one in a report or a chart
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The figures show a steady rise in car ownership since 2000.
example_sentences: Unemployment figures are published every month.
Sales reached a record figure last year.
entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, "the figure" can mean the chart itself or a number. Say "the chart shows" to stay clear.

entry_json.definition: to make something full, or to put information in the spaces on a form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fill in the application form and bring it to the office in person.
example_sentences: Please fill the bottle before you leave.
The hall filled quickly once the doors opened.

confusables.difference: Fill means make full. Feel is about emotion or touch. They are spelled and pronounced differently: fill has a short i, feel a long ee.

entry_json.definition: a story told in moving pictures, shown at the cinema or on television
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We watch one film in English every weekend with the subtitles off.
example_sentences: The film is based on a true story.
British speakers say film; Americans usually say movie.

entry_json.definition: last, coming at the end
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The final section of the reading test is always the hardest.
example_sentences: The final decision rests with the manager.
In the final paragraph, restate your opinion.

entry_json.definition: after a long time, or as the last point
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Finally, I would argue that education matters more than income.
example_sentences: The bus finally arrived forty minutes late.
Finally, I would like to thank my supervisor.

confusables.difference: Finally can simply mark your last point in an essay. "At last" always carries relief that a long wait is over.

entry_json.definition: to discover where something or someone is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me three weeks to find a flat I could afford.
example_sentences: I cannot find my student card anywhere.
Researchers found that sleep improved test scores.
entry_json.avoid: Find is irregular: find, found, found. "Finded" does not exist.

entry_json.definition: good enough; healthy and well
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The room was small, but it was fine for one term.
example_sentences: How are you? I am fine, thanks.
