You pay a price for goods and a charge for a service. A bank makes charges; a shop sets prices.

entry_json.avoid: Free of charge and in charge of are fixed. Do not write in the charge of when you mean responsible for.

entry_json.definition: to act dishonestly in order to gain an advantage, especially in a test or game
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who cheat in exams usually harm themselves most.
example_sentences: He was caught cheating in the final paper.
It is easy to cheat at online tests, which is the problem.

contexts.text: Online examinations are easy to cheat in, which is why so many institutions returned to invigilated halls.
Somebody in my class was caught cheating and was expelled.
Instances of cheating fell after the assessment format was changed.

confusables.difference: Copy describes the specific act of taking someone else's answers. Cheat is the general dishonesty, including using notes.
Plagiarism is presenting someone else's writing as your own. Cheating is broader and covers exams, games and sport.

entry_json.avoid: Cheat IN an exam but cheat AT a game. And cheat someone out of something means to swindle them.

entry_json.definition: happy and showing it, or making people feel happy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The staff are always cheerful, even at seven in the morning.
example_sentences: She is remarkably cheerful for someone who works nights.
The room is bright and cheerful.

contexts.text: The driver was so cheerful that the whole bus ended up in a good mood.
I am not particularly cheerful before about ten in the morning.
A cheerful working environment is worth more to staff retention than a small pay rise.

confusables.difference: Happy is how you feel inside. Cheerful is how you appear to others, and suggests it is a habit rather than a mood.
Optimistic is about expecting good outcomes. Cheerful is about visible good mood now.

entry_json.avoid: Cheerful is spoken register and describes people and places. It suits Speaking Part 2 descriptions well.

entry_json.definition: a substance used in or produced by chemistry, especially a manufactured one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chemicals used on farmland end up in the rivers.
example_sentences: The factory releases several chemicals into the air.
This cleaner contains no harsh chemicals.

contexts.text: Agricultural chemicals raise yields in the short term and damage soil life over decades.
I try to use fewer chemicals at home, mostly for the sake of the cat.
Chemical concentrations were measured at three points along the river.

confusables.difference: Substance is any kind of material. A chemical is specifically one with a defined composition, usually manufactured.
A drug is a chemical used as medicine or taken for its effect. Not all chemicals are drugs.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: the ch is a /k/ sound, and the stress is on the first syllable.

entry_json.definition: the front upper part of the body, between the neck and the stomach
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He went to the doctor with chest pain and was sent straight to hospital.
example_sentences: I felt a tightness in my chest after running.
The X-ray showed nothing wrong with his chest.

contexts.text: Chest infections rise every winter in housing that cannot be heated properly.
I had a chest infection for about three weeks last winter.
Chest measurements were recorded for all participants.

confusables.difference: Chest is the neutral anatomical word for everyone. Breast is used in specific medical phrases such as breast cancer.
The chest is above the waist and holds the heart and lungs. The stomach is below it.

entry_json.avoid: Chest also means a large strong box. Context makes it obvious, but do not mix the two in one sentence.

entry_json.definition: most important, or highest in rank
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chief advantage of the scheme is that it costs almost nothing to run.
example_sentences: Poor housing is the chief cause of the problem.
She is the chief executive of a small charity.

contexts.text: The chief obstacle to reform is not public opinion but the cost of the transition.
The chief reason I moved was the cost of living.
The chief limitation of the study is its small sample.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning, but chief is more formal and appears more in written argument than in speech.
Principal is equally formal and slightly more common in academic writing. Both are safe alternatives to main.

entry_json.avoid: Chief goes before a noun only. Do not write the reason is chief.

entry_json.definition: the period of your life when you are a child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spent most of my childhood outdoors, which children rarely do now.
example_sentences: She had a very happy childhood in a small village.
Childhood obesity has risen steadily for twenty years.

contexts.text: Childhood obesity rates have doubled in two decades, and school meals are only part of the explanation.
My strongest childhood memory is of my grandmother's kitchen.
Childhood exposure to lead was associated with lower test scores.

confusables.difference: Youth covers the teenage years and early twenties. Childhood ends before that.
Upbringing is how your parents raised you. Childhood is simply the period of time.

entry_json.avoid: Childhood is usually uncountable: during childhood. It takes an article only with an adjective: a happy childhood.

entry_json.definition: the facts or conditions surrounding an event, which affect what happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Under normal circumstances the process takes about a month.
example_sentences: The circumstances of the accident are still being investigated.
In these circumstances I think you made the right choice.

contexts.text: Children who succeed despite difficult circumstances are often held up as proof that circumstances do not matter.
Under the circumstances, I think they handled it well.
Participants' economic circumstances were recorded at the outset.

confusables.difference: Situation is the state of affairs as a whole. Circumstances are the particular conditions that shaped it.
A condition is a requirement or a state of health. Circumstances are the surrounding facts of someone's life.

entry_json.avoid: Usually plural. Under the circumstances or in the circumstances are both correct; under no circumstances is emphatic and takes inversion.

entry_json.definition: to mention something as a reason or example, or to refer to a source in academic writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report cites overcrowding as the main cause.
example_sentences: She cited three studies in support of the claim.
Cost is the reason most often cited for not recycling.

contexts.text: Cost is the reason most often cited by households that do not install insulation.
They cited health reasons, but nobody really believed that.
The paper has been cited over two thousand times.

confusables.difference: Quote means repeating someone's exact words. Cite means referring to a source or giving something as a reason, without necessarily quoting.
Cite, site and sight sound identical. Cite is the verb about references; a site is a place; sight is vision.

entry_json.avoid: Cite is one of the strongest Task 2 verbs: the reason most frequently cited is. Do not confuse the spelling with site.

entry_json.definition: a person who legally belongs to a country and has rights there
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every citizen has the right to vote from the age of eighteen.
example_sentences: She became a citizen after living there for six years.
Ordinary citizens had no say in the decision.

contexts.text: Citizens who feel they have no influence over decisions eventually stop voting altogether.
My grandfather became a citizen here in the nineteen sixties.
Citizens aged over 65 were surveyed separately.

confusables.difference: A resident lives somewhere but may hold another nationality. A citizen has legal nationality and the rights that come with it.
A civilian is anyone not in the armed forces. A citizen is defined by nationality, not by occupation.

entry_json.avoid: Senior citizen is a polite phrase for an older person. Citizen alone never means a city dweller in modern English.

entry_json.definition: connected with the ordinary people of a country rather than the military or religious authorities
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Civil servants implement the policies that ministers announce.
example_sentences: The country suffered a long civil war.
Civil rights were extended only gradually.

contexts.text: Civil society organisations often deliver services more cheaply than either government or business.
My aunt worked as a civil servant for thirty years.
Civil conflict was recorded in eleven of the countries studied.

confusables.difference: Civilian is used in contrast to military, especially about people: civilian casualties. Civil appears in fixed phrases: civil war, civil rights.
Civil can also mean politely restrained: he was civil but not friendly. That meaning is separate and quite cold.

entry_json.avoid: Learn the fixed phrases whole. Civil war, civil rights and civil servant do not accept substitutes.

entry_json.definition: to say something is true without proving it; also to formally ask for something you are entitled to
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company claims its packaging is fully recyclable, which is not quite true.
example_sentences: He claims to have read the entire report.
You can claim a refund within thirty days.

contexts.text: Manufacturers claim their products are environmentally friendly, and very few of these claims are independently checked.
She claims she has never been late, which is not how I remember it.
The authors claim that the effect persists over five years.

confusables.difference: Say is neutral. Claim signals that you doubt the statement, so it is a powerful and slightly loaded verb in argument.
State is formal and neutral. Claim carries scepticism. Choose deliberately.

entry_json.avoid: Claim quietly tells the reader you do not believe it. Do not use it about facts you accept.

entry_json.definition: typical of its kind, or of lasting quality and widely admired
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That is a classic example of a policy solving one problem and creating two more.
example_sentences: The film is a classic of its period.
He made the classic mistake of revising only what he enjoyed.

contexts.text: This is a classic case of a technology outrunning the law that should govern it.
It is a classic tourist trap, but I still enjoyed it.
The paper is now regarded as a classic study in the field.

confusables.difference: Classical refers to ancient Greece and Rome, or to a style of music. Classic means typical or of lasting quality. They are not interchangeable.
Traditional means passed down over time. Classic means it defines the type.

entry_json.avoid: Classical music, but a classic film. Writing classical film is a very visible error.

entry_json.definition: a group of words with a subject and a verb; also a section of a legal document
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
example_sentences: The contract has a clause about early cancellation.
Try joining the two clauses with although.

contexts.text: Every sentence needs at least one main clause; that is what separates a sentence from a fragment.
There was a clause in the tenancy agreement that we had completely missed.
Relative clauses were coded separately in the analysis.

confusables.difference: A sentence can contain several clauses. A clause is the smaller unit built around one verb.
A phrase has no finite verb. A clause always has a subject and a verb.

entry_json.avoid: Clause is pronounced /klɔːz/, identical to claws. Do not confuse it with cause /kɔːz/.

entry_json.definition: to press a button on a computer mouse, or to make a short sharp sound
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Click on the link at the bottom of the page to confirm.
example_sentences: The door clicked shut behind us.
Just click here and the form opens.

contexts.text: Designers deliberately make the button you should not click harder to find.
You just click on that and it downloads automatically.
Click-through rates were recorded for each version of the page.

confusables.difference: You press a physical button or a key. You click a mouse or a link on screen.
On a touchscreen you tap rather than click. Using click for a phone sounds slightly dated.

entry_json.avoid: Click ON a link, or simply click the link. Both are correct; click to a link is not.

entry_json.definition: a person or organisation that pays for professional services
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of our clients are small businesses.
example_sentences: The firm lost two major clients last year.
She meets clients three or four times a week.

contexts.text: Professional services firms compete for a small number of large clients, which makes them fragile.
I deal with clients all day, which I actually enjoy.
Client satisfaction was measured through an annual survey.

confusables.difference: A customer buys goods in a shop. A client pays for a professional service: legal, financial or design work.
Doctors have patients, not clients. Using client there sounds cold and commercial.

entry_json.avoid: Shops have customers; lawyers and accountants have clients. Choosing the wrong one is immediately noticeable.

entry_json.definition: in a way that involves careful attention, or with a strong connection
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The two variables are closely linked but not identical.
example_sentences: Look closely at the second paragraph.
The team worked closely with local residents.

contexts.text: Income and life expectancy are closely linked, though the relationship is not a simple one.
I work quite closely with two other people on that project.
The observed pattern closely matches the model's prediction.

confusables.difference: Close is the adjective and also an adverb of distance: stand close to me. Closely means carefully or with strong connection, never physical distance.
Carefully is about taking care. Closely is about attention to detail, especially when examining something.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write stand closely to me. Physical nearness takes close; examination takes closely.

entry_json.definition: material made from cotton, wool or a similar substance; also a piece of it used for cleaning
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wipe the surface with a damp cloth.
example_sentences: The bag is made of a heavy cotton cloth.
She put a clean cloth on the table.

contexts.text: Replacing paper towels with washable cloth cuts household waste noticeably.
I keep a cloth by the sink for wiping things down.
Cloth production accounted for a third of exports in 1850.

confusables.difference: Cloth is the material; clothes are the garments you wear. Clothes has no singular and never means fabric.
Fabric is the more technical or commercial word for the same material. Cloth is everyday.

entry_json.avoid: Cloth is uncountable for the material: some cloth. Clothes is always plural: my clothes are, not my clothes is.

entry_json.definition: a piece of information that helps you solve a problem or answer a question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph gives a useful clue about why sales fell.
example_sentences: Police found no clues at the scene.
I had no clue what the question was asking.

contexts.text: Fossil records provide the only clues we have about how quickly earlier climates changed.
I had absolutely no clue what he was talking about.
Contextual clues helped readers infer unfamiliar vocabulary.

confusables.difference: A hint is deliberately given by someone to help you. A clue may simply exist in the evidence.
Evidence supports a conclusion directly. A clue only points you towards one.

entry_json.avoid: I have no clue is informal. In writing use there is no evidence or it is unclear.

entry_json.definition: a hard black substance dug from the ground and burned to produce heat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coal still generates a large share of electricity in several major economies.
example_sentences: The town grew up around the coal mines.
Burning coal produces more carbon dioxide than any other fuel.

contexts.text: Countries that closed coal mines without planning for the towns around them created decades of unemployment.
My grandfather worked in a coal mine until it closed.
Coal accounted for 60 per cent of electricity generation in 1990 and 12 per cent by 2020.

confusables.difference: Charcoal is made by burning wood slowly. Coal is a fossil fuel dug out of the ground.
Coal is /kəʊl/ and cold is /kəʊld/. The final d is the only difference, and it matters.

entry_json.avoid: Coal is uncountable. Write a lot of coal, not many coals.

entry_json.definition: a small flat piece of metal used as money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fewer people carry coins now that most payments are by card.
example_sentences: I found an old coin under the floorboards.
The machine only takes coins.

contexts.text: As cash use falls, the coins in circulation cost more to produce than they are worth.
I never carry coins any more, which is a problem in car parks.
Coins recovered from the site date from the third century.

confusables.difference: In British English paper money is a note: a ten-pound note. Americans say bill. Coins are metal in both.
Cash covers both coins and notes. A coin is one metal piece.

entry_json.avoid: British English uses note, not bill, for paper money. Getting this wrong is a common Americanism.

entry_json.definition: to fall down suddenly, or to fail completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bridge collapsed after three days of heavy rain.
example_sentences: Tourism collapsed almost overnight.
He collapsed at work and was taken to hospital.

contexts.text: When a single industry collapses, the towns built around it rarely recover within a generation.
The old shed collapsed in the storm last winter.
Fish stocks collapsed after 1992 and have not returned to earlier levels.

confusables.difference: Fall is gradual or ordinary: prices fall. Collapse is sudden and total, and cannot be reversed easily.
Decline is a slow downward trend, ideal for Task 1. Collapse means it dropped to almost nothing.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, only write collapsed if the line really does drop to near zero. Otherwise use fell sharply.

entry_json.definition: a group of similar things kept or brought together; also the act of collecting something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The museum has one of the largest collections in the country.
example_sentences: Waste collection happens once a fortnight here.
He has a huge collection of records.

contexts.text: Reducing waste collection to once a fortnight increased fly-tipping in several boroughs.
I have a small collection of postcards from everywhere I have been.
Data collection took place between March and June.

confusables.difference: A group can be people or things gathered by chance. A collection is deliberately assembled and usually kept.
Collection is the noun; collect the verb. Data collection, or we collect data.

entry_json.avoid: Data collection, waste collection and rubbish collection are fixed compounds and take no article.

entry_json.definition: having a particular colour, or having colour rather than being black and white
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart uses coloured bars to distinguish the three regions.
example_sentences: She handed out coloured pencils to the class.
Brightly coloured packaging attracts younger buyers.

contexts.text: Brightly coloured packaging aimed at children should be restricted for high-sugar foods.
The walls are painted quite a bright colour, which I like.
Coloured markers indicate the three experimental conditions.

confusables.difference: Colourful means having many bright colours and is a compliment. Coloured just means it has some colour.
British spelling is colour and coloured. Keep the u throughout the exam if you are using British spelling.

entry_json.avoid: Never use coloured about a person. It is offensive and dated in British English. Say Black, or people of colour if you need the term.

entry_json.definition: two or more things joined or used together, and the result of doing so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fall was caused by a combination of higher costs and weaker demand.
example_sentences: A combination of diet and exercise works better than either alone.
The colour is a combination of blue and grey.

contexts.text: The improvement resulted from a combination of investment, regulation and simple public pressure.
It was a combination of things, really, not one single reason.
The two treatments were most effective in combination.

confusables.difference: A mixture is things blended so you may not tell them apart. A combination keeps the parts identifiable.
Mix is informal and often physical. Combination is the abstract word for causes and factors, which is what Task 2 needs.

entry_json.avoid: A combination OF things, or in combination WITH something. Not a combination between.

entry_json.definition: to join two or more things together so they work as one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many students combine full-time study with part-time work.
example_sentences: The course combines theory and practical experience.
Combine the flour and the water before adding anything else.

contexts.text: Policies that combine higher fuel taxes with better public transport succeed where either alone would fail.
I combine work and study, which is exhausting but worth it.
The two datasets were combined before analysis.

confusables.difference: Mix implies stirring things into one substance. Combine keeps the elements working together but distinct.
Join is about physical connection at a point. Combine is about bringing things together to act as a whole.

entry_json.avoid: Combine A WITH B, or combine A AND B. Not combine A to B.

entry_json.definition: the state of being physically relaxed and free from pain or worry; also something that makes you feel better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The seats are designed for comfort rather than for fitting more people in.
example_sentences: You can watch it from the comfort of your own home.
It was some comfort to know that others had failed too.

contexts.text: Modern housing is built for comfort, and comfort now accounts for a large share of household energy use.
I value comfort over style when it comes to shoes.
Thermal comfort was assessed using a standard questionnaire.

confusables.difference: Comfort is the noun, comfortable the adjective. Travel in comfort, or a comfortable journey.
Convenience is about being easy and saving effort. Comfort is about physical ease and wellbeing.

entry_json.avoid: The stress is on the first syllable and the second vowel is weak: /ˈkʌmfət/, not com-FORT.

entry_json.definition: an order given to someone; also control over people or a good knowledge of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She has an excellent command of three languages.
example_sentences: The officer gave the command to advance.
The general took command of the region in 1943.

contexts.text: A good command of English is now expected in professions that never required it a generation ago.
I would say I have a reasonable command of French, but not much more.
Voice commands were recognised correctly in 94 per cent of trials.

confusables.difference: An order is the everyday word for telling someone to do something. Command is military or technical.
Control is the general power over something. Command is formal authority, or expert knowledge of a subject.

entry_json.avoid: A good command OF a language is the phrase examiners expect. Not a good command in.

entry_json.definition: connected with buying and selling, or done mainly to make money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The building was converted for commercial use in the 1990s.
example_sentences: The film was a commercial success but poorly reviewed.
Commercial farming has replaced smallholdings across the region.

contexts.text: Universities under commercial pressure begin to treat students as customers rather than learners.
There is a commercial estate on the edge of town where most people work.
Commercial vehicles accounted for a fifth of all traffic.

confusables.difference: Economic relates to a whole economy. Commercial relates to trade and profit-making by individual businesses.
Business is a noun used before other nouns: business hours. Commercial is a true adjective and is more formal.

entry_json.avoid: Commercial before a noun means profit-driven, sometimes as a criticism. Take care in essays about the arts.

entry_json.definition: an official group appointed to investigate something; also money paid to someone for selling something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A government commission was set up to review the evidence.
example_sentences: Estate agents work on commission.
The commission published its findings after two years.

contexts.text: An independent commission would examine the evidence more credibly than a government department.
The salespeople work on commission, which explains a lot.
The commission's report was published in 2019.

confusables.difference: A committee is usually a permanent internal body. A commission is set up for one investigation and then disbanded.
Different words entirely. A commitment is a promise; a commission is a body or a payment.

entry_json.avoid: Work on commission takes no article. Set up or appoint a commission, not make one.

entry_json.definition: to do something wrong or illegal; also to promise seriously to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The government committed itself to halving emissions by 2035.
example_sentences: Most crimes are committed by a very small number of people.
I cannot commit to anything until I know my timetable.

contexts.text: Governments commit to targets that fall due long after the ministers announcing them have left office.
I did not want to commit to a two-year contract.
Offences committed by first-time offenders were analysed separately.

confusables.difference: Promise is everyday and personal. Commit is formal and implies binding yourself, often publicly.
You do a job but commit a crime. Commit is only used with wrongdoing, not with ordinary actions.

entry_json.avoid: Double the t: committed, committing, commitment has two t's but commitment keeps only one m pair. Commit TO doing, not commit to do.

entry_json.definition: a promise to do something, or the willingness to give time and energy to something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company made a public commitment to reduce packaging.
example_sentences: Studying part time is a serious commitment.
Her commitment to the project never wavered.

contexts.text: Without a firm financial commitment, environmental targets are simply statements of intention.
Owning a dog is a bigger commitment than people expect.
Participants' commitment to the programme was measured at three points.

confusables.difference: A promise can be casual. A commitment implies ongoing effort, not just a single undertaking.
Dedication is the personal quality of giving yourself to something. A commitment can be a formal obligation with no feeling attached.

entry_json.avoid: Make a commitment TO something or TO DOING something. Not commitment for.

entry_json.definition: a group of people chosen to make decisions or deal with a particular subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The committee meets once a month and decides almost nothing.
example_sentences: A committee was formed to review the curriculum.
She sits on two committees at the university.

contexts.text: Decisions taken by committee tend to be slower but harder to reverse.
I am on the residents' committee, which meets far too often.
The ethics committee approved the study in January.

confusables.difference: A committee is standing and internal. A commission is appointed for one task, often independently.
A board governs an organisation and has legal responsibility. A committee usually advises or manages one area.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: two m's, two t's, two e's. It is one of the most misspelt words on this list.

entry_json.definition: often, by many people, or in most cases
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The condition is commonly mistaken for something far less serious.
example_sentences: This is commonly known as the greenhouse effect.
The word is commonly used in the media but rarely defined.

contexts.text: It is commonly assumed that longer sentences deter crime, though the evidence is weak.
That is commonly called the ring road, though its official name is different.
The most commonly reported symptom was fatigue.

confusables.difference: Usually is about how often something happens to one person or in one case. Commonly is about how widespread something is across many cases.
Often is neutral and everyday. Commonly is formal and works better before a past participle: commonly used, commonly held.

entry_json.avoid: It is commonly believed that is a strong Task 2 opener for a view you intend to challenge.

entry_json.definition: the activity of sharing information, or the ways in which people do so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Poor communication between departments caused most of the delays.
example_sentences: Communication skills matter as much as technical knowledge.
There has been no communication from the company for weeks.

contexts.text: Instant communication has made us better informed and considerably worse at listening.
Communication is the main thing I would want to improve about my English.
Communication between the two teams was recorded and coded.

confusables.difference: A conversation is one specific spoken exchange. Communication is the whole process, including writing and gesture.
Information is the content. Communication is the act of passing it on.

entry_json.avoid: Usually uncountable when it means the process. Communications with an s means the technology or the messages themselves.

entry_json.definition: the act of examining two things to see how they are similar or different
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A comparison of the two charts shows the same pattern in both countries.
example_sentences: By comparison, the second option looks reasonable.
There is no comparison between the two courses.

contexts.text: In comparison with the previous decade, spending on public health barely rose at all.
By comparison, my old job was far less stressful.
A direct comparison between the two systems is difficult because they measure different things.

confusables.difference: Comparison is the noun; compare the verb. Make a comparison, or compare two things.
A comparison looks at similarities and differences. A contrast highlights differences only.

entry_json.avoid: In comparison WITH or TO, and by comparison alone. Not in comparison of.

entry_json.definition: a person or company competing against others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company lost ground to cheaper competitors overseas.
example_sentences: Only twelve competitors finished the race.
Our main competitor opened a branch across the road.

contexts.text: Firms that treat regulation as a burden lose out to competitors who treat it as a design problem.
There were about two hundred competitors in the race, which surprised me.
Competitors' prices were tracked over a six-month period.

confusables.difference: Competition is the abstract activity or the event. A competitor is one person or firm taking part.
An opponent is who you face directly in a match or debate. A competitor is anyone else in the same contest or market.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse with competitive, which is the adjective. A competitive market has many competitors.

entry_json.definition: a statement that you are not satisfied with something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am writing to make a formal complaint about the service.
example_sentences: The council received over a hundred complaints about the noise.
My only complaint is the price.

contexts.text: I wish to make a formal complaint about the condition of the accommodation.
My only complaint about the flat is that it is quite dark.
Complaints about waiting times rose by 40 per cent over the period.

confusables.difference: Criticism is a judgement about quality, often given to help. A complaint expects something to be done about it.
Complaint is the noun; complain the verb. Make a complaint, or complain about something.

entry_json.avoid: Make or lodge a complaint ABOUT something TO someone. Not do a complaint.

entry_json.definition: made of many connected parts and therefore difficult to understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Migration is a complex issue with no single cause.
example_sentences: The tax system here is unnecessarily complex.
It is a complex piece of machinery.

contexts.text: Poverty is a complex problem, and policies that address only income miss most of it.
The booking system is more complex than it needs to be.
The model captures a complex interaction between three variables.

confusables.difference: Complex means having many parts, which is neutral and often unavoidable. Complicated means confusing, and usually implies it should have been simpler.
Difficult is about how hard something is to do. Complex is about how many parts it has.

entry_json.avoid: A complex issue is a strong neutral phrase for Task 2. Complicated sounds like a criticism of whoever designed it.

entry_json.definition: made up of many confusing parts and hard to understand or deal with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The application process is far more complicated than it needs to be.
example_sentences: It is a complicated situation, and there is no quick answer.
The instructions were so complicated that nobody finished.

contexts.text: Benefit systems that are unnecessarily complicated exclude exactly the people they were designed to help.
It is complicated, but basically we had to change flights twice.
The procedure proved more complicated than the pilot study suggested.

confusables.difference: Complex is neutral: many parts. Complicated is negative: confusingly many parts. In academic writing, complex is usually the better choice.
Difficult things take effort. Complicated things take untangling.

entry_json.avoid: Complicated carries mild criticism. If you simply mean the subject has many aspects, write complex.

entry_json.definition: one of several parts that together make up a whole
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing is the largest single component of most household budgets.
example_sentences: The engine has fewer moving components than a petrol one.
Listening is one component of the test.

contexts.text: Reliable public transport is a key component of any workable plan to reduce urban emissions.
The most difficult component of the course was the statistics.
Each component of the score was weighted equally.

confusables.difference: Part is the everyday word for any piece. A component is a defined part of a designed system, which sounds more technical.
Element is more abstract: an element of risk. A component is usually a physical or structural part.

entry_json.avoid: A component OF something, not a component IN it, except when describing physical assembly.

entry_json.definition: to give all your attention to one thing, or to bring things together in one place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cannot concentrate with the television on.
example_sentences: The report concentrates on the first five years.
Wealth is increasingly concentrated in a few cities.

contexts.text: Wealth is increasingly concentrated in a small number of cities, which distorts national housing markets.
I find it hard to concentrate in the afternoon, so I do my reading early.
The study concentrates on students in their final year.

confusables.difference: Nearly identical. Focus on is slightly more common in academic writing; concentrate on is more common in speech about attention.
Pay attention to means noticing something. Concentrate on means sustained mental effort over time.

entry_json.avoid: Concentrate ON something, never concentrate in something.

entry_json.definition: the ability to give all your attention to something; also the amount of a substance in a mixture
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My concentration goes completely after about ninety minutes.
example_sentences: The test requires sustained concentration.
Concentrations of nitrogen dioxide are highest near main roads.

contexts.text: Concentrations of pollutants near schools regularly exceed the legal limit in several cities.
I lose concentration if I study for more than an hour without a break.
Constant notifications damage concentration more than the time they actually take.

confusables.difference: Attention is noticing something, which can be brief. Concentration is holding that attention over time.
Focus is where your attention is directed. Concentration is the effort of keeping it there.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable when it means attention. Countable when it means the amount of a substance: concentrations of lead.

entry_json.definition: an idea or principle connected with something abstract
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The concept of a job for life has almost disappeared.
example_sentences: Students struggle with the concept at first.
The whole concept rests on one questionable assumption.

contexts.text: The concept of retirement was invented barely a century ago and is already being abandoned.
The concept of working from home was strange to my parents' generation.
The concept is defined differently across the three studies.

confusables.difference: An idea can be a passing thought or a plan. A concept is a defined abstract principle used in thinking about a subject.
A theory explains how something works and can be tested. A concept is one building block used inside theories.

entry_json.avoid: The concept OF something. Not the concept about, and not a concept to.

entry_json.definition: a feeling of worry about something important, or a matter that worries people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is growing concern about the amount of plastic in the sea.
example_sentences: Safety was the main concern raised by parents.
Her only concern was whether the money would arrive.

contexts.text: There is growing concern that automation will remove entry-level jobs faster than it creates new ones.
My main concern about moving was leaving my family behind.
Concerns raised in the consultation are summarised below.

confusables.difference: Worry is personal and emotional. Concern is more measured and can be public and institutional, which suits formal writing.
A problem exists whether anyone notices it. A concern is the human reaction to it.

entry_json.avoid: Concern ABOUT or OVER something. Raise concerns, not make concerns.

entry_json.definition: worried about something; or involved in or affected by something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parents are increasingly concerned about screen time.
example_sentences: All the departments concerned were consulted.
As far as I am concerned, the decision was the right one.
collocations: as far as I am concerned

contexts.text: Health professionals are concerned that the guidance has not changed since 2011.
As far as I am concerned, the buses should be free.
The authorities concerned declined to comment.

confusables.difference: Concerned describes the person feeling worry. Concerning as an adjective describes the thing causing it: a concerning trend.
Interested means you want to know more. Concerned means you are worried.

entry_json.avoid: Position changes the meaning: a concerned parent is worried; the parents concerned means those involved.

entry_json.definition: to decide something after considering the evidence; also to end something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The researchers concluded that the effect was too small to matter.
example_sentences: The report concludes with three recommendations.
I concluded that it was not worth the money.

contexts.text: The evidence allows us to conclude that early intervention works, though not that it is cheap.
I concluded that I would be better off taking the earlier flight.
The authors conclude that further research is required.

confusables.difference: Finish is the everyday word for ending something. Conclude is formal and also means to reach a decision from evidence.
Decide is a choice between options. Conclude is a judgement drawn from evidence, which is stronger in an argument.

entry_json.avoid: Conclude THAT plus a clause, or conclude WITH something. Not conclude to.

entry_json.definition: a decision or judgement reached after thinking about the evidence; also the end of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The obvious conclusion is that the policy has not worked.
example_sentences: In conclusion, the benefits outweigh the risks.
He jumped to the wrong conclusion.

contexts.text: In conclusion, investment in prevention is a better use of public money than expanding treatment.
I came to the conclusion that the course was not right for me.
The conclusions drawn here are limited by the size of the sample.

confusables.difference: A summary repeats the main points. A conclusion states what follows from them, which is what Task 2 requires.
A result is what happened. A conclusion is what you decide it means.

entry_json.avoid: Draw or reach a conclusion, not take one. In conclusion belongs at the start of your final paragraph, once only.

entry_json.definition: to organise and carry out a particular activity, especially research or an investigation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The survey was conducted over three months in five cities.
example_sentences: They conducted interviews with forty participants.
An inquiry is being conducted into the accident.

contexts.text: Research conducted independently of the industry it examines carries far more weight.
They conducted a survey and then ignored the results entirely.
The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions.

confusables.difference: Do is the everyday verb. Conduct is the formal one that belongs with research, surveys, interviews and investigations.
Lead means being in charge of people. Conduct means carrying out a process from start to finish.

entry_json.avoid: Stress differs by word class: the verb is /kənˈdʌkt/, the noun conduct meaning behaviour is /ˈkɒndʌkt/.

entry_json.definition: the feeling that you can do things well, or trust in someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Speaking regularly is the only thing that builds confidence in a language.
example_sentences: Public confidence in the system has fallen sharply.
She lost confidence after failing twice.

contexts.text: Public confidence in official statistics is easy to lose and extremely slow to rebuild.
My confidence improved a lot once I started speaking every day.
Confidence in the results is limited by the response rate.

confusables.difference: Confidence is the noun, confident the adjective. Gain confidence, or become confident.
Trust is belief that someone will not let you down. Confidence is belief in their ability or in your own.

entry_json.avoid: Confidence IN something or someone. Build, gain or lose confidence, not make confidence.

entry_json.definition: sure that you can do something well, or certain that something will happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am fairly confident that the results will improve.
example_sentences: She is much more confident speaking in public now.
He seemed confident about the interview.

contexts.text: Students who are confident about making mistakes learn faster than those who are afraid of them.
I am not particularly confident in interviews, if I am honest.
Respondents were asked how confident they felt about the change.

confusables.difference: A confidant is a person you tell secrets to. Confident is the adjective. They are spelt one letter apart.
Confident is positive: sure of your ability. Arrogant is negative: believing you are better than others.

entry_json.avoid: Confident ABOUT something, or confident THAT plus a clause. Not confident of doing in most contexts.

entry_json.definition: to state or show that something is definitely true or will definitely happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please confirm your attendance by Friday.
example_sentences: The results confirm what earlier studies suggested.
The hotel confirmed the booking by email.

contexts.text: I would be grateful if you could confirm the refund in writing.
They never confirmed the booking, so we turned up hoping for the best.
These findings confirm the pattern reported in earlier work.

confusables.difference: Prove establishes something beyond doubt. Confirm supports what was already expected, which is a weaker and safer claim.
You check something to find out whether it is true. You confirm it once you know that it is.

entry_json.avoid: Confirm THAT plus a clause, or confirm a noun. Not confirm about something.

entry_json.definition: a serious disagreement, or fighting between countries or groups
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is an obvious conflict between growth and conservation.
example_sentences: The region has seen armed conflict for over a decade.
A conflict of interest should always be declared.

contexts.text: The conflict between short-term profit and long-term sustainability shapes almost every environmental debate.
There was a bit of conflict in the team, mostly about workload.
Countries experiencing armed conflict were excluded from the sample.

confusables.difference: An argument is one specific disagreement, often brief. Conflict is deeper and longer-lasting, and may involve violence.
Competition can be healthy and rule-governed. Conflict implies the parties are working against each other.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is /ˈkɒnflɪkt/ with front stress; the verb, meaning to disagree, is /kənˈflɪkt/. A conflict BETWEEN two things.

entry_json.definition: to make someone unable to think clearly, or to mistake one thing for another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People often confuse the two words because they sound similar.
example_sentences: The signs at the station confuse almost everybody.
Do not confuse cause with correlation.

contexts.text: Writers frequently confuse correlation with causation, and the error changes the whole argument.
I always confuse his name with his brother's.
The two conditions are easily confused in clinical settings.

confusables.difference: Confuse is the verb: the map confused me. Confused is how you then feel.
Mix up is the informal spoken equivalent of confusing two things. Confuse is the one to write.

entry_json.avoid: Confuse A WITH B. Not confuse A and B in the sense of mistaking one for the other.

entry_json.definition: unable to understand something clearly or think straight
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was completely confused by the timetable in the first week.
example_sentences: Students get confused when the instructions change halfway through.
He looked confused and asked her to repeat the question.

contexts.text: Patients left confused about their medication are far more likely to take it incorrectly.
I was completely confused about which bus to take.
Participants who reported feeling confused were given the instructions again.

confusables.difference: Confused describes the person. Confusing describes the thing that caused it. I was confused because the sign was confusing.
Uncertain means you do not know which is true. Confused means you cannot make sense of it at all.

entry_json.avoid: The -ed and -ing pair is a classic error: writing I am confusing when you mean I am confused says the opposite.

entry_json.definition: difficult to understand, and likely to make people uncertain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The instructions were so confusing that half the class gave up.
example_sentences: The layout of the website is genuinely confusing.
It is confusing that the two forms have almost the same name.

contexts.text: Confusing eligibility rules keep many entitled households from claiming support at all.
The signposting at that station is really confusing.
The original wording was found to be confusing and was revised.

confusables.difference: Confusing describes the cause; confused describes the person affected.
Complicated means it has many parts. Confusing means it is badly explained, which is a criticism of the presentation.

entry_json.avoid: Only things and situations are confusing. Saying I am confusing means you confuse other people.

entry_json.definition: a link between two things or people; also a link to a network or a transport service
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a clear connection between air quality and childhood asthma.
example_sentences: I missed my connection in Frankfurt.
The internet connection here is unreliable.

contexts.text: The connection between poor housing and poor health is well documented and largely ignored.
My internet connection drops out every evening around eight.
A significant connection was found between the two variables.

confusables.difference: Relationship is broader and often about people. Connection points at a specific link, which suits data and causes.
Almost identical in the abstract sense. Link is slightly shorter and preferred in headlines and in Task 1 descriptions.

entry_json.avoid: A connection BETWEEN two things, or WITH one thing. In connection with is a formal fixed phrase meaning about.

entry_json.definition: awake and able to notice things; also deliberately aware of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was a conscious decision to stop driving to work.
example_sentences: He remained conscious throughout the journey to hospital.
People are far more conscious of what they eat than they were.

contexts.text: Consumers are increasingly conscious of packaging waste, though few change what they buy.
I made a conscious effort to speak English every day.
Patients were conscious but disoriented on arrival.

confusables.difference: Aware is the neutral everyday word for knowing something. Conscious suggests deliberate attention, and also means awake.
Conscience is a noun meaning your sense of right and wrong. Conscious is an adjective meaning awake or aware. One letter apart, entirely different.

entry_json.avoid: Conscious OF something, or a conscious decision. Never conscious about.

entry_json.definition: a result of something that has happened, especially an unwelcome one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The environmental consequences of the decision will last for generations.
example_sentences: He lost his job as a consequence of the merger.
Every policy has consequences nobody predicted.

contexts.text: The unintended consequences of banning cars from the centre fell hardest on shift workers.
As a consequence, I ended up staying an extra week.
The consequences of the intervention were assessed after twelve months.

confusables.difference: Result is neutral and can be positive. Consequence is more formal and usually points at something serious or unwelcome.
Effect is the direct change something produces. A consequence is the wider situation that follows.

entry_json.avoid: As a consequence OF something, but as a consequence alone as a linker. Not in consequence to.

entry_json.definition: not liking change, and preferring traditional ways; also deliberately cautious in an estimate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Even on the most conservative estimate, the cost will exceed a billion.
example_sentences: Attitudes in the region remain fairly conservative.
The forecast is deliberately conservative.

contexts.text: Even on a conservative estimate, replacing the network would take fifteen years.
My family are quite conservative about that sort of thing.
A conservative approach to the analysis was adopted throughout.

confusables.difference: Traditional describes customs themselves. Conservative describes an attitude of wanting to keep them.
With a capital C it names a political party. Lower case, it describes an attitude. Keep them apart in writing.

entry_json.avoid: A conservative estimate means a cautious low one, not a politically right-wing one. Context decides.

entry_json.definition: careful thought about something, or a factor that must be taken into account
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cost was the main consideration in choosing the site.
example_sentences: After careful consideration, the offer was declined.
Safety must be the first consideration.

contexts.text: Planners must take the needs of non-drivers into consideration before removing bus routes.
The main consideration for me was how far it was from home.
Ethical considerations are discussed in section four.

confusables.difference: Consideration is the noun; consider the verb. Take into consideration, or consider something.
Thought is any mental activity. Consideration is deliberate weighing up before a decision.

entry_json.avoid: Take something INTO consideration. Not take in consideration, and not take to consideration.

entry_json.definition: to be made up of particular parts or things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course consists of six modules and a final project.
example_sentences: Breakfast consisted of bread and coffee.
The committee consists of eight elected members.

contexts.text: The average household's waste consists mainly of packaging and food, both of which are avoidable.
My week basically consists of lectures and shifts at the café.
The sample consisted of 240 undergraduates.

confusables.difference: Comprise takes no of: the course comprises six modules. Consist always needs of. Mixing them is a very common error.
Include lists some of the parts. Consist of lists all of them.

entry_json.avoid: Consist OF. Never consists in this sense without of, and never used in the passive: not it is consisted of.

entry_json.definition: always behaving or happening in the same way; also in agreement with something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Her results have been consistent all year.
example_sentences: The findings are consistent with earlier research.
We need a consistent approach across all departments.

contexts.text: The pattern is consistent across all five countries, which makes a local explanation unlikely.
I am not very consistent with exercise, unfortunately.
These results are consistent with those reported by earlier studies.

confusables.difference: Constant means unchanging or continuous in amount. Consistent means reliably the same in behaviour or quality.
Persistent means continuing despite obstacles. Consistent means not varying.

entry_json.avoid: Consistent WITH something is the academic phrase. Consistent IN doing something describes a person's reliability.

entry_json.definition: happening all the time, or staying the same over a period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The constant noise from the road was the only drawback.
example_sentences: Temperature was held constant throughout the experiment.
She lives under constant pressure to meet targets.

contexts.text: The constant availability of work email has eroded the boundary between employment and private life.
There is constant traffic outside my window, which I have got used to.
Numbers remained constant between 2005 and 2010 before rising sharply.

confusables.difference: Continuous means without any break. Constant can mean very frequent as well as unbroken, and often carries irritation.
Constant is about not changing in amount. Consistent is about not varying in quality or behaviour.

entry_json.avoid: Remained constant is an excellent Task 1 phrase for a flat line. Do not write stayed in constant.

entry_json.definition: all the time, or very often and repeatedly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rules change so constantly that nobody can keep up.
example_sentences: He is constantly checking his phone.
Prices are constantly rising.

contexts.text: Students who are constantly interrupted by notifications retain considerably less of what they read.
My neighbours are constantly having work done on their house.
The variable was constantly monitored throughout the trial.

confusables.difference: Continuously means without any interruption at all. Constantly usually means repeatedly, with gaps, and often suggests annoyance.
Always is neutral. Constantly implies excessive frequency, so it carries a mild complaint.

entry_json.avoid: Constantly often sounds critical. If you simply mean regularly, write regularly or frequently.

entry_json.definition: to build something, or to form something such as an argument from parts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bridge was constructed in less than two years.
example_sentences: The essay is carefully constructed around three examples.
Several new schools are being constructed on the edge of the city.

contexts.text: Housing constructed on flood plains creates costs that fall on everyone, not just the owners.
They are constructing a new station where the car park used to be.
A model was constructed using data from the first two years.

confusables.difference: Build is the ordinary word and works everywhere. Construct is formal and used for large structures and for abstract things like arguments.
Construct is the verb; construction is the noun. Under construction, or they constructed it.

entry_json.avoid: The verb is stressed on the second syllable. Construct is too formal for small everyday things: you build a fire, not construct one.

entry_json.definition: the process or industry of building things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Construction of the new line began in 2018.
example_sentences: The site has been under construction for three years.
He works in construction.

contexts.text: The construction industry produces nearly a third of all waste sent to landfill.
There is construction work going on outside all day.
Construction of the facility was completed in 2012.

confusables.difference: Building is the everyday noun and also means the structure itself. Construction is the process or the industry, and is uncountable in that sense.
Development is the whole project including planning and finance. Construction is only the physical building.

entry_json.avoid: Under construction takes no article. And construction meaning the industry is uncountable: work in construction.

entry_json.definition: to use up energy, food or resources
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The average household consumes far more electricity than it needs to.
example_sentences: We consume around a third of the meat our grandparents did.
Older appliances consume much more power.

contexts.text: Wealthy countries consume resources at a rate the planet cannot sustain indefinitely.
I try to consume less meat, though I have not given it up.
Households in the top income group consumed twice as much energy.

confusables.difference: Eat is the natural word for food in speech. Consume is formal and works for food, fuel, water and electricity alike.
Use is neutral. Consume implies the thing is used up and gone, which is why it suits resources.

entry_json.avoid: Consume is formal. Saying I consumed a sandwich sounds odd; keep it for resources and statistics.

entry_json.definition: a person who buys goods or services for their own use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Consumers now expect delivery within a day, which has an environmental cost.
example_sentences: Consumer spending fell for three consecutive quarters.
The law protects consumers from misleading advertising.

contexts.text: Consumers say they will pay more for sustainable products, and then reliably choose the cheaper option.
As a consumer I do look at where things are made now.
Consumer confidence declined steadily throughout 2008.

confusables.difference: A customer buys from one specific shop or company. A consumer is anyone who uses goods, considered as a group in economics.
Clients pay for professional services. Consumers buy products.

entry_json.avoid: Consumer is the word for essays about economics and advertising. Customer is the word for a specific transaction.

entry_json.definition: communication with someone, or the state of touching something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am still in contact with two people from that course.
example_sentences: Please give a contact number on the form.
Avoid contact with the eyes.

contexts.text: Regular contact with the wider family protects older people from isolation more effectively than any service.
I am still in contact with my best friend from school.
My contact details are given at the end of this letter.

confusables.difference: Communication is the process of exchanging information. Contact is simply being in touch, however briefly.
Connection is a link between things. Contact is between people.

entry_json.avoid: In contact WITH someone. Get in contact, keep in contact and stay in contact are all correct; make contact is for the first time.

entry_json.definition: a box, bottle or similar object used for holding something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reusable containers cut a surprising amount of household waste.
example_sentences: Store the leftovers in an airtight container.
The port handles thousands of containers a day.

contexts.text: Charging for single-use containers reduced their use by more than eighty per cent within a year.
I take my own container to the market, which saves a lot of plastic.
Containers were sealed and stored at a constant temperature.

confusables.difference: Packaging is the material wrapped around a product for sale. A container is the object that holds things, and is usually reusable.
A box is one kind of container, made of card or wood. Container is the general term.

entry_json.avoid: Container is countable. In shipping it means the large steel unit, which is a useful Task 1 vocabulary item.

entry_json.definition: a competition in which people try to win something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The contest attracted entries from over thirty countries.
example_sentences: She won a writing contest at fifteen.
The election turned into a two-way contest.

contexts.text: Turning school achievement into a contest motivates the strongest students and discourages everyone else.
I entered a photography contest once and came nowhere.
The contest between the two candidates was decided by fewer than 500 votes.

confusables.difference: Competition is the more common British word for the event and also names the activity in general. Contest is slightly more formal or literary.
A match is between two teams or players in sport. A contest can have many entrants and need not be sporting.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is /ˈkɒntest/ with front stress; the verb, meaning to dispute or challenge, is /kənˈtest/.

entry_json.definition: happening without stopping or without any break
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The machine emits a continuous low noise.
example_sentences: There has been continuous growth for six years.
Continuous assessment replaced the final exam.

contexts.text: Learning a language is a continuous process rather than a course you finish.
There is a continuous hum from the fridge that I only notice at night.
The line shows continuous growth from 1995 to 2015.

confusables.difference: Continuous means with no break at all. Continual means repeated with gaps, often annoyingly. Rain can be continuous; interruptions are continual.
Constant emphasises not changing in amount. Continuous emphasises not stopping in time.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, continuous growth means the line never falls. If it dips, write overall growth instead.

entry_json.definition: a formal written agreement that is legally binding
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I signed a twelve-month contract before I read all of it.
example_sentences: The company won a contract to supply the schools.
Read the contract carefully before you sign.

contexts.text: Short fixed-term contracts give employers flexibility and give workers no way to plan their lives.
My contract runs out in June, so I am looking around already.
Workers on temporary contracts reported lower job satisfaction.

confusables.difference: An agreement can be informal or spoken. A contract is written and legally enforceable.
Deal is the informal word for the commercial arrangement. Contract is the document that records it.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is /ˈkɒntrækt/ with front stress; the verb meaning to shrink or to catch an illness is /kənˈtrækt/.

entry_json.definition: a clear difference between two things when they are compared
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a sharp contrast between the two halves of the city.
example_sentences: In contrast, spending on transport fell every year.
The contrast between the figures is striking.

contexts.text: In contrast, the rural figure barely changed over the entire period.
The contrast between the two cities was quite a shock at first.
There is a striking contrast between what people say about recycling and what they do.

confusables.difference: A comparison looks for both similarities and differences. A contrast points only at the differences.
Difference is the plain noun. Contrast implies the difference is large and immediately visible.

entry_json.avoid: In contrast and by contrast both start a sentence. In contrast TO or WITH something. Not in contrast of.

entry_json.definition: to give money, help or ideas towards something; also to be one of the causes of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic contributes more to urban air pollution than industry does.
example_sentences: Everyone contributed something towards the gift.
Several factors contributed to the decline.

contexts.text: Deforestation contributes significantly to emissions, yet receives a fraction of the attention given to transport.
We all contributed a bit towards the cost of the trip.
Three variables contributed significantly to the model.

confusables.difference: Cause claims full responsibility. Contribute to says it is one factor among several, which is usually the more defensible claim.
Donate is only about giving money or goods to a cause. Contribute also covers ideas, effort and causal influence.

entry_json.avoid: Contribute TO something. The stress is on the second syllable: /kənˈtrɪbjuːt/.

entry_json.definition: something you give or do to help achieve something, or an amount of money given
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Her contribution to the project was far larger than the credit she received.
example_sentences: Small daily changes make a real contribution over a year.
Employers pay a contribution towards the pension.

contexts.text: Individual behaviour makes a real contribution, but it cannot substitute for regulation.
I would like to think I made some contribution to the team.
Each factor's contribution to the total variance is shown in Table 3.

confusables.difference: A donation is money or goods given to a charity. A contribution can be effort, ideas or part of a shared cost.
Participation is taking part. A contribution is what you actually add.

entry_json.avoid: Make a contribution TO something. Not do a contribution, and not contribution for.

entry_json.definition: useful because it saves you trouble, or easy to reach and use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flat is convenient for the station, which is why we took it.
example_sentences: Would Thursday be convenient for you?
Online banking is more convenient but less secure.

contexts.text: Online shopping is convenient for the customer and expensive for the environment.
My flat is really convenient for work, about ten minutes on foot.
Please let me know a convenient time to discuss the matter.

confusables.difference: Comfortable is about physical ease. Convenient is about saving time and effort. A long train journey can be comfortable but inconvenient.
Suitable means right for the purpose. Convenient means it fits easily into your arrangements.

entry_json.avoid: Convenient FOR a place or a person, and convenient TO DO something. Never convenient of.

entry_json.definition: to change something into a different form, or to change it so that it can be used for a different purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old cotton mill has been converted into student flats.
example_sentences: Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity.
You can convert the figures into percentages to make the comparison clearer.

contexts.text: The old cotton mill has been converted into student flats.
Wind turbines convert the movement of air into usable power.
Governments should convert unused office blocks into affordable housing.

confusables.difference: Change is the neutral word for any difference. Convert means changing form or purpose deliberately, usually into something specific: you convert a garage into a bedroom, you do not convert your mind.
Transform is bigger and more dramatic, and often has no stated end product. Convert almost always names what it becomes, with into.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say "convert to flats" when you mean the building becomes flats. The normal pattern is convert something into something.

entry_json.definition: to make somebody believe that something is true, or to persuade them to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a week to convince my parents that studying abroad was worth the cost.
example_sentences: The evidence convinced the committee that the policy needed changing.
My friend convinced me to join the gym with her.

contexts.text: It took me a week to convince my parents that studying abroad was worth the cost.
These figures alone are unlikely to convince readers that the scheme has worked.

confusables.difference: Persuade is about getting somebody to act. Convince is about getting them to believe. You persuade a friend to come out; you convince a friend that the film is good.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write "convince about". Use convince somebody of something, or convince somebody that.

entry_json.definition: completely sure that something is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am convinced that online learning suits some students far better than lectures do.
example_sentences: She was convinced of his honesty long before the evidence appeared.
Not everyone is convinced that the new bypass will reduce traffic.

contexts.text: I am convinced that online learning suits some students far better than lectures do.
Honestly, I am not convinced by that argument at all.

confusables.difference: Convinced describes the person who now believes. Convincing describes the thing that made them believe. A convincing argument leaves you convinced.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two -ed and -ing forms: "I am convincing" means you persuade others, not that you believe.

entry_json.definition: the most important or central part of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the core of the problem is a shortage of affordable housing, not a shortage of land.
example_sentences: Maths and language form the core of the primary curriculum.
The report goes to the core of why young people leave rural areas.

contexts.text: At the core of the problem is a shortage of affordable housing, not a shortage of land.
The core modules are compulsory, but you choose the rest yourself.

confusables.difference: Centre is usually physical position. Core is importance: the core of an argument is its essential part, not its middle.
Heart of the matter is warmer and more idiomatic; core is the drier, more academic choice for essays.

entry_json.avoid: In an essay, avoid "the core reason" when you simply mean the main reason; core works best as a noun in at the core of.

entry_json.definition: connected with a large company or with companies in general
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Corporate donations now fund a large share of university research.
example_sentences: Many graduates are drawn to corporate life by the salary rather than the work.
The company publishes an annual report on its corporate responsibility.

contexts.text: Corporate donations now fund a large share of university research.
I did not enjoy the corporate world, so I moved to a small charity.

confusables.difference: Commercial means done for profit or connected with buying and selling. Corporate means belonging to companies as organisations, so corporate culture is about how a firm behaves internally.

entry_json.avoid: Corporate describes companies, not individual businesspeople; a person is a business executive, not a corporate.

entry_json.definition: a set of clothes worn by an actor or performer, or the traditional clothes of a place or period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: At the spring festival everyone wears traditional costume and dances in the square.
example_sentences: The museum has a room of nineteenth-century costume.
She spent a fortnight making her son's costume for the school play.

contexts.text: At the spring festival everyone wears traditional costume and dances in the square.
The exhibition traces changes in working-class costume between 1850 and 1900.

confusables.difference: Clothes is what you wear every day. Costume is worn for a performance, a festival or a period, so "I bought new costume" is wrong for ordinary shopping.
An outfit is a set of ordinary clothes chosen to go together; a costume represents a character, a country or a tradition.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use costume for daily clothing. In British English a swimming costume is a swimsuit, not fancy dress.

entry_json.definition: a small, usually old house in the countryside or in a village
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We rented a stone cottage in the hills for a week with no internet at all.
example_sentences: Her grandparents live in a cottage with a garden full of vegetables.
Holiday cottages have pushed local house prices beyond what young families can pay.

contexts.text: We rented a stone cottage in the hills for a week with no internet at all.
Second-home buyers have converted many village cottages into holiday lets.

confusables.difference: A bungalow is any house on one floor, town or country, new or old. A cottage is small, rural and usually old, and may well have stairs.

entry_json.avoid: A cottage is not a general word for house; a modern flat or a city house is never a cottage.

entry_json.definition: a soft white material from the cotton plant, used to make cloth and thread
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cotton production uses far more water than most shoppers realise.
example_sentences: I prefer cotton shirts because they are cooler in summer.
The country's economy still depends heavily on exports of raw cotton.

contexts.text: I prefer cotton shirts because they are cooler in summer.
Cotton production uses far more water than most shoppers realise.

confusables.difference: Cotton comes from a plant; wool comes from sheep. Both are uncountable when you mean the material.

entry_json.avoid: Cotton is uncountable as a material: say "a cotton shirt" or "some cotton", not "a cotton".

entry_json.definition: a group of people elected to govern a town or area, or a group chosen to advise or make decisions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The local council has closed two libraries to balance its budget.
example_sentences: Residents wrote to the council about the state of the pavements.
The student council meets once a month to discuss campus issues.

contexts.text: The local council has closed two libraries to balance its budget.
I rang the council about the bins and they came the next day.

confusables.difference: Counsel with an s is advice, or a lawyer. Council with a c is the body of people. They sound the same, so the spelling is the only signal in writing.
Government usually means the national one. Council is local: it runs schools, roads and rubbish collection in one town or district.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write counsel when you mean the elected body; the spelling error is common and costs marks in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: land outside towns and cities, with fields, farms and woods
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young people keep leaving the countryside because the jobs are all in the cities.
example_sentences: At weekends we drive out into the countryside to walk.
Protecting the countryside from new housing is a constant political argument.

contexts.text: At weekends we drive out into the countryside to walk.
Young people keep leaving the countryside because the jobs are all in the cities.

confusables.difference: Nature is the natural world in general, including wild places. Countryside is farmed, settled land outside cities, and it is uncountable and normally takes the.
Country can mean a nation. The countryside never does: "I live in the countryside" means rural area, "I live in this country" means the nation.

entry_json.avoid: Countryside is uncountable and normally takes the: not "a countryside" or "countrysides".

entry_json.definition: one of the areas that a country such as Britain or the United States is divided into for local government
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Funding for schools varies sharply from one county to another.
example_sentences: She grew up in a small village in a rural county in the north.
The county council is responsible for maintaining these roads.

contexts.text: Funding for schools varies sharply from one county to another.
My family has lived in the same county for four generations.

confusables.difference: A country is a nation. A county is an administrative area inside one. One letter changes the meaning completely, and examiners notice.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use county for a nation state; that is country.

entry_json.definition: the ability to do something dangerous or difficult even though you are afraid
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes real courage to move to a country where you know nobody.
example_sentences: She never found the courage to tell her manager she was leaving.
The rescue team showed extraordinary courage during the floods.
collocations: have the courage to do something

contexts.text: It takes real courage to move to a country where you know nobody.
Reform of this kind requires political courage rather than new funding.

confusables.difference: Confidence is believing you can do it. Courage is doing it although you are afraid. A shy person can act with courage without confidence.
Brave is the adjective for the person; courage is the noun for the quality. Say "she was brave" or "she showed courage", never "she was courage".

entry_json.avoid: Courage is uncountable: not "a courage" or "courages".

entry_json.definition: a place where legal cases are decided by a judge, or a marked area where a sport such as tennis is played
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The case went to court and took two years to settle.
example_sentences: There are four tennis courts behind the sports centre.
The company was taken to court over the way it disposed of waste.

contexts.text: The case went to court and took two years to settle.
We book a court on Sunday mornings when it is cheaper.

confusables.difference: In British English football and cricket are played on a pitch; tennis, basketball and badminton on a court.
The court is the institution or the room; the trial is the process that happens in it.

entry_json.avoid: In the legal sense, the fixed phrases drop the article: go to court, appear in court, not "go to the court".

entry_json.definition: having something over or on the surface, or having a roof
entry_json.own_context_sentence: By March the fields were still covered with snow.
