entry_json.definition: the outside limit of an object, surface or area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: New housing keeps appearing on the edge of the city while the centre empties.
example_sentences: She sat on the edge of the desk while she explained the task.
Careful editing gives one application the edge over another.

contexts.text: New housing keeps appearing on the edge of the city while the centre empties.
We live right on the edge of town, so the countryside starts at the end of our road.

confusables.difference: A border is the official line between countries or regions. An edge is the physical limit of any object or area.

entry_json.avoid: Use on the edge of, not "in the edge of".

entry_json.definition: to prepare a piece of writing, film or recording by correcting it and deciding what to include
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning to edit my own writing improved my marks more than learning new words did.
example_sentences: She edits the department newsletter in her own time.
The footage was edited down from six hours to twenty minutes.

contexts.text: Learning to edit my own writing improved my marks more than learning new words did.
The footage was edited down from six hours to twenty minutes.

confusables.difference: Correct only fixes mistakes. Edit also cuts, reorders and reshapes, so a well-edited text may have had nothing wrong with it.

entry_json.avoid: Edit does not double the t: edited, editing.

entry_json.definition: one of the printings of a book or newspaper, or one broadcast of a regular programme
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Check that you are using the third edition, because the chapter numbering changed.
example_sentences: The paperback edition costs half as much as the hardback.
The evening edition carried a longer version of the story.

contexts.text: Check that you are using the third edition, because the chapter numbering changed.
The revised edition includes data collected after 2018.

confusables.difference: A version can differ in content or language and applies to software, songs and stories. An edition is a specific printing or issue of a published work.
A copy is one physical book; an edition is the whole batch printed with the same content.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse edition with addition; they sound similar but mean entirely different things.

entry_json.definition: a person who prepares written work or film for publication, or who is in charge of a newspaper
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A good editor removes a third of your words and improves the argument.
example_sentences: She worked as an editor at a small publishing house.
The letter was addressed to the editor of the local paper.

contexts.text: A good editor removes a third of your words and improves the argument.
Letters to the editor remain one of the few open channels for public complaint.

confusables.difference: The author writes the text. The editor shapes and corrects what somebody else wrote.
The publisher is the company that produces and sells the book; the editor is a person who works on the text.

entry_json.avoid: Editor has -or, not -er, at the end.

entry_json.definition: to teach somebody over a period of time, especially at a school or college, or to give people information about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Campaigns that educate the public about recycling work better than fines.
example_sentences: She was educated at a state school in the north of the city.
Educating girls has a measurable effect on a country's health statistics.

contexts.text: Educating girls has a measurable effect on a country's health statistics.
I was educated at a state school in the north of the city.

confusables.difference: Teach is what happens in a single lesson or on a single subject. Educate covers a whole formal process over years, or informing a whole population.
Train is about practical skills for a job; educate is broader and includes knowledge and thinking.

entry_json.avoid: Use be educated at a school and educated in a subject, not "educated from a school".

entry_json.definition: having received education, especially to a high level
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A well-educated workforce attracts investment more reliably than low taxes do.
example_sentences: The population is far better educated than it was two generations ago.
I can only make an educated guess about next year's figures.

contexts.text: A well-educated workforce attracts investment more reliably than low taxes do.
I can only make an educated guess about next year's figures.

confusables.difference: Intelligent is natural ability. Educated is the result of schooling, and the two do not always go together.
Clever is informal praise for quick thinking; educated is a statement about qualifications and training.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate before a noun: a well-educated workforce, but the workforce is well educated.

entry_json.definition: connected with education, or providing something useful to learn
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Educational opportunities still depend heavily on where a child happens to be born.
example_sentences: The museum runs educational programmes for local schools.
The trip was genuinely educational rather than just a day out.

contexts.text: Educational opportunities still depend heavily on where a child happens to be born.
The trip was genuinely educational rather than just a day out.

confusables.difference: Academic means connected with study and research, and often contrasts with practical. Educational simply means concerning education or teaching you something.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is education; do not write "the educational of children".

entry_json.definition: producing the result that was intended
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Congestion charges have proved more effective than appeals to drivers' conscience.
example_sentences: Regular short revision sessions are more effective than one long one.
The treatment is effective in most cases if it is started early.

contexts.text: Congestion charges have proved more effective than appeals to drivers' conscience.
Regular short revision sessions are more effective than one long one.

confusables.difference: Effective asks whether it works. Efficient asks whether it works without wasting time or money. A bulldozer is an effective way to open a tin but not an efficient one.

entry_json.avoid: Use effective in doing something or effective at doing something, not "effective to do".

entry_json.definition: in a way that produces the intended result; or used to say what the real situation amounts to
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Money spent early is used more effectively than money spent after the damage is done.
example_sentences: The department manages its budget effectively despite the cuts.
Removing the last bus effectively cuts the village off after seven o'clock.

contexts.text: Removing the last bus effectively cuts the village off after seven o'clock.
I learned to manage my time more effectively during my final year.

confusables.difference: Efficiently means with little waste of time or resources. Effectively means the aim was achieved. A team can work efficiently on the wrong task.
The second sense of effectively is close to in effect. If your reader might expect the well sense, use in effect to be unambiguous.

entry_json.avoid: The two senses can clash: "the rule effectively bans cycling" means in practice, not successfully. Rephrase if the context is unclear.

entry_json.definition: doing something well without wasting time, money or energy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: An efficient rail network takes more cars off the road than any advertising campaign.
example_sentences: Modern boilers are far more efficient than those installed in the 1990s.
She is a quiet but extremely efficient administrator.

contexts.text: Modern boilers are far more efficient than those installed in the 1990s.
She is a quiet but extremely efficient administrator.

confusables.difference: Effective means it achieves the aim; efficient means it achieves it cheaply or quickly. Say which one you mean, because the two can point in opposite directions.
Productive is about how much is produced; efficient is about the ratio of output to input.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is efficiency, not "efficientness". Do not use efficient of a person to mean skilled; it suggests they waste no time, which is not the same.

entry_json.definition: physical or mental energy needed to do something, or an attempt to do it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a language takes sustained effort rather than occasional bursts of enthusiasm.
example_sentences: She made a real effort to speak to everyone in the room.
Efforts to reduce waste have had only limited success so far.

contexts.text: Efforts to reduce waste have had only limited success so far.
She made a real effort to speak to everyone in the room.

confusables.difference: An attempt is one try at achieving something. Effort is the energy involved, and can be uncountable: it took a lot of effort.

entry_json.avoid: Use make an effort, not "do an effort". The pattern is an effort to do something, not "an effort of doing".

entry_json.definition: old, used as a polite way of describing older people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Elderly residents are the group most affected when a local bus route is cut.
example_sentences: The building has no lift, which is difficult for elderly visitors.

contexts.text: Elderly residents are the group most affected when a local bus route is cut.
An elderly neighbour looks after our cat when we are away.

confusables.difference: Old is blunt and can sound rude about a person. Elderly is the polite alternative, but it is only used of people, never of objects.

entry_json.avoid: Never use elderly for things: an elderly building is wrong, and an elderly car is a joke.

entry_json.definition: to choose somebody for a position by voting

Members of the council are elected every four years.

contexts.text: Members of the council are elected every four years.
She was elected chair of the student committee last term.

confusables.difference: Choose is any selection by anyone. Elect specifically means selected by a formal vote.

entry_json.avoid: No article before the role: "she was elected president", not "elected the president".

entry_json.definition: an occasion when people vote to choose somebody for an official position
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Turnout at local elections is far lower than at national ones.
example_sentences: The election is expected to take place in the spring.
Compulsory voting raises turnout but does not necessarily improve the result.

contexts.text: Turnout at local elections is far lower than at national ones.
The election is expected to take place in the spring.

confusables.difference: A vote is what one person casts, or a single decision. An election is the whole event in which many people vote.

entry_json.definition: one necessary part of something; also a basic chemical substance
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Trust is the one element of a good workplace that money cannot buy.

There is an element of risk in any investment.

contexts.text: There is an element of risk in any investment.
The course has a strong practical element as well as lectures.

confusables.difference: A factor influences a result. An element is a component part of a whole. Cost is a factor in a decision, but a module is an element of a course.

entry_json.definition: in, at or to some other place

Many learners are too embarrassed to ask the speaker to repeat something.

entry_json.definition: making you feel shy, awkward or ashamed

The mistake was embarrassing for the company rather than dangerous.

entry_json.definition: to come out from somewhere and become visible, or to become known

She emerged from the interview looking far more relaxed than she went in.

entry_json.definition: a sudden serious situation that needs immediate action

Every student should know where the emergency exits are.

In an emergency, knowing basic first aid matters more than owning a first aid kit.

entry_json.definition: a strong feeling such as love, fear or anger

Children need help naming their emotions before they can manage them.

entry_json.definition: connected with feelings, or showing strong feelings

The debate became emotional rather than factual.

Leaving the country was an emotional moment for the whole family.

entry_json.definition: special importance given to something; or extra force given to a word when speaking

entry_json.definition: to give special importance to something, or to say something with extra force
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report emphasizes that the fall in numbers began before the policy changed.

entry_json.definition: the state of having a paid job, or the situation of work in general
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employment in manufacturing has fallen steadily while service jobs have grown.

entry_json.definition: to make it possible for somebody to do something

entry_json.definition: to meet with something, especially a problem, or to meet somebody unexpectedly

entry_json.definition: to give somebody support or confidence to do something, or to make something more likely to happen

Low interest rates encourage borrowing.

contexts.text: Safe cycle lanes encourage far more people to leave the car at home than advertising does.
My teacher encouraged me to apply, and I am glad she did.

confusables.difference: Persuade means you succeeded in changing their mind. Encourage says nothing about whether they acted; it only describes the support given.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is encourage somebody to do something. "Encourage somebody doing" is wrong.

entry_json.definition: a person who hates you or opposes you, or a country you are at war with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Boredom is the real enemy of independent study, not difficulty.

The two countries were enemies for most of the last century.

contexts.text: The two countries were enemies for most of the last century.
Boredom is the real enemy of independent study, not difficulty.

confusables.difference: An opponent competes against you in a game, an election or a debate, without hatred. An enemy wishes you harm.

entry_json.definition: to take part in something, or to attract and hold somebody's interest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Lessons that engage students in real problems produce better recall than lectures.

The course really engaged me because everything had a practical use.

entry_json.definition: having agreed to marry somebody; or busy and involved in something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister got engaged last summer and is getting married next spring.
example_sentences: They were engaged for two years before the wedding.
Students who are actively engaged in the lesson remember far more of it.

Students who are actively engaged in the lesson remember far more of it.

entry_json.definition: the work of designing and building machines, roads, bridges and other structures
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I chose civil engineering because I wanted to see what I had built.

contexts.text: Engineering graduates are in short supply in several countries.
I chose civil engineering because I wanted to see what I had built.

confusables.difference: The engineer is the person; engineering is the field. "I study engineer" is a very common error for "I study engineering".

entry_json.definition: a question asked in order to get information; or an official investigation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I made an enquiry about the evening course but never received a reply.
example_sentences: All enquiries should be sent to the address below.

contexts.text: All enquiries should be sent to the address below.
I made an enquiry about the evening course but never received a reply.

confusables.difference: British English traditionally uses enquiry for a question and inquiry for a formal investigation; American English uses inquiry for both. Pick one system and hold to it.

entry_json.definition: to make certain that something happens or is the case
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments must ensure that new housing is built near transport, not far from it.
example_sentences: Check the seal to ensure that no water can get in.
The system is designed to ensure equal access for all applicants.

contexts.text: Governments must ensure that new housing is built near transport, not far from it.
I set two alarms to ensure I do not sleep through the exam.

entry_json.avoid: In a To what extent question, answer with a position such as to a large extent; do not ignore the phrase and simply agree or disagree.

entry_json.definition: connected with the outside of something, or coming from outside an organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fall in sales had external causes that no amount of better management could prevent.

The external walls need repointing before winter.

contexts.text: The fall in sales had external causes that no amount of better management could prevent.
An external examiner reviews a sample of every year's scripts.

confusables.difference: The direct opposite, and the pair is useful in analysis: internal factors are within the organisation's control, external ones are not.
Outside is the everyday word and works as preposition, adverb and adjective. External is the formal adjective used in reports.

entry_json.definition: very unusual or remarkable, far beyond what is normal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The speed at which the vaccine was developed was extraordinary by any historical measure.

It is extraordinary that so little was done after the first warning.

contexts.text: The speed at which the vaccine was developed was extraordinary by any historical measure.
She showed extraordinary patience with a very difficult class.

confusables.difference: Special means chosen or different for a purpose. Extraordinary means so far outside the normal range that it surprises people.
Unusual only means rare. Extraordinary adds that it is remarkable, and is much stronger.

entry_json.avoid: British pronunciation compresses the middle: ik-STROR-din-ree, not ex-tra-OR-din-ary.

entry_json.definition: a building, service or piece of equipment provided for a particular purpose

The sports facilities at my university were better than the teaching, honestly.

confusables.difference: Equipment is the tools and machines and is uncountable. A facility is the place or service that houses them, and is countable.

entry_json.definition: a lack of success, or the fact of not doing something you were expected to do

contexts.text: The failure to build enough homes over thirty years explains most of the current shortage.
My first attempt was a failure, but I learned more from it than from the second.

confusables.difference: A mistake is a wrong action or choice. A failure is not achieving the aim, which may follow from a mistake or from bad luck.
Defeat means an opponent beat you; failure needs no opponent at all.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is failure to do something, not "failure of doing".

entry_json.definition: to some degree but not very; also in a just and reasonable way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The results are fairly consistent across all four regions.

contexts.text: The results are fairly consistent across all four regions.
The exam was fairly straightforward, though the last section was long.

confusables.difference: In British English, quite before a gradable adjective is close to fairly but can also mean completely before an absolute one, as in quite impossible. Fairly is never absolute.

entry_json.avoid: Fairly only modifies gradable adjectives and adverbs. It cannot modify a verb: not "I fairly agree".

entry_json.definition: strong trust in somebody or something; or a religion, or belief in a religion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public faith in official statistics falls whenever figures are revised without explanation.

People of every faith use the community centre.

contexts.text: Public faith in official statistics falls whenever figures are revised without explanation.
She has enormous faith in her students' ability to improve.

confusables.difference: Trust is usually based on evidence or experience. Faith can be held without proof, which is why it suits both religion and confidence in people.

entry_json.definition: well known to you, or having a good knowledge of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The pattern will be familiar to anyone who has watched a town centre decline.
example_sentences: I am not familiar with that software, but I could learn it.
Her face looked familiar, though I could not place her.

contexts.text: The pattern will be familiar to anyone who has watched a town centre decline.
I am not familiar with that software, but I could learn it.

confusables.difference: Familiar means already known to you. Similar means alike. Learners often write "my job is familiar to hers" when they mean similar.

entry_json.definition: to want something or want to do something; used mainly in informal British English
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I fancy a walk before it gets dark, if anyone wants to come.
example_sentences: Do you fancy going to the exhibition on Saturday?

contexts.text: Do you fancy going to the exhibition on Saturday?
I did not fancy the long journey, so I stayed at home.

confusables.difference: Would like is the neutral form usable anywhere. Fancy is informal, British and spoken, so it fits Speaking Part 1 but not Task 2.

entry_json.definition: extremely interesting, in a way that holds your full attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I found the section on how cities are mapped absolutely fascinating.
example_sentences: The documentary on ocean currents was fascinating from start to finish.
It is fascinating how differently the same data can be presented.

contexts.text: I found the section on how cities are mapped absolutely fascinating.
It is fascinating how differently the same data can be presented.

confusables.difference: Interesting is mild and can sound like faint praise. Fascinating is much stronger and is a useful upgrade in Speaking.
Fascinating is the thing; fascinated is you. "I am fascinating" claims you fascinate others.

entry_json.avoid: Fascinating is already extreme, so avoid "very fascinating"; use absolutely fascinating.

entry_json.definition: popular or considered stylish at a particular time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It has become fashionable to blame technology for problems that existed long before it.
example_sentences: That part of the city has become fashionable and expensive within a decade.
Fashionable clothes lose their value the moment the season changes.

contexts.text: It has become fashionable to blame technology for problems that existed long before it.
That part of the city has become fashionable and expensive within a decade.

confusables.difference: Popular means liked by many people and can last for generations. Fashionable means liked right now, with the suggestion that it will pass.
Modern means of the present era. Fashionable is about taste and can apply to a revived old style.

entry_json.avoid: Saying an argument is fashionable implies it is shallow; be sure that is your meaning.

entry_json.definition: to close or join something firmly, or to attach one thing to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Passengers are asked to fasten their seat belts before the aircraft moves.
example_sentences: Fasten the strap tightly or the bag will slip off.
The shelves are fastened to the wall with heavy brackets.

contexts.text: Passengers are asked to fasten their seat belts before the aircraft moves.
Fasten the strap tightly or the bag will slip off.

confusables.difference: Tie uses string or laces and makes a knot. Fasten covers any secure closing, including buttons, clips and belts.
Close just means shut; fasten means shut and secured so it cannot open by itself.

entry_json.avoid: The t is silent: FAH-sn. The opposite is unfasten, not "defasten".

entry_json.definition: responsibility for something wrong; or something wrong with a machine or a person's character
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The delay was nobody's fault, but somebody had to explain it to the passengers.
example_sentences: There is a fault in the heating system that nobody has traced.
It was my own fault for leaving the application until the last day.

contexts.text: There is a fault in the heating system that nobody has traced.
It was my own fault for leaving the application until the last day.

confusables.difference: A mistake is the wrong action itself. Fault is the blame for it, which is why we say "I made a mistake" but "it was my fault".
Defect is the formal technical word for something wrong in a manufactured product; fault is the everyday one.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say "I have fault"; say it was my fault, or I made a mistake.

entry_json.definition: a helpful act you do for somebody; or approval and support for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most residents are in favour of pedestrianising the high street.
example_sentences: Could you do me a favour and check these figures?
Opinion has shifted in favour of later school start times.

contexts.text: Most residents are in favour of pedestrianising the high street.
Could you do me a favour and check these figures?

confusables.difference: Favour is the British spelling; favor is American. Use whichever variety you have chosen, consistently.
Support is the general noun for backing something. In favour of is the fixed phrase for taking a side in an argument.

entry_json.avoid: The essay phrase is in favour of, not "in favour to". Use do somebody a favour, not "make a favour".

entry_json.definition: one of the light soft parts that cover a bird's body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Feathers keep birds warm and dry as well as allowing them to fly.
example_sentences: The children collected feathers along the shore.
Down feathers are still used in cheap winter jackets.

contexts.text: Feathers keep birds warm and dry as well as allowing them to fly.
The children collected feathers along the shore.

confusables.difference: Fur covers mammals; feathers cover birds. Fur is uncountable, feathers countable.

entry_json.avoid: The vowel is short: FEH-thuh, not FEE-thuh.

entry_json.definition: an amount of money paid for professional services or to join something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tuition fees rose again, and applications from mature students fell the same year.
example_sentences: The gym charges a monthly fee with no long contract.
Legal fees can easily exceed the value of the dispute.

contexts.text: Tuition fees rose again, and applications from mature students fell the same year.
The gym charges a monthly fee with no long contract.

confusables.difference: Price is what you pay for goods. A fee is what you pay for a service, membership or professional work.
A fare is specifically the price of a journey by bus, train or taxi.

entry_json.avoid: You pay a fee and an organisation charges one; do not write "pay a price for the course" when you mean tuition fees.

entry_json.definition: comments about how well or badly somebody is doing, intended to help them improve
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Detailed feedback within a week does more for progress than a grade a month later.
example_sentences: We received positive feedback from almost every participant.
Ask for feedback on your writing before you submit it.

contexts.text: Detailed feedback within a week does more for progress than a grade a month later.
Ask for feedback on your writing before you submit it.

confusables.difference: Criticism points out what is wrong. Feedback is neutral and includes praise, which is why organisations ask for feedback rather than criticism.
An opinion is a personal view on anything. Feedback is a response to somebody's specific work or performance.

entry_json.avoid: Feedback is uncountable: not "a feedback" or "feedbacks". Say some feedback or a piece of feedback.

entry_json.definition: used to describe somebody who is in the same situation or group as you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I learned as much from fellow students as from the lectures themselves.
example_sentences: She discussed the problem with a fellow researcher.
Fellow passengers helped him carry the bags off the train.

contexts.text: I learned as much from fellow students as from the lectures themselves.
Fellow passengers helped him carry the bags off the train.

confusables.difference: A colleague is a noun and means somebody you work with. Fellow is an adjective placed before a noun: a fellow teacher.
As a noun, fellow is a dated informal word for a man, or a senior academic post. Do not mix that sense in.

entry_json.avoid: Fellow as an adjective always needs a noun after it: fellow students, not "my fellows" in the student sense.

entry_json.definition: a structure of wood, wire or metal that surrounds a piece of land
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A low fence separates the playground from the main road.
example_sentences: The garden fence blew down in the first storm of the winter.
Wildlife corridors are useless if fences cut across them.

contexts.text: Wildlife corridors are useless if fences cut across them.
The garden fence blew down in the first storm of the winter.

confusables.difference: A wall is solid, of brick or stone. A fence is lighter, often with gaps, and made of wood, wire or metal.
A hedge is a line of living bushes doing the same job as a fence.

entry_json.avoid: Sit on the fence is an idiom meaning to avoid choosing a side; do not use it literally in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: the act of fighting, especially violence between groups or in a war
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fighting broke out again after the talks collapsed.
example_sentences: The fighting displaced thousands of families within a fortnight.

contexts.text: The fighting displaced thousands of families within a fortnight.
Fighting between rival groups of supporters closed the stadium for a season.

confusables.difference: A war is the whole declared conflict. Fighting is the physical violence itself, and can happen without a war.
An argument is verbal disagreement. Fighting in this noun sense is physical.

entry_json.avoid: Fighting is uncountable: not "fightings". Use the fighting when referring to a specific conflict.

entry_json.definition: a collection of information stored on a computer, or a folder holding papers
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keep a backup of every file somewhere other than the machine you work on.
example_sentences: The file was too large to send by email.
Patient files are now stored electronically rather than on paper.

contexts.text: Patient files are now stored electronically rather than on paper.
The file was too large to send by email.

confusables.difference: A folder contains files. On a computer the distinction is exact, and mixing them up makes instructions impossible to follow.
A document is text you read; a file is any stored item, including images and programs.

entry_json.avoid: File as a verb means to store officially or to submit, as in file a complaint; keep that sense separate.

entry_json.definition: money used to run a business or a project, or the management of large amounts of money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The project stalled because finance could not be secured in time.

Public finances have been under pressure since the last recession.

contexts.text: Public finances have been under pressure since the last recession.
She works in finance and travels most weeks.

confusables.difference: Funding is money given for a specific purpose, often by a government or a grant body. Finance is the broader field and includes borrowing and investment.

entry_json.avoid: Singular finance means money or the field; plural finances means somebody's financial situation. Choose deliberately.

entry_json.definition: connected with money and how it is managed

example_sentences: The charity offers financial support to families in difficulty.
The financial year runs from April to March in the United Kingdom.

contexts.text: Financial pressure is the main reason students give for dropping out.
The charity offers financial support to families in difficulty.

confusables.difference: Economic concerns a whole economy: growth, trade, employment. Financial concerns money itself: budgets, loans, payments.
Monetary is a technical term about currency and interest rates, used mainly of central bank policy.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write "financial crisis" when you mean an individual's money problems; that is financial difficulties.

entry_json.definition: information or a conclusion that research or an official investigation produces
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main finding is that class size matters less than teacher experience.

contexts.text: These findings contradict earlier work on the same population.
The main finding is that class size matters less than teacher experience.

entry_json.definition: a business company, especially a small or professional one

contexts.text: Small firms create most of the new jobs but attract the least support.
She joined a law firm straight after graduating.

confusables.difference: Company is the general word and covers any size. Firm suggests a partnership or a professional practice, such as law or accountancy.

entry_json.definition: the state of being physically healthy and strong

example_sentences: Regular walking is enough to maintain basic fitness for most adults.
Fitness levels among schoolchildren have fallen over the past twenty years.

contexts.text: Fitness levels among schoolchildren have fallen over the past twenty years.
Cycling to work improved my fitness more than a gym membership ever did.

confusables.difference: Health covers whether you are ill or well, including mental health. Fitness is specifically physical capability: how far you can run or lift.

entry_json.avoid: Fitness is uncountable: not "a fitness". Fitness also means suitability, as in fitness for purpose.

entry_json.definition: staying the same and not able to be changed; or firmly attached in one place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rent on a fixed contract cannot rise mid-year, which makes budgeting far easier.
example_sentences: The course has fixed start dates in September and January.

The course has fixed start dates in September and January.

confusables.difference: Fixed as a past participle can mean repaired, but as an adjective before a noun it means unchanging. A fixed price is not a repaired price.

entry_json.avoid: Context has to separate the two senses; if there is any risk of confusion, write set or unchanging instead.

entry_json.definition: a piece of cloth with a pattern on it, used as the symbol of a country or organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flags were flying outside every public building on the national holiday.
example_sentences: The national flag is raised at the start of the ceremony.
A red flag on the beach means it is unsafe to swim.

contexts.text: Flags were flying outside every public building on the national holiday.
A red flag on the beach means it is unsafe to swim.

confusables.difference: A banner carries a message or a slogan and is often carried in a march. A flag is a fixed symbol of a country or group.

entry_json.avoid: A red flag meaning a warning sign is idiomatic; in an essay say warning sign unless the context is literal.

entry_json.definition: a hot bright stream of burning gas that comes from something on fire
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The building was in flames before the first engine arrived.
example_sentences: Keep the flame low or the sauce will burn.
Flames from the wildfire were visible from the motorway.

contexts.text: Flames from the wildfire were visible from the motorway.
Keep the flame low or the sauce will burn.

confusables.difference: Fire is the whole burning event and is usually uncountable. A flame is one visible tongue of burning gas within it.

entry_json.avoid: The fixed phrases use the plural: in flames, burst into flames.

entry_json.definition: to shine brightly for a very short time, or to make a light do this
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A warning light flashes on the dashboard when the battery runs low.

contexts.text: A warning light flashes on the dashboard when the battery runs low.
The driver flashed his headlights to let us pull out.

confusables.difference: Shine is continuous light. Flash is brief and often repeated, which is why warning lights flash rather than shine.

entry_json.definition: able to change or be changed easily to suit a new situation; or able to bend without breaking
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flexible working hours help parents far more than an extra week of holiday.
example_sentences: The course is flexible enough to fit around a full-time job.

The course is flexible enough to fit around a full-time job.

entry_json.definition: to stay on the surface of a liquid, or to move slowly through air or water
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Plastic bottles float for years before they eventually break into fragments.
example_sentences: Ice floats because it is less dense than water.

contexts.text: Ice floats because it is less dense than water.
Leaves floated down the stream past the bridge.

confusables.difference: The direct opposite: things that float stay on the surface, things that sink go under.

entry_json.avoid: Float is intransitive in this sense: things float, but you do not "float something" unless you mean launch it.

entry_json.definition: a large amount of water covering land that is usually dry
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Building on flood plains guarantees that the next flood will be expensive.
example_sentences: The floods destroyed crops across the whole valley.
Flood defences were raised after the third serious event in a decade.

contexts.text: Building on flood plains guarantees that the next flood will be expensive.
The floods destroyed crops across the whole valley.

confusables.difference: A storm is violent weather. A flood is water on the ground, which a storm may cause but which can also come from a river or melting snow.

entry_json.avoid: The vowel is short, rhyming with blood, not with food.

entry_json.definition: fine powder made from grain, used to make bread, cakes and pasta
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A poor wheat harvest pushes up the price of flour within months.
example_sentences: Mix the flour and water until the dough comes together.
The bakery uses flour milled about ten miles away.

contexts.text: A poor wheat harvest pushes up the price of flour within months.
Mix the flour and water until the dough comes together.

confusables.difference: Flour and flower sound identical in British English. Flour is the baking powder; a flower grows on a plant. Only the spelling separates them.

entry_json.avoid: Flour is uncountable: say a bag of flour or some flour, never "a flour".

entry_json.definition: the steady movement of a liquid, or of people, traffic or information in one direction
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new junction was designed to improve the flow of traffic at rush hour.
example_sentences: The dam controls the flow of water into the valley below.
There is a constant flow of information between the two departments.

contexts.text: The dam controls the flow of water into the valley below.
The new junction was designed to improve the flow of traffic at rush hour.

confusables.difference: A current is a moving body of water or air with a direction of its own. Flow is the movement itself, and can be measured as a rate.

entry_json.avoid: Use the flow of something, not "the flow from", unless you are naming the source.

entry_json.definition: to bend something so that one part lies on top of another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fold the form in three and post it in the envelope provided.
example_sentences: She folded the map and put it in her pocket.
The chairs fold flat and stack against the wall.

contexts.text: Fold the form in three and post it in the envelope provided.
She folded the map and put it in her pocket.

confusables.difference: Bend curves something without necessarily bringing two parts together. Fold makes a crease and lays one part over another.

entry_json.avoid: Fold in half, not "fold on half". Fold up means to make smaller by folding; fold in the business sense means to close down.

entry_json.definition: designed so that it can be folded to take up less space
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A folding bike solves the problem of taking a bicycle onto a crowded train.
example_sentences: We keep a few folding chairs for when visitors come.
The folding table stores flat behind the door.

contexts.text: A folding bike solves the problem of taking a bicycle onto a crowded train.
We keep a few folding chairs for when visitors come.

confusables.difference: Folding describes the design: it can be folded. Folded describes the current state: it has been folded.

entry_json.avoid: Folding goes before the noun: a folding chair, not "the chair is folding".

entry_json.definition: physical strength or violence; or an influence that produces change; or an organised group such as the police
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economic forces, not government policy, emptied the mining towns.
example_sentences: The wind hit the coast with tremendous force.
The new rules come into force at the start of next month.

contexts.text: Economic forces, not government policy, emptied the mining towns.
The new rules come into force at the start of next month.

confusables.difference: Strength is the capacity a person or thing has. Force is that capacity in action, or the push actually applied.

entry_json.definition: for all future time; or, informally, for a very long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Once a species is gone it is gone forever, whatever is spent afterwards.
example_sentences: Nothing lasts forever, least of all a technology company's advantage.
The queue at the passport office took forever.

contexts.text: Once a species is gone it is gone forever, whatever is spent afterwards.
The queue at the passport office took forever.

confusables.difference: Permanently is the formal word for a lasting state and fits academic writing. Forever is warmer and slightly literary, and in the take forever sense it is informal.
Always means on every occasion. Forever means for unlimited time ahead, which is not the same.

entry_json.avoid: Take forever is an exaggeration and belongs in Speaking only.

entry_json.definition: to stop feeling angry with somebody for something they have done wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took years for the town to forgive the company for closing the plant without warning.
example_sentences: She forgave him almost immediately, which surprised everyone.
Voters rarely forgive a government that raises taxes after promising not to.

contexts.text: Voters rarely forgive a government that raises taxes after promising not to.
She forgave him almost immediately, which surprised everyone.

confusables.difference: Excuse means to accept a reason so that no blame attaches. Forgive accepts that there was blame and lets it go anyway.
Forgive and forget are different acts; you can forgive without forgetting.

entry_json.avoid: Irregular: forgive, forgave, forgiven. The pattern is forgive somebody for doing something.

entry_json.definition: that used to exist or hold a position in the past; or the first of two things mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The former factory is now a gallery, which has changed the whole district.
example_sentences: A former colleague of mine now runs the department.
Of the two proposals, the former is cheaper but the latter is more durable.

contexts.text: Of the two proposals, the former is cheaper but the latter is more durable.
A former colleague of mine now runs the department.

confusables.difference: Former means the first of two; latter means the second. They work only when exactly two things have been mentioned.
Previous means the one before this one in a sequence. Former means no longer holding the role at all.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use former and latter with three or more items; name them instead, or the reader loses track.

entry_json.definition: a very large amount of money; or chance and the way it affects your life
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Renting in the capital costs a fortune, which is why so many graduates share.
example_sentences: He made a fortune importing machinery in the 1980s.
By good fortune, the delay meant we caught a better connection.

contexts.text: Renting in the capital costs a fortune, which is why so many graduates share.
The family fortune was built on trade rather than land.

confusables.difference: Luck is the everyday word for chance. Fortune is more formal in that sense, and it also means great wealth, which luck never does.
Wealth is uncountable and describes the general state of being rich. A fortune is one specific large sum.

entry_json.avoid: Cost a fortune is informal exaggeration; in Task 2, write extremely expensive.

entry_json.definition: to start an organisation, institution or town that is intended to continue for a long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The charity was founded in 1953 by a group of returning nurses.
example_sentences: The company was founded by two engineering graduates.

contexts.text: The charity was founded in 1953 by a group of returning nurses.

entry_json.definition: a border that surrounds a picture or window, or the strong structure that supports a building or vehicle

The bicycle has an aluminium frame, so it is light enough to carry.

confusables.difference: Structure is the general word for how something is built. A frame is specifically the skeleton that carries the weight.

entry_json.avoid: A time frame is a period allowed for something; keep that phrase separate from the physical sense.

entry_json.definition: the right or ability to do what you want without being controlled

contexts.text: Freedom of movement between the two countries ended in 2021.
Working from home gave me freedom over my hours but far less contact with people.

confusables.difference: Independence is not depending on others, including financially. Freedom is not being restricted, which is a different thing: you can be free but dependent.

entry_json.definition: to become hard and solid because of cold, or to keep food very cold to preserve it; also to hold prices or pay at the same level

contexts.text: The council has frozen council tax for a second year.
Freezing food that would otherwise be thrown away cuts household waste sharply.

entry_json.definition: the rate at which something happens over a period of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The frequency of extreme weather events has increased in every decade since the 1970s.
example_sentences: Bus frequency was cut from every ten minutes to every twenty.
The table shows the frequency of each response by age group.

contexts.text: The frequency of extreme weather events has increased in every decade since the 1970s.
Bus frequency was cut from every ten minutes to every twenty.

confusables.difference: Number counts the total. Frequency measures how often per unit of time, so a rising number over a longer period may not mean rising frequency.

entry_json.avoid: Frequency is uncountable in this sense. Use the frequency of something, not "the frequency for".

entry_json.definition: often; many times over a period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Buses run frequently during the day but almost stop after eight in the evening.
example_sentences: This mistake occurs frequently in student writing.
The two words are frequently confused.

contexts.text: This mistake occurs frequently in student writing.
Buses run frequently during the day but almost stop after eight in the evening.

confusables.difference: Often is the everyday word and is normal in speech. Frequently is the formal equivalent and is better in an essay, though not more accurate.

entry_json.definition: a relationship between friends, or the state of being friends
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The friendships I made in my first year abroad have outlasted the course itself.

Online platforms make contact easy but do not necessarily create friendship.

contexts.text: Online platforms make contact easy but do not necessarily create friendship.
The friendships I made in my first year abroad have outlasted the course itself.

confusables.difference: Relationship covers any connection, including romantic ones and those between countries. Friendship is specifically between friends.

entry_json.avoid: Friendship can be countable or uncountable: a close friendship, but also the value of friendship in general.

entry_json.definition: to make somebody feel afraid
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Campaigns that frighten people into changing habits rarely work for long.
example_sentences: The noise of the fireworks frightened the dog.
High prices frighten off first-time buyers before they even view a property.

contexts.text: Campaigns that frighten people into changing habits rarely work for long.
The noise of the fireworks frightened the dog.

confusables.difference: Scare is the more informal everyday verb. Frighten is slightly more formal, and both take the person as the object.

entry_json.avoid: Frighten needs an object: "the film frightened me", not "I frightened" when you mean you were afraid.

entry_json.definition: feeling afraid

example_sentences: The children were frightened by the storm.
Many patients are frightened of asking their doctor too many questions.

contexts.text: Many patients are frightened of asking their doctor too many questions.
I was frightened of speaking in front of a class until I had to do it every week.

confusables.difference: Frightened is the person; frightening is the thing that causes the fear.
Afraid cannot go before a noun: an afraid child is wrong, a frightened child is right.

entry_json.avoid: Use frightened of a thing you fear generally, and frightened by a specific event that scared you.

entry_json.definition: making you feel afraid
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The speed at which the water rose was frightening even to people who had seen floods before.
example_sentences: It is frightening how quickly a small debt can grow.
The first week in a new country can be frightening as well as exciting.

contexts.text: It is frightening how quickly a small debt can grow.
The first week in a new country can be frightening as well as exciting.

confusables.difference: The -ing form describes the cause; the -ed form describes the person feeling it.
Terrifying is much stronger. Save it for genuine terror or it loses its force.

entry_json.avoid: "I am frightening" says you scare other people, not that you feel afraid.

entry_json.definition: kept very cold so that it is solid, or turned to ice
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Frozen vegetables often contain more nutrients than fresh ones that have travelled for days.
example_sentences: The lake was frozen solid for most of January.
We keep a few frozen meals for evenings when nobody wants to cook.

contexts.text: Frozen vegetables often contain more nutrients than fresh ones that have travelled for days.
We keep a few frozen meals for evenings when nobody wants to cook.

confusables.difference: Cold is a matter of degree. Frozen means below freezing point and turned solid, so "the soup is frozen" and "the soup is cold" are very different problems.

entry_json.avoid: In informal speech, "I am frozen" means very cold; do not use that in writing.

entry_json.definition: to cook something in hot oil or fat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Frying is quick, but grilling the same food uses far less oil.
example_sentences: Fry the onions gently for about five minutes.
Most street food in the city is fried rather than baked.

contexts.text: Most street food in the city is fried rather than baked.
Fry the onions gently for about five minutes.

confusables.difference: Grilling uses direct heat and no oil; frying uses hot oil in a pan. The health argument in Task 2 usually turns on exactly that difference.

entry_json.avoid: Spelling changes with the ending: fries, fried, frying.

entry_json.definition: any material burned to produce heat or power
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fuel costs make up nearly a third of what a haulage company spends.
example_sentences: Fossil fuels still supply most of the world's electricity.
The price of fuel rose sharply during the winter.

contexts.text: Fossil fuels still supply most of the world's electricity.
Fuel costs make up nearly a third of what a haulage company spends.

confusables.difference: Energy is the power produced; fuel is the material burned to produce it. Solar power involves energy but no fuel.

entry_json.avoid: Fuel is uncountable when you mean the substance; fuels in the plural means different types, as in fossil fuels.

entry_json.definition: completely; to the greatest possible degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The consequences of the change were not fully understood when it was approved.
example_sentences: The flat is fully furnished, so we brought almost nothing.
I fully accept that the data has limitations.

contexts.text: The consequences of the change were not fully understood when it was approved.
The flat is fully furnished, so we brought almost nothing.

confusables.difference: These overlap, but fully collocates with a set of participles such as fully aware, fully qualified, fully booked, where completely sounds odd.
Full is the adjective: a full cup. Fully is the adverb: fully booked. Do not write "full booked".

entry_json.avoid: Note the vowel: FOOL-i, not FYOO-li.

entry_json.definition: the special purpose or job of a person, a thing or a part of the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main function of a library today is providing space and access, not storing books.
example_sentences: The kidneys perform several functions at once.
This button has no obvious function, which is a design fault.

contexts.text: The main function of a library today is providing space and access, not storing books.
This button has no obvious function, which is a design fault.

confusables.difference: Purpose is the intention behind something, which a person supplies. Function is the job it actually performs, which can be described without knowing anyone's intention.
Role is used mainly of people and organisations within a system; function suits parts, organs and devices.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is the function of something, not "the function for". As a verb, function means to work properly.

entry_json.definition: an amount of money saved or made available for a particular purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A hardship fund allows students to stay on the course when something unexpected happens.
example_sentences: The school set up a fund to replace the science equipment.
Public funds should not be spent without a clear account of the benefits.

contexts.text: Public funds should not be spent without a clear account of the benefits.
The school set up a fund to replace the science equipment.

confusables.difference: A fund is the pot of money itself and is countable. Funding is the act or the supply of money and is uncountable.

entry_json.avoid: Singular a fund means one specific pot; plural funds often just means money in general.

entry_json.definition: forming the necessary base of something; central and essential rather than superficial
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a fundamental difference between reducing waste and simply moving it elsewhere.
example_sentences: Access to clean water is a fundamental right, not a service to be bought.
The reform involves a fundamental change to how schools are funded.

contexts.text: There is a fundamental difference between reducing waste and simply moving it elsewhere.
For me the fundamental problem is time, not motivation.

confusables.difference: Basic can mean simple or even inadequate. Fundamental means underlying and essential, with no suggestion of being simple.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is fundamental to, not "fundamental for".

entry_json.definition: money provided by a government or organisation for a particular purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Funding for adult education has fallen every year for a decade.
example_sentences: The research depends on funding from a single charity.
Schools in poorer areas receive extra funding per pupil.

contexts.text: Funding for adult education has fallen every year for a decade.
The research depends on funding from a single charity.

confusables.difference: Funding is uncountable and means the money supplied. A fund is one countable pot of money set aside.

entry_json.avoid: Funding is uncountable: not "fundings". Use funding for a purpose and funding from a source.

entry_json.definition: the soft thick hair covering many animals, or the skin used to make clothing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public opinion turned against fur long before any law was passed.
example_sentences: The cat's fur was thick enough to keep out the rain.
Several countries have banned fur farming outright.

contexts.text: Several countries have banned fur farming outright.
The cat's fur was thick enough to keep out the rain.

confusables.difference: Hair is the word for people and for individual strands. Fur is the whole coat on an animal, and is uncountable.
Fur covers mammals; feathers cover birds.

entry_json.avoid: Fur is uncountable: not "furs" unless you mean fur garments.

entry_json.definition: to obtain or achieve something useful, or to gradually get more of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Volunteering is one of the few ways to gain experience before you have any.
example_sentences: The party gained twelve seats at the last election.
She gained a great deal of confidence during her year abroad.

contexts.text: The party gained twelve seats at the last election.
Volunteering is one of the few ways to gain experience before you have any.

confusables.difference: Earn means receiving something in return for work, usually money. Gain is broader and covers experience, weight, speed and support.
Win requires a contest with an opponent. You gain a place at university, but you win a competition.

entry_json.avoid: Gain is transitive: "she gained experience", not "she gained" alone. Gain weight is neutral; put on weight is the spoken form.

entry_json.definition: an organised group of criminals, or a group of young people who spend time together and often cause trouble
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Youth centres are closed on cost grounds and gang membership rises soon afterwards.

Boys with nothing to do after school are the easiest for a gang to recruit.

contexts.text: Youth centres are closed on cost grounds and gang membership rises soon afterwards.
The police broke up a gang that had been stealing from building sites.

confusables.difference: Group is entirely neutral. Gang carries a strong suggestion of crime or trouble, so calling your friends a gang is informal and jokey at best.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use gang for a study group or a set of colleagues in formal writing; the negative sense dominates.

entry_json.definition: to come together in a group, or to bring things or information together from different places

Governments need to gather reliable evidence before changing the law.

entry_json.definition: in most cases, or when you consider something as a whole rather than in detail

The report is generally positive about the scheme, but it warns about the cost.

Rents in the suburbs are generally lower than in the centre.

The scheme is expected to generate enough revenue to pay for itself within a decade.

entry_json.avoid: 'Generation' is a countable noun: say 'the older generation' or 'older generations', never 'the older generation people'.

entry_json.definition: willing to give more money, time or help than is usual or expected; also, larger than expected in amount

The scholarship is generous enough to cover both fees and living costs.
Countries with generous parental leave tend to have higher birth rates.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'generous with' (time, money) or 'generous to' (a person), not 'generous for'.

entry_json.definition: a style or type of art, writing, film or music with its own recognisable features
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Science fiction is the one genre I never get tired of.

The essay examines how each genre shapes what readers expect.
Streaming services have made minority genres commercially viable.

confusables.difference: Style is how one artist or writer does things, and is personal. Genre is a category shared by many works, such as horror or jazz.

Doctors often recommend gentle exercise such as swimming for older patients.
The graph rises at a gentle rate until 2010 and then climbs sharply.

Please could you show this gentleman to the waiting room.

entry_json.definition: the spirit of a dead person that some people believe can be seen or felt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I don't believe in ghosts, but I still wouldn't sleep in that house.

entry_json.definition: extremely large, much bigger than other things of the same kind

The museum's giant model of the solar system takes up a whole hall.

Giant retailers can afford to sell below cost until small shops close.
There was a giant queue outside the exam hall.

confusables.difference: Huge is the safer written choice and simply means very big. Giant is more visual and slightly informal, and suits objects you can picture.

entry_json.definition: pleased and happy about something, usually about a particular event or piece of news
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I'm glad I chose the evening course, because the mornings were impossible.
example_sentences: She was glad to hear that her application had finally been accepted.
I'd be glad to help you practise before the speaking test.

contexts.text: I'm glad I chose the evening course, because the mornings were impossible.
I'd be glad to show you around if you ever visit.
We were all glad when the exams were finally over.

confusables.difference: Happy can describe a lasting state ('a happy childhood'); glad almost always reacts to one specific thing and cannot go before a noun.
Pleased is slightly more formal and often about satisfaction with a result. Glad is warmer and more personal.

entry_json.avoid: You cannot put 'glad' before a noun. Say 'a happy day', never 'a glad day'.

entry_json.definition: affecting or including the whole world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Climate change is a global problem that no single country can solve alone.

English has become the global language of academic publishing.

contexts.text: Climate change is a global problem that no single country can solve alone.
Working for a global company means answering emails at strange hours.
The chart compares global energy consumption in 1990 and 2020.

confusables.difference: International means between countries and implies borders being crossed. Global means the whole planet taken as one unit.
Worldwide is usually about reach or spread ('sold worldwide'). Global is more often used of systems, problems and markets.

entry_json.avoid: 'Global' has no plural and is not a noun. Write 'global issues', not 'the globals'.

entry_json.definition: a piece of clothing that covers the hand, with a separate part for each finger
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I never leave home in January without a pair of gloves.

contexts.text: I never leave home in January without a pair of gloves.
Staff are required to wear disposable gloves when handling food.
I lost one glove on the bus, which is somehow worse than losing both.

confusables.difference: A mitten keeps all four fingers together in one pocket; a glove has a separate sleeve for each finger.

entry_json.avoid: Gloves come in pairs: say 'a pair of gloves', not 'a gloves'.

entry_json.definition: things that are produced to be sold; products moved or traded, rather than services
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap imported goods have made it hard for local workshops to survive.
example_sentences: The port handles millions of tonnes of goods every year.
Electronic goods are the country's largest single export.

contexts.text: Cheap imported goods have made it hard for local workshops to survive.
The chart shows the value of goods exported between 2000 and 2015.
Deliveries of household goods have got much faster where I live.

entry_json.definition: to control and legally run a country or region; also, to control how something works or happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The party has governed the country for almost twenty years.
example_sentences: Strict rules govern how personal data may be stored and shared.

Strict rules govern how personal data may be stored and shared.
I think local councils should govern local matters, not central government.

confusables.difference: Rule suggests power held by one person or a small group, often without consent. Govern is neutral and suggests administration under law.

entry_json.avoid: 'Govern' is a verb; the noun is 'government'. Write 'the government decided', not 'the govern decided'.

entry_json.definition: to take hold of something suddenly and roughly; informally, to get something quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He grabbed his coat and ran for the last train.
example_sentences: Someone grabbed her bag as she was leaving the station.

contexts.text: He grabbed his coat and ran for the last train.
Shall we grab something to eat before the film?
A headline has about two seconds to grab a reader's attention.

confusables.difference: Take is neutral. Grab adds speed and force, and often a hint of rudeness or urgency.
You catch something moving through the air; you grab something that is still. 'Catch the ball', 'grab the rail'.

entry_json.definition: a mark showing the quality of a student's work, or a level in a scale of quality or rank
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I needed a good grade in maths to get onto the engineering course.

The wood is sold in three grades, and only the top one is used for flooring.

contexts.text: I needed a good grade in maths to get onto the engineering course.
Employers increasingly look beyond grades to what candidates can actually do.
Students are placed in classes according to the grade they achieved in the entrance test.

Accommodation is where a particular person stays, including hotels and student halls. Housing is the permanent supply of homes.

entry_json.avoid: 'Housing' is uncountable: write 'more housing', not 'more housings'.

entry_json.definition: funny, or intended to make people laugh, usually in a gentle rather than a loud way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The lecturer had a humorous way of explaining difficult ideas.
example_sentences: The advertisement takes a humorous approach to a serious health message.
She wrote a humorous account of her first month living abroad.

contexts.text: The lecturer had a humorous way of explaining difficult ideas.
I like humorous novels more than serious ones.
The campaign used a humorous tone to reach younger viewers.

confusables.difference: Funny is the everyday spoken word and can also mean strange. Humorous is more formal and only means amusing.
A humorist is a person who writes amusing things. Do not confuse the noun with the adjective.

entry_json.avoid: The spelling drops the 'u' of 'humour': it is 'humorous', not 'humourous'.

entry_json.definition: the quality of being amusing, or the ability to find things funny
entry_json.own_context_sentence: British humour relies heavily on understatement, which takes time to hear.
example_sentences: He kept his sense of humour even during the worst of the delays.
Humour rarely survives translation intact.

contexts.text: British humour relies heavily on understatement, which takes time to hear.
My father has a very dry sense of humour.
Humour is one of the hardest things to acquire in a second language.

confusables.difference: A joke is one thing you say to make people laugh. Humour is the whole quality or style.
'Good humour' can mean a cheerful mood, but this use is old-fashioned; 'mood' is the normal modern word.

entry_json.avoid: British spelling keeps the 'u': 'humour'. The adjective, however, is 'humorous' with no 'u'.

entry_json.definition: to chase and kill wild animals for food or sport; also to search hard for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Some communities still hunt for food rather than for sport.
example_sentences: Wolves hunt in packs, which lets them bring down much larger animals.
I spent the whole weekend hunting for a flat I could afford.

contexts.text: Wolves hunt in packs, which lets them bring down much larger animals.
I spent the whole weekend hunting for a flat I could afford.
Species that were hunted almost to extinction have slowly recovered.

confusables.difference: Chase is only the running after. Hunt includes tracking, waiting and killing, and can happen without any chase at all.
Search is the neutral word for looking. Hunt for something suggests long, determined effort.

entry_json.avoid: When it means looking for something, 'hunt' needs 'for': 'hunt for a job', not 'hunt a job'.

entry_json.definition: the activity of chasing and killing wild animals, for food or as a sport
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Hunting was banned in the national park in the 1990s.
example_sentences: Illegal hunting remains the main threat to the surviving population.
Hunting for sport divides opinion sharply in rural areas.

contexts.text: Illegal hunting remains the main threat to the surviving population.
Hunting for sport divides opinion sharply in rural areas.
Nobody in my family goes hunting, but it's common where my grandparents live.

confusables.difference: Poaching is hunting that breaks the law, on land you have no right to or of protected species. Hunting itself may be legal and regulated.

entry_json.avoid: 'Hunting' is uncountable and takes no article: 'hunting is banned', not 'the hunting is banned'.

entry_json.definition: a violent storm with extremely strong winds, forming over warm ocean water
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The hurricane destroyed thousands of homes along the coast.
example_sentences: Hurricanes are expected to become more intense as sea temperatures rise.
The islands were still rebuilding two years after the hurricane.

contexts.text: Hurricanes are expected to become more intense as sea temperatures rise.
The hurricane destroyed thousands of homes along the coast.
We were on holiday when a hurricane warning came through.

confusables.difference: A storm is any violent weather. A hurricane is a specific, named tropical system with sustained winds above a set speed.
The same kind of storm, but the word depends on the ocean: hurricane in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoon in the western Pacific.

entry_json.avoid: A hurricane 'hits' or 'strikes' a place. Do not write 'a hurricane happened'.

entry_json.definition: to do something or move more quickly than usual because there is not much time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had to hurry to catch the last bus after the class overran.
example_sentences: Don't hurry the answer; the examiner would rather hear you think.
She hurried through the airport with only minutes to spare.

contexts.text: I had to hurry to catch the last bus after the class overran.
Don't hurry the answer; the examiner would rather hear you think.
There's no hurry, so take your time reading the instructions.

confusables.difference: Rush is stronger and suggests panic or carelessness. Hurry is simply moving faster because time is short.
The phrasal verb is what you say to another person to make them go faster. Plain 'hurry' describes what you yourself do.

entry_json.avoid: 'In a hurry' is the fixed phrase. Do not write 'in hurry' or 'on a hurry'.

entry_json.definition: who or what somebody or something is; also the qualities and beliefs that make a person or group distinct
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Language is central to how a community keeps its identity.
example_sentences: Migrants often describe holding two identities at once.
You will need photographic identity documents to sit the exam.

contexts.text: Language is central to how a community keeps its identity.
Moving abroad made me think much harder about my own identity.
You will need photographic identity documents to sit the exam.

confusables.difference: Personality is the set of traits that make you behave as you do. Identity is who you understand yourself to be, including nationality, culture and role.
Identification is the act of recognising someone, or the document itself. Identity is the fact of who they are.

entry_json.avoid: 'Identity' is countable in the personal sense ('two identities') but takes no plural in fixed phrases like 'identity theft'.

entry_json.definition: to deliberately pay no attention to someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments cannot afford to ignore the warnings in the latest report.
example_sentences: He ignored the message and carried on working.
The design ignores the needs of anyone using a wheelchair.

contexts.text: Governments cannot afford to ignore the warnings in the latest report.
I tend to ignore notifications until the evening.
The design ignores the needs of anyone using a wheelchair.

confusables.difference: Ignoring is a choice not to respond to something you know about. Being ignorant of something means you simply do not know it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Ignore' does not mean 'not know'. Write 'I did not know the rule', not 'I ignored the rule', unless you knew it and chose to break it.

entry_json.definition: not allowed by law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parking on the pavement is illegal, but it happens on every street.
example_sentences: Illegal dumping of waste has increased since the tip closed.
Downloading the film without paying is illegal in most countries.

contexts.text: Parking on the pavement is illegal, but it happens on every street.
Illegal dumping of waste has increased since the tip closed.
The report distinguishes between illegal and merely unregulated practices.

confusables.difference: Unlawful is the more technical legal term and covers acts that break a rule without necessarily being a crime. Illegal is the everyday word for breaking the law.
A different word entirely: illegible means impossible to read. The similarity of the letters catches learners out.

entry_json.avoid: 'Illegal' describes acts and goods. Applying it to a person ('an illegal') is offensive; write 'an undocumented migrant'.

entry_json.definition: to make something clearer by giving an example; also to add pictures to a text
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This case illustrates how quickly a small problem can grow.
example_sentences: The graph illustrates the relationship between income and life expectancy.
The book is illustrated with photographs taken by the author.

contexts.text: The graph illustrates the relationship between income and life expectancy.
This case illustrates how quickly a small problem can grow.
I'll illustrate what I mean with something that happened last year.

confusables.difference: Show is the plain word for presenting information. Illustrate means showing it in a way that makes an idea easier to grasp, usually through an example.
