contexts.text: Deciding when to stop revising is a matter of judgement, not rules.
The court delivered its judgement three months after the hearing.
I trust her judgement more than my own on things like this.

confusables.difference: An opinion can be formed instantly and needs no evidence. Judgement implies weighing things up carefully first.
A decision is the choice you make. Judgement is the quality of thinking that leads to it.

entry_json.avoid: British English spells it 'judgement' outside law and 'judgment' in legal contexts; either is accepted in IELTS, but stay consistent.

entry_json.definition: low in rank or position within an organisation; also for younger people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Junior staff are given very little say in how the department is run.
example_sentences: She started as a junior analyst and now leads the team.
The club runs junior sessions on Saturday mornings.

contexts.text: Junior staff are given very little say in how the department is run.
She started as a junior analyst and now leads the team.
I played in the junior team until I was sixteen.

confusables.difference: The opposite: senior means higher in rank and usually older or more experienced.
Younger is only about age. Junior is about position, and a junior colleague can easily be the older person.

entry_json.avoid: In British English 'junior school' means primary years, not secondary. Do not use it for a university year.

entry_json.definition: fair treatment of people, and the system by which the law is applied
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Access to justice depends heavily on whether you can afford a lawyer.
example_sentences: The families waited twenty years for justice.
The criminal justice system is under severe pressure.

contexts.text: Access to justice depends heavily on whether you can afford a lawyer.
The criminal justice system is under severe pressure.
I think fairness matters more than punishment when we talk about justice.

confusables.difference: The law is the set of rules. Justice is the fairness those rules are supposed to deliver. A law can be legal and unjust at the same time, which is often the point of an essay.
Fairness is the everyday quality of treating people evenly. Justice is the formal, institutional version of it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Justice' is uncountable in this sense: write 'access to justice', not 'a justice'.

entry_json.definition: to give a good reason for something that others might think is wrong or unreasonable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is hard to justify building another car park in a city trying to cut emissions.
example_sentences: The results do not justify the cost of the programme.
Candidates must justify their answers with evidence from the text.

contexts.text: It is hard to justify building another car park in a city trying to cut emissions.
The results do not justify the cost of the programme.
I had to justify the extra expense to my manager.

confusables.difference: Explain says why something happened. Justify argues that it was right. An explanation is not a defence.
An excuse asks to be forgiven for something admitted to be wrong. Justifying claims it was not wrong at all.

entry_json.avoid: 'Justify' is followed by a noun or -ing form: 'justify spending more', not 'justify to spend more'.

entry_json.definition: very interested in doing something or enthusiastic about it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I'm keen to improve my speaking before I apply for a job abroad.
example_sentences: She is a keen cyclist and rides thirty miles most weekends.
The company is keen on hiring people with practical experience.

contexts.text: I'm keen to improve my speaking before I apply for a job abroad.
She is a keen cyclist and rides thirty miles most weekends.
The department is keen to attract students from a wider range of backgrounds.

confusables.difference: Enthusiastic is more formal and works in written English. Keen is very British and mainly spoken, though 'keen to' appears in formal writing too.
Interested is passive: you want to know more. Keen is active: you want to do it.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'keen on' plus a noun or -ing form, and 'keen to' plus a verb. 'Keen for doing' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: the set of keys used to type on a computer, or a musical instrument with keys
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I type much faster on a full keyboard than on a phone screen.
example_sentences: The keyboard on the library computers is missing several letters.
He plays keyboards in a band at weekends.

contexts.text: I type much faster on a full keyboard than on a phone screen.
Students who learn on a keyboard rather than by hand may remember less.
The keyboard on the library computers is missing several letters.

confusables.difference: A keypad is a small set of keys, usually numbers, on a phone or a door lock. A keyboard has the full alphabet.
A piano is a specific instrument with strings and hammers. A keyboard in music means an electronic one.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'type on a keyboard', not 'type in a keyboard'.

entry_json.definition: to hit someone or something with your foot
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He kicked the ball straight over the fence and into the road.
example_sentences: Someone had kicked the door until the lock gave way.
The horse kicked out when the vet came near.

contexts.text: He kicked the ball straight over the fence and into the road.
Someone had kicked the door until the lock gave way.
I used to kick a ball around with my brother every evening.

confusables.difference: Hit is with any part of the body or an object. Kick is specifically with the foot.
The phrasal verb means to start, especially a match or an event. It is informal and should stay out of essays.

entry_json.avoid: 'Kick' needs a direct object. To describe the action alone, add 'out' or 'at': 'kicked out', 'kicked at the wall'.

entry_json.definition: an act of causing someone's death deliberately
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The killing of large predators has upset the balance of the whole ecosystem.
example_sentences: Police are treating the killing as suspicious.
The killing of elephants for ivory has fallen but not stopped.

contexts.text: The killing of large predators has upset the balance of the whole ecosystem.
Police are treating the killing as suspicious.
The killing of elephants for ivory has fallen but not stopped.

confusables.difference: Murder is the legal term for deliberately killing a person unlawfully. Killing is broader and covers animals, war and lawful deaths.
Death is the event of dying, from any cause. Killing says someone or something caused it deliberately.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the noun with the informal adjective in 'a killing pace'. In an essay, use the noun only.

entry_json.definition: to touch someone with your lips as a greeting or to show affection
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In some countries people kiss both cheeks when they meet.
example_sentences: She kissed her son goodbye at the school gate.
Greeting customs vary: some cultures kiss, others bow, others shake hands.

contexts.text: In some countries people kiss both cheeks when they meet.
She kissed her son goodbye at the school gate.
Greeting customs vary: some cultures kiss, others bow, others shake hands.

confusables.difference: A hug uses the arms; a kiss uses the lips. Both are greetings in some cultures and intimate in others, so describe carefully.
Greet is the neutral verb for any welcome. Use it in writing unless the physical act itself is the point.

entry_json.avoid: 'Kiss' takes a direct object: 'she kissed him', not 'she kissed to him'.

entry_json.definition: a piece of paper or plastic on an object giving information about it; also a word used to describe someone or something, often unfairly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The label lists every ingredient, but the print is too small to read.
example_sentences: Clothes labels tell you where the item was made.
Once a child is given the label 'difficult', it is very hard to remove.

contexts.text: The label lists every ingredient, but the print is too small to read.
I always check the label to see how much sugar is in something.
Once a child is given the label 'difficult', it is very hard to remove.

confusables.difference: A tag hangs off an item, often with a price. A label is usually stuck or sewn on and carries information.
A brand is the company name and reputation. The label is the physical piece of paper, though 'label' is also used for a record company.

entry_json.avoid: The verb doubles the l in British English: 'labelled', 'labelling'.

entry_json.definition: work, especially hard physical work; also the workers of a country considered as a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap labour was the main reason the factories moved abroad.
example_sentences: The construction industry faces a serious shortage of skilled labour.
Machines have replaced manual labour in most of these processes.

contexts.text: Cheap labour was the main reason the factories moved abroad.
The construction industry faces a serious shortage of skilled labour.
My grandfather did manual labour all his life and never complained.

confusables.difference: Work is the general word and is used of individuals. Labour is an economic term for effort as a resource, and is more abstract.
American spelling. In IELTS use the British 'labour', and keep spelling consistent across the whole answer.

entry_json.avoid: 'Labour' in this sense is uncountable and has no plural. Capitalised, 'Labour' is a British political party.

entry_json.definition: the state of not having something, or of not having enough of it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A lack of affordable childcare keeps many parents out of work.
example_sentences: The main obstacle is a lack of funding rather than a lack of ideas.
Poor results were blamed on a lack of teaching staff.

contexts.text: A lack of affordable childcare keeps many parents out of work.
The main obstacle is a lack of funding rather than a lack of ideas.
My biggest problem was a lack of speaking practice.

confusables.difference: A shortage means there is some but not enough, and is usually temporary. A lack can mean there is none at all.
Absence is neutral and simply notes that something is not there. Lack implies it ought to be there and is missed.

entry_json.avoid: The noun needs 'of': 'a lack of time'. The verb takes no preposition: 'the plan lacks detail', not 'lacks of detail'.

entry_json.definition: everything you can see when you look across an area of land; also the general situation in a field of activity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The landscape changes completely once you cross the mountains.
example_sentences: Wind turbines have altered the landscape of much of the north.
The digital landscape has changed beyond recognition in ten years.

contexts.text: Wind turbines have altered the landscape of much of the north.
The landscape changes completely once you cross the mountains.
The digital landscape has changed beyond recognition in ten years.

confusables.difference: Scenery is what a place looks like as an experience for the viewer, and is uncountable. Landscape is the land itself and can be counted and studied.
Environment covers the whole natural system, including air and water. Landscape is only what the land looks like.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'landscape' for a city view; that is 'a cityscape' or simply 'the skyline'.

entry_json.definition: mostly, or to a great extent
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The improvement is largely due to better public transport rather than to the charge.
example_sentences: The scheme has been largely successful, though costs ran over.
Rural areas were largely unaffected by the changes.

contexts.text: The improvement is largely due to better public transport rather than to the charge.
Rural areas were largely unaffected by the changes.
My decision was largely about money, if I'm honest.

confusables.difference: Mainly points to the biggest part of a group or activity. Largely points to the degree to which something is true, and is common with 'due to' and 'because of'.
Mostly is more conversational. Largely is the better choice in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: 'Largely' has nothing to do with size. Do not write 'the building is largely' meaning it is big.

entry_json.definition: the most recent, newest in a series
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The latest figures show a small fall in unemployment.
example_sentences: Her latest book is much shorter than the previous one.
The latest models use about a third less fuel.

contexts.text: The latest figures show a small fall in unemployment.
The latest models use about a third less fuel.
I try not to buy the latest phone every year.

confusables.difference: Last means final, with nothing after it. Latest means most recent so far, with more expected. 'Her last book' can imply she has died or stopped writing.
Newest compares age directly. Latest places something in a sequence of releases or reports.

entry_json.avoid: 'At the latest' means no later than a stated time: 'send it by Friday at the latest'.

entry_json.definition: to start something new such as a product, campaign or investigation; also to send a ship or rocket off
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council launched a campaign to cut single-use plastic in schools.
example_sentences: The company launched the service in three cities before going national.
An inquiry was launched within days of the report appearing.

contexts.text: The council launched a campaign to cut single-use plastic in schools.
The company launched the service in three cities before going national.
They launched the new timetable without telling passengers properly.

confusables.difference: Start is the plain verb for beginning anything. Launch implies a public beginning with some effort behind it, so it suits products and campaigns.
Introduce is used for rules, laws and policies that come into force. Launch is for things offered to the public.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'launch' for personal beginnings. 'I launched my degree' is wrong; use 'began' or 'started'.

entry_json.definition: to put something down carefully in a flat position
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They laid new cycle paths along both sides of the river.
example_sentences: She laid the papers on the desk and left without a word.
Workers laid the foundations before the winter set in.

contexts.text: They laid new cycle paths along both sides of the river.
She laid the papers on the desk and left without a word.
I lay the table while my father cooks.

confusables.difference: Lay always needs an object ('lay the book down'); lie does not ('lie on the sofa'). The confusion worsens because 'lay' is also the past tense of 'lie'.
Put is general. Lay implies placing something down flat and carefully, often across a surface.

entry_json.avoid: The past of 'lay' is 'laid'. The past of 'lie' is 'lay'. 'I laid down for an hour' is a very common error; the correct form is 'I lay down'.

entry_json.definition: a quantity of something spread over a surface, with other things above or below it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A thin layer of ice made the pavements dangerous.
example_sentences: The ozone layer protects the surface from harmful radiation.
Wearing several thin layers is warmer than one thick coat.

contexts.text: The ozone layer protects the surface from harmful radiation.
A thin layer of ice made the pavements dangerous.
Wearing several thin layers is warmer than one thick coat.

confusables.difference: A level is a position on a scale, usually vertical and measurable. A layer is physical material covering a surface.
A coat is one covering of paint or similar, applied deliberately. A layer can form naturally and can be one of many.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'a layer of' something. Do not write 'a layer with dust'.

entry_json.definition: the ability to lead a group well, or the people who run an organisation or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The turnaround was credited to strong leadership rather than extra funding.
example_sentences: Poor leadership was identified as the main cause of the failure.
The party's leadership has changed three times in five years.

contexts.text: The turnaround was credited to strong leadership rather than extra funding.
Poor leadership was identified as the main cause of the failure.
The best manager I had was good at leadership without being loud about it.

confusables.difference: Management is running systems, budgets and processes. Leadership is about direction and getting people to follow it. An organisation can be well managed and badly led.
The leader is one person. Leadership is either the quality or the whole group at the top.

entry_json.avoid: 'Leadership' is uncountable in the quality sense: 'strong leadership', not 'a strong leadership'.

entry_json.definition: most important, most successful or in first place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The country is now a leading exporter of solar equipment.
example_sentences: Smoking remains the leading cause of preventable death.
She is a leading researcher in the field.

contexts.text: Smoking remains the leading cause of preventable death.
The country is now a leading exporter of solar equipment.
My town has one of the leading football clubs in the region.

confusables.difference: Main means the biggest or most central and can apply to anything. Leading suggests a ranking against competitors.
First is a position in order or time. Leading is about importance or success, not sequence.

entry_json.avoid: 'Leading' goes before a noun. You cannot write 'this company is leading'; use 'is a leading company' or 'is in the lead'.

entry_json.definition: a flat green part of a plant that grows from a stem or branch
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The leaves turn a deep red here for about two weeks each autumn.
example_sentences: Trees lose their leaves earlier when the summer has been dry.
A single leaf can tell a botanist which species the tree is.

contexts.text: Trees lose their leaves earlier when the summer has been dry.
The leaves turn a deep red here for about two weeks each autumn.
Fallen leaves block the drains every October.

confusables.difference: 'Leaves' is the plural of 'leaf' and also a form of the verb 'leave'. Context separates them, but the spelling trips learners up.
A branch is the woody arm of the tree. Leaves grow from it.

entry_json.avoid: The plural changes the spelling: one leaf, many leaves.

entry_json.definition: a group of sports teams that compete against each other over a season; also a group of people or countries working together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Our local team was promoted to the second league last season.
example_sentences: The league has expanded to twenty clubs.
She is simply in a different league from the rest of the field.

contexts.text: Our local team was promoted to the second league last season.
The league has expanded to twenty clubs.
University league tables influence where students apply, for better or worse.

confusables.difference: A tournament is a short competition, often knockout, decided in days or weeks. A league runs across a whole season with everyone playing everyone.
A team is one group of players. A league is all the teams together plus the competition between them.

entry_json.avoid: 'A league table' in British English means any published ranking, including of schools and hospitals, not only sport.

entry_json.definition: to bend from an upright position, or to rest against something for support
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She leaned against the wall while she waited for the bus.
example_sentences: Do not lean out of the window when the train is moving.
The old tower leans noticeably to one side.

contexts.text: She leaned against the wall while she waited for the bus.
Do not lean out of the window when the train is moving.
The old tower leans noticeably to one side.

confusables.difference: Bend usually means the body or an object curves at a joint. Lean means the whole thing tilts from vertical.
Figuratively 'lean on someone' means to depend on them for support. That sense is informal; in an essay use 'rely on' or 'depend on'.

entry_json.avoid: As an adjective, 'lean' means thin with little fat ('lean meat'). Do not confuse the two uses.

entry_json.definition: material made from animal skin, used for shoes, bags and furniture
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A good pair of leather boots will outlast three cheap pairs.
example_sentences: The bag is real leather, which is why it cost so much.
Producing leather uses large amounts of water and chemicals.

contexts.text: A good pair of leather boots will outlast three cheap pairs.
Producing leather uses large amounts of water and chemicals.
The bag is real leather, which is why it cost so much.

confusables.difference: Fur keeps the animal's hair; leather is the treated skin with the hair removed.
Suede is leather with a soft brushed surface. Calling suede 'leather' is not wrong, but the reverse is.

entry_json.avoid: 'Leather' is uncountable: 'a leather jacket', not 'a leathers jacket'.

entry_json.definition: allowed by law, or connected with the law
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling on the pavement is not legal, though it is rarely punished.
example_sentences: The company took legal action against its former supplier.
Anyone signing the contract should take legal advice first.

contexts.text: The company took legal action against its former supplier.
Cycling on the pavement is not legal, though it is rarely punished.
I had to get legal advice about my tenancy agreement.

confusables.difference: Direct opposite: not allowed by law. Watch the prefix, which is easy to lose when typing quickly.
Lawful is more formal and stresses conformity with a particular law. Legal is the everyday word and also means 'to do with law' ('legal advice').

entry_json.avoid: 'Legal' can mean both 'permitted' and 'relating to law'. 'Legal problems' means problems with the law, not permitted problems.

entry_json.definition: time when you are not working and can do what you enjoy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People have more leisure time than a century ago but feel busier.
example_sentences: The council is building a new leisure centre on the old industrial site.
Most leisure activities in the town cost money, which excludes some families.

contexts.text: People have more leisure time than a century ago but feel busier.
The council is building a new leisure centre on the old industrial site.
I spend most of my leisure time reading or walking.

confusables.difference: Free time is the ordinary spoken phrase and is always safe. Leisure is more formal and appears in survey and policy language.
A hobby is one particular activity you pursue. Leisure is the time and the whole category of activities.

entry_json.avoid: 'Leisure' is uncountable and usually used before another noun: 'leisure time', not 'a leisure'.

entry_json.definition: how long something is from end to end, or how long something lasts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The length of the working week has barely changed in thirty years.
example_sentences: The bridge is nearly two kilometres in length.
Essays are marked on quality, not on length.

contexts.text: The bridge is nearly two kilometres in length.
The length of the working week has barely changed in thirty years.
The length of the journey put me off going more often.

confusables.difference: Length is the noun and 'long' the adjective. Write 'two metres in length' or 'two metres long', not 'two metres length'.
Distance is the space between two separate points. Length is the measurement of one object from one end to the other.

entry_json.avoid: 'At length' means either 'for a long time' or 'finally'. It does not mean 'in length'.

entry_json.definition: an official document giving permission to do, own or use something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You need a licence to drive anything larger than a van.
example_sentences: The restaurant lost its licence after repeated hygiene failures.
A television licence is still required in the United Kingdom.

contexts.text: You need a licence to drive anything larger than a van.
The restaurant lost its licence after repeated hygiene failures.
I got my driving licence a year later than most of my friends.

confusables.difference: In British English the noun is 'licence' and the verb is 'license'. A pub is licensed and holds a licence. American English uses 'license' for both.
A permit is usually for a specific limited activity or place, like parking. A licence covers an ongoing right, like driving or selling alcohol.

entry_json.avoid: British spelling: 'a driving licence'. Using 'license' as the noun is an American form and may be marked in a British-standard answer.

entry_json.definition: the greatest or smallest amount of something that is allowed or possible
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The speed limit outside schools was reduced to twenty miles per hour.
example_sentences: There is a strict word limit on the essay.
Everyone has a limit to how much they can concentrate in one sitting.

contexts.text: The speed limit outside schools was reduced to twenty miles per hour.
There is a strict word limit on the essay.
I set myself a limit of an hour a day on social media.

confusables.difference: A boundary is a line marking where one area or responsibility ends. A limit is a maximum amount, usually a number.
A restriction is a rule that stops you doing something at all. A limit allows the thing but caps how much.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'a limit on' something, or 'a limit to' what is possible. 'A limit of' takes the number: 'a limit of 250 words'.

entry_json.definition: small in amount or extent, and not able to be increased
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Places on the course are limited, so early application matters.
example_sentences: The study is useful but its sample size is very limited.
Public transport in rural areas is extremely limited.

contexts.text: The study is useful but its sample size is very limited.
Public transport in rural areas is extremely limited.
I had pretty limited English when I arrived.

confusables.difference: Little is a plain quantity word. Limited implies a boundary imposed by circumstances, so it explains as well as describes.
Restricted means access is controlled by a rule. Limited means there simply is not much of it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Limited' is a diplomatic way of saying 'not enough'. It is useful in Task 2 for criticising politely.

entry_json.definition: one of the two soft edges of the mouth
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dry air left my lips cracked within a day.
example_sentences: Reading lips becomes essential when a room is very noisy.
She bit her lip rather than say what she was thinking.

contexts.text: The dry air left my lips cracked within a day.
Reading lips becomes essential when a room is very noisy.
She bit her lip rather than say what she was thinking.

confusables.difference: The mouth is the whole opening including the tongue and teeth. The lips are only the outer edges.
Different word, close vowel sound for many learners: 'leap' means to jump. Keep the short vowel in 'lip'.

entry_json.avoid: In pronunciation work, 'lip rounding' describes how the lips shape vowels; that is a technical use, not general vocabulary.

entry_json.definition: a substance that flows freely, such as water or oil, and is neither a solid nor a gas
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bottle contains a clear liquid that turns blue when heated.
example_sentences: Passengers may not carry liquids over 100 millilitres in hand luggage.
Patients recovering from surgery are given liquids before solid food.

contexts.text: Passengers may not carry liquids over 100 millilitres in hand luggage.
The diagram shows the substance changing from a solid to a liquid.
The bottle contains a clear liquid that turns blue when heated.

confusables.difference: Fluid is the scientific term and includes gases as well as liquids. In everyday speech 'fluids' means drinks: 'drink plenty of fluids'.
Water is one particular liquid. Do not use the two words interchangeably in a process description.

entry_json.avoid: 'Liquid' can be countable ('carry liquids') or uncountable ('in liquid form'). Both are correct in the right context.

entry_json.definition: novels, plays and poetry considered as art; also all the published writing on a subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reading literature in a second language builds vocabulary faster than textbooks do.
example_sentences: She studied English literature before training as a teacher.
The existing literature on the topic is surprisingly thin.

contexts.text: She studied English literature before training as a teacher.
The existing literature on the topic is surprisingly thin.
I've always preferred literature to history at school.

confusables.difference: Books is the plain plural for physical objects. Literature is the art form, or the whole body of research on a topic.
Fiction means invented stories. Literature includes poetry and drama, and can include non-fiction of high quality.

entry_json.avoid: 'Literature' is uncountable: 'a great deal of literature', never 'many literatures'.

entry_json.definition: full of energy and activity, or full of interest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The market on Saturday mornings is the liveliest place in town.
example_sentences: The seminar produced a lively discussion that ran over time.
She is a lively speaker who keeps the whole room awake.

contexts.text: The seminar produced a lively discussion that ran over time.
The market on Saturday mornings is the liveliest place in town.
The area became noticeably more lively after the new cafes opened.

confusables.difference: Alive means not dead. Lively means energetic. Calling a person 'alive' when you mean 'lively' says something very odd.
Busy is about quantity of activity, and can be stressful. Lively is positive and about energy and atmosphere.

entry_json.avoid: 'Lively' ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb. The adverb form is 'in a lively way'.

entry_json.definition: the money you earn to support yourself; also the way you live
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He makes a living translating documents from home.
example_sentences: The cost of living has risen faster than wages for a decade.
It is increasingly hard to earn a living from farming alone.

contexts.text: The cost of living has risen faster than wages for a decade.
He makes a living translating documents from home.
It is increasingly hard to earn a living from farming alone.

confusables.difference: Life is existence itself. Living in this sense is how you pay for it: 'What do you do for a living?'
A salary is a fixed amount from one employer. A living is whatever total you manage to earn, from any source.

entry_json.avoid: 'What do you do for a living?' is the fixed question. Do not write 'for a life'.

entry_json.definition: something heavy that is carried, or the amount of work or pressure something has to bear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The teaching load in the first year is heavier than most students expect.
example_sentences: Lorries carrying a heavy load are banned from the bridge.
Electric heating puts a much greater load on the grid in winter.

contexts.text: The teaching load in the first year is heavier than most students expect.
Electric heating puts a much greater load on the grid in winter.
I had to carry a heavy load up four flights of stairs.

confusables.difference: Weight is how heavy something is as a measurement. A load is the thing being carried, whatever it weighs.
A burden is always negative and often emotional or financial. A load is neutral and can be purely physical.

entry_json.avoid: 'Loads of' meaning 'a lot of' is informal spoken English. Keep it out of Task 2.

entry_json.definition: money that is borrowed and must be paid back, usually with interest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most graduates leave with a student loan that takes decades to clear.
example_sentences: The business took out a loan to buy new equipment.
Interest rates on personal loans have risen sharply.

contexts.text: Most graduates leave with a student loan that takes decades to clear.
The business took out a loan to buy new equipment.
I'm still paying off a loan from my first year of study.

confusables.difference: A loan must be repaid; a grant never is. This distinction decides whole arguments in essays about university funding.
'Loan' is the noun for the money. 'Lend' is the verb for giving it, and 'borrow' for receiving it. 'Can you borrow me some money?' is a very common error.

entry_json.avoid: You 'take out' or 'repay' a loan. Do not write 'do a loan' or 'make a loan' unless you are the bank.

entry_json.definition: to find the exact position of something, or to put something in a particular place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rescuers were able to locate the group within a few hours.
example_sentences: The company chose to locate its warehouse near the motorway.
I could not locate the file anywhere on the shared drive.

contexts.text: Rescuers were able to locate the group within a few hours.
The company chose to locate its warehouse near the motorway.
I couldn't locate the room and arrived ten minutes late.

confusables.difference: Find is the everyday word and covers accidents as well as searches. Locate is formal and implies a deliberate effort to fix a position.
The past participle is far more common than the active verb. 'The office is located in the centre' is the usual pattern.

entry_json.avoid: 'Locate' is formal. In speech 'find' sounds much more natural.

entry_json.definition: situated in a particular place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The campus is located about three kilometres from the city centre.
example_sentences: The new hospital will be located on the site of the old barracks.
Most of the factories were located close to the river.

contexts.text: The campus is located about three kilometres from the city centre.
Most of the factories were located close to the river.
My flat is located right above a bakery, which is both good and bad.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning. 'Situated' is slightly more formal and common in property descriptions; 'located' is more common in academic writing.
Placed suggests someone deliberately put it there recently. Located simply states where it is.

entry_json.avoid: Always use 'be located', never 'located' alone as a verb: 'the school is located near the park'.

entry_json.definition: the place where something is or where something happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The location of the new station will decide which suburbs benefit.
example_sentences: The hotel's location is its main advantage; the rooms are ordinary.
Filming took place on location in three different countries.

contexts.text: The location of the new station will decide which suburbs benefit.
The hotel's location is its main advantage; the rooms are ordinary.
The map shows the location of each recycling point in the district.

confusables.difference: Place is the general everyday word. Location is more precise and suits maps, planning and business decisions.
Position often means relative arrangement, or a job. Location is where something sits geographically.

entry_json.avoid: 'On location' is a film-making phrase meaning away from the studio. It does not mean 'in that place' generally.

entry_json.definition: reasonable and sensible; following correctly from what has been said
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving the deadline was the logical response to the delay.
example_sentences: The essay is well written but the argument is not logical.
It seems logical to test the idea in one district before extending it.

contexts.text: The essay is well written but the argument is not logical.
It seems logical to test the idea in one district before extending it.
Moving closer to work seemed like the logical thing to do.

confusables.difference: Reasonable means fair or moderate and involves judgement about people. Logical means the reasoning holds together, whether or not the result is fair.
'Logic' is the noun and 'logical' the adjective. 'His logic was logical' is a tangle; choose one.

entry_json.avoid: The negative is 'illogical', not 'unlogical'.

entry_json.definition: unhappy because you are alone or have no friends nearby; also of a place, far from others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving to a new city can be lonely for the first few months.
example_sentences: Older people living alone are especially at risk of feeling lonely.
The cottage stands on a lonely stretch of coast.

contexts.text: Older people living alone are especially at risk of feeling lonely.
Moving to a new city can be lonely for the first few months.
The cottage stands on a lonely stretch of coast.

confusables.difference: Alone describes the fact of having nobody with you, with no feeling attached. Lonely describes the unhappiness. You can be alone and perfectly content.
'Lonely' is the adjective; 'loneliness' is the noun. Essays about ageing usually need the noun.

entry_json.avoid: 'Lonely' ends in -ly but is an adjective. There is no adverb 'lonelily' in normal use.

entry_json.definition: continuing or having effects over a long period of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The long-term consequences of the policy will not be clear for a decade.
example_sentences: Long-term unemployment damages health as well as income.
Investment in education is a long-term solution, not a quick fix.

contexts.text: The long-term consequences of the policy will not be clear for a decade.
Long-term unemployment damages health as well as income.
I'm thinking about it as a long-term plan rather than something for this year.

confusables.difference: The opposite, and the natural partner in an essay: short-term costs versus long-term benefits.
Permanent means it will never end. Long-term means it lasts a long time but may still change.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate before a noun ('long-term effects') but not after a verb ('in the long term', 'this will last long term').

entry_json.definition: not firmly fixed in place, or not tight
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the handrails on the stairs is loose and needs fixing.
example_sentences: Loose clothing is more comfortable in hot climates.
The screw had worked loose over months of vibration.

contexts.text: One of the handrails on the stairs is loose and needs fixing.
Loose clothing is more comfortable in hot climates.
The report describes a loose connection between the two variables.

confusables.difference: Completely different word: 'lose' is a verb meaning to no longer have something, and rhymes with 'news'. 'Loose' rhymes with 'juice'. This is one of the most common spelling errors in English.
The direct opposite for clothing and fastenings.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'I don't want to loose marks'. That should be 'lose'.

entry_json.definition: a man of high rank in the British nobility, or his title; in religion, a name for God
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bill was debated at length in the House of Lords.
example_sentences: He was made a lord after leaving the government.
The estate belonged to the local lord for four hundred years.

contexts.text: The bill was debated at length in the House of Lords.
The estate belonged to the local lord for four hundred years.
We visited a house that once belonged to a lord, which was fascinating.

confusables.difference: A landlord rents property to tenants and has nothing to do with nobility, despite the shared root.
A king rules a country. A lord holds a rank below that, historically with land and local power.

entry_json.avoid: Capitalise it in titles and in the religious sense ('Lord Smith', 'the Lord'), lowercase for the general noun.

entry_json.definition: the fact of no longer having something, or the amount of money a business fails to make
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The loss of local shops has changed the character of the high street.
example_sentences: Habitat loss is the main driver of falling insect numbers.
The company reported a loss for the third year running.

contexts.text: Habitat loss is the main driver of falling insect numbers.
The company reported a loss for the third year running.
The loss of the old cinema was a real shame for the town.

confusables.difference: 'Loss' is the noun and 'lost' the past form of the verb. 'The lost of jobs' is wrong; it is 'the loss of jobs'.
Damage is harm to something that still exists. Loss means it is gone entirely.

entry_json.avoid: 'At a loss' means either selling below cost or being unable to think what to do. Both are idiomatic; keep the context clear.

entry_json.definition: to reduce something in amount, level or strength; to move something down
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The government lowered the voting age to sixteen for local elections.
example_sentences: Insulating homes lowers energy consumption immediately.
The bank lowered interest rates twice in the same year.

contexts.text: Insulating homes lowers energy consumption immediately.
The bank lowered interest rates twice in the same year.
I've lowered the amount I spend on eating out.

confusables.difference: Reduce is the standard verb for cutting an amount and is safest in essays. Lower suits levels, rates and standards, and things measured on a scale.
Fall is what a figure does by itself; lower is what someone does to it. 'Prices fell' has no agent; 'the shop lowered prices' does.

entry_json.avoid: 'Lower' as an adjective is the comparative of 'low'. Do not write 'more lower'.

entry_json.definition: one of the two organs in the chest used for breathing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air pollution damages children's lungs while they are still developing.
example_sentences: Smoking is the leading cause of lung disease.
The patient's lungs were badly affected by years of dust exposure.

contexts.text: Air pollution damages children's lungs while they are still developing.
Smoking is the leading cause of lung disease.
My grandfather had lung problems from working in the mines.

confusables.difference: The heart pumps blood; the lungs take in air. Keep them separate in any description of health.
Breath is the air you take in. The lungs are the organ that does it.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is 'lungs' with no change in spelling, and there are two, so 'her lungs' is usually right where 'her lung' would be odd.

entry_json.definition: something expensive and pleasant that you do not really need, or great comfort of that kind
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Owning a car in this city is a luxury rather than a necessity.
example_sentences: Air conditioning was once a luxury and is now standard.
Having time to read for pleasure feels like a luxury during term.

contexts.text: Owning a car in this city is a luxury rather than a necessity.
Having time to read for pleasure feels like a luxury during term.
Sales of luxury goods have grown even as average incomes stagnate.

confusables.difference: The natural opposite, and the pairing most essays need: what is a luxury for one household is a necessity for another.
Comfort is the ordinary absence of difficulty. Luxury goes beyond it, into what is expensive and unnecessary.

entry_json.avoid: 'Luxury' is countable when it means a particular item and uncountable when it means a state ('live in luxury').

entry_json.definition: very foolish, or very angry; in older or informal use, mentally ill
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It would be mad to drive when the train takes half the time.
example_sentences: My parents were mad at me for missing the deadline.
The traffic in the centre drives me mad.

contexts.text: It would be mad to drive when the train takes half the time.
The traffic in the centre drives me mad.
My parents were mad at me for missing the deadline.

confusables.difference: Angry is the neutral written word. 'Mad' meaning angry is informal and mainly American; in Britain it more often means foolish.
Both are informal. Neither belongs in Task 2, where 'unwise', 'irrational' or 'unreasonable' should be used instead.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'mad' to describe mental illness in an essay. It is offensive; write 'mental illness' or 'a mental health condition'.

entry_json.definition: the power to make impossible things happen, in stories and beliefs; also tricks performed as entertainment
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children believe in magic long after they have stopped believing in much else.
example_sentences: The show combines magic with comedy.
There is no magic that will make a language easy to learn.

contexts.text: Children believe in magic long after they have stopped believing in much else.
There is no magic that will make a language easy to learn.
The show combines magic with comedy.

confusables.difference: 'Magic' is mostly the noun; 'magical' is the adjective for something wonderful. 'A magical evening' is a compliment; 'a magic evening' is not standard.
A miracle is a single event believed to come from God. Magic is a power or a performance.

entry_json.avoid: 'Magic' is uncountable in the sense of power: 'believe in magic', not 'believe in a magic'.

entry_json.definition: more than anything else; for the most part
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course is mainly practical, with only two written assignments.
example_sentences: Visitors come mainly in July and August.
The decline was mainly the result of falling exports.

contexts.text: The course is mainly practical, with only two written assignments.
Visitors come mainly in July and August.
I chose the flat mainly because of the location.

confusables.difference: Largely is about degree and pairs naturally with 'due to'. Mainly points to the biggest part or the main reason among several.
Only excludes everything else. Mainly allows exceptions, so it is the safer word when your claim is not absolute.

entry_json.avoid: 'Mainly' goes before the main verb but after 'be': 'is mainly used', 'mainly consists of'.

entry_json.definition: to keep something at the same level or in good condition; also to state firmly that something is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is far cheaper to maintain a road than to rebuild it.
example_sentences: The country has maintained a stable birth rate for a decade.
He maintains that he was never told about the change.

contexts.text: It is far cheaper to maintain a road than to rebuild it.
The country has maintained a stable birth rate for a decade.
It's hard to maintain a routine when your shifts keep changing.

confusables.difference: Keep is the everyday verb and fits almost anywhere. Maintain is formal and implies deliberate effort to prevent decline.
Sustain suggests supporting something so it can continue, often against pressure. Maintain suggests keeping it as it is.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, 'the figure maintained a steady level' is fine, but 'remained steady' is more natural.

entry_json.definition: the larger number or part of a group; more than half
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The majority of students now work part-time during term.
example_sentences: A large majority voted in favour of the change.
In the vast majority of cases, the treatment works within a week.

contexts.text: The majority of students now work part-time during term.
In the vast majority of cases, the treatment works within a week.
The majority of people I know rent rather than own.

confusables.difference: Most is simpler and often better. 'The majority of' is three words where 'most' does the same job, so do not use it just to sound academic.
The smaller part, less than half. The two words together structure a great many Task 1 sentences.

entry_json.avoid: 'The majority of' is followed by a plural verb when the noun is plural: 'the majority of students are', not 'is'.

entry_json.definition: a large covered building containing many shops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The mall drew shoppers away from the old town centre within two years.
example_sentences: Teenagers meet at the mall because there is nowhere else free to go.
The mall has replaced the high street in many suburbs.

contexts.text: The mall drew shoppers away from the old town centre within two years.
Teenagers meet at the mall because there is nowhere else free to go.
There's a big mall near my house that I hardly ever visit.

confusables.difference: The usual British term. 'Mall' is American in origin and is understood everywhere, but 'shopping centre' is safer in a British-standard exam.
A market is open-air or in a hall, with independent stalls. A mall is enclosed and made up of shops.

entry_json.avoid: In British English prefer 'shopping centre' in writing; 'mall' is fine in speech.

entry_json.definition: the activity of running a business or organisation, or the people who do it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Poor management, not lack of demand, closed the factory.
example_sentences: The management has agreed to review the shift patterns.
Time management is the skill most new students are missing.

contexts.text: Poor management, not lack of demand, closed the factory.
Time management is the skill most new students are missing.
The management where I worked never listened to the staff.

confusables.difference: Management runs the systems day to day. Leadership sets the direction. Essays about organisations often need both, used precisely.
A manager is one person. Management is the activity, or the whole group of managers taken together.

entry_json.avoid: As a group of people, 'the management' takes either a singular or plural verb in British English; be consistent.

entry_json.definition: the activity of presenting and advertising a product so that people will buy it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Clever marketing persuaded people that bottled water was safer than tap water.
example_sentences: The company spends more on marketing than on research.
She works in marketing for a small publisher.

contexts.text: Clever marketing persuaded people that bottled water was safer than tap water.
The company spends more on marketing than on research.
She works in marketing for a small publisher.

confusables.difference: Advertising is one part of marketing: the paid messages themselves. Marketing also covers pricing, packaging and choosing who to sell to.
Sales is the act of actually selling to a customer. Marketing prepares the ground for it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Marketing' is uncountable and takes no article when it names the field: 'she works in marketing'.

entry_json.definition: the legal relationship between two people who are married, or the ceremony that begins it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The average age at first marriage has risen by almost a decade.
example_sentences: Marriage rates have fallen steadily since the 1970s.
Their marriage lasted more than fifty years.

contexts.text: The average age at first marriage has risen by almost a decade.
Marriage rates have fallen steadily since the 1970s.
My parents' marriage has lasted forty years, which impresses me.

confusables.difference: The wedding is the ceremony on one day. The marriage is the relationship that follows and may last decades.
'Marriage' is the noun and 'married' the adjective. 'They did a marriage' is wrong; use 'they got married'.

entry_json.avoid: In British English you 'get married to' someone, not 'marry with' them.

entry_json.definition: involving or affecting a very large number of people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Mass tourism has changed the economy of the whole coastline.
example_sentences: Mass production made clothing cheap enough to replace rather than repair.
The scheme relies on mass participation to work at all.

contexts.text: Mass tourism has changed the economy of the whole coastline.
Mass production made clothing cheap enough to replace rather than repair.
Mass transport is the only realistic answer for a city that size.

confusables.difference: Massive means very large in size. Mass as an adjective means involving very many people, and only appears before a noun.
Public means open to everyone or run by the state. Mass stresses the sheer number involved.

entry_json.avoid: 'Mass' as an adjective cannot follow a verb. Write 'mass production', never 'the production is mass'.

entry_json.definition: extremely large in size, amount or degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council faces a massive shortfall in its housing budget.
example_sentences: There has been a massive increase in online shopping since 2019.
The stadium is massive but rarely more than half full.

contexts.text: There has been a massive increase in online shopping since 2019.
The council faces a massive shortfall in its housing budget.
The queue outside was massive, so we gave up.

confusables.difference: Almost identical, though 'massive' is a little more informal in speech. In Task 1, 'substantial' or 'considerable' is more precise than either.
Different word class and meaning: 'mass' before a noun means involving many people.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, prefer 'substantial', 'sharp' or 'considerable' to 'massive', which reads as conversational exaggeration.

entry_json.definition: to learn something so well that you can do it without difficulty
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me two years to master the sounds that do not exist in my first language.
example_sentences: Nobody masters a language in six weeks, whatever the advertisement claims.
Once you have mastered the basic technique, the rest follows quickly.

contexts.text: It took me two years to master the sounds that do not exist in my first language.
Nobody masters a language in six weeks, whatever the advertisement claims.
Once you have mastered the basic technique, the rest follows quickly.

confusables.difference: Learn covers any level, including a first lesson. Master means reaching complete competence, so it claims far more.
Manage means you succeeded at one attempt, often with difficulty. Master means you can do it reliably from now on.

entry_json.avoid: 'Master' takes a direct object: 'master the technique', not 'master in the technique'.

entry_json.definition: having the same colour, pattern or design as something else, so that they go together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The room had matching curtains and cushions, which felt slightly too planned.
example_sentences: Staff wear matching uniforms so visitors can identify them.
The report includes matching figures for the previous year.

contexts.text: Staff wear matching uniforms so visitors can identify them.
The room had matching curtains and cushions, which felt slightly too planned.
The table gives matching figures for the same months in 2019.

confusables.difference: Similar means alike in some ways. Matching means designed to go together as a set, which is a stronger claim.
The same means identical. Matching things may differ in shape but share a colour or pattern.

entry_json.avoid: 'Matching' goes before a noun. After a verb use 'match': 'the colours match', not 'the colours are matching'.

entry_json.definition: as large or as much as is allowed or possible
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The maximum class size is thirty, though most groups are smaller.
example_sentences: The maximum temperature recorded that summer was 38 degrees.
There is a maximum penalty of two years for the offence.

contexts.text: The maximum temperature recorded that summer was 38 degrees.
The maximum class size is thirty, though most groups are smaller.
There's a maximum of two hours' free parking near my flat.

confusables.difference: The opposite: the smallest allowed. Task 1 answers often need both in the same sentence, so keep them straight.
'Most' is a general quantity word. 'Maximum' names a fixed limit, usually a number that is set by a rule.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is 'maxima' in technical writing but 'maximums' is accepted. Avoid the issue by writing 'the maximum figure'.

entry_json.definition: a method or way of doing something; also money available to spend
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For many households, the bicycle is the only affordable means of transport.
example_sentences: Email remains the main means of communication in most offices.
The family simply did not have the means to send both children to university.

contexts.text: For many households, the bicycle is the only affordable means of transport.
Email remains the main means of communication in most offices.
The family simply did not have the means to send both children to university.

confusables.difference: Way is the everyday word and fits speech. Means is formal and belongs in phrases like 'a means of transport'.
A method is a worked-out procedure with steps. A means is simply whatever gets you there.

entry_json.avoid: 'Means' has the same form singular and plural: 'one means of transport', 'several means of transport'. Never write 'a mean of transport'.

entry_json.definition: at the same time as something else, or in the period between two events
entry_json.own_context_sentence: House prices have doubled; wages, meanwhile, have barely moved.
example_sentences: The road will be closed for a year. Meanwhile, buses will follow a longer route.
Exports rose sharply. Imports, meanwhile, remained flat.

contexts.text: Exports rose sharply. Imports, meanwhile, remained flat.
House prices have doubled; wages, meanwhile, have barely moved.
The road will be closed for a year. Meanwhile, buses will follow a longer route.

confusables.difference: However signals contrast in argument. Meanwhile signals that two things happen in the same period, and only implies contrast.
'In the meantime' stresses the waiting period before something happens. 'Meanwhile' is more often used to compare two parallel trends.

entry_json.avoid: 'Meanwhile' is an adverb, not a conjunction. Do not join two clauses with it; use a semicolon or a full stop.

entry_json.definition: to find the size, amount or degree of something using an instrument or a standard
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is easy to measure attendance and very hard to measure learning.
example_sentences: Rainfall is measured at the same station every day.
The room measures four metres by three.

contexts.text: Rainfall is measured at the same station every day.
It is easy to measure attendance and very hard to measure learning.
I measure my progress by how much I understand without subtitles.

confusables.difference: Weigh is only about weight. Measure covers length, volume, temperature and abstract things like performance.
'Measure' is the verb; 'measurement' is the result you get. 'Take a measurement', not 'take a measure'.

entry_json.avoid: As a noun, 'measures' means actions taken by an authority ('safety measures'), which is a different sense entirely.

entry_json.definition: the size, length or amount of something, found by measuring; also the act of measuring
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Accurate measurement of air quality requires sensors across the whole city.
example_sentences: Take the measurements before you order the furniture.
The measurement of poverty depends heavily on where the line is drawn.

contexts.text: Accurate measurement of air quality requires sensors across the whole city.
The measurement of poverty depends heavily on where the line is drawn.
Take the measurements before you order the furniture.

confusables.difference: 'Measurement' is the number you obtain; 'measure' as a noun is an action taken to solve a problem. 'Government measures' are policies, not readings.
Size is a general impression or a category (small, medium, large). A measurement is an exact figure with a unit.

entry_json.avoid: You 'take' a measurement, not 'make' or 'do' one.

entry_json.definition: in the middle between two sizes, amounts or levels
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A medium-sized town has enough services without the congestion of a city.
example_sentences: The recipe calls for two medium onions.
Medium-term projections are more reliable than long-term ones.

contexts.text: A medium-sized town has enough services without the congestion of a city.
Medium-term projections are more reliable than long-term ones.
I usually order a medium coffee rather than a large one.

confusables.difference: Average is a calculated figure from a set of numbers. Medium is a rough category between small and large.
The plural noun 'media' means television, newspapers and the internet, and comes from the noun 'medium' meaning a channel. Different sense entirely.

entry_json.avoid: As a noun meaning a channel of communication, the plural is 'media'. As a clothing size the plural is 'mediums'.

entry_json.definition: to change from solid to liquid because of heat, or to make something do this
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The glaciers are melting far faster than the earlier models predicted.
example_sentences: Snow melts within hours at this time of year.
Heat the pan gently until the butter melts.

contexts.text: The glaciers are melting far faster than the earlier models predicted.
The diagram shows the ice melting and the water draining away.
Heat the pan gently until the butter melts.

confusables.difference: Something dissolves when it disappears into a liquid, like sugar in tea. It melts when heat alone turns it into liquid.
The opposite process: liquid becomes solid. Process diagrams often need both verbs in sequence.

entry_json.avoid: 'Melt' can be used with or without an object: 'the ice melted' and 'the sun melted the ice' are both correct.

entry_json.definition: connected with the mind or with thinking, rather than the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Mental health services were the first thing cut when budgets tightened.
example_sentences: Long hours affect physical and mental wellbeing alike.
She made a mental note of the platform number.

contexts.text: Mental health services were the first thing cut when budgets tightened.
Long hours affect physical and mental wellbeing alike.
Exercise helps my mental state more than anything else does.

confusables.difference: The standard pairing: physical health concerns the body, mental health the mind. Essays about wellbeing usually need both.
The adverb: 'mentally exhausting'. Do not write 'mental exhausting'.

entry_json.avoid: In informal British speech 'mental' can mean crazy, which is offensive in a health context. In writing keep it to 'mental health'.

entry_json.definition: a dirty or untidy state, or a situation that is confused and badly handled
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The kitchen was in a complete mess after the party.
example_sentences: The timetable change was a mess and nobody knew which bus to take.
Make a mess in the laboratory and you clean it up yourself.

contexts.text: The kitchen was in a complete mess after the party.
The timetable change was a mess and nobody knew which bus to take.
Make a mess in the laboratory and you clean it up yourself.

confusables.difference: Chaos is complete disorder on a large scale and is fine in writing. A mess is smaller and more informal.
Different word: 'mass' means a large quantity or number. The vowel and the meaning both differ.

entry_json.avoid: 'Mess' is conversational. In Task 2 use 'poorly managed', 'disorganised' or 'chaotic' instead.

entry_json.definition: not severe or extreme; of weather, warmer than usual for the season
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Winters here are mild, so heavy snow is rare.
example_sentences: Most patients experience only mild side effects.
The curry was surprisingly mild for something described as hot.

contexts.text: Winters here are mild, so heavy snow is rare.
Most patients experience only mild side effects.
The curry was surprisingly mild for something described as hot.

confusables.difference: Warm describes an actual temperature that feels pleasant. Mild says it is less cold or less severe than expected.
The opposite for illness and weather. 'Mild symptoms' versus 'severe symptoms' is a useful pair in health writing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Mild' is a comparison with the norm. Calling a hot summer 'mild' makes no sense; use it for winters and for low severity.

entry_json.definition: connected with soldiers, the armed forces and war
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Military spending rose while spending on schools was frozen.
example_sentences: The site was a military base until the 1990s.
Some countries still require a period of military service.

contexts.text: Military spending rose while spending on schools was frozen.
Some countries still require a period of military service.
My uncle did military service for two years before university.

confusables.difference: The army is the land force specifically. Military covers the army, navy and air force together.
The opposite: anyone not in the armed forces. Essays about conflict need both words.

entry_json.avoid: 'Military' is normally an adjective. As a noun it takes 'the': 'the military', not 'militaries'.

entry_json.definition: a natural substance found in the earth, such as iron or salt; also a substance the body needs from food
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The country's wealth depends almost entirely on exporting minerals.
example_sentences: Vegetables supply vitamins and minerals that supplements cannot fully replace.
Mining has stripped the region of its most valuable minerals.

contexts.text: The country's wealth depends almost entirely on exporting minerals.
Vegetables supply vitamins and minerals that supplements cannot fully replace.
I always buy mineral water when I travel, which is bad for the environment.

confusables.difference: A metal is one kind of mineral with particular physical properties. Not all minerals are metals: salt and quartz are not.
Vitamins are organic compounds made by living things. Minerals are inorganic and come from rock and soil.

entry_json.avoid: 'Mineral water' means bottled water from a spring, not water with minerals added.

entry_json.definition: the smallest amount or level that is allowed or possible
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The minimum wage has not kept pace with the cost of renting.
example_sentences: Applicants need a minimum score of six in each section.

State your objectives clearly before designing the study.
My objective this year is simply to speak more confidently.

contexts.text: Employers have a legal obligation to provide a safe workplace.
Wealthier countries have a moral obligation to help with adaptation costs.
There is no obligation to buy anything at the presentation.

confusables.difference: Responsibility is broader and includes things you take on yourself. An obligation is imposed from outside, by law, promise or morality.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'an obligation to do something' or 'under an obligation'. Do not write 'an obligation of doing'.

The conclusions rest on observation rather than on experiment.
The patient was kept under observation overnight.

As several writers have observed, the trend began well before the crisis.

contexts.text: Researchers observed the same behaviour in four separate colonies.
Trainee teachers observe experienced staff before taking a class themselves.
I like to sit in cafes and observe people, which sounds strange when I say it.

confusables.difference: Watch is casual and can be entertainment. Observe implies a purpose: you are watching in order to learn something.

The most obvious solution is also the most expensive one.
It was obvious from her face that the news was bad.

contexts.text: Obviously, not everyone can afford to move closer to work.

The scheme has obviously worked in dense areas; the countryside is another matter.

entry_json.definition: a particular time when something happens, or an important event or celebration

contexts.text: On several occasions the bus simply failed to arrive.
The opening of the library was a real occasion for the whole town.
We only use the good plates on special occasions.

confusables.difference: 'Occasion' is the noun for a particular time; 'occasionally' is the adverb meaning sometimes. Do not use one for the other.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'on that occasion', not 'in that occasion'.

entry_json.definition: sometimes, but not often

example_sentences: The river occasionally floods the lower part of the town.
Occasionally a student asks a question that changes how I teach the topic.

contexts.text: I occasionally work from home when the office is too noisy.
The river occasionally floods the lower part of the town.
Occasionally a student asks a question that changes how I teach the topic.

confusables.difference: Almost the same, but 'occasionally' is less frequent than 'sometimes' and slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: two c's and one s. 'Occassionally' is a very common misspelling.

entry_json.definition: to happen, especially without being planned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most accidents on this stretch of road occur after dark.
example_sentences: Flooding now occurs several times a year rather than once a decade.
The same error occurs throughout the document.

contexts.text: Most accidents on this stretch of road occur after dark.
Flooding now occurs several times a year rather than once a decade.
It occurred to me halfway through that I had misread the question.

confusables.difference: Happen is the everyday word and is normal in speech. Occur is formal and preferred in academic writing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Occur' is never used with an object and has no passive form. 'The event was occurred' is wrong. Double the r: 'occurred', 'occurring'.

entry_json.definition: strange or unusual; also, of numbers, not divisible by two

example_sentences: There was an odd smell in the corridor that nobody could explain.
Houses on the odd-numbered side of the street get the afternoon sun.

contexts.text: It seems odd that the busiest station has the fewest staff.
There was an odd smell in the corridor that nobody could explain.
Houses on the odd-numbered side of the street get the afternoon sun.

confusables.difference: Practically the same in the 'unusual' sense. 'Odd' is slightly milder and very British in tone.
The mathematical opposite. In a data description, keep the numerical sense clearly separate from the 'strange' sense.

entry_json.avoid: 'The odd' before a noun means 'occasional': 'I have the odd cup of coffee' does not mean the coffee is strange.

entry_json.definition: an illegal act; also the feeling of being upset by something rude
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Driving without insurance is a serious offence in most countries.
example_sentences: The court treats a second offence far more severely.
No offence was intended by the remark, but it was clumsy.

contexts.text: Driving without insurance is a serious offence in most countries.
The court treats a second offence far more severely.
I hope I didn't cause offence; I was translating literally.

confusables.difference: Crime is the general concept and can be uncountable ('crime is falling'). An offence is one specific breach of a particular law.
American spelling. In a British-standard answer use 'offence' for the noun; the verb is 'offend' in both varieties.

entry_json.avoid: You 'commit' an offence, 'cause' offence and 'take' offence. Do not write 'do an offence'.

entry_json.definition: to say or do something that makes someone feel upset, hurt or insulted
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Humour that works at home can easily offend people from another culture.
example_sentences: I hope I didn't offend her by turning the invitation down.
Advertisers have to be careful not to offend the audiences they depend on.

contexts.text: Humour that works at home can easily offend people from another culture.
I didn't mean to offend anyone, but I do think the rule is unfair.
The study asked whether such images offend religious sensibilities.

confusables.difference: Insult is deliberate and direct: you choose the words to wound. Offend is about the effect, and it is often accidental.
minimal_pair: He insulted my accent.
He offended me without meaning to.

confusables.difference: Annoy is mild irritation about behaviour; offend touches dignity, beliefs or identity.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say "I am offend". The person is offended and the remark is offensive.

entry_json.definition: extremely rude or unpleasant, in a way that hurts or insults people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Language that was common thirty years ago is now considered offensive.
example_sentences: Several viewers complained that the joke was offensive.
Social media companies are expected to remove offensive content quickly.

contexts.text: Language that was common thirty years ago is now considered offensive.
Personally, I found the advert quite offensive, and I wasn't the only one.
Platforms are under growing pressure to remove offensive material within hours.

confusables.difference: Rude is bad manners in an ordinary situation. Offensive is stronger and usually involves race, religion, gender or something a person cannot change.
minimal_pair: It was rude to interrupt.
The comment about her religion was offensive.

confusables.difference: Aggressive describes threatening behaviour; offensive describes words or images that insult.

entry_json.avoid: In sport and the military 'offensive' means attacking, not insulting. Context decides the meaning.

entry_json.definition: agreed to or arranged by people in authority, and therefore accepted as correct
entry_json.own_context_sentence: According to official figures, unemployment fell slightly last year.
example_sentences: You need an official translation of your degree certificate.
The official language of the country is Portuguese.

contexts.text: According to official figures, unemployment fell slightly last year.
I'm still waiting for the official result of my exam.
The ministry has not yet issued an official statement on the proposal.

confusables.difference: Official means it comes from an authority. Formal is about style and manners. An official letter is usually formal, but a formal dinner is not official.
Officer is a person; official as an adjective describes a thing. As a noun, an official is someone in a position of authority.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'official' to mean 'certain'. Say 'It is confirmed', not 'It is official' in an essay.

entry_json.definition: no longer modern, and belonging to a style or way of thinking from the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My parents' views on marriage are quite old-fashioned.
example_sentences: The hotel was a bit old-fashioned, but the staff were lovely.
Some people still prefer old-fashioned paper maps to phone apps.

contexts.text: My parents' views on marriage are quite old-fashioned.
Critics dismiss the policy as old-fashioned, but it has worked for decades.
Younger consumers see printed catalogues as old-fashioned and wasteful.

confusables.difference: Traditional is neutral or positive and respects the past. Old-fashioned usually sounds negative, as if something should have changed.
minimal_pair: It is a traditional wedding ceremony.
His attitude to women is old-fashioned.

confusables.difference: Ancient means thousands of years old. Old-fashioned means merely out of date.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the hyphen. 'Old fashioned' as two words is a spelling error in writing.

entry_json.definition: a space or hole that something can pass through, or the beginning of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Light came in through a narrow opening in the roof.
example_sentences: The opening of the film sets up everything that follows.
A small opening in the fence was enough for the animals to escape.

contexts.text: Light came in through a narrow opening in the roof.
We got there late and missed the opening of the concert.
The opening paragraph should state the writer's position clearly.

confusables.difference: Beginning is only about time. Opening can be a physical gap as well as a start, and it is the natural word for a film, a book or a ceremony.

entry_json.avoid: 'An opening' for a job is American English. In IELTS writing use 'a vacancy' or 'a post'.

entry_json.definition: to work or function, or to control a machine or a business so that it works
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory operates twenty-four hours a day.
example_sentences: Only trained staff are allowed to operate the machinery.
The company operates in more than forty countries.

contexts.text: The factory operates twenty-four hours a day.
I've never actually operated a drone, but I'd love to try.
Low-cost airlines operate on very narrow profit margins.

confusables.difference: Work is the everyday word for a machine functioning. Operate is more formal and is also used for running a business or a service.

The service operates only at weekends.

minimal_pair: She operates the equipment.
Surgeons operated on her knee.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'operate on a patient', not 'operate a patient'. Dropping 'on' changes the meaning completely.

entry_json.definition: a medical procedure in which a surgeon cuts into the body, or an organised activity involving many people

example_sentences: The rescue operation lasted three days.
The new rules will come into operation next April.

contexts.text: She had an operation on her knee and was back at work in a month.
The rescue operation involved more than two hundred volunteers.
The regulations will come into operation at the start of the financial year.

confusables.difference: Surgery is uncountable and names the field or the practice. An operation is one countable event.
minimal_pair: He needs surgery.
He needs an operation.

confusables.difference: A process happens over time by stages; an operation is organised and directed by people.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'have an operation', not 'do an operation', when you are the patient. The surgeon performs it.

entry_json.definition: a person who competes against you, or who disagrees with a plan or an idea

The bill has powerful opponents in parliament.

Opponents of nuclear power point to the cost of storing waste safely.

confusables.difference: An enemy wants to harm you. An opponent simply takes the other side in a game, an election or a debate.
minimal_pair: Wartime enemies.
His opponent in the debate.

confusables.difference: A competitor is trying to win the same prize or market. An opponent is directly against you in the same contest.

entry_json.avoid: 'Opponent of' is the fixed pattern, not 'opponent against'.

entry_json.definition: to disagree strongly with a plan or policy and try to prevent it

Economists who oppose the tax argue that it penalises the poorest households.

confusables.difference: Refuse is about saying no to something offered to you; oppose is about campaigning against something in general.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'oppose to' + noun. It is 'oppose the plan' or 'be opposed to the plan'.

The chart compares rail use as opposed to car use over a twenty-year period.

entry_json.avoid: 'Opposed to' is followed by a noun or -ing, never by an infinitive: 'opposed to building', not 'opposed to build'.

entry_json.definition: strong disagreement with a plan, or the main political party that is not in power

contexts.text: The proposal met fierce opposition from local farmers.

Opposition to the reform came mainly from older voters.

confusables.difference: An objection is one specific reason given against something. Opposition is the general resistance, and is usually uncountable.
minimal_pair: She raised an objection.
