confusables.difference: Competition is rivalry for a prize or a market; opposition is resistance to a plan.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'opposition to', never 'opposition against'.

entry_json.definition: a part of the body with a particular function, such as the heart or the liver

Shortages of donated organs remain the main obstacle to treatment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse with 'organisation'. They look similar but share no meaning in modern use.

entry_json.definition: able to plan your work and your time well, or arranged in a careful, ordered way

The conference was well organized and ran exactly to time.

Organized crime accounts for a small but costly share of offences.

entry_json.avoid: Choose one spelling, -ized or -ised, and keep it throughout the whole answer.

entry_json.definition: a person or group that plans and arranges an event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The organizers expect around five thousand people to attend.
example_sentences: I emailed the organizers to ask about wheelchair access.
Festival organizers had to cancel because of the weather.

contexts.text: The organizers expect around five thousand people to attend.
I was one of the organizers of our school's charity run last year.
I am writing to the organizers to request a refund for the cancelled session.

confusables.difference: An organization is a company or institution. An organizer is the person doing the arranging.

entry_json.avoid: Spell it consistently with 'organized'. Do not mix 'organiser' and 'organized' in one answer.

entry_json.definition: the point or place where something begins, or where a person's family comes from
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The origin of the tradition is still disputed by historians.

The report traces the origins of the crisis to the 1990s.

My family is of Tamil origin, though I was born in London.
Labels must state the country of origin of every ingredient.

The origin of the custom.

confusables.difference: Beginning is a point in time in a story or process. Origin explains where something came from and why.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'of' after origin: 'the origin of the problem', not 'the origin from the problem'.

entry_json.definition: in the beginning, before things changed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The building was originally a railway station.

contexts.text: The building was originally a railway station.
I'm originally from a small town near the coast.
The scheme was originally intended to last three years.

It was originally free.

confusables.difference: At first is the spoken equivalent and usually contrasts with 'but later'. Originally is neutral and slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: 'I am originally from X' is natural; 'I am original from X' is a common error.

entry_json.definition: used to say what will happen if something is not done; also 'in other respects'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Book early, otherwise you will pay almost double.
example_sentences: The traffic was terrible, but otherwise the journey was fine.

contexts.text: Book early, otherwise you will pay almost double.
Governments must act now; otherwise the cost of adaptation will rise sharply.
The room was a little small, but otherwise the accommodation was excellent.

Leave now, otherwise you will miss it.

confusables.difference: However contrasts two statements. Otherwise states the consequence of not doing something.

entry_json.avoid: Otherwise joins two sentences, so use a semicolon or a full stop before it, not a bare comma.

entry_json.definition: the one or ones that belong to us
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Their garden is much bigger than ours.
example_sentences: That car isn't ours; ours is the blue one.
The decision is not ours to make.

contexts.text: Their garden is much bigger than ours.
A friend of ours recommended the hotel to us.
The responsibility is ours, not the next generation's.

confusables.difference: Our comes before a noun: our house. Ours replaces the noun completely: this house is ours.

This room is ours.

confusables.difference: 'Our's' does not exist. Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'our's'. The correct form has no apostrophe.

entry_json.definition: the final result of a process, meeting or event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The outcome of the negotiations will affect thousands of workers.
example_sentences: Nobody could predict the outcome of the election.
Early treatment leads to much better outcomes for patients.

contexts.text: The outcome of the negotiations will affect thousands of workers.
Whatever the outcome, I'll be glad the exam is over.
Early intervention is associated with significantly better health outcomes.

confusables.difference: Result is the plain word and is used for scores and figures. Outcome suits a situation whose end was uncertain, and is preferred in academic writing.
minimal_pair: My exam results arrived.
The outcome of the trial.

confusables.difference: A consequence is what follows on afterwards, often bad. An outcome is how the thing itself ended.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'outcome result'. Choose one word.

entry_json.definition: used, done or existing outside rather than in a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The town has an outdoor pool that opens in June.
example_sentences: Outdoor activities are an important part of the course.
There is an outdoor market every Saturday morning.

contexts.text: The town has an outdoor pool that opens in June.
I much prefer outdoor sports to going to the gym.
Access to outdoor space is strongly linked to mental wellbeing.

confusables.difference: Outdoor is an adjective and goes before a noun. Outdoors is an adverb and goes after the verb.

We ate outdoors.

confusables.difference: Outside works as both preposition and adverb; outdoor cannot stand alone after a verb.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'We played outdoor'. Use 'outdoors' after a verb.

entry_json.definition: outside, not in a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children today spend far less time outdoors than their parents did.
example_sentences: We ate outdoors because the evening was so warm.
In summer the whole class is taught outdoors.

contexts.text: Children today spend far less time outdoors than their parents did.
At weekends I try to be outdoors as much as possible.
Staff who work outdoors need proper protection from the sun.

confusables.difference: Outdoors follows the verb; outdoor sits in front of a noun.
minimal_pair: We slept outdoors.
an outdoor pool

confusables.difference: Outside can take an object ('outside the house'); outdoors never can.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'outdoors activities'. The adjective is 'outdoor'.

entry_json.definition: on the outside of something, or furthest from the centre
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents are much lower in the outer suburbs.
example_sentences: Remove the outer leaves before you cook it.
The outer walls of the castle are still standing.

contexts.text: Rents are much lower in the outer suburbs.
I live in one of the outer districts, so it's about an hour in.
The outer layer of the material keeps the rain out.

confusables.difference: Outer is only an adjective before a noun. Outside is a noun, adjective or preposition.
minimal_pair: the outer wall
outside the wall

confusables.difference: External is the formal, technical word, often paired with 'internal'. Outer describes physical position.

entry_json.avoid: Outer has no comparative. Do not write 'more outer' or 'outerer'.

entry_json.definition: a short description of the main ideas, without the details; also the shape of something seen from a distance
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The minister gave a broad outline of the new policy.
example_sentences: Write an outline of your essay before you start the first draft.
We could just make out the outline of the mountains.

contexts.text: The minister gave a broad outline of the new policy.
I always write a quick outline before I answer a Task 2 question.
The following section presents an outline of the research method.

confusables.difference: A summary condenses something that already exists. An outline is a skeleton of the main points, often written before the full version.
minimal_pair: a summary of the article
an outline of the essay

confusables.difference: A draft is a full but unfinished version. An outline is only headings and main points.

entry_json.avoid: 'Outline' as a verb needs no preposition: 'outline the plan', not 'outline about the plan'.

entry_json.definition: considering everything, rather than one particular part
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Overall, the figures show a steady improvement.
example_sentences: Overall, I think the advantages outweigh the drawbacks.
The city has grown overall, although two districts have shrunk.

contexts.text: Overall, the figures show a steady improvement between 2005 and 2020.
Overall, I'd say it was a good decision, even though it was hard at the time.
Overall, the benefits of the scheme appear to justify its cost.

confusables.difference: In general introduces a broad tendency with exceptions. Overall sums up after weighing all the parts, which is why Task 1 overviews use it.
minimal_pair: In general, people prefer cheaper options.
Overall, sales rose.

confusables.difference: Total is a number. Overall is a judgement made after considering the numbers.

entry_json.avoid: In an IELTS Task 1 the overview normally starts with 'Overall,' followed by a comma. Do not write 'Overall of'.

entry_json.definition: to have to pay money back to someone, or to feel that you should thank someone for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many graduates owe tens of thousands of pounds in student loans.
example_sentences: I still owe my brother fifty pounds.
She owes her success largely to her parents' support.

contexts.text: Many graduates owe tens of thousands of pounds in student loans.
I owe my parents a lot, honestly, because they paid for everything.
The company still owes its suppliers for goods delivered last year.

confusables.difference: You borrow first; afterwards you owe. Borrow is the action, owe is the state that follows.
minimal_pair: I borrowed £50.
I owe him £50.

confusables.difference: Owe and own sound different and mean opposite things: owe is debt, own is possession.

entry_json.avoid: Owe is not used in continuous tenses. Write 'I owe him money', never 'I am owing him money'.

entry_json.definition: the speed at which something happens or at which someone walks or runs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Technology is changing at a pace that older workers find hard to match.
example_sentences: The pace of life in the capital is exhausting.
She set off at a fast pace and finished first.

contexts.text: Technology is changing at a pace that older workers find hard to match.
The pace of life back home is much slower, which I actually prefer.
Wages have failed to keep pace with rising rents.

confusables.difference: Speed is measurable in numbers. Pace is about how fast something feels or develops, and it collocates with change, life and reform.
minimal_pair: a speed of 90 km/h
the pace of reform

confusables.difference: Rate is a figure per unit of time: the unemployment rate. Pace is the felt rhythm of a process.

entry_json.avoid: 'Keep pace with' takes 'with'. Do not write 'keep pace to'.

entry_json.definition: something wrapped up to be sent or sold, or a set of things offered together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The government announced a package of measures to help small businesses.
example_sentences: A package arrived for you this morning.
We booked a package holiday because it worked out cheaper.

contexts.text: The government announced a package of measures to help small businesses.
A package turned up for me this morning and I've no idea what's in it.
I am writing because the package I ordered on 3 May has still not arrived.

confusables.difference: In British English a parcel is what the post delivers. Package is common in American English and in the figurative sense of a set of measures.
minimal_pair: The postman left a parcel.
a package of reforms

confusables.difference: A packet is a small paper or plastic bag: a packet of crisps. A package is bigger and usually posted.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'a package of information'. Use 'a set of information' or 'a pack'.

entry_json.definition: causing physical pain, or causing sadness and difficulty
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Recovery was slow and painful, but she went back to running.
example_sentences: My knee is still painful when I climb stairs.
Losing the family home was a painful experience.

contexts.text: Recovery was slow and painful, but she went back to running within a year.
My knee's still a bit painful, so I've stopped playing football.
The transition to automation has been painful for older employees.

confusables.difference: Sore is used for a small area that hurts to touch: a sore throat. Painful is broader and stronger, and works for emotions too.
minimal_pair: a sore throat
a painful injury

confusables.difference: Painless is the opposite and is often used figuratively: a painless process.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'My leg is painful' or 'My leg hurts', not 'I am painful'.

entry_json.definition: light in colour, or with less colour in the face than usual because of illness or shock
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She looked pale and said she had not slept.
example_sentences: The walls were painted a pale green.
He went pale when he heard the news.

contexts.text: She looked pale and said she had not slept for two nights.
The room was a pale yellow, which made it feel bigger.
Prolonged indoor working can leave staff pale and vitamin-deficient.

confusables.difference: Light is neutral for colours. Pale suggests weak or washed-out, and is the only one used about a person's face.
minimal_pair: light brown hair
a pale face

confusables.difference: White is a colour; pale describes a lack of colour, so a pale face is not literally white.

entry_json.avoid: For skin, 'pale' describes a temporary look from illness or shock; use 'fair' for someone's natural complexion.

entry_json.definition: a metal container with a handle, used for cooking food on a stove
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heat a little oil in a large pan before you add the onions.
example_sentences: I burnt the pan and it took an hour to clean.
Use a heavy pan so the rice does not stick.

contexts.text: Heat a little oil in a large pan before you add the onions.
I only really own one decent pan, so I cook fairly simple things.
Cheap pans wear out quickly and are rarely recycled.

confusables.difference: A pot is deep and used for boiling and stews. A pan is shallower and used for frying.
minimal_pair: a pot of soup
a frying pan

confusables.difference: A pane is a sheet of glass in a window. Same sound, no shared meaning.

entry_json.avoid: This word is rarely useful in Task 2. Keep it for Speaking Part 1 or 2 about food and cooking.

entry_json.definition: a group of people chosen to discuss something or make a decision, or a flat piece of material
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A panel of experts reviewed all the applications.
example_sentences: Solar panels now cover most of the roof.
She sat on the interview panel for three days.

contexts.text: A panel of experts reviewed all the applications independently.
There were four people on the interview panel, which was pretty intimidating.
Solar panels have fallen sharply in price over the last decade.

confusables.difference: A committee meets regularly and has ongoing duties. A panel is usually assembled for one purpose, such as judging or interviewing.
A jury decides a court case. A panel judges applications, competitions or debates.

entry_json.avoid: 'On the panel', not 'in the panel', when you mean being a member of it.

entry_json.definition: the group of elected people who make or change a country's laws
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bill was approved by parliament last month.
example_sentences: Parliament will debate the proposal in October.
She was elected to parliament at the age of thirty.

contexts.text: The bill was approved by parliament after two years of debate.
I honestly couldn't name more than three members of parliament.
Parliament has the final say on how public money is spent.

confusables.difference: The government is the group that runs the country day to day. Parliament is the wider body that makes laws and holds the government to account.
minimal_pair: The government raised taxes.
Parliament voted on the tax.

confusables.difference: Congress is the equivalent body in the United States; parliament suits the UK and most Commonwealth contexts.

entry_json.avoid: Note the silent middle: it is spelled par-lia-ment, not 'parlament'.

entry_json.definition: a person who takes part in an activity, event or study
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Participants were asked to keep a diary for four weeks.
example_sentences: All participants received a certificate at the end of the course.
Half the participants dropped out before the second stage.

contexts.text: Participants were asked to keep a sleep diary for four weeks.
There were about thirty participants, mostly students like me.
The survey found that regular participants reported lower stress levels.

confusables.difference: A competitor is trying to win. A participant is simply taking part, which is why research reports prefer it.
A member belongs to an organisation over time; a participant takes part in one activity or study.

entry_json.avoid: In academic writing use 'participants' rather than 'subjects', which now sounds outdated.

entry_json.definition: to take part in an activity or event with other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every student is expected to participate in at least one club.
example_sentences: Around two hundred schools participated in the competition.
Older residents are less likely to participate in online consultations.

contexts.text: Every student is expected to participate in at least one extracurricular club.
I participated in a debating competition last year and really enjoyed it.
Employees who participate in training are more likely to stay with the company.

confusables.difference: Take part is the everyday spoken phrase; participate is its formal equivalent and fits an essay better.
minimal_pair: I took part in a race.
Students participate in the scheme.

confusables.difference: You attend by being present. You participate by doing something active.

entry_json.avoid: Always use 'in': participate in an event. Never 'participate to' or 'participate at'.

entry_json.definition: more than usual, or more than other things; especially
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing costs are rising, particularly in the south of the country.
example_sentences: I'm not particularly keen on crowded places.
Air quality is particularly poor during the winter months.

contexts.text: Housing costs are rising, particularly in the south of the country.
I'm not particularly good at cooking, to be honest.
Young graduates are particularly affected by the shortage of affordable housing.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable, but 'not particularly' is the natural negative; 'not especially' sounds odd.
minimal_pair: not particularly interested
especially in winter

confusables.difference: Specially means 'for one specific purpose': specially designed. Particularly means 'to an unusual degree'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not begin a sentence with 'Particularly' alone. Attach it to what it modifies, or use 'In particular,'.

entry_json.definition: to some extent but not completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The delay was partly caused by bad weather.
example_sentences: I chose the course partly because of its reputation.
The rise in obesity is only partly explained by diet.

contexts.text: The delay was partly caused by bad weather and partly by staff shortages.
I moved here partly for the job and partly because my sister lives nearby.
The fall in sales can be attributed partly to the price increase.

confusables.difference: Partially is more common for physical or technical incompleteness: partially blind, partially built. Partly suits reasons and causes.
minimal_pair: partially sighted
partly because of the cost

confusables.difference: Mostly means the larger share; partly means only a share, without saying how big.

entry_json.avoid: 'Partly because' is followed by a clause; 'partly due to' is followed by a noun. Do not mix them.

entry_json.definition: a short section of a book, speech or piece of music, or a narrow way between two places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Read the passage carefully before you answer the questions.
example_sentences: A narrow passage led from the kitchen to the garden.
The passage of time has softened his opinion.

contexts.text: Read the passage carefully before you answer the questions.
There's a little passage at the back of the building that most people miss.
The passage of time has made the original agreement unworkable.

confusables.difference: An extract is deliberately taken out and reproduced. A passage is any section identified within the whole text.
minimal_pair: an extract from the novel
the passage on page 4

confusables.difference: A corridor is a proper hallway inside a building; a passage is narrower and can be outdoors.

entry_json.avoid: A reading passage is 'a passage', not 'a paragraph'. A paragraph is one block; a passage may hold several.

entry_json.definition: a very strong feeling of enthusiasm for something, or of love
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Photography started as a hobby and turned into a real passion.
example_sentences: She speaks about her subject with genuine passion.
His passion for cycling began at university.

contexts.text: Photography started as a hobby and turned into a real passion.
Teachers who speak with passion are the ones students remember.
A genuine passion for the subject matters more than early ability.

confusables.difference: An interest is mild and can be temporary. A passion is intense and lasting.
minimal_pair: I have an interest in history.
History is a passion of mine.

confusables.difference: A hobby is the activity itself; a passion is the strength of feeling behind it.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'a passion for something', never 'a passion of doing'.

entry_json.definition: a narrow way for walking, or the direction in which something moves or develops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A path runs along the river all the way to the next village.
example_sentences: Studying part-time was the only realistic path for me.
The storm destroyed everything in its path.

contexts.text: A path runs along the river all the way to the next village.
There's a lovely path near my house that I walk along most evenings.
Vocational training offers a realistic path into skilled employment.

confusables.difference: A road is built for vehicles. A path is for walking and is usually unpaved or narrow.
minimal_pair: a busy road
a woodland path

confusables.difference: Way is the route or method in general; a path is a physical line you can see, or a metaphor built on it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Career path' is a fixed collocation; 'career road' and 'career way' are not English.

entry_json.definition: an amount of money paid, or the act of paying
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first payment is due at the end of the month.
example_sentences: Contactless payment has almost replaced cash in many shops.
They offered to spread the cost over twelve monthly payments.

contexts.text: The first payment is due at the end of the month.
I make almost all my payments by card now; I rarely use cash.
Digital payment systems have reduced the cost of small transactions.

confusables.difference: A fee is the amount charged for a service. A payment is the money actually handed over, whatever it is for.
minimal_pair: a tuition fee of £9,000
a payment of £500

confusables.difference: A salary is regular pay for a job; a payment is any single transfer of money.

entry_json.avoid: You 'make a payment', not 'do a payment'.

entry_json.definition: quiet and calm, or not involving violence
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The village is peaceful once the day-trippers have gone.
example_sentences: Thousands took part in a peaceful protest.
I wanted somewhere peaceful to revise.

contexts.text: The village is peaceful once the day-trippers have gone.
Thousands took part in a peaceful protest outside the town hall.
A peaceful resolution to the dispute remains the preferred outcome.

confusables.difference: Quiet is about the absence of noise. Peaceful adds a feeling of calm and safety, and it is the only one used about protests and settlements.
minimal_pair: a quiet room
a peaceful demonstration

confusables.difference: Calm can describe a person's state of mind; peaceful describes a place or a situation.

entry_json.avoid: Do not describe a person as 'peaceful' when you mean calm. Say 'She stayed calm'.

entry_json.definition: an amount expressed as a part of a total of one hundred
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The percentage of households with broadband rose sharply after 2010.
example_sentences: Only a small percentage of applicants are accepted.
The chart shows the percentage of income spent on housing.

contexts.text: The percentage of households with broadband rose sharply after 2010.
A surprisingly high percentage of my friends still live with their parents.
Only a small percentage of plastic waste is actually recycled.

confusables.difference: Proportion is the more academic word and does not require a number. Percentage implies a figure out of a hundred.
minimal_pair: a large proportion of students
a percentage of 42%

confusables.difference: Percent follows a number: 40 percent. Percentage is the noun on its own: the percentage rose.
minimal_pair: 40 per cent of people
the percentage of people

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the percentage of 40%'. Write either '40%' or 'the percentage'.

entry_json.definition: completely, or in a way that could not be better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is perfectly normal to feel nervous before a speaking test.
example_sentences: The plan worked perfectly.
She speaks three languages perfectly.

contexts.text: It is perfectly normal to feel nervous before a speaking test.
The system worked perfectly for the first six months.
It is perfectly possible to reduce emissions without harming growth.

confusables.difference: Before adjectives such as normal, clear or reasonable, 'perfectly' is the natural intensifier; completely sounds heavier.
minimal_pair: perfectly reasonable
completely destroyed

confusables.difference: Very simply raises the degree. Perfectly claims the full extent, so it cannot be used with gradable comparison.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'more perfectly'. Perfect is already absolute.

entry_json.definition: how well someone or something does a task, or an occasion when a play or music is presented
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The school's exam performance has improved for three years running.
example_sentences: We went to an evening performance of the play.
Poor sleep has a measurable effect on academic performance.

contexts.text: The school's exam performance has improved for three years running.
We went to an evening performance and it was completely sold out.
Regular feedback is one of the cheapest ways to raise employee performance.

confusables.difference: A result is the final figure. Performance is the quality of how it was achieved, and can be described as good or poor.
minimal_pair: exam results
exam performance

confusables.difference: A show is the whole entertainment event; a performance is one occasion of it, or one person's contribution.

entry_json.avoid: 'Performance' in the academic sense is uncountable: 'his performance was poor', not 'his performances were poor' unless you mean several occasions.

entry_json.definition: lasting for a long time or for ever, without an expected end
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After two years on short contracts she finally found a permanent job.
example_sentences: The damage to the reef may be permanent.
There is no permanent solution to the problem yet.

contexts.text: After two years on short contracts she finally found a permanent job.
I'd rather have a permanent contract than a higher salary, honestly.
Rising sea temperatures may cause permanent damage to coral systems.

confusables.difference: Constant means happening again and again without stopping. Permanent means it will not end.
minimal_pair: constant interruptions
a permanent change

confusables.difference: Temporary is the direct opposite and is the word for short contracts and stopgap measures.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: -ent at the end, not -ant.

entry_json.definition: to allow something officially
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Smoking is not permitted anywhere on the premises.
example_sentences: The visa permits you to work up to twenty hours a week.
Weather permitting, the match will start at two.

contexts.text: Smoking is not permitted anywhere on the premises.
They don't permit dogs in the park, which seems a bit strict to me.
Current regulations permit councils to charge for the service.

confusables.difference: Allow is the everyday word and works in speech. Permit is formal and belongs to rules, signs and official texts.
minimal_pair: My parents allowed me to go.
Visitors are not permitted to enter.

confusables.difference: As a noun the stress moves to the first syllable, ˈpɜːmɪt, and it means the document itself: a parking permit.

entry_json.avoid: Permit takes an object plus 'to': 'permit students to use', not 'permit to students'.

entry_json.definition: used to give your own opinion, or to say that you did something yourself rather than through someone else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Personally, I think the drinking age should stay as it is.
example_sentences: The manager personally apologised to every customer.
Personally, I would rather live in a smaller town.

contexts.text: Personally, I think the drinking age should stay as it is.
The manager personally apologised to every customer who had waited.
I don't know her personally, but I've read a lot about her work.

confusables.difference: In my opinion is safe in an essay. 'Personally, I think' sounds conversational and is better kept for Speaking.
minimal_pair: Personally, I'd say so.
In my opinion, the policy has failed.

confusables.difference: Individually means one at a time; personally means by that person themselves.

entry_json.avoid: Avoid 'Personally, I think' in Task 2. Examiners prefer 'In my view' or a direct statement of position.

entry_json.definition: a particular way of thinking about something, shaped by who you are and what you know
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living abroad gave me a completely different perspective on my own country.
example_sentences: The report looks at the issue from an economic perspective.
It helps to see the problem from the student's perspective.

contexts.text: Living abroad gave me a completely different perspective on my own country.
The report examines the housing shortage from an economic perspective.
Seeing the figures for other countries puts our own problem in perspective.

confusables.difference: An opinion is what you think. A perspective is the position you are thinking from, which shapes many opinions at once.
minimal_pair: my opinion on tax
an economic perspective

confusables.difference: Point of view is the everyday equivalent; perspective sounds more academic and is preferred in essays.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'from the perspective of' or 'a perspective on'. Do not write 'in the perspective of'.

entry_json.definition: to make someone agree to do or believe something by giving them reasons
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took months to persuade the council to fund the project.
example_sentences: My friends persuaded me to enter the competition.
The evidence did not persuade the committee.

contexts.text: It took months to persuade the council to fund the project.
My friends persuaded me to enter the competition, and I'm glad they did.
Advertising aims to persuade consumers that they need a product.

confusables.difference: Convince changes what someone believes; persuade changes what they do. In practice they overlap, but 'persuade someone to do' is the safer pattern.
minimal_pair: He convinced me that it was true.
He persuaded me to go.

confusables.difference: Encourage is gentler support; persuade implies argument against initial resistance.

entry_json.avoid: Persuade takes 'to' + verb, not '-ing': 'persuade her to come', never 'persuade her coming'.

entry_json.definition: one stage in a process of change or development
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first phase of the building work should finish in March.
example_sentences: Teenagers often go through a difficult phase.
The scheme will be introduced in three phases.

contexts.text: The first phase of the building work should finish in March.
I went through a phase of only listening to jazz, which didn't last.
The reforms will be introduced in phases over a five-year period.

confusables.difference: Stage and phase overlap, but phase suggests a period with its own character that will pass; stage suggests a fixed step in a planned sequence.
minimal_pair: stage two of the process
a phase of rapid growth

confusables.difference: A period is simply a length of time; a phase is defined by what is happening in it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Phase out' is a phrasal verb meaning to end something gradually. Do not confuse it with 'faze', which means to disturb.

entry_json.definition: a fact or situation that exists and can be observed, especially one that is new or hard to explain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Remote working is a phenomenon that has changed city centres permanently.
example_sentences: Researchers are still trying to explain the phenomenon.
Rapid urbanisation is a global phenomenon.

contexts.text: Remote working is a phenomenon that has changed city centres permanently.
Cheap flights are a fairly recent phenomenon in my country.
Scientists have observed the same phenomenon in several unrelated species.

confusables.difference: An event happens once at a particular time. A phenomenon is a pattern that can be observed repeatedly.
minimal_pair: a sporting event
a social phenomenon

confusables.difference: A trend is a direction of change over time. A phenomenon is the thing itself, whether or not it is moving.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is 'phenomena', not 'phenomenons'. 'This phenomena is' is a very common error.

entry_json.definition: the study of the nature of knowledge and existence, or a set of beliefs that guides how someone acts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company's philosophy is that staff should never work weekends.
example_sentences: She studied philosophy and politics at university.
His teaching philosophy puts questions before answers.

contexts.text: The company's philosophy is that staff should never be expected to work weekends.
My philosophy is fairly simple: do one thing properly rather than three badly.
Modern educational philosophy places the learner rather than the teacher at the centre.

confusables.difference: A theory tries to explain how something works and can be tested. A philosophy is a set of values guiding behaviour.
minimal_pair: a theory of learning
a philosophy of teaching

confusables.difference: A belief is one thing you hold to be true; a philosophy is the whole connected system.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: philo-sophy, with 'ph' twice and no 'f'.

entry_json.definition: a person who takes photographs, especially as a job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The newspaper sent a photographer to cover the festival.
example_sentences: She works as a freelance photographer.
A wedding photographer can cost more than the venue.

contexts.text: The newspaper sent a photographer to cover the festival.
My cousin is a photographer, so all our family pictures are excellent.
Smartphone cameras have reduced demand for professional photographers.

confusables.difference: A photograph is the picture; a photographer is the person. The stress also moves: PHO-to-graph, but pho-TO-gra-pher.
A cameraman films moving pictures; a photographer takes stills.

entry_json.avoid: Stress the second syllable: fə-TO-grə-fə. Saying 'PHOto-grapher' is a common pronunciation error.

entry_json.definition: the art or activity of taking photographs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Photography is one of the few hobbies I have kept up.
example_sentences: He teaches photography at the local college.
Digital photography made the hobby much cheaper.

contexts.text: Photography is one of the few hobbies I have kept up since school.
Digital photography has made the hobby far cheaper than it was.
Photography is increasingly used as a research method in social science.

confusables.difference: Photography is the activity and is uncountable. A photograph is one picture and is countable.
minimal_pair: I enjoy photography.
I took a photograph.

confusables.difference: Photo is the informal short form of photograph, and never replaces photography.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'I like photographies'. Photography has no plural.

entry_json.definition: a number of things lying on top of one another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a pile of unmarked essays on her desk.
example_sentences: He left a pile of dirty plates in the sink.
Piles of waste build up outside the flats every week.

contexts.text: There was a pile of unmarked essays on her desk.
I've got a pile of books I keep meaning to read.
Piles of uncollected waste create a serious public health risk.

confusables.difference: A heap is untidy and roughly thrown together. A pile can be neat and deliberate.
minimal_pair: a heap of rubbish
a neat pile of shirts

confusables.difference: A stack is always tidy and even: a stack of chairs. A pile may or may not be.

entry_json.avoid: 'A pile of' takes a plural verb when what follows is plural in meaning, but formal writing keeps the singular: 'a pile of books was'.

entry_json.definition: a short thin piece of metal with a sharp point, used to fasten things together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She fixed the notice to the board with four pins.
example_sentences: A pin holds the two pieces of fabric in place.
I've forgotten the PIN for my card.

contexts.text: She fixed the notice to the board with four pins.
I always keep a safety pin in my bag; it's saved me more than once.
The mechanism is held together by a single steel pin.

confusables.difference: A needle has an eye and carries thread through fabric. A pin only holds things in place.
minimal_pair: thread the needle
fasten it with a pin

confusables.difference: In capitals PIN is a bank code and is unrelated to the metal object.

entry_json.avoid: Strictly, 'PIN number' repeats the word number, but it is so common in speech that it is accepted; avoid it in writing.

entry_json.definition: a tube through which liquid or gas flows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A burst pipe flooded the ground floor.
example_sentences: The city is replacing water pipes laid over a century ago.
Gas reaches the plant through a pipe under the sea.

contexts.text: A burst pipe flooded the ground floor of the building.
Our heating stopped because a pipe froze, which happens most winters.
Ageing water pipes are responsible for a fifth of all supply losses.

confusables.difference: Tube is the general shape word and is used in science and medicine. Pipe is the practical word for water, gas and drainage.
Different word and vowel: a pip is a small seed in fruit.

entry_json.avoid: For the London underground, British speakers say 'the Tube', never 'the pipe'.

entry_json.definition: an area of ground marked out for playing a sport, or how high or low a sound is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The pitch was too wet for the match to go ahead.
example_sentences: Thousands of children have no access to a proper football pitch.
Her voice rose in pitch as she got more excited.

contexts.text: The pitch was too wet for the match to go ahead.
There's a pitch just behind my flat where people play every evening.
Her voice rose in pitch as the argument went on.

confusables.difference: British English says football pitch; American English says field. Use pitch for football, cricket and rugby in IELTS.
A court is for tennis, basketball and badminton. A pitch is for football, cricket and rugby.
minimal_pair: a tennis court
a cricket pitch

entry_json.avoid: Never 'a swimming pitch' or 'a tennis pitch'. Match the word to the sport.

entry_json.definition: simple and without decoration, or easy to see and understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The instructions should be written in plain English.
example_sentences: He wore a plain white shirt.
It was plain that she had not read the report.

contexts.text: Public information should be written in plain English so that everyone can act on it.
I usually go for plain colours because they're easier to match.
It was plain from the figures that demand had collapsed.

confusables.difference: Simple means not complicated. Plain means without decoration or extras, and can also mean obvious.
minimal_pair: a simple explanation
a plain envelope

confusables.difference: Same sound, different word: a plane is an aircraft or a flat surface.

entry_json.avoid: Calling a person 'plain' means unattractive and can offend. Use it for objects and language.

entry_json.definition: the process of deciding in advance how something will be done
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The project failed because of poor planning rather than lack of money.
example_sentences: Careful planning saved us a lot of money on the trip.
The council refused planning permission for the extension.

contexts.text: The project failed because of poor planning rather than a lack of money.
A bit of planning beforehand makes travelling so much less stressful.
Urban planning decisions made now will shape the city for fifty years.

confusables.difference: A plan is the thing you produce; planning is the activity of producing it.
minimal_pair: We made a plan.
The planning took three months.

confusables.difference: Preparation is getting ready to carry something out; planning is deciding what to do.

entry_json.avoid: Planning is uncountable. Do not write 'the plannings' or 'a planning'.

entry_json.definition: enjoyable, or friendly and easy to be with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was a pleasant walk along the canal.
example_sentences: The staff were pleasant and the room was clean.
We had a pleasant surprise when the upgrade came through.

contexts.text: It was a pleasant walk along the canal, and the weather held.
The staff were pleasant and the room was spotlessly clean.
Green space makes urban living considerably more pleasant.

confusables.difference: Nice is overused and adds little. Pleasant is more precise and is worth a mark in Speaking.
minimal_pair: a nice day
a pleasant afternoon

confusables.difference: Pleasant describes the thing or person causing enjoyment. Pleased describes how you feel.
minimal_pair: a pleasant evening
I was pleased with the result.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: the first syllable is 'plez', not 'pleez'.
