entry_json.own_context_sentence: The school has around six hundred pupils on its register.
example_sentences: Pupils are tested at the ages of seven and eleven.
Each teacher is responsible for thirty pupils.

contexts.text: The school has around six hundred pupils on its register.
There were only about twenty pupils in my class, which I really appreciated.
Pupils in the region are tested at the ages of seven and eleven.

confusables.difference: In British English 'pupil' is used for school-age children and 'student' for those in college or university. American English uses student for both.
minimal_pair: primary school pupils
university students

confusables.difference: The same word names the black circle in the centre of the eye.

entry_json.avoid: Do not call a university learner a pupil. In IELTS, use 'student' unless you specifically mean schoolchildren.

entry_json.definition: to buy something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tickets purchased online are ten per cent cheaper.
example_sentences: Customers who purchase two items receive a discount.
The council purchased the land in 2018.

contexts.text: Tickets purchased online are approximately ten per cent cheaper than those bought at the station.
I purchased the item on 4 March and it arrived damaged.
Everything I purchased that day is itemised on the receipt.

confusables.difference: Buy is the normal word in speech and most writing. Purchase is formal and belongs in official letters, receipts and reports.
minimal_pair: I bought a coffee.
goods purchased under this agreement

confusables.difference: Shop is the activity of going round looking; purchase is completing the transaction.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'purchase' in Speaking. It sounds stiff and rehearsed; say 'buy' or 'get'.

entry_json.definition: not mixed with anything else, or complete and total
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bottle claims to contain pure orange juice with nothing added.
example_sentences: We found it by pure chance.
Rivers that were once pure are now heavily polluted.

contexts.text: Rivers that were once pure enough to drink from are now heavily polluted.
We found the place by pure chance, actually, and it was the best meal of the trip.
The label claims the product contains pure orange juice with nothing added.

confusables.difference: Clean means free of dirt. Pure means free of any other substance at all.
minimal_pair: clean water from the tap
chemically pure water

confusables.difference: The adverb 'purely' usually means only or entirely: purely for financial reasons.

entry_json.avoid: 'Pure' before an abstract noun means total: 'pure luck', 'pure nonsense'. This is emphatic and best kept for speech.

entry_json.definition: to continue with an activity or plan over a long period in order to achieve something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She decided to pursue a career in research rather than teaching.
example_sentences: The government is pursuing a policy of gradual reform.
He pursued the matter until he received a written answer.

contexts.text: She decided to pursue a career in research rather than in teaching.
I'd like to pursue photography more seriously once I have the time.
The government is pursuing a policy of gradual reform rather than sudden change.

confusables.difference: Chase is physical and immediate: chase a thief. Pursue is sustained effort towards a goal over time.
minimal_pair: The dog chased the ball.
She pursued a doctorate.

confusables.difference: Follow is going along after something; pursue adds determination and a purpose.

entry_json.avoid: British pronunciation is pə-SYOO. Note that pursue is transitive and needs an object.

entry_json.definition: an official record showing that you have completed a course or passed an exam
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Employers increasingly ask for qualifications that did not exist ten years ago.
example_sentences: She has a teaching qualification from a British university.
You need no formal qualifications to apply.

contexts.text: Employers increasingly ask for qualifications that did not exist ten years ago.
I got my teaching qualification a couple of years after my degree.
No formal qualifications are required, although experience is an advantage.

confusables.difference: A degree is one specific qualification from a university. Qualification is the general word for any certificate or award.
minimal_pair: a degree in law
professional qualifications

confusables.difference: Experience is what you have done; a qualification is the paper proving what you have studied.

entry_json.avoid: Countable: 'She has three qualifications'. Do not treat it as uncountable like 'experience'.

entry_json.definition: having passed the exams or training needed to do a particular job
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are simply not enough qualified nurses to fill the vacancies.
example_sentences: She is a fully qualified accountant.
Only qualified electricians may carry out the work.

contexts.text: There are simply not enough qualified nurses to fill the existing vacancies.
My sister is a fully qualified accountant, which took her about five years.
Only qualified electricians are permitted to carry out this work.

confusables.difference: Experienced means having done the job for a long time. Qualified means holding the required certificate. Someone can be one without the other.
minimal_pair: an experienced but unqualified worker
a newly qualified doctor

confusables.difference: Skilled describes ability; qualified describes official recognition of it.

entry_json.avoid: 'Qualified to do something' or 'qualified in a subject'. Do not write 'qualified for teaching' when you mean holding the certificate.

entry_json.definition: to pass the exams needed to do a job, or to have the right to something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes seven years to qualify as a doctor in most countries.
example_sentences: Households on low incomes qualify for a reduced rate.
The team qualified for the final with a game to spare.

contexts.text: It takes at least seven years to qualify as a doctor in most countries.
I qualified as a teacher in 2019 and started work that September.
Households on low incomes qualify for a substantially reduced rate.

confusables.difference: 'Qualify as' names the profession you become. 'Qualify for' names the benefit or competition you become eligible for.
minimal_pair: qualify as a lawyer
qualify for a discount

confusables.difference: Graduate means finish a degree; qualify means gain the right to practise a profession.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'qualify to a job'. Use 'qualify as' or 'qualify for'.

entry_json.definition: a line of people waiting for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a queue right round the building when the tickets went on sale.
example_sentences: I joined the queue at the ticket office.
Online booking has removed the queues that used to form outside.

contexts.text: There was a queue right round the building when the tickets went on sale.
Online booking has removed the queues that used to form outside the office.
Long queues at border control were the most common complaint in the survey.

confusables.difference: American English says 'line'; British English says 'queue'. IELTS examiners are British, so queue is the safer choice.
minimal_pair: stand in line
join the queue

confusables.difference: A cue is a signal to act. It sounds identical but is spelt differently.

entry_json.avoid: Spelling: q-u-e-u-e, five letters, only one syllable. British speakers 'queue up', not 'do a queue'.

entry_json.definition: to leave a job, school or activity, or to stop doing something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He quit his job after six months to travel.
example_sentences: She quit smoking three years ago.
Around a third of students quit the course before the second year.

contexts.text: He quit his job after six months and spent a year travelling.
She quit smoking three years ago and has not started again.
A lot of people quit the course in the first year, which honestly surprised me.

confusables.difference: Resign is the formal word for leaving a job officially, and is what you write in a letter. Quit is informal.
minimal_pair: I wish to resign from my post.
I quit my job.

confusables.difference: Give up is the natural phrasal verb for habits: give up smoking. Quit also works but sounds more American.

entry_json.avoid: Avoid 'quit' in Task 2 or a formal letter. Use 'resign', 'leave' or 'give up' instead.

entry_json.definition: a group of words taken from a text or speech and repeated by someone else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A short quotation from the study supports the point better than a summary.
example_sentences: The essay opens with a quotation from Orwell.
We asked three firms for a quotation before choosing one.

contexts.text: A short quotation from the study supports the point better than a long summary.
I got a quotation from three different companies before deciding.
Please send me a written quotation for the repair work.

confusables.difference: Quote is the verb, and is also used informally as a noun. Quotation is the correct noun in formal writing.
minimal_pair: He quoted Orwell.
a quotation from Orwell

confusables.difference: A citation gives the source reference; a quotation reproduces the actual words.

entry_json.avoid: In academic writing prefer 'quotation' to 'quote' as a noun.

entry_json.definition: to repeat the exact words that someone else has written or said
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The article quotes three separate studies without naming any of them.
example_sentences: She quoted the minister word for word.
Do not quote me on this, but I think the date has changed.

contexts.text: The article quotes three separate studies without naming any of them.
Don't quote me on this, but I think the deadline has moved.
The report quotes the director as saying that no jobs will be lost.

confusables.difference: Cite means refer to a source, with or without the exact words. Quote means reproduce the words themselves.
minimal_pair: He cited three studies.
He quoted one sentence from each.

confusables.difference: Mention is a passing reference; quote reproduces language exactly.

entry_json.avoid: 'Quote from a book' takes 'from' when you name the source, but 'quote someone' takes no preposition.

entry_json.definition: the sport of competing in races, especially with horses, cars or bicycles
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Motor racing attracts more television viewers than most other sports.
example_sentences: Horse racing has a long history in the region.
He gave up cycle racing after an injury.

contexts.text: Motor racing attracts more television viewers than almost any other sport in the country.
My grandfather loved horse racing and took me to the track most summers.
Cycle racing has grown steadily in popularity since the 2012 Olympics.

confusables.difference: A race is one event. Racing is the whole sport and is uncountable.
minimal_pair: He won the race.
He follows motor racing.

confusables.difference: Running is the activity; racing means competing against others.

entry_json.avoid: Racing is uncountable in this sense. Do not write 'racings'.

entry_json.definition: a set of different things of the same general type, or the limits between which something varies
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library offers a wide range of services beyond lending books.
example_sentences: Prices range from twenty to eighty pounds.
The temperature range in the desert is extreme.

contexts.text: The library offers a wide range of services well beyond lending books.
There's a good range of restaurants near where I live, which I appreciate.
Prices in the chart range from twenty to eighty pounds per unit.

confusables.difference: Variety emphasises how different the things are. Range emphasises that they cover the whole span from one end to the other.
minimal_pair: a variety of opinions
a range of sizes

confusables.difference: Scale is about size; range is about breadth and coverage.

entry_json.avoid: 'A wide range of' is followed by a plural noun: 'a wide range of options', not 'a wide range of option'.

entry_json.definition: a position in a scale that shows importance, quality or seniority
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The university has fallen ten places in the world rankings.
example_sentences: He rose to the rank of captain in six years.
The country ranks second in the world for renewable energy.

contexts.text: The university's rank has fallen ten places in the world tables since 2015.
He worked his way up through the ranks, which people respected.
The country ranks second in the world for renewable energy generation.

confusables.difference: Position is the general word for where something sits. Rank implies a formal scale that others are measured on too.
minimal_pair: a good position in the market
second rank in the league

confusables.difference: Class is a category; rank is an ordered level within one.

entry_json.avoid: Careful with 'rank' as an adjective: 'a rank smell' means a very unpleasant one, unrelated to position.

entry_json.definition: happening or moving very quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rapid growth of online shopping has emptied many high streets.
example_sentences: Rapid change makes long-term planning difficult.
There has been a rapid rise in the number of electric vehicles.

contexts.text: The rapid growth of online shopping has emptied many high streets.
Change has been really rapid here; the area looks nothing like it did.
A rapid rise in electric vehicle sales was recorded after 2020.

confusables.difference: Fast describes speed of movement, especially of vehicles and people. Rapid describes the speed of change and is the word for Task 1 trends.
minimal_pair: a fast car
a rapid decline

confusables.difference: Quick suggests a short duration. Rapid suggests a high rate over a period.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a rapid car'. Reserve 'rapid' for change, growth, increase, decline and expansion.

entry_json.definition: very quickly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The population of the city grew rapidly between 1980 and 2000.
example_sentences: Costs are rising rapidly.
The technology is developing more rapidly than regulation can follow.

contexts.text: The population of the city grew rapidly between 1980 and 2000.
Prices have gone up rapidly over the last year or so, especially food.
The technology is developing more rapidly than regulation can follow.

confusables.difference: Quickly is neutral and works in speech. Rapidly is the formal choice for describing figures and trends.
minimal_pair: He walked quickly.
Sales rose rapidly.

confusables.difference: Sharply describes a steep change in a graph; rapidly describes a fast one. A line can rise sharply but briefly.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 pair 'rapidly' with a verb of change: 'rose rapidly'. Do not write 'increased in a rapid way'.

entry_json.definition: not happening or found very often; also, of meat, cooked only briefly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Serious side effects are rare but must still be reported.
example_sentences: It is rare for the river to freeze completely.
The island is home to several rare bird species.

contexts.text: Serious side effects are rare, but they must still be reported.
It's rare for us all to be free on the same weekend, so we make an effort.
The island is home to several rare bird species found nowhere else.

confusables.difference: Unusual means different from what is expected. Rare means it happens infrequently, which is about number, not strangeness.
minimal_pair: an unusual name
a rare disease

confusables.difference: Scarce means there is not enough of something needed, such as water or housing. Rare simply means uncommon.

entry_json.avoid: 'It is rare for someone to do something' is the fixed pattern. Do not write 'It is rare that someone to do'.

entry_json.definition: not often; almost never
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students rarely read the whole reading list.
example_sentences: I rarely watch television during the week.
Rarely has a policy been reversed so quickly.

contexts.text: Students rarely read the entire reading list, however carefully it is chosen.
I rarely watch television during the week; I'd rather read.
Rarely has a government policy been reversed so quickly.

confusables.difference: Seldom is a more literary equivalent. Rarely is the safer choice in both speech and writing.
minimal_pair: I seldom travel by air.
I rarely travel by air.

confusables.difference: Hardly ever is the informal spoken version; rarely suits an essay.

entry_json.avoid: Rarely is already negative. Do not write 'I don't rarely go'. It goes before the main verb: 'I rarely go'.

entry_json.definition: not cooked, or in its natural state before being processed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The country exports raw materials and imports finished goods.
example_sentences: Raw fish must be stored below a certain temperature.
The raw data has not yet been analysed.

contexts.text: The country exports raw materials and imports the finished goods made from them.
I'd never eaten raw fish before I went to Japan, and I loved it.
The raw data has not yet been analysed, so the figures may change.

confusables.difference: Uncooked simply states that heat has not been applied. Raw is the natural collocation for food and the only one used for materials and data.
minimal_pair: uncooked pastry
raw materials

confusables.difference: Rare meat is cooked briefly; raw meat is not cooked at all.

entry_json.avoid: 'Raw materials' is a fixed phrase. Do not write 'natural materials' when you mean the industrial input.

entry_json.definition: the way someone behaves or feels in response to something that happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The public reaction to the announcement was overwhelmingly negative.
example_sentences: Her first reaction was to laugh.
Some people have an allergic reaction to nuts.

contexts.text: Public reaction to the announcement was overwhelmingly negative.
My first reaction was to laugh, which probably wasn't appropriate.
Some children have a severe allergic reaction to nuts.

confusables.difference: A response is considered and often deliberate. A reaction is immediate and may be emotional.
minimal_pair: a written response to the report
an angry reaction

confusables.difference: A reply answers a specific question or message; a reaction is any way of responding.

entry_json.avoid: 'Reaction to', not 'reaction on' or 'reaction against' unless you mean organised opposition.

entry_json.definition: sensible and based on what is actually possible, or showing things as they really are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is not realistic to expect everyone to give up their car.
example_sentences: We need a realistic timetable for the project.
The film gives a realistic picture of hospital work.

contexts.text: It is not realistic to expect every household to give up its car.
I try to be realistic about how much I can actually get done in a day.
The committee should set a realistic timetable before work begins.

confusables.difference: Real means genuinely existing. Realistic means either sensible about what is possible, or lifelike.
minimal_pair: a real problem
a realistic solution

confusables.difference: Practical asks whether something is useful in practice; realistic asks whether it can be achieved at all.

entry_json.avoid: 'Be realistic about something'. Do not write 'be realistic to something'.

entry_json.definition: the true situation, as opposed to what people imagine or claim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The reality of studying abroad is far less glamorous than the brochures suggest.
example_sentences: In reality, very few graduates walk into a job.
Virtual reality is being used to train surgeons.

contexts.text: The reality of studying abroad is far less glamorous than the brochures suggest.
In reality, very few graduates walk straight into a job.
Virtual reality is increasingly used to train surgeons before they operate.

confusables.difference: Truth is about whether a statement is correct. Reality is the actual state of things, whatever anyone says about it.
minimal_pair: He told the truth.
the reality of the situation

confusables.difference: A fact is one verifiable piece of information; reality is the whole situation.

entry_json.avoid: 'In reality' contrasts with what people believe. Do not use it simply to mean 'actually' in every sentence.

entry_json.definition: fair and sensible, or acceptable in price or amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is reasonable to expect employers to cover the cost of training.
example_sentences: The hotel was clean and the price was reasonable.
A reasonable person would have checked first.

contexts.text: It seems reasonable to expect employers to cover the cost of essential training.
The hotel was clean and the price was very reasonable for the location.
I would be grateful if you could offer a reasonable explanation for the delay.

confusables.difference: Fair is about treating people equally. Reasonable is about being sensible and moderate, and also covers price.
minimal_pair: a fair decision
a reasonable price

confusables.difference: Logical follows from the argument; reasonable also takes practicality and fairness into account.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reasonable amount' means quite a lot, not a small amount. Learners often use it the wrong way round.

entry_json.definition: to remember something, especially when you make an effort to do so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Participants were asked to recall as many words as they could.
example_sentences: I cannot recall exactly when the change was made.
The manufacturer recalled thousands of vehicles after the fault was found.

contexts.text: Participants were asked to recall as many words from the list as they could.
I can't recall exactly when we moved, but I was about seven.
The manufacturer recalled thousands of vehicles once the fault was identified.

confusables.difference: Remember is the everyday word and can be effortless. Recall implies deliberate effort to retrieve something, and is preferred in research writing.
minimal_pair: I remember her face.
I could not recall her name.

confusables.difference: Remind means make someone else remember; recall is something you do yourself.

entry_json.avoid: Recall is not followed by 'to' + verb. Write 'I recall meeting him', not 'I recall to meet him'.

entry_json.definition: a piece of paper showing that goods or money have been received
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the item.
example_sentences: I've lost the receipt, so they may not refund it.
Please acknowledge receipt of this letter.

contexts.text: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the item within thirty days.
I enclose a copy of the receipt as proof of purchase.
Consumers who retain receipts are significantly more likely to claim refunds.

confusables.difference: An invoice asks for payment before it is made. A receipt proves payment has already happened.
minimal_pair: The invoice is due in 30 days.
Here is your receipt.

confusables.difference: A recipe tells you how to cook something. The two words are often confused because they look alike.

entry_json.avoid: The p is silent: say ri-SEET. Note the spelling ei, not ie.

entry_json.definition: a suggestion that something is good, or advice about the best thing to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report makes six recommendations, only two of which were adopted.
example_sentences: I booked the restaurant on a friend's recommendation.
The committee's recommendation was rejected.

contexts.text: The report makes six recommendations, only two of which have been adopted.
I booked the restaurant on a friend's recommendation and it was excellent.
I would be grateful if you could send a written recommendation to the admissions office.

confusables.difference: A suggestion is one idea offered casually. A recommendation carries authority, from an expert, a report or someone you trust.
A reference in a job application is a letter about your character or work; a recommendation states that something should be done.

entry_json.avoid: 'Make a recommendation', not 'do a recommendation'. Note the double m and single c.

entry_json.definition: to get better after an illness or difficulty, or to get back something that was lost
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The economy took nearly a decade to recover from the crisis.
example_sentences: She recovered fully after six weeks of treatment.
Police recovered most of the stolen equipment.

contexts.text: The regional economy took nearly a decade to recover from the crisis.
I recovered pretty quickly, but I was told to rest for a month.
Police later recovered most of the stolen equipment from a storage unit.

confusables.difference: A doctor or a treatment cures a patient. The patient recovers. The subjects are different.
minimal_pair: Antibiotics cured the infection.
He recovered in a week.

confusables.difference: Improve means get better from any level; recover means return to a previous healthy or normal state.

entry_json.avoid: 'Recover from' something. Do not write 'recover of an illness'.

entry_json.definition: the act of making something smaller or less, or the amount by which it is made less
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There has been a sharp reduction in the number of smokers since 2000.
example_sentences: A reduction in working hours did not reduce output.
Students are entitled to a reduction on rail fares.

contexts.text: There has been a sharp reduction in the number of smokers since 2000.
Students get a reduction on rail fares, which makes a real difference.
A reduction in working hours did not lead to any fall in output.

confusables.difference: Decrease and reduction are close, but reduction suggests someone made it happen, while a decrease can occur on its own.
minimal_pair: a decrease in rainfall
a reduction in fares

confusables.difference: A discount is money taken off a price for a customer; a reduction is any decrease in amount.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reduction in' the quantity, but 'a reduction of' the amount: a reduction in prices of ten per cent.

entry_json.definition: a mention of something, or a letter about your character written to support an application
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The article makes no reference to the cost of the scheme.
example_sentences: My tutor agreed to write me a reference.
Please quote this reference number in any correspondence.

contexts.text: The article makes no reference at all to the likely cost of the scheme.
My tutor agreed to write me a reference, which was very generous.
With reference to your letter of 3 May, I would like to clarify one point.

confusables.difference: A reference describes what you are like as a worker or student. A recommendation states what should be done.
Mention is the everyday verb; 'make reference to' is the formal noun phrase for the same act.

entry_json.avoid: 'With reference to' opens a formal letter. It is too heavy for the body of an essay.

entry_json.definition: to show or be a sign of something, or to think carefully about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The results reflect the amount of preparation each student did.
example_sentences: The figures reflect a change in how the data is collected.
It is worth reflecting on why the policy failed.

contexts.text: The results reflect the amount of preparation each student put in.
Looking back, I reflect on that year as the point where things changed.
The rise in the figures reflects a change in how the data is collected.

confusables.difference: Without 'on', reflect means show or indicate. With 'on', it means think deeply about.
minimal_pair: The price reflects the quality.
She reflected on her choices.

confusables.difference: Show presents evidence directly; reflect suggests the thing is a sign of a deeper cause.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'reflect about'. The preposition is 'on' or 'upon'.

entry_json.definition: to think of someone or something in a particular way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme is widely regarded as a failure.
example_sentences: Many people regard homework as a waste of time.
She is regarded as one of the leading researchers in the field.

contexts.text: The scheme is now widely regarded as an expensive failure.
A lot of people I know regard homework as a waste of time.
With regard to your enquiry, I can confirm that places are still available.

confusables.difference: Consider can take an adjective directly: 'consider it unfair'. Regard always needs 'as': 'regard it as unfair'.
minimal_pair: consider it important
regard it as important

confusables.difference: 'Regards' with an s is a closing in letters, or means 'concerning' in 'as regards'. Keep the two apart.

entry_json.avoid: 'Regard as' is compulsory. 'They regard it a failure' is a common and visible error.

entry_json.definition: relating to one part of a country rather than the whole of it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Regional differences in income have widened over the last twenty years.
example_sentences: The regional airport handles about two million passengers a year.
There are strong regional accents within a very small area.

contexts.text: Regional differences in income have widened over the last twenty years.
There are really strong regional accents where I'm from, even between nearby towns.
Regional government has responsibility for transport and planning.

confusables.difference: Local means the immediate area around you: a local shop. Regional covers a much larger area within a country.
minimal_pair: the local school
regional transport policy

confusables.difference: National covers the whole country; regional is one part of it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'regional' for a small neighbourhood. Use 'local'.

entry_json.definition: to feel sorry about something you have done or failed to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I regret not taking the opportunity to study abroad.
example_sentences: We regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful.
She has never regretted the decision.

contexts.text: I regret not taking the opportunity to study abroad when it was offered.
We regret to inform you that your application has been unsuccessful.
Many graduates later regret choosing a subject purely for its earning potential.

confusables.difference: 'Regret doing' is being sorry about the past. 'Regret to inform' introduces bad news you are about to give.
minimal_pair: I regret telling him.
I regret to tell you that...

confusables.difference: Apologise is said to the person affected; regret describes your own feeling.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'regret to' for past actions. 'I regret to go' does not mean 'I wish I hadn't gone'.

entry_json.definition: at repeated times with roughly equal gaps between them; often
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People who exercise regularly report lower levels of stress.
example_sentences: The bus runs regularly throughout the day.
I regularly check the site for new listings.

contexts.text: People who exercise regularly report significantly lower levels of stress.
I regularly go running at weekends, mainly to clear my head.
The timetable is regularly updated and can be found on the website.

confusables.difference: Often counts how many times. Regularly adds the idea of a repeated pattern at fixed intervals.
minimal_pair: I often forget.
I regularly attend.

confusables.difference: Usually describes what normally happens in a situation; regularly describes frequency over time.

entry_json.avoid: Regularly usually sits before the main verb or at the end. Avoid placing it between the verb and its object.

entry_json.definition: an official rule made by a government or organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tighter regulation of the industry is long overdue.
example_sentences: New safety regulations came into force in January.
The regulations require every landlord to fit smoke alarms.

contexts.text: Tighter regulation of the rental market is long overdue.
There are so many regulations now that small businesses struggle to keep up.
New safety regulations came into force at the start of January.

confusables.difference: A law is passed by parliament. A regulation is a detailed rule made under a law by a government body.
minimal_pair: the Data Protection Act
data protection regulations

confusables.difference: A rule can be made by anyone, including a school or a club. A regulation is official and legally backed.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable when it means the activity ('regulation of the industry'), countable when it means individual rules ('the regulations say').

entry_json.definition: to refuse to accept an idea, an offer or an application
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council rejected the proposal for a third time.
example_sentences: My application was rejected without an interview.
The theory has been rejected by most researchers.

contexts.text: The council rejected the proposal for a third time in November.
My application was rejected without even an interview, which stung.
The original theory has since been rejected by most researchers in the field.

confusables.difference: Refuse is about saying no to something offered to you. Reject is deciding that something submitted is not good enough.
minimal_pair: She refused the job.
They rejected her application.

confusables.difference: Deny is saying something is not true, or not allowing access. Reject is turning something down.

entry_json.avoid: The noun 'a reject' means a faulty product and is offensive when used of a person. Use 'rejection' for the act.

entry_json.definition: to show or have a connection with something, or to understand and sympathise with someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chapter relates directly to what we discussed last week.
example_sentences: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than treatment.
I can relate to what she went through.

contexts.text: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than to the quality of treatment.
I can really relate to that, because I went through something similar.
This chapter relates directly to the argument set out in the introduction.

confusables.difference: The same phrase does two jobs: showing a link between things, and understanding a person's feelings. Context decides.
minimal_pair: The figures relate to 2019.
I relate to her frustration.

confusables.difference: Concern states the subject matter directly and takes no preposition: 'the report concerns housing'.

entry_json.avoid: Relate needs 'to' in almost every use. 'This relates the issue' is not correct English.

entry_json.definition: connected with something, or belonging to the same family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Stress-related illness accounts for a large share of absence from work.
example_sentences: The two problems are closely related.
Are you related to the woman who runs the shop?

contexts.text: Stress-related illness accounts for a large share of absence from work.
Are you related to the woman who runs the corner shop? You look alike.
The two problems are closely related and cannot be solved separately.

confusables.difference: Related is the adjective meaning connected. A relative is a person in your family.
minimal_pair: We are related.
She is a distant relative.

confusables.difference: Relevant means important to the matter in hand. Related only means connected.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate compounds: work-related, stress-related, weather-related.

entry_json.definition: the way in which two things are connected, or a member of your family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no clear relation between class size and exam results.
example_sentences: Trade relations between the two countries have improved.
Most of my relations still live in the same town.

contexts.text: There is no clear relation between class size and final exam results.
Most of my relations still live in the same town, so we see each other often.
Trade relations between the two countries have improved since the agreement.

confusables.difference: Relationship is preferred for connections between people. Relation suits abstract links between facts or figures, and 'relations' in the plural means diplomatic or trade links.
minimal_pair: a close relationship with my sister
the relation between income and health

confusables.difference: Relative is the more common word for a family member; relation is slightly more formal in that sense.

entry_json.avoid: 'In relation to' means concerning. Do not use it when you simply mean 'compared with'.

entry_json.definition: a member of your family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several relatives travelled from abroad for the wedding.
example_sentences: I have a distant relative who emigrated in the 1950s.
Older people who live near relatives report less loneliness.

contexts.text: Several relatives travelled from abroad for the wedding.
Older people who live close to relatives report significantly less loneliness.
Caring for elderly relatives falls disproportionately on women.

confusables.difference: Both mean a family member, but 'relative' is more common in modern English.
minimal_pair: my relatives
my relations

confusables.difference: As an adjective, relative means compared with something else: relative poverty.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'relative' for a friend. It means family only.

entry_json.definition: to a fairly large or small degree, when compared with something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents here are relatively low compared with the capital.
example_sentences: The process is relatively straightforward.
Relatively few people take up the offer.

contexts.text: Rents in the area are relatively low compared with those in the capital.
It was relatively easy once someone showed me how.
Relatively few households have taken up the grant since it was introduced.

confusables.difference: Fairly is a simple degree word. Relatively always implies a comparison, stated or understood.
minimal_pair: fairly cheap
relatively cheap for this city

confusables.difference: Comparatively is a close synonym and slightly more formal. Both need a point of comparison.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'relatively' with no comparison in mind. It should replace 'quite' only when something is being measured against something else.

entry_json.definition: calm and not worried, or informal and without strict rules
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The atmosphere in the office is relaxed but the deadlines are strict.
example_sentences: I felt completely relaxed by the second day of the holiday.
The school has a fairly relaxed attitude to uniform.

contexts.text: The atmosphere in the office is relaxed, although the deadlines are strict.
I felt completely relaxed by about the second day of the holiday.
A relaxed classroom environment has been shown to improve participation.

confusables.difference: Relaxed describes how you feel. Relaxing describes the thing that produces the feeling.
minimal_pair: I feel relaxed.
It was a relaxing evening.

confusables.difference: Calm suggests staying steady under pressure. Relaxed suggests there is no pressure to begin with.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'The holiday was relaxed'. A holiday is relaxing; a person is relaxed.

entry_json.definition: making you feel calm and free from worry
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A long walk at the end of the day is the most relaxing thing I do.
example_sentences: It was a relaxing weekend with nothing planned.
Some people find cooking relaxing.

contexts.text: A long walk at the end of the day is the most relaxing thing I do.
The hotel was quiet and relaxing, exactly what we needed.
Activities that people find relaxing vary considerably between age groups.

confusables.difference: Relaxing is the cause; relaxed is the effect on you.
minimal_pair: a relaxing bath
I was relaxed afterwards

confusables.difference: Restful is quieter and more literary; relaxing is the everyday word.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'I am relaxing' when you mean 'I am relaxed'. The -ing form as an adjective describes the thing, not the person.

entry_json.definition: to allow someone or something to leave or escape, or to make information or a product available
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory releases treated water back into the river.
example_sentences: The band released their first album in 2019.
He was released from hospital after two nights.

contexts.text: The factory releases treated water back into the river downstream.
They released the album about three years ago and I still listen to it.
The government released the figures only after repeated requests.

confusables.difference: Publish is used for books, articles and reports. Release is used for films, music, products and official data.
Free as a verb is used for people trapped or imprisoned; release is more formal and also works for information.

entry_json.avoid: The s is pronounced /s/, not /z/: ri-LEESE.

entry_json.definition: closely connected with the subject being discussed, and therefore important to it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only evidence that is directly relevant to the question should be included.
example_sentences: Please attach any relevant documents.
That point is interesting, but it is not relevant here.

contexts.text: Only evidence directly relevant to the question should be included in the answer.
That's interesting, but I'm not sure it's relevant to what we're deciding.
Please attach any relevant documents to support your application.

confusables.difference: Related just means connected. Relevant means the connection actually matters to the point being made.
minimal_pair: a related issue
a relevant argument

confusables.difference: Important judges value in general; relevant judges usefulness to this particular question.

entry_json.avoid: 'Relevant to', never 'relevant for' or 'relevant with'. In IELTS, going off topic means losing Task Response marks.

entry_json.definition: able to be trusted to do what is expected, or to be accurate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public transport here is cheap but not reliable.
example_sentences: We need reliable data before drawing any conclusion.
He is the most reliable person on the team.

contexts.text: Public transport in the city is cheap but not especially reliable.
My old car wasn't reliable at all, so I finally gave up on it.
Reliable data is needed before any firm conclusion can be drawn.

confusables.difference: Trustworthy is about honesty and character. Reliable is about consistent performance, and applies to machines and services too.
minimal_pair: a trustworthy friend
a reliable train service

confusables.difference: Dependable is a close synonym used mainly of people; reliable is broader.

entry_json.avoid: The opposite is 'unreliable', not 'non-reliable'.

entry_json.definition: the feeling of happiness when something unpleasant stops or does not happen, or help given to people in need
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was a relief to discover the deadline had been extended.
example_sentences: Aid agencies provided emergency relief within days.
Paracetamol offers short-term relief from the pain.

contexts.text: It was an enormous relief to discover that the deadline had been extended.
Aid agencies provided emergency relief within days of the earthquake.
The medication offers only short-term relief from the symptoms.

confusables.difference: Relief is the noun with an f. Relieve is the verb with a v. The spelling change catches many learners.
minimal_pair: a great relief
to relieve the pressure

confusables.difference: Comfort is ongoing physical or emotional ease; relief is the moment when something bad ends.

entry_json.avoid: 'What a relief!' is a natural exclamation in speech but too informal for an essay.

entry_json.definition: the belief in and worship of a god or gods, or a particular system of such belief
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Religion still shapes public holidays even in secular countries.
example_sentences: The school teaches about several major religions.
She does not follow any religion.

contexts.text: Religion still shapes public holidays even in largely secular countries.
Religion isn't a big part of my life, though it matters a lot to my grandparents.
The curriculum covers the beliefs and practices of several major religions.

confusables.difference: Faith is personal belief and trust. Religion is the organised system of belief and practice.
minimal_pair: her personal faith
the world's largest religions

confusables.difference: Religion is the noun, religious the adjective. Do not write 'a religion person'.

entry_json.avoid: Handle this topic carefully in Speaking. Describe practices rather than judging any belief.

entry_json.definition: connected with religion, or believing strongly in a religion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Religious festivals remain the busiest travel periods of the year.
example_sentences: My grandmother is deeply religious.
The building was originally a religious site.

contexts.text: Religious festivals remain the busiest travel periods of the year in many countries.
My grandmother is deeply religious, but the rest of us aren't really.
The building was originally a religious site before it became a museum.

confusables.difference: Spiritual describes inner belief that need not belong to any organised religion. Religious implies a specific faith and its practices.
Religious is the adjective; religion is the noun. 'Religious' cannot be the subject of a sentence.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: reli-gious, with -gious at the end, not -geous.

entry_json.definition: to need or depend on someone or something in order to work or survive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rural communities still rely heavily on the bus service.
example_sentences: Many households rely on a single income.
You cannot rely on the figures without checking the source.

contexts.text: Rural communities still rely heavily on a bus service that is being cut back.
I rely on my phone for absolutely everything, which is probably unhealthy.
Many households now rely on a single income to cover rising costs.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning. 'Depend on' is slightly more common in speech; 'rely on' emphasises trust that it will work.
minimal_pair: It depends on the weather.
We rely on the weather forecast.

confusables.difference: Trust is about belief in honesty; rely is about needing something to function.

entry_json.avoid: Always 'rely on' or 'rely upon'. Never 'rely to' or 'rely in'.

entry_json.definition: to stay in the same place or condition, or to be left after everything else has gone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment remains the biggest concern for people in the region.
example_sentences: Only two of the original buildings remain.
The cause of the fault remains unclear.

contexts.text: Unemployment remains the single biggest concern for people in the region.
Only two of the original buildings remain, which is a shame.
The cause of the fault remains unclear despite two investigations.

confusables.difference: Stay is the everyday word, especially about people in places. Remain is formal and is the natural verb for figures and conditions.
minimal_pair: I stayed at home.
The figure remained stable.

confusables.difference: The rest is a noun for what is left; remain is the verb.

entry_json.avoid: Remain is not used in the continuous. Write 'The problem remains', not 'is remaining'.

entry_json.definition: something that someone says, expressing an opinion or observation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: His remark about immigration was widely criticised.
example_sentences: She made a passing remark about the cost.
The report closes with a few general remarks.

contexts.text: His remark about immigration was widely criticised in the following days.
She made a passing remark about the cost, and I've thought about it since.
The report closes with a few general remarks about future research.

confusables.difference: Comment is the more common word and is often invited. A remark is spontaneous and may be casual or pointed.
minimal_pair: Comments are welcome.
an unhelpful remark

confusables.difference: A statement is formal and prepared; a remark is brief and often unplanned.

entry_json.avoid: You 'make a remark', not 'say a remark'.

entry_json.definition: to make someone remember something they must do, or to make them think of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please remind me to send the form before Friday.
example_sentences: The photograph reminds me of my first year here.
Staff are reminded that the building closes at ten.

contexts.text: Please remind me to send the form before Friday.
Staff are reminded that the building closes at ten each evening.
The findings remind us that correlation does not establish causation.

confusables.difference: You remember something yourself. You remind someone else. The subject is different.
minimal_pair: I remembered the date.
She reminded me of the date.

confusables.difference: 'Remind me of' brings a memory back. 'Remind me to' prompts a future action.
minimal_pair: It reminds me of home.
Remind me to call her.

entry_json.avoid: Remind needs a person as its object: 'remind me', not 'remind that the meeting is at three' with no object.

entry_json.definition: far away from towns and people, or done from a distance using technology
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Delivering healthcare to remote villages remains expensive.
example_sentences: The job is fully remote, so I can live anywhere.
There is only a remote chance of that happening.

contexts.text: Delivering healthcare to remote villages remains prohibitively expensive.
My job is fully remote now, so I only go in about once a month.
Remote working has changed demand for office space in city centres.

confusables.difference: Distant states physical or emotional distance. Remote adds the idea of being hard to reach and cut off.
minimal_pair: a distant relative
a remote island

confusables.difference: Rural means countryside, which may still be well connected. Remote means isolated.

entry_json.avoid: 'A remote chance' means a very small one. Do not confuse it with the physical sense.

entry_json.definition: money paid regularly for the use of a house, flat or room
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rent takes up more than half my monthly income.
example_sentences: Rents in the city have risen faster than wages.
The rent includes water but not electricity.

contexts.text: Rent now takes up more than half of my monthly income.
Rents in the city have risen considerably faster than average wages.
I am writing to query the rent increase notified in your letter of 2 April.

confusables.difference: In British English you rent a home for a long period and hire a car or equipment for a short one.
minimal_pair: rent a flat
hire a car for the weekend

confusables.difference: A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home; rent is money paid to a landlord for using one.

entry_json.avoid: Rent as a noun is usually uncountable for one property: 'the rent is £900', not 'the rents are'.

entry_json.definition: happening or done many times
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Repeated failures to fix the problem have damaged public trust.
example_sentences: Despite repeated requests, no reply was received.
Repeated exposure to loud noise damages hearing.

contexts.text: Repeated failures to fix the problem have damaged public trust in the service.
Despite repeated requests, I have received no reply to my complaint.
I made repeated attempts to contact them and eventually gave up.

confusables.difference: Frequent describes how often something happens over time. Repeated stresses that the same thing happened again and again.
minimal_pair: frequent trains
repeated warnings

confusables.difference: Continuous means without stopping; repeated means happening over and over with gaps.

entry_json.avoid: Repeated goes before the noun. Do not write 'The requests were repeated many times' when 'repeated requests' is shorter and stronger.

entry_json.definition: to act or speak officially for someone, or to be a sign or symbol of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Each column represents one year of data.
example_sentences: She was elected to represent the students on the committee.
This figure represents a five per cent rise.

contexts.text: Each column in the chart represents one year of recorded data.
I was elected to represent our year on the student committee.
The organisation represents the interests of tenants in the private sector.

confusables.difference: Stand for is the informal equivalent for symbols and abbreviations. Represent is formal and covers both meanings.
minimal_pair: BBC stands for...
The line represents growth.

confusables.difference: Present means show or give; represent means act on behalf of, or symbolise.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, use 'represents' for what a bar or line shows. Do not write 'represents about', which is redundant.

entry_json.definition: a person chosen to act or speak for a group of people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Each department sends one representative to the monthly meeting.
example_sentences: A union representative attended the hearing.
The sample was not representative of the wider population.

contexts.text: Each department sends one representative to the monthly meeting.
There was a student representative on the panel, which made a difference.
The sample was not representative of the wider population, which limits the findings.

confusables.difference: A delegate is sent to one particular conference or meeting. A representative holds the role over time.
As an adjective it means typical of a larger group: 'a representative sample'. This is the key research use.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the stress: rep-ri-ZEN-ta-tiv. It is a long word and mispronouncing it is very audible.

entry_json.definition: the opinion that people generally have about someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The university has built a strong reputation for research.
example_sentences: The city has a reputation for being expensive.
One serious mistake can destroy a reputation built over decades.

contexts.text: The university has built a strong international reputation for medical research.
The city has a reputation for being expensive, which is fairly deserved.
One serious error can destroy a reputation built over several decades.

confusables.difference: Fame is being widely known. Reputation is what people think of you, and can be good or bad.
minimal_pair: He achieved fame.
He has a reputation for honesty.

confusables.difference: Image is how something is deliberately presented; reputation is what people actually conclude.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reputation for' takes a noun or -ing: 'a reputation for being late', not 'a reputation to be late'.

entry_json.definition: to need something, or to make something necessary by rule
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The role requires at least two years of relevant experience.
example_sentences: All passengers are required to show identification.
Reducing emissions will require action from every sector.

contexts.text: The role requires at least two years of directly relevant experience.
It required a lot more effort than I expected, honestly.
Reducing emissions on this scale will require coordinated action from every sector.

confusables.difference: Need is the everyday word and can be used about people directly. Require is formal and is standard for rules and job descriptions.
minimal_pair: I need a break.
Applicants are required to submit two references.

confusables.difference: Request means politely ask for; require means make necessary or demand.

entry_json.avoid: Require is not used in the continuous: 'The job requires', not 'is requiring'.

entry_json.definition: something that is needed or that must be done because of a rule
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Meeting the language requirement is the last step for most applicants.
example_sentences: The course has no formal entry requirements.
Safety requirements have become considerably stricter.

contexts.text: Meeting the language requirement is the final step for most international applicants.
The entry requirements weren't as high as I'd feared, luckily.
Please confirm that the property meets all current safety requirements.

confusables.difference: A condition is something that must be true for an agreement to hold. A requirement is something that must be provided or achieved.
A need is what someone lacks; a requirement is what an authority insists on.

entry_json.avoid: You 'meet' or 'satisfy' requirements. Do not write 'reach the requirements'.

entry_json.definition: to save someone or something from a dangerous or harmful situation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Volunteers rescued more than forty people from the flooded streets.
example_sentences: The dog was rescued from a shelter.
A last-minute loan rescued the company.

contexts.text: Volunteers rescued more than forty people from the flooded streets.
We rescued our dog from a shelter, and she's been brilliant.
A last-minute government loan rescued the company from collapse.

confusables.difference: Save is broader and includes money, time and files. Rescue means physically removing someone from danger.
minimal_pair: He saved my life.
They rescued the crew.

confusables.difference: Recover is getting back something lost or stolen; rescue is saving something in danger.

entry_json.avoid: Pronounced RES-kyoo, with stress on the first syllable.

entry_json.definition: an arrangement to keep a table, room or seat for someone, or a feeling of doubt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I made a reservation for four at eight o'clock.
example_sentences: The hotel has no record of my reservation.
I have serious reservations about the plan.

contexts.text: I made a reservation for four people at eight o'clock.
The hotel has no record of my reservation, despite the confirmation email.
Several experts have expressed reservations about the reliability of the data.

confusables.difference: British English usually says 'booking' for restaurants and hotels; reservation is slightly more formal and standard in writing.
minimal_pair: I've made a booking.
your reservation is confirmed

confusables.difference: In the plural it often means doubts: 'I have reservations about it'. This is a useful essay phrase.

entry_json.avoid: 'Reservations about', not 'reservations on', when you mean doubts.

entry_json.definition: to arrange for something to be kept for you, or to keep something for a particular purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two carriages are reserved for passengers with bicycles.
example_sentences: I reserved a table for Friday evening.
The right to refuse entry is reserved.

contexts.text: Two carriages on each train are reserved for passengers travelling with bicycles.
I reserved a table for Friday, but I can change it if that's easier.
The organisers reserve the right to alter the programme without notice.

confusables.difference: Book is the ordinary British verb for tickets and tables. Reserve is more formal and is used on signs and in notices.
minimal_pair: I booked the flight.
This seat is reserved.

confusables.difference: Preserve means keep something from being damaged or lost; reserve means set it aside for someone.

entry_json.avoid: 'Reserved for' takes 'for'. A 'nature reserve' uses the noun and has nothing to do with booking.

entry_json.definition: a person who lives in a particular place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Local residents were not consulted before the road was closed.
example_sentences: Residents have complained about noise from the site.
Only residents may park in these streets.

contexts.text: Local residents were not consulted before the road was closed to traffic.
The residents in my building organised a meeting about it, which was quite effective.
I am writing on behalf of residents affected by the noise from the building site.

confusables.difference: A citizen has legal nationality of a country. A resident simply lives there, whatever their nationality.
minimal_pair: a British citizen
a resident of Manchester

confusables.difference: Inhabitant is used in geography for the population of a place; resident is used for people affected by local decisions.

entry_json.avoid: 'A resident of' a place. Do not write 'a resident in' unless you mean 'resident in the UK' as an adjective.

entry_json.definition: to refuse to accept something and try to stop it, or to stop yourself doing something you want to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many companies resisted the change until it became a legal requirement.
example_sentences: I could not resist buying it.
The material resists heat up to 300 degrees.

contexts.text: Many companies resisted the change until it became a legal requirement.
I couldn't resist buying it, even though I really didn't need it.
Older employees are often assumed to resist new technology, which the evidence does not support.

confusables.difference: Refuse is saying no to an offer or request. Resist is actively opposing something being imposed on you.
minimal_pair: She refused the offer.
They resisted the reform.

confusables.difference: Oppose is usually public and organised; resist can be quiet and individual.

entry_json.avoid: Resist is followed by -ing, never 'to': 'resist buying it', not 'resist to buy it'.

entry_json.definition: to find a satisfactory solution to a problem or disagreement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The dispute was finally resolved through mediation.
example_sentences: Most complaints are resolved within five working days.
The two sides failed to resolve their differences.

contexts.text: The dispute was finally resolved through mediation rather than through the courts.
It took a few emails, but they resolved it in the end.
I trust that the matter can be resolved without further correspondence.

confusables.difference: Solve is used for problems and puzzles that have an answer. Resolve is used for disputes, conflicts and issues between people.
minimal_pair: solve the equation
resolve the conflict

confusables.difference: Settle suggests both sides agree to stop; resolve suggests the underlying problem has actually been dealt with.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'resolve a question'. Questions are answered; disputes are resolved.

entry_json.definition: a place where people go on holiday, or a course of action taken when nothing else has worked
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The town has grown from a fishing village into a major resort.
example_sentences: Ski resorts at lower altitudes are already losing snow.
Legal action should be a last resort.

contexts.text: The town has grown from a fishing village into a major coastal resort.
We stayed at a small resort on the south coast, which was lovely and quiet.
Legal action should be a last resort rather than a first response.

confusables.difference: A hotel is one building. A resort is a whole holiday town or a large complex with several facilities.
As a verb, 'resort to' means turn to something undesirable because nothing else worked: 'resort to violence'.

entry_json.avoid: 'As a last resort' is the fixed phrase. Do not write 'as the last resort' in this idiom.

entry_json.definition: a supply of something such as money, materials or staff that can be used
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Water is the resource most likely to cause conflict this century.
example_sentences: Schools in the area lack basic resources.
The library is an excellent resource for students.

contexts.text: Water is the resource most likely to cause international conflict this century.
Our school didn't have many resources, but the teachers were excellent.
The online library is an excellent free resource for anyone preparing for the exam.

confusables.difference: A source is where something comes from. A resource is a stock of something you can draw on.
minimal_pair: a source of income
natural resources

confusables.difference: Supply is the amount available now; a resource is the stock that supply is drawn from.

entry_json.avoid: British English stresses the second syllable: ri-ZORS. The American first-syllable stress sounds foreign here.

entry_json.definition: admiration for someone's qualities or achievements, or polite behaviour towards them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Teachers earn respect by listening, not by shouting.
example_sentences: I have enormous respect for what she has achieved.
Young people are often accused of showing no respect.

contexts.text: Teachers earn respect by listening rather than by raising their voices.
I've got enormous respect for what my parents managed on very little.
Mutual respect between staff and management is essential to a functioning workplace.

confusables.difference: Admire is the verb for the feeling. Respect can be a verb too, but as a noun it is what you show or have.
minimal_pair: I admire her.
I have respect for her.

confusables.difference: 'With respect to' and 'in respect of' are formal phrases meaning 'concerning', unrelated to admiration.

entry_json.avoid: 'Respect for', not 'respect to', when you mean admiration.

entry_json.definition: a duty to deal with something, or the state of being to blame for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reducing waste is the responsibility of individuals and governments alike.
example_sentences: She took responsibility for the mistake.
My main responsibility was managing the schedule.

contexts.text: Reducing waste is the responsibility of individuals and governments alike.
My main responsibility was managing the schedule, which I actually enjoyed.
The company has accepted responsibility for the delay and offered a refund.

confusables.difference: A duty is imposed on you by a role or the law. A responsibility can also be something you choose to take on.
minimal_pair: a legal duty
a personal responsibility

confusables.difference: Blame looks backwards at fault; responsibility can look forward at what you must do.

entry_json.avoid: You 'take' or 'accept' responsibility, not 'do responsibility'. And it is 'responsibility for', not 'of'.

entry_json.definition: having the duty to deal with something, or being the cause of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Road transport is responsible for a quarter of national emissions.
example_sentences: Who is responsible for locking up at night?
She is a responsible and reliable employee.

contexts.text: Road transport is responsible for roughly a quarter of national emissions.
I was responsible for a team of six, which was new for me at the time.
Please confirm who is responsible for maintaining the shared garden.

confusables.difference: Responsible means having a duty, or being the cause. Reliable means you can be counted on to perform.
minimal_pair: responsible for the budget
a reliable colleague

confusables.difference: In charge of emphasises authority over people; responsible for emphasises the duty and the accountability.

entry_json.avoid: Always 'responsible for', never 'responsible of' or 'responsible to do'.

entry_json.definition: to keep something rather than losing it or giving it up
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools struggle to retain teachers in their first five years.
example_sentences: The soil retains water for much longer after treatment.
Please retain your ticket for inspection.
