She studied sculpture before turning to painting.

contexts.text: A large bronze sculpture stands at the entrance to the park.
There's a sculpture near my flat that I walk past every day and still like.
Public sculpture has been shown to increase how safe people feel in an area.

confusables.difference: A statue represents a person or animal realistically. A sculpture is any three-dimensional artwork, including abstract ones.
minimal_pair: a statue of the queen
an abstract sculpture

confusables.difference: A sculptor is the artist; sculpture is the work.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable as an art form ('she studies sculpture'), countable for individual works ('three sculptures').

entry_json.definition: less important than something else, or relating to the education of children aged about eleven to eighteen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cost was a secondary consideration when we chose the school.
example_sentences: She teaches history at a secondary school.
The secondary effects of the policy were not anticipated.

contexts.text: Cost was a secondary consideration when we chose the school.
I went to a secondary school about twenty minutes from my house.
Secondary education in the region is free but not compulsory beyond sixteen.

confusables.difference: Primary means most important, or for younger children. Secondary means less important, or for older children.
minimal_pair: the primary cause
of secondary importance

confusables.difference: 'High school' is American English. In IELTS, 'secondary school' is the safer British term.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a secondary reason' when you mean an additional one. Secondary means less important, not simply extra.

entry_json.definition: safe from being harmed, lost or stolen, or certain to continue in the future
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Very few young workers now have a secure job.
example_sentences: Make sure the connection is secure before entering your details.
The building is secure and monitored at night.

contexts.text: Very few young workers now have what previous generations would call a secure job.
I don't feel secure in the flat because the front door doesn't lock properly.
Please check that the connection is secure before entering any payment details.

confusables.difference: Safe means free from danger right now. Secure means protected by something and likely to stay that way.
minimal_pair: the child is safe
a secure building

confusables.difference: As a verb, secure means obtain something with effort: 'secure a place at university'.

entry_json.avoid: Stress the second syllable: si-KYOOR. As a verb it means 'obtain', which is a different meaning entirely.

entry_json.definition: protection against deliberate threats such as crime or attack, or the feeling of being safe
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Airport security has become far more time-consuming since 2001.
example_sentences: Job security matters more to some people than salary.
The building has security cameras at every entrance.

contexts.text: Airport security has become considerably more time-consuming since 2001.
Job security matters more to me than a higher salary, honestly.
The building has security cameras at every entrance and a staffed reception.

confusables.difference: Safety protects against accidents; security protects against deliberate harm such as theft or attack.
minimal_pair: fire safety
data security

confusables.difference: Security is the noun, secure the adjective. 'A security job' means working as a guard, not a stable job.

entry_json.avoid: 'Job security' means a stable job. 'A security job' means working as a security guard. Word order changes everything.

entry_json.definition: the small hard part of a plant from which a new plant grows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farmers who save their own seed are less dependent on suppliers.
example_sentences: Sunflower seeds are a cheap source of protein.
The seeds should be planted in early spring.

contexts.text: Farmers who save their own seed are much less dependent on commercial suppliers.
I planted some seeds on the balcony and, surprisingly, they grew.
The seeds should be planted in early spring and watered regularly.

confusables.difference: A pip is the small seed in fruit such as apples and oranges. Seed is the general word.
minimal_pair: apple pips
grass seed

confusables.difference: A plant is what grows; the seed is what it grows from.

entry_json.avoid: Seed is countable ('three seeds') but uncountable in farming ('save seed for next year').

entry_json.definition: to try to find or obtain something, or to try to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Graduates seeking work in the sector face intense competition.
example_sentences: Patients should seek medical advice before stopping the treatment.
The company is seeking to reduce its energy use by half.

contexts.text: Graduates seeking work in the creative sector face intense competition.
Patients should seek medical advice before stopping any prescribed treatment.
Most people my age would seek advice online before asking anyone in person.

confusables.difference: Look for is the everyday phrasal verb. Seek is formal and belongs in writing, especially with advice, help and permission.
minimal_pair: I'm looking for a flat.
applicants seeking permission

confusables.difference: Search means examine a place thoroughly; seek means try to obtain something.

entry_json.avoid: Irregular past forms: sought, sought. Do not write 'seeked'.

entry_json.definition: to choose someone or something carefully from a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Participants were selected at random from the electoral register.
example_sentences: Only twelve applicants were selected for interview.
Select the option that best describes your situation.

contexts.text: Participants were selected at random from the electoral register.
Only twelve of us were selected for interview out of about two hundred.
Please select the option that best describes your current situation.

confusables.difference: Choose is the everyday word and can be casual. Select implies careful comparison against criteria and is standard in research writing.
minimal_pair: Choose whichever you like.
Candidates were selected on merit.

confusables.difference: Pick is informal and quick; select is deliberate and formal.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'choose' in Speaking. 'Select' can sound rehearsed in a natural conversation.

entry_json.definition: the process of choosing, or a group of things that have been chosen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The selection process took almost three months.
example_sentences: The shop offers a wide selection of local produce.
Selection for the team is based entirely on performance.

contexts.text: The selection process took almost three months from application to offer.
There's a really good selection of restaurants near where I live.
Selection criteria should be published before applications open.

confusables.difference: A choice is the act or the freedom of choosing. A selection is the range available, or the formal process of choosing.
minimal_pair: It's your choice.
a wide selection of books

confusables.difference: Range emphasises coverage from one extreme to the other; selection emphasises that someone has chosen what to offer.

entry_json.avoid: 'A wide selection of' is followed by a plural or uncountable noun, never a singular countable one.

entry_json.definition: the kind of person you really are, including your character and your feelings
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long-term stress can leave people feeling cut off from their usual self.
example_sentences: After a month of rest she was back to her old self.
Social media rewards a polished version of the self rather than the real person.

contexts.text: Long-term stress can leave people feeling cut off from their usual self.
Honestly, I didn't feel like my usual self at all that week.
The study examines how adolescents build a sense of self online.

confusables.difference: Self is a neutral noun for who you are. Selfish is a negative adjective meaning you think only about yourself.
minimal_pair: He is rediscovering his true self.
He is selfish about money.

confusables.difference: Myself is a reflexive pronoun used with a verb. The self is a noun you can put 'the' or 'my' in front of.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'self' where English wants a reflexive pronoun: say "I did it myself", not "I did it self".

entry_json.definition: high in rank or position, or older than other people in a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Decisions of this size are normally taken by senior managers rather than by the team.
example_sentences: She was promoted to a senior role after only three years.
Senior citizens travel free on buses in most British cities.

contexts.text: Decisions of this size are normally taken by senior managers rather than by the team.
My sister is a senior nurse now, so she does a lot of the training.
Women remain under-represented in senior academic posts.

confusables.difference: Senior is about rank at work, or polite age. Elder is only about age within a family or community, and cannot follow 'more'.
minimal_pair: She is senior to me at the bank.
My elder brother lives abroad.

confusables.difference: Older simply compares age. Senior adds authority: a senior colleague may be younger than you.

entry_json.avoid: Say "senior to me", not "senior than me". Senior takes 'to', never 'than'.

entry_json.definition: showing good judgement; practical and reasonable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A sensible revision plan leaves time for sleep as well as for study.
example_sentences: It would be sensible to book the ticket before prices rise.
She gave me some very sensible advice about choosing a course.

contexts.text: A sensible revision plan leaves time for sleep as well as for study.
I think the sensible thing is to save first and travel later.
A sensible policy would combine higher fuel taxes with better public transport.

confusables.difference: Sensible means practical and wise. Sensitive means easily hurt or quick to notice feelings. Learners swap these two constantly.
minimal_pair: He is sensible with money.
He is sensitive about his accent.

confusables.difference: Reasonable is about being fair or acceptable; sensible is about showing good judgement.

entry_json.avoid: Sensible does not mean 'able to feel'. "I am sensible about the noise" is wrong; you mean sensitive.

entry_json.definition: easily affected, hurt or upset; or needing to be treated with care
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Immigration is a sensitive topic, so writers should present both sides carefully.
example_sentences: My skin is sensitive to strong sunlight.
Teachers need to be sensitive to the pressure that exams put on students.

contexts.text: Immigration is a sensitive topic, so writers should present both sides carefully.
I'm quite sensitive to caffeine, so I stop drinking coffee after lunch.
Coral reefs are extremely sensitive to small rises in water temperature.

confusables.difference: Sensitive is about feeling and reacting. Sensible is about thinking clearly and acting wisely.
minimal_pair: She is sensitive to noise.
She is sensible with her time.

confusables.difference: Touchy is informal and negative, suggesting someone is too easily offended. Sensitive is neutral and safe in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'sensitive to', not 'sensitive for'. Also, praising a person as 'sensible' when you mean kind and aware is a different word.

entry_json.definition: a set of events, actions or numbers that follow one another in a particular order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The diagram shows the sequence of stages in the recycling of glass.
example_sentences: The photographs are arranged in the sequence in which they were taken.
A short sequence of simple exercises is enough to warm up before running.

contexts.text: The diagram shows the sequence of stages in the recycling of glass.
We had to put the slides back in the right sequence before the presentation.
Figure 2 sets out the sequence of chemical reactions involved.

confusables.difference: A sequence has a fixed order that matters. A series is simply a number of similar things, ordered or not.
minimal_pair: The sequence of steps cannot be changed.
There was a series of accidents last winter.

confusables.difference: Order is the arrangement itself; a sequence is the set of items in that arrangement.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 process questions, write 'the sequence of stages', not 'the sequences' — the singular covers the whole process.

entry_json.definition: in a way that is severe or important; or in a way that shows you mean what you say
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few governments took the warnings about air quality seriously enough.
example_sentences: He was seriously injured in a cycling accident last year.
Seriously, you should apply for that scholarship.

contexts.text: Few governments took the warnings about air quality seriously enough.
Seriously, the traffic in my city has got much worse in five years.
The findings should be taken seriously by policymakers.

confusables.difference: Severely describes how bad something is. Seriously does that too, but only seriously can mean 'genuinely, not joking'.
minimal_pair: He was seriously ill.
The town was severely damaged.

confusables.difference: Badly is more informal for physical harm; seriously is safer in an essay.

entry_json.avoid: 'Seriously?' as a one-word reaction is spoken only. Keep it out of Task 2.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to work in someone else's house, cooking, cleaning or similar
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the nineteenth century, thousands of young women worked as servants in city houses.
example_sentences: The museum shows how servants lived below the main rooms of the house.
Her grandmother was a servant in a large country home.

contexts.text: In the nineteenth century, thousands of young women worked as servants in city houses.
My grandfather was a civil servant, so we moved around the country a lot.
Domestic servants formed a large share of the urban workforce in 1900.

confusables.difference: Employee is the ordinary modern word for anyone with a job. Servant now sounds historical, or means someone working in a private house.
minimal_pair: She is an employee of the bank.
The house had three servants.

confusables.difference: A civil servant works for the government, not in a private home. The two-word phrase has a completely different meaning.

entry_json.avoid: Do not call ordinary staff 'servants' in an essay — it sounds insulting. Use staff, employees or workers.

entry_json.definition: a period of time spent doing one particular activity
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most courses now include a weekly session in which students practise speaking.
example_sentences: I book a two-hour session in the library every Tuesday evening.
The training session was cancelled because the coach was ill.

contexts.text: Most courses now include a weekly session in which students practise speaking.
I usually do a short gym session before work.
Participants attended six therapy sessions over three months.

confusables.difference: A lesson is taught by someone and has content. A session is any block of time given to an activity, taught or not.
minimal_pair: I have a piano lesson on Fridays.
I did a long study session on Friday.

confusables.difference: A meeting is people discussing something; a session is time spent doing something.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'make a session'. You have, hold, attend or run a session.

entry_json.definition: the place and conditions in which something happens; or a position on a machine's controls
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a language in a natural setting is very different from learning it in a classroom.
example_sentences: The hotel has a beautiful setting between the lake and the mountains.
Change the setting on the washing machine to a lower temperature.

contexts.text: Learning a language in a natural setting is very different from learning it in a classroom.
I prefer studying in a quiet setting, ideally at home.
The experiment was repeated in a laboratory setting to control for noise.

confusables.difference: Scenery is the natural view you can see. Setting is the whole situation or surroundings, and can be a hospital or an office too.
minimal_pair: The scenery on the coast is stunning.
The novel has a wartime setting.

confusables.difference: Environment is broader and often means the natural world. Setting points at one specific place and situation.

entry_json.avoid: 'Settings' in the plural usually means the controls of a device. Do not use it when you mean one place.

entry_json.definition: to make your permanent home in a place, or to end an argument by reaching agreement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many graduates settle in the city where they studied rather than returning home.
example_sentences: The two companies settled the dispute without going to court.
My parents settled here in the 1990s and never moved again.

contexts.text: Many graduates settle in the city where they studied rather than returning home.
It took me about a month to settle in after I moved.
Migrants who settle permanently tend to send less money home over time.

confusables.difference: You solve a problem by finding an answer. You settle an argument or a claim by agreeing to stop it.
minimal_pair: They solved the technical problem.
They settled the dispute out of court.

confusables.difference: Move is the act of going somewhere new. Settle is staying and making a life there.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'settle to a country'. It is settle in a place, and settle down when you start a stable life.

entry_json.definition: very bad, serious or harsh
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Severe flooding forced hundreds of families to leave their homes last winter.
example_sentences: Patients with severe symptoms were treated first.
The penalties for drink-driving are severe in most countries.

contexts.text: Severe flooding forced hundreds of families to leave their homes last winter.
We had a really severe storm last year and the power went off for two days.
Severe air pollution is now the leading environmental risk to health.

confusables.difference: Serious is the general word and works everywhere. Severe is stronger and is used for weather, illness, damage and shortages.
minimal_pair: It is a serious problem.
The drought caused severe damage.

confusables.difference: Strict describes rules and people who enforce them. Severe describes the size of harm or punishment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use severe for a person's character in an essay; a person is strict, not severe, about rules.

entry_json.definition: the state of being male or female
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The table gives the number of applicants by age and sex.
example_sentences: The survey asked participants to state their age, sex and occupation.
In many countries, pay still differs between the sexes.

contexts.text: The table gives the number of applicants by age and sex.
At my school the classes were mixed, so both sexes studied together.
Life expectancy differs markedly by sex in almost every country.

confusables.difference: Sex refers to biological categories. Gender refers to social roles and identity, and is the safer word in most Task 2 essays about equality.
minimal_pair: Please state your sex on the form.
The essay discusses gender roles at work.

confusables.difference: Sex is the noun; sexual is the adjective. Do not write 'sex equality' when you mean gender equality.

entry_json.avoid: This word has a second, physical meaning, so keep it to data and forms in writing and prefer 'gender' when discussing society.

entry_json.definition: connected with whether someone is male or female, or with physical attraction between people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The law prohibits sexual discrimination in recruitment and pay.
example_sentences: The company has a clear policy on sexual harassment.
Health education in schools now covers sexual health.

contexts.text: The law prohibits sexual discrimination in recruitment and pay.
We had classes on sexual health when I was about fifteen.
Legislation on sexual equality in the workplace dates from the 1970s.

confusables.difference: In modern essays 'gender equality' and 'gender roles' are far more usual than 'sexual equality'. Keep sexual for health and harassment.
minimal_pair: The report examines gender equality.
The clinic offers sexual health advice.

entry_json.avoid: Because the word carries a physical meaning, choose 'gender' when writing about equality at work or in education.

entry_json.definition: an area that is dark and cooler because the sun does not reach it; or a particular form of a colour
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Planting trees along wide streets provides shade and lowers summer temperatures.
example_sentences: We sat in the shade of an old tree and waited for the bus.
The walls were painted in a pale shade of green.

contexts.text: Planting trees along wide streets provides shade and lowers summer temperatures.
When it's hot I always look for a seat in the shade.
Street trees can reduce surface temperatures by providing shade during peak hours.

confusables.difference: Shade is a whole cool area out of the sun. A shadow is the dark shape one particular object makes.
minimal_pair: We ate lunch in the shade.
The tower cast a long shadow.

confusables.difference: Shade is normally uncountable when it means coolness; shadow is countable when it means a shape.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'under the shadow of a tree' when you mean sitting out of the sun. That is 'in the shade'.

entry_json.definition: the dark shape that something makes on a surface when it blocks the light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: By late afternoon the tower blocks cast long shadows across the whole square.
example_sentences: Her shadow moved along the wall as she walked past the window.
Photographers work early in the morning when the shadows are soft.

contexts.text: By late afternoon the tower blocks cast long shadows across the whole square.
The new building puts our whole garden in shadow after about four o'clock.
The scandal cast a long shadow over the government's environmental record.

confusables.difference: A shadow is a dark shape with an outline. Shade is the cool area you sit in.
minimal_pair: The tree cast a shadow on the path.
The tree gave us welcome shade.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in the shadow' when you mean protected from the sun; use 'in the shade'.

entry_json.definition: not deep, measured from the top to the bottom; or not showing serious thought
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children swim safely at the shallow end of the pool while adults use the deep end.
example_sentences: The river is shallow enough to walk across in summer.
The essay gives a shallow account of a complicated problem.

contexts.text: Children swim safely at the shallow end of the pool while adults use the deep end.
I only swim in the shallow part because I never learned properly.
Shallow coastal waters warm faster than the open ocean.

confusables.difference: Both can mean 'lacking depth of thought', but superficial is the normal academic choice. Shallow sounds like a personal criticism.
minimal_pair: The analysis is superficial.
He is quite a shallow person.

confusables.difference: Low is about height from the ground. Shallow is about depth from the surface downwards.

entry_json.avoid: Do not describe a person as 'shallow' in an essay; it is a judgement, not an argument.

entry_json.definition: the bad feeling you have when you know you have done something wrong or embarrassing; or a situation you are sorry about
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many people who lose their jobs feel a sense of shame that stops them asking for help.
example_sentences: It is a shame that the old library was demolished.
He admitted the mistake without any attempt to hide his shame.

contexts.text: Many people who lose their jobs feel a sense of shame that stops them asking for help.
It's a shame the museum closes so early, because I'd love to spend longer there.
Public shame remains a powerful reason for under-reporting mental illness.

confusables.difference: Guilt is about the act: you did something wrong. Shame is about the self: you feel you are bad or exposed.
minimal_pair: He felt guilt over the lie he had told.
He felt shame at being seen there.

confusables.difference: 'It's a shame' and 'it's a pity' both mean 'that is unfortunate'. Both are conversational.

entry_json.avoid: "What a shame!" is spoken English. In Task 2 write 'unfortunately' or 'regrettably'.

entry_json.definition: having a thin edge or fine point that cuts easily; or sudden and large, of a change
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a sharp rise in electric car sales after 2020.
example_sentences: Be careful with that knife because the blade is very sharp.
There was a sharp fall in visitor numbers during the pandemic.

contexts.text: The graph shows a sharp rise in electric car sales after 2020.
I keep one really sharp knife for vegetables and use the others for everything else.
Unemployment recorded a sharp increase in the first quarter of 2009.

confusables.difference: Both describe a fast change on a graph. Steep describes the line itself; sharp describes the change and is more common with 'rise' and 'fall'.
minimal_pair: There was a sharp fall in prices.
The line shows a steep decline.

confusables.difference: Sudden is only about speed. Sharp adds size: a sharp rise is both quick and big.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'sharp' for gradual movement on a chart; that is a gradual or steady rise.

entry_json.definition: a flat board fixed to a wall or in a cupboard, used for putting things on
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The top shelf in the library holds the reference books that cannot be borrowed.
example_sentences: I put the dictionary back on the shelf where I found it.
The shelves in the supermarket were almost empty by Sunday evening.

contexts.text: The top shelf in the library holds the reference books that cannot be borrowed.
I've got one shelf just for the books I actually reread.
Products placed at eye level on the shelf sell substantially better.

confusables.difference: A cupboard is the whole enclosed space with a door. A shelf is one flat board, inside a cupboard or on an open wall.
minimal_pair: Put the plates in the cupboard.
Put the plates on the shelf.

entry_json.avoid: The plural is irregular: shelves, not 'shelfs'.

entry_json.definition: the hard outer covering of an egg, a nut, or an animal such as a snail or crab
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Turtles are easy to identify by the pattern on the shell.
example_sentences: Crack the shell and pour the egg into the pan.
We collected shells along the beach at low tide.

contexts.text: Turtles are easy to identify by the pattern on the shell.
As a kid I used to collect shells every summer holiday.
More acidic seawater makes it harder for molluscs to form a shell.

confusables.difference: Skin is soft and flexible, on people, fruit and animals. A shell is hard and protective.
minimal_pair: Peel the skin off the orange.
Crack the shell of the nut.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'shell' for the outside of fruit — that is skin or peel.

entry_json.definition: protection from bad weather or danger, or a building that gives that protection
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Food, clean water and shelter are the first needs after any natural disaster.
example_sentences: We took shelter in a doorway until the rain stopped.
The council opened a night shelter for people sleeping on the street.

contexts.text: Food, clean water and shelter are the first needs after any natural disaster.
There's a bus shelter outside my flat, so at least you stay dry waiting.
Emergency shelter is normally the first form of aid to arrive.

confusables.difference: Housing means permanent homes and the system that supplies them. Shelter is basic, often temporary protection.
minimal_pair: The city needs more affordable housing.
The charity provides shelter for a single night.

confusables.difference: Refuge is safety from people or persecution; shelter is usually from weather or from having nowhere to sleep.

entry_json.avoid: Shelter is uncountable when it means protection: write 'provide shelter', not 'provide a shelter', unless you mean one building.

entry_json.definition: a change in position, opinion or method; or a period of work in a place that operates day and night
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There has been a clear shift towards working from home since 2020.
example_sentences: Nurses on the night shift often struggle to sleep properly.
The data show a shift in public opinion on renewable energy.

contexts.text: There has been a clear shift towards working from home since 2020.
My brother works shifts, so we hardly ever eat dinner together.
The figures indicate a gradual shift from coal to gas between 1990 and 2010.

confusables.difference: Change is the neutral word for anything becoming different. A shift is a movement in direction, usually gradual and in one clear direction.
minimal_pair: There was a change in the timetable.
There was a shift towards online study.

confusables.difference: A move is a single decision or action; a shift is a broader trend.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'a shift towards' or 'a shift in', not 'a shift of', when describing a trend.

entry_json.definition: to produce or reflect light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Solar panels generate very little power on days when the sun does not shine.
example_sentences: The sun was shining when we arrived at the coast.
Someone shone a torch through the window.

contexts.text: Solar panels generate very little power on days when the sun does not shine.
Where I live the sun shines almost every day in summer.
The report shines a light on conditions in the garment industry.

confusables.difference: Shine is the verb, shiny is the adjective. "The floor shines" and "a shiny floor" are both right; "the floor is shine" is not.
minimal_pair: Her shoes shine.
She has shiny shoes.

entry_json.avoid: The past tense is shone /ʃɒn/ for light, not 'shined'. Use shined only for polishing shoes.

entry_json.definition: smooth and bright, reflecting the light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertisements always show a shiny new car parked on an empty road.
example_sentences: The kitchen surfaces were shiny and completely clean.
He bought a pair of shiny black shoes for the interview.

contexts.text: Advertisements always show a shiny new car parked on an empty road.
I like phones with a matt back rather than a shiny one, because of fingerprints.
Consumers respond to shiny packaging even when the product is identical.

confusables.difference: Bright means giving out a lot of light. Shiny means reflecting light from a smooth surface.
minimal_pair: The room is bright.
The table is shiny.

entry_json.avoid: Shiny is an everyday adjective. In academic writing prefer 'polished' or 'reflective' for surfaces.

entry_json.definition: a strong feeling of surprise caused by something unpleasant and unexpected
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The sudden rise in energy prices came as a shock to households across Europe.
example_sentences: The news of the closure was a shock to everyone in the department.
She is still in shock after the accident.

contexts.text: The sudden rise in energy prices came as a shock to households across Europe.
Moving to a colder country was a bit of a shock at first.
An external price shock can push a fragile economy into recession.

confusables.difference: A surprise can be pleasant. A shock is nearly always unpleasant and much stronger.
minimal_pair: Her visit was a lovely surprise.
The bill was a nasty shock.

confusables.difference: Shock is the noun for the event or feeling; shocked is the adjective describing the person.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'it came as a shock', not 'it came as shock'. The countable use needs an article.

entry_json.definition: feeling upset or very surprised by something unpleasant
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Readers were shocked by how little of the plastic collected is actually recycled.
example_sentences: I was shocked to hear that the course had been cancelled.
Local residents are shocked at the scale of the flooding.

contexts.text: Readers were shocked by how little of the plastic collected is actually recycled.
I was honestly shocked at how expensive rent was when I moved there.
Respondents were shocked by the level of misinformation they encountered online.

confusables.difference: Shocked describes the person who feels it. Shocking describes the thing that causes it.
minimal_pair: I was shocked by the figures.
The figures are shocking.

confusables.difference: Surprised is neutral. Shocked adds distress, so do not use it for good news.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write "the news was shocked". News is shocking; people are shocked.

entry_json.definition: to fire a gun at someone or something; or to film or photograph something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The documentary was shot over three years in six different countries.
example_sentences: The film was shot entirely on a mobile phone.
Police are trained not to shoot unless there is no alternative.

contexts.text: The documentary was shot over three years in six different countries.
A friend of mine shoots weddings at weekends to earn extra money.
Much of the footage was shot on hand-held cameras.

confusables.difference: Shoot is the verb; shot is both the past tense and a separate noun meaning a photograph or an attempt.

confusables.difference: Cotton comes from a plant and is cheap and everyday. Silk comes from insects, is smooth and shiny, and is expensive.

entry_json.definition: showing a lack of thought or good sense; not serious

entry_json.definition: to some degree; rather, but not extremely

entry_json.definition: in or from the south of a country or region

entry_json.definition: a person with deep knowledge of one particular subject or area of work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Patients often wait months to see a specialist even when a diagnosis is urgent.

entry_json.definition: a group of animals or plants that are alike and can breed with each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Around a million species are now considered at risk of extinction.

example_sentences: I need to move all my stuff out of the flat by Friday.
There is a lot of interesting stuff on that website.

contexts.text: Most of the stuff in the average cupboard is used once and then forgotten.
I've got far too much stuff for a one-bedroom flat.
Journalists use stuff freely, but examiners expect a more precise noun in an essay.

confusables.difference: Things is neutral and acceptable in semi-formal speech. Stuff is more casual and always uncountable.
minimal_pair: I packed a few things.
I packed a load of stuff.

confusables.difference: Belongings is the formal word and is the one to use in a letter or an essay.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'stuff' in Task 2. Write 'possessions', 'materials' or 'items' instead.

entry_json.definition: to give a document or piece of work to someone in authority so that it can be considered
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Applicants must submit references before the closing date, not afterwards.
example_sentences: I submitted my essay two hours before the deadline.
Please submit the completed form to the admissions office.

contexts.text: Applicants must submit references before the closing date, not afterwards.
I submitted the application online and heard back within a week.
Authors are asked to submit manuscripts through the online portal.

confusables.difference: Send is neutral and covers any delivery. Submit means handing work to an authority that will judge it.
minimal_pair: I sent her the file.
I submitted the assignment.

confusables.difference: Hand in is the informal equivalent, common in speech and at school. Submit is the formal choice.

entry_json.avoid: Double the t: submitted, submitting. And write 'submit to the office', not 'submit for the office'.

entry_json.definition: a type of solid, liquid or gas with particular qualities
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cleaning products often contain substances that are harmful if they enter waterways.
example_sentences: The bottle contained a clear substance with no smell.
Certain substances are banned from hand luggage.

contexts.text: Cleaning products often contain substances that are harmful if they enter waterways.
They tested the water and found some substance they couldn't identify.
The substance breaks down slowly and accumulates in the food chain.

confusables.difference: Material is what an object is made from, like wood or cotton. Substance is a chemical or physical stuff, often studied scientifically.
minimal_pair: The chairs are made of a cheap material.
The lab identified the substance.

confusables.difference: Matter is everything physical, in the broadest scientific sense; a substance is one specific kind.

entry_json.avoid: 'Substance' also means the important content of an argument, as in 'an argument of substance'. Keep the two senses apart.

entry_json.definition: in a way that achieves the result you wanted
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several cities have successfully cut traffic by charging drivers to enter the centre.
example_sentences: She successfully completed the course in eighteen months.
The scheme has been successfully trialled in three regions.

contexts.text: Several cities have successfully cut traffic by charging drivers to enter the centre.
I successfully passed my driving test on the second attempt.
The vaccine was successfully deployed across the whole population within a year.

confusables.difference: Effectively means it produced the intended effect and is often about method. Successfully means the goal was reached.
minimal_pair: The drug works effectively.
She successfully finished the programme.

entry_json.avoid: Mind the spelling: two c's, two s's, then -fully with two l's.

entry_json.definition: happening quickly and without warning
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A sudden change in the weather can turn an easy walk into a dangerous one.
example_sentences: There was a sudden drop in temperature overnight.
His sudden departure surprised everyone in the office.

contexts.text: A sudden change in the weather can turn an easy walk into a dangerous one.
All of a sudden the lights went out and the whole street was dark.
The sudden withdrawal of funding halted the project in 2015.

confusables.difference: Unexpected is about surprise: you did not predict it. Sudden is about speed: it happened at once.
minimal_pair: The result was unexpected.
The change was sudden.

confusables.difference: Quick describes how fast something is done. Sudden describes something starting with no warning.

entry_json.avoid: 'All of a sudden' is an informal spoken phrase. In writing use 'suddenly' or 'without warning'.

entry_json.definition: to experience something unpleasant, such as pain, illness or damage
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coastal communities suffer most when storms become more frequent.
example_sentences: Around one in six adults suffers from chronic back pain.
The local economy suffered badly after the factory closed.

contexts.text: Coastal communities suffer most when storms become more frequent.
My mother suffers from arthritis, so she finds stairs difficult.
Low-income households suffer disproportionately from rising fuel costs.

confusables.difference: Hurt is what you feel at one moment, or what you do to someone. Suffer is enduring something bad over time.
minimal_pair: My knee hurts.
He has suffered from asthma since childhood.

confusables.difference: Bear means to tolerate something without complaining. Suffer is simply experiencing it.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'suffer from' for illnesses, but no preposition for events: 'suffer damage', not 'suffer from damage'.

entry_json.definition: right or acceptable for a particular purpose, person or occasion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Not every candidate is suitable for a job that involves working alone.
example_sentences: The film is not suitable for young children.
We are still looking for a suitable venue for the conference.

contexts.text: Not every candidate is suitable for a job that involves working alone.
The flat wasn't really suitable for two people, so we moved again.
The site was judged suitable for wind generation after two years of measurement.

confusables.difference: Appropriate is about being socially or ethically right. Suitable is about being practically fit for the purpose.
minimal_pair: That language is not appropriate at work.
These shoes are not suitable for walking.

confusables.difference: Convenient means easy and time-saving for you. Suitable means genuinely fit for the job.

entry_json.avoid: Suitable takes 'for', not 'to': 'suitable for beginners'.

entry_json.definition: an amount of money; or the total you get by adding numbers together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments spend vast sums on road building while cycling schemes wait for funding.
example_sentences: She was offered a large sum of money to leave the case.
The sum of the two figures is just over four million.

contexts.text: Governments spend vast sums on road building while cycling schemes wait for funding.
I had to borrow quite a large sum to pay the deposit.
Considerable sums have been invested in flood defences since 2007.

confusables.difference: Amount is the everyday word for a quantity of anything uncountable. Sum is specifically money or the result of addition.
minimal_pair: A large amount of water was lost.
A large sum of money was lost.

confusables.difference: Total is the final figure after adding. Sum can mean the same, but also means simply 'an amount of money'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Sums' meaning arithmetic ('do your sums') is informal British English. Keep it out of essays.

entry_json.definition: to give the main points of something without the details
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Task 1 asks candidates to summarize the information rather than describe every figure.
example_sentences: Could you summarize the report in a couple of sentences?
The final paragraph summarizes the main arguments.

contexts.text: Task 1 asks candidates to summarize the information rather than describe every figure.
Let me summarize what I've said so far, because I've covered a lot.
Table 3 summarizes the findings of the eleven studies reviewed.

confusables.difference: Describe means giving the details. Summarize means cutting them and keeping only the main points.
minimal_pair: Describe the process in detail.
Summarize the main trends.

confusables.difference: Conclude states what you infer from the evidence. Summarize just restates what is there.

entry_json.avoid: The British spelling 'summarise' is equally correct. Pick one spelling convention and keep to it throughout your essay.

entry_json.definition: a short account giving only the main points of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A good summary of a chart names the highest and lowest values and the overall direction.
example_sentences: Write a one-page summary of the article for Friday.
In summary, the costs outweigh the benefits.

contexts.text: A good summary of a chart names the highest and lowest values and the overall direction.
I always read the summary first to see if the article is worth my time.
The executive summary should be no longer than a single page.

confusables.difference: A conclusion states the judgement you reach. A summary restates the content without adding a judgement.
minimal_pair: In conclusion, the policy should be abandoned.
In summary, costs rose and use fell.

confusables.difference: An overview gives the shape of the whole subject; a summary condenses one particular text.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 the required sentence is the 'overview', which is a summary. Do not confuse it with 'In conclusion', which belongs in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: an amount of something that is available to be used, or the system that provides it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: When supply falls behind demand, prices rise regardless of what governments promise.
example_sentences: The city's water supply comes from three reservoirs.
There is a limited supply of affordable housing near the centre.

contexts.text: When supply falls behind demand, prices rise regardless of what governments promise.
Our water supply was cut off for a whole day last month.
Global supply of rare earth metals is concentrated in a handful of countries.

confusables.difference: Supply is how much is available; demand is how much people want. Task 1 essays about markets need both.
minimal_pair: Supply exceeded demand.
Demand exceeded supply.

confusables.difference: Stock is the amount held in store right now. Supply is the flow reaching the market.

entry_json.avoid: 'Supply and demand' is a fixed pair in that order. Reversing it sounds odd.

entry_json.definition: a person who supports a team, a political party or an idea
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Supporters of the scheme argue that it will pay for itself within a decade.
example_sentences: Thousands of supporters travelled to the final.
She has been a lifelong supporter of the local club.

contexts.text: Supporters of the scheme argue that it will pay for itself within a decade.
I've been a supporter of the same team since I was six.
Supporters of congestion charging point to the improvement in air quality.

confusables.difference: Fan is warmer and covers music and film as well as sport. Supporter suggests loyalty and is the usual word for a football club or a cause.
minimal_pair: I am a fan of her novels.
I am a supporter of the local team.

confusables.difference: A member has formally joined and usually pays. A supporter may simply agree.

entry_json.avoid: For an argument in Task 2, 'supporters of X argue that' is a useful frame. 'Fans of X' would sound wrong.

entry_json.definition: used to show that you believe something is true and expect others to agree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Surely a city that limits cars should also invest in the buses that replace them.
example_sentences: Surely it would be cheaper to repair the building than to replace it.
There must surely be a better way of organising the timetable.

contexts.text: Surely a city that limits cars should also invest in the buses that replace them.
Surely it makes more sense to cycle if the distance is that short?
Such a policy must surely be judged against its cost to poorer households.

confusables.difference: Certainly states that you are sure. Surely appeals to the listener to agree with you, and often expects a yes.
minimal_pair: It will certainly rain.
Surely it will rain?

confusables.difference: Definitely is a firm statement of fact; surely is a rhetorical push.

entry_json.avoid: Do not answer a question with 'Surely' meaning 'of course'. That is 'Certainly' or 'Definitely'.

entry_json.definition: the outside or top layer of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: More than seventy per cent of the earth's surface is covered by ocean.
example_sentences: Wipe the surface with a damp cloth before you start.
Oil spread across the surface of the water.

contexts.text: More than seventy per cent of the earth's surface is covered by ocean.
The kitchen surfaces get dirty so quickly with two children around.
Surface temperatures have risen by roughly one degree since 1900.

confusables.difference: Top is the highest part of an object. Surface is the whole outer layer, which may be the side or the underneath as well.
minimal_pair: Put it on top of the box.
Clean the whole surface.

confusables.difference: Outside is the exterior seen as a place; surface is the layer itself.

entry_json.avoid: Note the stress and vowel: /ˈsɜːfɪs/, with a weak second syllable, not 'sur-FACE'.

entry_json.definition: medical treatment in which a doctor cuts into the body to repair or remove something; in British English also a doctor's consulting room
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Waiting times for routine surgery have lengthened in almost every public health system.
example_sentences: She needs surgery on her knee after the accident.
The doctor's surgery is open until six on weekdays.

contexts.text: Waiting times for routine surgery have lengthened in almost every public health system.
I had surgery on my shoulder two years ago and it still aches sometimes.
Elective surgery was postponed in order to free intensive care capacity.

confusables.difference: An operation is one countable event. Surgery is usually uncountable and refers to the treatment in general.
minimal_pair: He had an operation on Tuesday.
He needs surgery.

confusables.difference: In British English 'the surgery' is the GP's building; a clinic is usually specialised.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a surgery' when you mean one operation. Say 'an operation' or 'a surgical procedure'.

entry_json.definition: to be all around something or someone on every side
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Green belts surround many British cities and limit how far they can expand.
example_sentences: High walls surround the old part of the town.
Considerable uncertainty surrounds the cost of the project.

contexts.text: Green belts surround many British cities and limit how far they can expand.
My village is surrounded by fields, so it's very quiet.
Uncertainty continues to surround the long-term effects of the treatment.

confusables.difference: Cover means lying over the top of something. Surround means being around its edges.
minimal_pair: Snow covered the field.
Trees surrounded the field.

confusables.difference: Enclose implies a complete barrier that keeps things in; surround is simply being on all sides.

entry_json.avoid: The passive is very common: 'the house is surrounded by trees'. Do not omit 'by'.

entry_json.definition: that is near or all around a particular place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new hospital serves the city and the whole surrounding region.
example_sentences: Air quality is poor in the surrounding streets as well as on the main road.
Flooding affected the village and the surrounding farmland.

contexts.text: The new hospital serves the city and the whole surrounding region.
I live in the city but most of my family are in the surrounding towns.
Noise levels were measured in the surrounding residential area.

confusables.difference: Surroundings is a plural noun meaning the place you are in. Surrounding is an adjective placed before a noun.
minimal_pair: I like my surroundings.
I like the surrounding hills.

confusables.difference: Nearby can come after a noun and means simply close. Surrounding means on all sides.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the surroundings area'. The adjective has no s.

entry_json.definition: to continue to live or exist, especially after a difficult or dangerous situation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Small independent shops struggle to survive once a supermarket opens nearby.
example_sentences: Only two of the original buildings survive today.
Most patients now survive the illness if it is caught early.

contexts.text: Small independent shops struggle to survive once a supermarket opens nearby.
I don't know how students survive on that budget in this city.
Coral colonies that survive bleaching events remain more vulnerable for years.

confusables.difference: Live is about being alive generally. Survive means continuing to live through something that could have ended it.
minimal_pair: She lives in Leeds.
She survived the crash.

confusables.difference: Remain means staying in place or condition. Survive implies danger has been overcome.

entry_json.avoid: Survive takes no preposition before the danger: 'survive the storm', not 'survive from the storm'.

entry_json.definition: to think that something is probably true, especially something bad, without being certain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Researchers suspect that the real figure is far higher than official reports admit.
example_sentences: Doctors suspected an infection and ordered further tests.
I suspect the delay has more to do with cost than with safety.

contexts.text: Researchers suspect that the real figure is far higher than official reports admit.
I suspect I'll end up staying here longer than I planned.
The authors suspect that self-reporting understates actual consumption.

confusables.difference: Suspect and doubt point in opposite directions. If you suspect something is true, you think it probably is. If you doubt it, you think it probably is not.
minimal_pair: I suspect he is right.
I doubt he is right.

confusables.difference: Expect is about the future and is neutral. Suspect is about what may already be the case and carries suspicion.

entry_json.avoid: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, /səˈspekt/. The noun 'a suspect' is stressed on the first, /ˈsʌspekt/.

entry_json.definition: to use rude or offensive language; or to make a serious promise
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Broadcasters still receive complaints when contributors swear before nine in the evening.
example_sentences: He swore loudly when the printer jammed again.
Witnesses swear to tell the truth before they give evidence.

contexts.text: Broadcasters still receive complaints when contributors swear before nine in the evening.
My grandmother never swore once in her life, as far as I know.
Witnesses must swear an oath before testifying in court.

confusables.difference: Curse can mean the same as swear, but it also means wishing harm on someone. Swear is the ordinary British word for bad language.
minimal_pair: He swore under his breath.
She cursed her bad luck.

confusables.difference: Promise is the everyday word. Swear is formal and legal, or emphatic in speech.

entry_json.avoid: Irregular forms: swear, swore, sworn. And 'swear at someone' is abuse, while 'swear to something' is a promise.

entry_json.definition: to clean a floor or surface using a brush; or to move quickly and powerfully across an area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wildfires now sweep through regions that were considered too wet to burn.
example_sentences: He sweeps the shop floor before opening every morning.
The new technology swept across the industry within five years.

contexts.text: Wildfires now sweep through regions that were considered too wet to burn.
I sweep the kitchen every evening, otherwise it gets out of control.
Reform swept through the higher education sector in the early 1990s.

confusables.difference: Brush is what you do with a small brush to clothes, hair or teeth. Sweep is for floors and larger surfaces.
minimal_pair: Brush your coat.
Sweep the floor.

confusables.difference: Wipe uses a cloth and removes marks; sweep uses a brush and removes loose dirt.

entry_json.avoid: Irregular past: swept, not 'sweeped'.

entry_json.definition: to change from one thing to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Households that switch to a cheaper energy tariff save more than most people expect.
example_sentences: I switched from a bus pass to a bicycle last spring.
Many students switch courses after the first year.

contexts.text: Households that switch to a cheaper energy tariff save more than most people expect.
I switched to a different provider and my bill dropped by a third.
Consumers rarely switch supplier even when substantial savings are available.

confusables.difference: Change is the general verb and can be used for anything. Switch means moving between two clear options, usually deliberately.
minimal_pair: I changed my mind.
I switched to the other course.

confusables.difference: Swap is exchanging with another person. Switch is moving your own choice from A to B.

entry_json.avoid: 'Switch off' means to turn off a device. Do not use it for stopping an activity in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: the feeling of being sorry for someone who is in a difficult or sad situation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public sympathy for striking workers depends heavily on how the dispute is reported.
example_sentences: She wrote a short letter of sympathy after hearing the news.
I have some sympathy with the argument, though I do not fully accept it.

contexts.text: Public sympathy for striking workers depends heavily on how the dispute is reported.
I have a lot of sympathy for people who commute two hours each way.
Media coverage shapes public sympathy towards refugees more than direct experience does.

confusables.difference: Empathy is understanding a feeling because you can imagine being in that position. Sympathy is feeling sorry from outside.
minimal_pair: She showed real empathy with the patients.
She expressed sympathy for the family.

confusables.difference: Pity can sound as though you look down on the person; sympathy does not.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'sympathy for a person' but 'sympathy with an argument'. The prepositions are not interchangeable.

entry_json.definition: the part at the back of an animal's body that sticks out beyond the rest
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A dog's tail tells you more about its mood than the noise it makes.
example_sentences: The cat sat on the wall, flicking its tail.
Fish use the tail to push themselves forward through the water.

contexts.text: A dog's tail tells you more about its mood than the noise it makes.
Our dog wags his tail the moment anyone touches the door handle.
The length of the tail varies considerably between the two subspecies.

confusables.difference: Tail and tale sound identical. A tale is a story; a tail is part of an animal.
minimal_pair: The dog wagged its tail.
She told a wonderful tale.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the spelling with 'tale'. This is one of the most common homophone errors in Writing.

entry_json.definition: a story, especially one that is exciting or invented
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every culture has a tale that warns children about the dangers of the forest.
example_sentences: My grandfather used to tell tales about life before electricity.
The film is a familiar tale of ambition and regret.

contexts.text: Every culture has a tale that warns children about the dangers of the forest.
My grandmother told us folk tales every summer when we visited.
The collection preserves oral tales that would otherwise have been lost.

confusables.difference: Story is the ordinary word and covers news reports too. Tale sounds older and more literary, and suits folk and fairy stories.
minimal_pair: I read a news story about it.
She retold an old folk tale.

confusables.difference: A tale is a story; a tail belongs to an animal. They sound the same.

entry_json.avoid: 'A cautionary tale' is a set phrase meaning a warning example. Do not write 'a cautionary story'.

entry_json.definition: a natural ability to do something well
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that fail to train their young people end up importing talent instead.
example_sentences: She has a real talent for explaining difficult ideas simply.
The competition is designed to find new musical talent.

contexts.text: Countries that fail to train their young people end up importing talent instead.
My sister has a real talent for languages, which I definitely don't.
Cities compete for talent as much as for investment.

confusables.difference: A skill is learned through practice. A talent is something you are born with, though it still needs developing.
minimal_pair: Typing is a skill you can learn.
Perfect pitch is a rare talent.

confusables.difference: Ability is the general capacity to do something, learned or not. Talent implies unusual natural gift.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'a talent for music', not 'a talent in music'.

entry_json.definition: having a natural ability to do something well
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Talented students from poor households are still far less likely to reach university.
example_sentences: He is the most talented player the club has produced in years.
The school has several talented young musicians.

contexts.text: Talented students from poor households are still far less likely to reach university.
My cousin is a really talented cook, but she has never worked in a kitchen.
Programmes for talented pupils risk widening the gap unless access is controlled.

confusables.difference: Skilled means trained and experienced. Talented means naturally gifted, which is not the same thing.
minimal_pair: He is a skilled electrician.
He is a talented singer.

confusables.difference: Gifted is the term used in education for children of exceptional ability; talented is more general.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'he has talented'. It is an adjective: 'he is talented' or 'he has talent'.

entry_json.definition: a large container for holding liquid or gas
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rainwater collected in a tank can cover most of a household's garden use.
example_sentences: The water tank on the roof holds five hundred litres.
I filled the tank before setting off on the long drive.

contexts.text: Rainwater collected in a tank can cover most of a household's garden use.
Our hot water tank broke in the middle of winter, which was miserable.
Storage tanks allow supply to be maintained through periods of drought.

confusables.difference: Container is the general word for anything that holds things. A tank holds liquid or gas and is usually large and fixed.
minimal_pair: Put the rice in a container.
The tank holds two thousand litres.

confusables.difference: A tank is also an armoured vehicle. Context normally makes the meaning obvious.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'tank' for a small bottle or jar. It implies a large fixed container.

entry_json.definition: a long narrow strip of material used for sticking things together or for recording sound
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Recordings on tape degrade within decades, which is why archives are being digitised.
example_sentences: Stick the poster to the wall with tape.
My father still has boxes of old tapes he cannot play.

contexts.text: Recordings on tape degrade within decades, which is why archives are being digitised.
I found a box of my parents' old tapes in the loft.
Magnetic tape remains in use for long-term archival storage.

confusables.difference: Glue is a liquid that dries. Tape is a strip you press on, and can usually be removed.
minimal_pair: Use glue for the model.
Use tape for the poster.

confusables.difference: Ribbon is decorative fabric; tape is functional.

entry_json.avoid: Tape is uncountable when it means the sticky strip: 'a roll of tape', not 'a tape'.

entry_json.definition: money that people and businesses must pay to the government to fund public services
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A tax on sugary drinks reduced consumption faster than public information campaigns did.
example_sentences: Income tax rates vary considerably between European countries.
The government has promised not to raise taxes before the election.

contexts.text: A tax on sugary drinks reduced consumption faster than public information campaigns did.
I pay a lot more tax now than I did in my first job.
A carbon tax raises the price of emissions and shifts demand towards cleaner alternatives.

confusables.difference: A fee is what you pay for a specific service you choose. Tax is compulsory and general.
minimal_pair: The visa fee is forty pounds.
Income tax is deducted automatically.

confusables.difference: A fine is a punishment for breaking a rule; tax is not a punishment.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'pay tax' or 'pay taxes', not 'pay the taxes' unless you mean particular ones.

entry_json.definition: connected with the practical use of machines, science or a specialised subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Technical problems delayed the launch by almost a year.
example_sentences: The manual is full of technical terms that ordinary users cannot follow.
She has a technical background in civil engineering.

contexts.text: Technical problems delayed the launch by almost a year.
There were technical problems with the video call, so we gave up.
Technical training is often undervalued relative to academic qualifications.

confusables.difference: Technological refers to technology as a field and to progress in it. Technical refers to the practical detail of how something works.
minimal_pair: Technological change is accelerating.
There was a technical fault.

confusables.difference: Scientific concerns discovering knowledge; technical concerns applying it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'technical development' when you mean progress in technology; that is 'technological development'.

entry_json.definition: a particular way of doing something, especially one that needs skill
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Note-taking techniques matter more in Listening than raw vocabulary does.
example_sentences: The surgeon uses a technique developed only five years ago.
She has an excellent swimming technique but very little stamina.

contexts.text: Note-taking techniques matter more in Listening than raw vocabulary does.
My teacher showed me a technique for remembering vocabulary and it works.
The technique allows samples to be analysed in under an hour.

confusables.difference: Method is the overall plan or system. Technique is the specific skilled way of carrying out one part of it.
minimal_pair: The study used a qualitative method.
The pianist has a superb technique.

confusables.difference: Technology is machines and systems; technique is human skill.

entry_json.avoid: Stress the second syllable: /tekˈniːk/, not like 'technical'.

entry_json.definition: lasting for only a limited time, not permanent
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Temporary contracts give employers flexibility and give workers very little security.
example_sentences: The road closure is temporary and will end in June.
She took a temporary job while looking for something permanent.

contexts.text: Temporary contracts give employers flexibility and give workers very little security.
I'm in temporary accommodation until my flat is ready.
Temporary migration has grown faster than permanent settlement since 2000.

confusables.difference: These are direct opposites and Task 2 essays on employment usually need both.
minimal_pair: He has a permanent contract.
She has a temporary contract.

confusables.difference: Short-term describes duration or planning horizon; temporary emphasises that it will definitely end.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: three syllables in normal British speech, /ˈtemprəri/, not 'tem-po-ra-ry'.

entry_json.definition: to usually do a particular thing, or to be likely to happen in a particular way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Younger people tend to rent for far longer than their parents did.
example_sentences: Prices tend to rise sharply in the weeks before a holiday.
I tend to work better in the morning than late at night.

contexts.text: Younger people tend to rent for far longer than their parents did.
I tend to cook at the weekend and eat leftovers during the week.
Respondents in urban areas tend to report higher levels of stress.

confusables.difference: Usually is an adverb of frequency. Tend is a verb, and 'tend to' is often the more academic way to hedge a general claim.
minimal_pair: Students usually arrive late.
Students tend to arrive late.

confusables.difference: Intend means to plan to do something. Tend means to do it habitually. The two are easily confused.

entry_json.avoid: Tend is followed by 'to' plus the infinitive: 'tend to increase', never 'tend increasing'.

entry_json.definition: a shelter made of cloth held up by poles, used for camping
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap tents end up in landfill after a single festival weekend.
example_sentences: We put the tent up before it got dark.
Two people can sleep comfortably in this tent.

contexts.text: Cheap tents end up in landfill after a single festival weekend.
