example_sentences: I bought a tube of toothpaste and some soap.
The gas travels through a narrow tube into the burner.

contexts.text: Water is carried across the city in tubes laid more than a century ago.
I take the tube to work, which takes about half an hour.
Samples were sealed in test tubes and stored at four degrees.

confusables.difference: A pipe is usually rigid and fixed, carrying water or gas in a building. A tube is often flexible or small.
minimal_pair: The pipe under the sink burst.
Blood is drawn into a small tube.

confusables.difference: A bottle is rigid with a neck; a tube is squeezed and collapses.

entry_json.avoid: 'The Tube' with a capital letter means the London Underground. Elsewhere in Britain the underground railway has other names.

entry_json.definition: a series of musical notes that is pleasant and easy to remember
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A memorable tune does more for a public health campaign than any amount of text.
example_sentences: I cannot remember the words, but the tune has stayed with me all day.
She hummed a tune while she worked.

contexts.text: A memorable tune does more for a public health campaign than any amount of text.
There's one tune from my childhood that I still hear everywhere.
Advertisers use a repeated tune to make a brand easier to recall.

confusables.difference: A song has words. A tune is the melody alone, which may have no words at all.
minimal_pair: She sang a beautiful song.
She whistled a familiar tune.

confusables.difference: Melody is the technical musical term; tune is the everyday word.

entry_json.avoid: 'In tune' means at the right pitch. Do not confuse it with 'in time', which is about rhythm.

entry_json.definition: a passage built underground or through a hill for a road, railway or people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A rail tunnel costs several times more per kilometre than track laid on the surface.
example_sentences: The train goes through a long tunnel just before the border.
Work on the new tunnel will take at least six years.

contexts.text: A rail tunnel costs several times more per kilometre than track laid on the surface.
The signal always drops when we go through the tunnel.
The tunnel reduced journey times between the two cities by an hour.

confusables.difference: A bridge goes over an obstacle; a tunnel goes under or through it.
minimal_pair: They built a bridge over the river.
They dug a tunnel under the river.

confusables.difference: An underpass is a short pedestrian passage under a road; a tunnel is much longer.

entry_json.avoid: Double the l in British English: tunnelled, tunnelling.

entry_json.definition: in most cases; in the way that is usual for a person, group or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Households typically spend about a third of their income on housing.
example_sentences: A consultation typically lasts around ten minutes.
Typically, applications rise sharply in the final week.

contexts.text: Households typically spend about a third of their income on housing.
I typically get up at six, even at the weekend.
Symptoms typically appear between two and five days after exposure.

confusables.difference: Usually is the everyday word for frequency. Typically suggests this is the standard pattern, and is more common in reports.
minimal_pair: I usually walk to work.
Journeys typically take twenty minutes.

confusables.difference: Generally means in most respects; typically means in the standard case.

entry_json.avoid: Do not overuse 'typically' as a synonym for 'always'. It allows exceptions.

entry_json.definition: the thick rubber ring fitted around the wheel of a vehicle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Worn tyres are a factor in a significant proportion of wet-weather accidents.
example_sentences: I had a flat tyre on the way to the station.
Check your tyres before a long journey.

contexts.text: Worn tyres are a factor in a significant proportion of wet-weather accidents.
I got a flat tyre on my bike and had to walk the rest of the way.
Tyre particles are now recognised as a major source of microplastic pollution.

confusables.difference: The wheel is the metal disc that turns. The tyre is the rubber fitted around it.
minimal_pair: The wheel was bent.
The tyre was flat.

confusables.difference: 'Tire' is the American spelling of this noun, and also a British verb meaning to become tired.

entry_json.avoid: With British examiners write 'tyre', not 'tire'.

entry_json.definition: unpleasant to look at
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap post-war blocks were widely called ugly, and many are now protected buildings.
example_sentences: The new car park is an ugly addition to a beautiful street.
Nobody wants an ugly building opposite their window.

contexts.text: Cheap post-war blocks were widely called ugly, and many are now protected buildings.
I think the new shopping centre is genuinely ugly, but my friends disagree.
Public opposition to the design centred on claims that it was ugly and out of scale.

confusables.difference: Unattractive is milder and more polite, and is the better choice in writing. Ugly is blunt.
minimal_pair: The site is unattractive.
The site is ugly.

confusables.difference: Plain means simple and undecorated, which is not the same as unpleasant to look at.

entry_json.avoid: Never describe a person as ugly in an essay. Even about buildings, 'unattractive' sounds more measured.

entry_json.definition: in the end, after everything else has been considered; or finally, after a long process
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Ultimately, the success of any recycling scheme depends on how easy it is to use.
example_sentences: The proposal was ultimately rejected by the council.
Ultimately it is the taxpayer who pays for these subsidies.

contexts.text: Ultimately, the success of any recycling scheme depends on how easy it is to use.
Ultimately I decided to stay, mostly because of my family.
Ultimately the policy shifted costs from the state to individual households.

confusables.difference: Finally is about the last item in a sequence or the end of a wait. Ultimately is about the fundamental point once everything is weighed.
minimal_pair: Finally, we discuss the limitations.
Ultimately, the decision rests with parliament.

confusables.difference: Eventually is about time passing before something happens; ultimately is about the underlying conclusion.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'ultimately' to introduce your last body paragraph. That is 'finally'.

entry_json.definition: not having the ability, opportunity or permission to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Patients who are unable to travel are the ones least likely to receive follow-up care.
example_sentences: I was unable to attend the meeting because of a delayed flight.
Many households are unable to afford the increase in rent.

contexts.text: Patients who are unable to travel are the ones least likely to receive follow-up care.
I was unable to get a ticket, so I watched it at home.
A third of respondents were unable to name a single local service.

confusables.difference: Cannot is the ordinary way to say this and is fine in speech and writing. Unable is more formal and is followed by 'to'.
minimal_pair: I cannot come.
I am unable to attend.

confusables.difference: Disabled describes a long-term condition. Unable describes a temporary or specific inability.

entry_json.avoid: Unable is always followed by 'to' plus a verb. 'Unable of doing' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: not physically relaxed or pleasant; or feeling embarrassed or worried
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long flights in economy class are uncomfortable in a way that no amount of planning solves.
example_sentences: The chairs in the lecture hall are extremely uncomfortable.
I felt uncomfortable being asked about my salary.

contexts.text: Long flights in economy class are uncomfortable in a way that no amount of planning solves.
The bus is cheap but really uncomfortable on a long journey.
Participants reported feeling uncomfortable when asked about household income.

confusables.difference: Unpleasant is about something being nasty in itself. Uncomfortable is about how it makes you feel physically or socially.
minimal_pair: The smell was unpleasant.
The seat was uncomfortable.

confusables.difference: Awkward describes a socially difficult situation; uncomfortable describes the feeling it produces.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /ʌnˈkʌmftəbl/, four syllables, not 'un-com-for-ta-ble'.

entry_json.definition: not awake and not aware of what is happening; or done without realising it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unconscious bias in recruitment is difficult to prove and easy to demonstrate in experiments.
example_sentences: He was unconscious for several minutes after the fall.
Many of our daily choices are largely unconscious.

contexts.text: Unconscious bias in recruitment is difficult to prove and easy to demonstrate in experiments.
He was unconscious when the ambulance arrived, but he recovered completely.
Unconscious associations shape hiring decisions even among trained assessors.

confusables.difference: Asleep is normal rest that you wake from naturally. Unconscious is a medical state you cannot be woken from.
minimal_pair: The baby is asleep.
The patient was unconscious.

confusables.difference: Subconscious refers to mental processes just below awareness. Unconscious is used both medically and for bias.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'he fell unconscious asleep'. The two words describe different states.

entry_json.definition: clothes worn next to the skin under other clothes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cheap underwear made from synthetic fibres sheds plastic every time it is washed.
example_sentences: Pack enough underwear for a week.
The shop sells underwear and socks on the ground floor.

contexts.text: Cheap underwear made from synthetic fibres sheds plastic every time it is washed.
I always forget to pack enough underwear when I travel.
Synthetic underwear contributes to microfibre release during laundering.

confusables.difference: Clothes is everything you wear. Underwear is only the layer worn next to the skin.
minimal_pair: I bought some new clothes.
I bought some new underwear.

entry_json.avoid: Underwear is uncountable. Write 'some underwear' or 'two pairs of underwear', never 'underwears'.

entry_json.definition: without a paid job, although wanting to work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young people who are unemployed for more than a year earn less for decades afterwards.
example_sentences: He was unemployed for eight months after the factory closed.
The scheme offers free training to unemployed adults.

contexts.text: Young people who are unemployed for more than a year earn less for decades afterwards.
I was unemployed for about six months and it was a difficult time.
The proportion of unemployed graduates fell steadily after 2013.

confusables.difference: Jobless is the journalistic word and appears in headlines. Unemployed is the standard term in reports and essays.
minimal_pair: Jobless totals rose again.
The unemployed rate rose again.

confusables.difference: Retired people have stopped working by choice or age; the unemployed are looking for work.

entry_json.avoid: 'The unemployed' takes a plural verb: 'the unemployed are entitled to support'.

entry_json.definition: the situation in which people who want jobs cannot find them, or the number of such people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment fell steadily from 2013 onwards, reaching its lowest level in the final year shown.
example_sentences: Youth unemployment remains far higher than the national average.
The region suffered high unemployment throughout the 1980s.

contexts.text: Unemployment fell steadily from 2013 onwards, reaching its lowest level in the final year shown.
Unemployment is quite high in my hometown, which is why people leave.
Unemployment among the under-25s peaked at twenty-two per cent in 2012.

confusables.difference: Redundancy is losing a specific job because it no longer exists. Unemployment is the state of having no job at all.
minimal_pair: He was made redundant in March.
Unemployment rose sharply that year.

entry_json.avoid: Unemployment is uncountable. Write 'high unemployment', never 'a high unemployment'.

entry_json.definition: surprising, because you did not think it would happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most useful finding was unexpected: the cheapest option also produced the best results.
example_sentences: An unexpected delay meant we missed the connection.
The results were unexpected and the study was repeated.

contexts.text: The most useful finding was unexpected: the cheapest option also produced the best results.
I had an unexpected phone call from an old colleague last week.
An unexpected fall in demand undermined the original cost projections.

confusables.difference: Sudden is about speed with no warning. Unexpected is about surprise, and something slow can still be unexpected.
minimal_pair: There was a sudden noise.
The decision was unexpected.

confusables.difference: Surprising describes something that causes surprise; unexpected states that it was not predicted.

entry_json.avoid: Note the stress: /ˌʌnɪkˈspektɪd/, with the main stress on 'spec'.

entry_json.definition: not treating people equally or according to what is right
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is unfair to judge schools on results alone when their intakes differ so much.
example_sentences: Many workers feel that the new shift system is unfair.
The test gives an unfair advantage to students who can pay for coaching.

contexts.text: It is unfair to judge schools on results alone when their intakes differ so much.
I thought it was unfair that only full-time staff got the bonus.
Critics argue that the funding formula is unfair to rural authorities.

confusables.difference: Unjust is stronger and usually concerns law and morality. Unfair covers everyday inequality of treatment.
minimal_pair: The law is unjust.
The rule is unfair.

confusables.difference: Unequal states a difference in amount; unfair judges that difference to be wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'unfair to someone' or 'unfair on someone'. Not 'unfair for someone' when you mean badly treated.

entry_json.definition: an organisation of workers formed to protect their rights; or the joining together of states or groups
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Membership of a trade union has fallen in almost every developed economy since 1980.
example_sentences: The union negotiated a four per cent pay rise.
The European Union has twenty-seven member states.

contexts.text: Membership of a trade union has fallen in almost every developed economy since 1980.
I joined the union in my first week and I've never regretted it.
Union density correlates closely with lower income inequality.

confusables.difference: An association is any organised group with shared interests. A union specifically represents workers in bargaining with employers.
minimal_pair: She joined the residents' association.
She joined the teachers' union.

entry_json.avoid: Note the article: 'a union', not 'an union'. The word begins with a consonant sound, /j/.

entry_json.definition: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every city claims a unique character, but the evidence for it is often thin.
example_sentences: Each fingerprint is unique to the individual.
The building is unique in Europe.

contexts.text: Every city claims a unique character, but the evidence for it is often thin.
The atmosphere at that festival is unique — I've never felt anything like it.
The species is unique to a single valley in the north of the island.

confusables.difference: Special means unusually good or important. Unique means there is literally no other one, which is a much stronger claim.
minimal_pair: It was a special evening.
The manuscript is unique.

confusables.difference: Rare means very few exist; unique means exactly one does.

entry_json.avoid: Unique is absolute. Do not write 'very unique' or 'more unique'. Use 'truly unique' if you need emphasis.

entry_json.definition: everything that exists, including all the stars, planets and space between them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public funding for research into the universe competes directly with funding for health.
example_sentences: The universe is thought to be around 13.8 billion years old.
New telescopes let us see parts of the universe that were invisible a decade ago.

contexts.text: Public funding for research into the universe competes directly with funding for health.
I find documentaries about the universe strangely relaxing.
Observations suggest that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

confusables.difference: World normally means the earth and the people on it. Universe means everything that physically exists.
minimal_pair: People all over the world use it.
The universe contains billions of galaxies.

confusables.difference: Space is the emptiness between objects beyond the atmosphere; the universe includes the objects too.

entry_json.avoid: The universe usually takes 'the'. Do not write 'in universe'.

entry_json.definition: not known, or not familiar to people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The long-term effects of the drug remain unknown, which is why the trial continues.
example_sentences: The cause of the fire is still unknown.
The artist was almost unknown outside her own country.

contexts.text: The long-term effects of the drug remain unknown, which is why the trial continues.
The band were completely unknown when I first saw them.
The number of undetected cases remains unknown.

confusables.difference: Unfamiliar means you personally do not know it, though others might. Unknown means nobody knows it.
minimal_pair: The street was unfamiliar to me.
The author is unknown.

confusables.difference: Uncertain means we have information but cannot be sure. Unknown means we have none.

entry_json.avoid: Note the double n in spelling and the doubled consonant sound: /ˌʌnˈnəʊn/.

entry_json.definition: except if; used to say that something will happen if another thing does not
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Emissions will keep rising unless transport is included in the targets.
example_sentences: We will not finish on time unless everyone helps.
Unless you book early, the fare doubles.

contexts.text: Emissions will keep rising unless transport is included in the targets.
I won't go unless the weather improves.
Unless funding is increased, waiting times will continue to lengthen.

confusables.difference: Unless means the same as 'if not' in most conditional sentences, but unless cannot be used for hypothetical wishes.
minimal_pair: Unless it rains, we will walk.
If it does not rain, we will walk.

confusables.difference: Without takes a noun or -ing form; unless takes a full clause with a subject and a verb.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use a negative after unless. "Unless you don't come" is wrong; write "unless you come".

entry_json.definition: different from; in contrast to
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unlike most European capitals, the city has almost no underground railway.
example_sentences: Unlike her brother, she has never enjoyed sport.
This model, unlike the previous one, can be repaired at home.

contexts.text: Unlike most European capitals, the city has almost no underground railway.
Unlike my parents, I've never owned a car.
Unlike the 2008 downturn, the recent contraction affected services most.

confusables.difference: Unlike compares two things. Unlikely means probably not going to happen. They are unrelated despite looking similar.
minimal_pair: Unlike his brother, he cycles.
He is unlikely to come.

confusables.difference: In contrast to is the formal linking phrase for a whole clause; unlike is followed by a noun.

entry_json.avoid: Unlike is followed by a noun or pronoun, not a clause. "Unlike he does" is wrong.

entry_json.definition: not probable; not expected to happen or be true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is unlikely that any single measure will reduce congestion on its own.
example_sentences: Heavy snow is unlikely at this time of year.
She is unlikely to accept the offer.

contexts.text: It is unlikely that any single measure will reduce congestion on its own.
I'm unlikely to move again in the next few years.
It is unlikely that the target will be met before 2030.

confusables.difference: Unlikely is about probability. Unlike is a preposition meaning 'different from'.
minimal_pair: He is unlikely to win.
Unlike him, I enjoy running.

confusables.difference: Improbable is more formal and slightly stronger; unlikely is the standard hedging word in essays.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'it is unlikely that' plus a clause, or 'X is unlikely to' plus a verb. Not 'it is unlikely to happen that'.

entry_json.definition: not needed, or more than is needed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Much of the packaging around fresh food is unnecessary and ends up in landfill.
example_sentences: The form asks for a great deal of unnecessary information.
It is unnecessary to book in advance on weekdays.

contexts.text: Much of the packaging around fresh food is unnecessary and ends up in landfill.
I try to avoid unnecessary trips by planning my shopping.
The reform removed several unnecessary stages from the application process.

confusables.difference: Useless means it does not work at all. Unnecessary means it works but is not needed.
minimal_pair: The old charger is useless.
The extra form is unnecessary.

confusables.difference: Optional means you may choose it; unnecessary judges that it should not be there.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the spelling: one n at the start of the root, two in 'unn-', then one c and two s's — unnecessary.

entry_json.definition: not enjoyable or attractive; causing a bad feeling
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic noise makes streets unpleasant long before it becomes a measurable health risk.
example_sentences: There was an unpleasant smell coming from the drain.
The journey was unpleasant but mercifully short.

contexts.text: Traffic noise makes streets unpleasant long before it becomes a measurable health risk.
The bus station is a pretty unpleasant place to wait at night.
Residents described the area as unpleasant and unsafe after dark.

confusables.difference: Uncomfortable is about how you feel physically or socially. Unpleasant describes the thing itself as nasty.
minimal_pair: The chair was uncomfortable.
The smell was unpleasant.

confusables.difference: Horrible is informal and emotional; unpleasant is the measured word for writing.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /ʌnˈpleznt/, with a short e, not 'un-PLEASE-ant'.

entry_json.definition: to add the most recent information to something, or to make something more modern
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments that fail to update their statistics make good policy almost impossible.
example_sentences: The website is updated every morning.
I need to update my CV before I apply.

contexts.text: Governments that fail to update their statistics make good policy almost impossible.
I update my phone as soon as it asks, otherwise I forget.
The database is updated quarterly using returns from local authorities.

confusables.difference: Upgrade means replacing something with a better version. Update means refreshing the information or making small improvements.
minimal_pair: I upgraded to a newer laptop.
I updated the software on my old one.

confusables.difference: Renew means extending something that has expired, like a licence; update means bringing content up to date.

entry_json.avoid: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, /ˌʌpˈdeɪt/. The noun 'an update' is stressed on the first.

entry_json.definition: a formal word for 'on', used especially in fixed phrases and after certain verbs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The success of the scheme depends upon households sorting waste correctly.
example_sentences: The decision was based upon incomplete evidence.
Once upon a time, most people worked on the land.

contexts.text: The success of the scheme depends upon households sorting waste correctly.
It depends upon what the weather does, really.
The argument rests upon two assumptions that are not stated explicitly.

confusables.difference: On and upon mean the same after depend, base and rely, but on is far more common. Upon sounds deliberately formal.
minimal_pair: It depends on the price.
The finding depends upon the sample used.

confusables.difference: 'Up on' as two words is not the same word: 'she climbed up on the roof'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use upon for physical position. 'The book is upon the table' sounds archaic; write 'on'.

entry_json.definition: at or near the top; higher in position or rank than something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Households in the upper income groups reduced their spending least during the downturn.
example_sentences: Store the heavier boxes on the upper shelves.
Pain in the upper back is common among office workers.

contexts.text: Households in the upper income groups reduced their spending least during the downturn.
My flat is on the upper floor, so it's warmer in winter.
The upper quartile earned more than three times the median.

confusables.difference: Higher compares two things directly and can follow 'than'. Upper describes a fixed position or band and cannot.
minimal_pair: Prices are higher than last year.
The upper floors were flooded.

confusables.difference: Top means the highest of all; upper means the higher part of two.

entry_json.avoid: Upper cannot be used after 'than' or after a verb. Write 'the shelf is higher', not 'the shelf is upper'.

entry_json.definition: unhappy or worried because something unpleasant has happened
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parents were understandably upset when the after-school club was closed without warning.
example_sentences: She was upset about the way the decision was announced.
Do not be upset if you have to take the test twice.

contexts.text: Parents were understandably upset when the after-school club was closed without warning.
I was quite upset when I first got the results, to be honest.
Respondents reported feeling upset by the tone of the coverage.

confusables.difference: Angry is about being cross with someone. Upset is sadness and distress, which may include some anger.
minimal_pair: He was angry with the referee.
He was upset about the result.

confusables.difference: Disappointed is about hopes not met; upset is a stronger emotional reaction.

entry_json.avoid: 'Upset' as an adjective is stressed on the second syllable. As a noun meaning a stomach problem, it is stressed on the first.

entry_json.definition: towards a higher place, level or amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The line moves upwards steadily until 2015 and then flattens out.
example_sentences: Prices have been revised upwards twice this year.
The path climbs steadily upwards for about two kilometres.

contexts.text: The line moves upwards steadily until 2015 and then flattens out.
The road slopes upwards all the way to my house, which I notice on a bike.
Estimates were revised upwards following the release of the census data.

confusables.difference: Upward is the adjective before a noun: an upward trend. Upwards is the adverb after a verb: it moved upwards.
minimal_pair: There is an upward trend.
The line moves upwards.

confusables.difference: Up is the ordinary everyday adverb. Upwards is more formal and describes continuous movement.

entry_json.avoid: In British English the adverb usually keeps the s: 'upwards'. The adjective never does.

entry_json.definition: connected with a town or city rather than the countryside
entry_json.own_context_sentence: More than half the world's population now lives in urban areas, and the share is still rising.
example_sentences: Urban air quality has improved in most European capitals since 2000.
Rents in urban areas rose twice as fast as rural ones.

contexts.text: More than half the world's population now lives in urban areas, and the share is still rising.
I've always lived in urban areas, so the countryside feels strange to me.
Urban households consume less energy per person than rural ones.

confusables.difference: Urban and rural are the standard opposing pair in Task 1 and Task 2. Use both when comparing.
minimal_pair: Urban incomes are higher.
Rural incomes are lower.

confusables.difference: Urbane is a completely different word meaning polite and sophisticated. It is not the adjective for cities.

entry_json.avoid: Urban has no comparative. Write 'more heavily urbanised', not 'more urban'.

entry_json.definition: to advise or try hard to persuade someone to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Doctors urge patients to take exercise, but few clinics can prescribe it.
example_sentences: The report urges the government to act before the next winter.
She urged me to apply, and I am glad I did.

contexts.text: Doctors urge patients to take exercise, but few clinics can prescribe it.
My teacher urged me to take the exam a year early.
The authors urge caution in interpreting the correlation.

confusables.difference: Encourage is gentle and supportive. Urge is stronger and more insistent, and implies urgency.
minimal_pair: She encouraged him to try.
She urged him to leave immediately.

confusables.difference: Force removes choice. Urge is only persuasion, however strong.

entry_json.avoid: Urge takes an object plus 'to': 'urge them to act'. Not 'urge that they act' in everyday writing.

entry_json.definition: worth a lot of money, or very useful and important
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most valuable part of a placement is the contact with people already doing the job.
example_sentences: The museum holds several valuable manuscripts.
Her advice proved extremely valuable during my first year.

contexts.text: The most valuable part of a placement is the contact with people already doing the job.
That job gave me valuable experience even though the pay was terrible.
Longitudinal data are particularly valuable for identifying causal relationships.

confusables.difference: Invaluable is not the opposite of valuable. It means so useful that it cannot be measured, so it is even stronger.
minimal_pair: Her help was valuable.
Her help was invaluable.

confusables.difference: Expensive is what you pay. Valuable is what it is worth, which can be very different.

entry_json.avoid: The opposite of valuable is 'worthless', not 'invaluable'. This is a very common and costly error.

entry_json.definition: how much something is worth in money, or how useful and important it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The value of a degree is increasingly measured in earnings rather than in knowledge.
example_sentences: The value of the property has doubled in ten years.
Nobody disputes the value of early diagnosis.

contexts.text: The value of a degree is increasingly measured in earnings rather than in knowledge.
The flat has gone up in value since we bought it, luckily.
The chart shows the value of exports in billions of dollars.

confusables.difference: Price is what is actually charged. Value is what something is genuinely worth, which may be more or less.
minimal_pair: The price is thirty pounds.
The value is far higher.

confusables.difference: Cost is what you must pay or give up; value is the benefit you get.

entry_json.avoid: 'Values' in the plural usually means moral beliefs. Keep that sense separate from money.

entry_json.definition: several different; of several kinds
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Various explanations have been offered, but none accounts for the whole pattern.
example_sentences: The course is available at various times during the week.
We visited various museums, though I cannot remember all the names.

contexts.text: Various explanations have been offered, but none accounts for the whole pattern.
I've tried various apps for learning vocabulary and none of them stuck.
Various factors contribute to the decline, of which cost is the most significant.

confusables.difference: Several tells you roughly how many, more than two but not many. Various emphasises that they are different in kind.
minimal_pair: Several students were absent.
Students gave various reasons for being absent.

confusables.difference: Various is the adjective; a variety is the noun phrase. Write 'a variety of reasons' or 'various reasons', not 'a various of'.

entry_json.avoid: Various is always followed by a plural noun. 'Various reason' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to be different in different situations, or to change something so that it is not always the same
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fees vary considerably between institutions, even for identical courses.
example_sentences: Rainfall varies widely across the region.
Try to vary your sentence structure in the writing test.

contexts.text: Fees vary considerably between institutions, even for identical courses.
My working hours vary a lot from week to week.
Participation rates vary considerably according to household income.

confusables.difference: Change means becoming different over time. Vary means being different between cases, places or occasions.
minimal_pair: Prices changed in March.
Prices vary from shop to shop.

confusables.difference: Differ compares two specific things; vary describes a spread across many.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'vary from X to Y' or 'vary between X and Y'. Not 'vary from X until Y'.

entry_json.definition: extremely large in area, amount or degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The vast majority of plastic ever produced is still somewhere in the environment.
example_sentences: Vast areas of forest were cleared in a single decade.
The company spends a vast amount on advertising.

contexts.text: The vast majority of plastic ever produced is still somewhere in the environment.
The vast majority of my friends have moved away from our hometown.
A vast body of evidence now links air pollution to cardiovascular disease.

confusables.difference: Large is neutral and can describe anything. Vast is an extreme adjective and suggests almost unmanageable size.
minimal_pair: It is a large area.
It is a vast area.

confusables.difference: Wide is about breadth from side to side. Vast is about overall size or quantity.

entry_json.avoid: 'The vast majority' is a strong claim. In Task 1 use it only when the figure is genuinely above about eighty per cent.

entry_json.definition: the place where an event such as a concert, conference or match is held
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities that lack a large indoor venue lose touring events to their neighbours.
example_sentences: The concert was moved to a bigger venue after tickets sold out.
The organisers changed the venue three weeks before the event.

contexts.text: Cities that lack a large indoor venue lose touring events to their neighbours.
My favourite venue in the city is a converted cinema.
Smaller venues have closed at a rate of two per week since 2010.

confusables.difference: Place is the general word for anywhere. Venue is specifically where an organised event happens.
minimal_pair: It is a nice place to sit.
It is a good venue for a concert.

confusables.difference: Location is where something is on a map. A venue is a building or space chosen to host an event.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'venue' for a shop or a home. It implies an organised public event.

entry_json.definition: a form of something that is slightly different from other forms of the same thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The free version of the software does everything a student actually needs.
example_sentences: A shorter version of the report was published for the public.
The film is based on the American version of the novel.

contexts.text: The free version of the software does everything a student actually needs.
I'm still using an old version of the app because the new one is slower.
An earlier version of this paper was presented at the 2019 conference.

confusables.difference: Edition is used for books and newspapers printed at a particular time. Version is broader and covers software and accounts of events.
minimal_pair: The second edition came out in 2020.
The latest version fixes the bug.

confusables.difference: A copy is identical to the original. A version is deliberately different.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the version 3'. It is 'version 3' with no article.

entry_json.definition: travelling through a place on the way somewhere; or by means of a particular method
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Applications are submitted via the online portal rather than by post.
example_sentences: We flew to Sydney via Singapore.
The results were communicated to families via text message.

contexts.text: Applications are submitted via the online portal rather than by post.
I usually get there via the ring road because the centre is jammed.
The infection is transmitted via contaminated water.

confusables.difference: Through describes physically passing inside something. Via names a stopping point on a route, or a method.
minimal_pair: We drove through the tunnel.
We flew via Doha.

confusables.difference: By is the ordinary way to name a means of transport or method. Via is more formal and often names an intermediary.

entry_json.avoid: Via is formal. In Speaking, 'through' or 'by' sounds far more natural.

entry_json.definition: a person who has been hurt, damaged or killed as a result of a crime, accident or disaster
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Victims of online fraud rarely report it, which makes the official figures misleading.
example_sentences: The charity provides legal advice to victims of domestic abuse.
Flood victims were housed in the local sports hall.

contexts.text: Victims of online fraud rarely report it, which makes the official figures misleading.
A friend of mine was the victim of a phone scam last year.
Victims of violent crime are more likely to move house within two years.

confusables.difference: Survivor emphasises that the person came through and is often preferred by the people themselves. Victim emphasises the harm done.
minimal_pair: She describes herself as a survivor.
He was the victim of an assault.

confusables.difference: A patient is receiving medical care; a victim has been harmed by an event or crime.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'a victim of crime', not 'a victim from crime'.

entry_json.definition: success in a game, election, war or struggle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A narrow victory rarely gives a government the authority to make unpopular decisions.
example_sentences: The team celebrated a comfortable victory over their rivals.
The campaign claimed victory after the law was changed.

contexts.text: A narrow victory rarely gives a government the authority to make unpopular decisions.
That victory in the final is still the best sporting memory I have.
The party's victory in 1997 was the largest in modern British history.

confusables.difference: Win is the everyday word and is also a verb. Victory is a noun only, and sounds more formal and more significant.
minimal_pair: They got a win at home.
They secured a famous victory.

confusables.difference: Success is any achievement. A victory requires an opponent who is defeated.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'a victory over someone' or 'against someone'. Not 'a victory to someone'.

entry_json.definition: a person who watches television or online video
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Streaming services know exactly when a viewer stops watching, which shapes what they commission.
example_sentences: The programme attracted eight million viewers.
Viewers complained about the amount of advertising.

contexts.text: Streaming services know exactly when a viewer stops watching, which shapes what they commission.
I'm a regular viewer of that documentary series, actually.
The average viewer now watches less than twenty minutes of live television per day.

confusables.difference: Audience is the whole group watching or listening, and takes a singular or plural verb. A viewer is one individual.
minimal_pair: The audience was silent.
Each viewer sees a different set of recommendations.

confusables.difference: A spectator watches an event in person, usually sport. A viewer watches a screen.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'viewers' for television and 'readers' for print. Do not mix them.

entry_json.definition: behaviour that is intended to hurt or kill people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reported violence has fallen for two decades, yet public fear of it has not.
example_sentences: The film was criticised for its portrayal of violence.
Violence at football matches has declined sharply since the 1980s.

contexts.text: Reported violence has fallen for two decades, yet public fear of it has not.
There's very little violence where I live, which I don't take for granted.
Exposure to violence in early childhood predicts poorer outcomes in adolescence.

confusables.difference: Crime is any illegal act, including theft and fraud. Violence specifically involves physical harm.
minimal_pair: Property crime rose.
Violence fell.

confusables.difference: Aggression is the hostile attitude or behaviour; violence is the physical act itself.

entry_json.avoid: Violence is uncountable. Write 'acts of violence', never 'violences'.

entry_json.definition: involving or caused by physical force intended to hurt; or very strong and sudden
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Violent crime accounts for a small share of offences but almost all of the coverage.
example_sentences: He was convicted of a violent assault.
A violent storm brought down trees across the county.

contexts.text: Violent crime accounts for a small share of offences but almost all of the coverage.
There was a violent storm the night we arrived and the ferry was cancelled.
Violent offences represent under five per cent of recorded crime.

confusables.difference: Aggressive describes a hostile manner, which may never become physical. Violent means physical force is actually used.
minimal_pair: He was aggressive in the meeting.
He became violent and was arrested.

confusables.difference: Severe is about the scale of harm; violent is about force being used.

entry_json.avoid: Do not describe an argument as 'violent' unless someone was physically hurt. Use 'heated' or 'fierce'.

entry_json.definition: made to appear to exist by computer, rather than existing physically; or almost, but not quite, complete
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Virtual meetings cut travel costs but make informal conversation almost impossible.
example_sentences: The museum offers a virtual tour for people who cannot visit.
The scheme was a virtual failure within a year.

contexts.text: Virtual meetings cut travel costs but make informal conversation almost impossible.
I did a virtual tour of the campus before I applied.
Virtual consultations now account for a third of all appointments.

confusables.difference: Online simply means connected to the internet. Virtual means a computer-made version of something that exists physically.
minimal_pair: I bought it online.
We took a virtual tour of the building.

confusables.difference: Careful: 'virtually' often means 'almost', which is nearly the opposite of 'actually'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Virtually' usually means 'almost', not 'in a virtual way'. Check which you mean before you write it.

entry_json.definition: the ability to see; or a clear idea of how something should be in the future
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The plan sets out a vision for the city in 2050 without saying who will pay for it.
example_sentences: Poor vision is often the reason older drivers give up their licence.
She had a clear vision of what the department could become.

contexts.text: The plan sets out a vision for the city in 2050 without saying who will pay for it.
My vision has got worse since I started working on screens all day.
The strategy articulates a vision of carbon neutrality by 2040.

confusables.difference: Sight is the plain word for the ability to see. Vision is used medically and also means a plan for the future.
minimal_pair: He lost his sight.
Her vision is deteriorating.

confusables.difference: A view is an opinion or something you can see. A vision is an ambitious picture of the future.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'my vision is that' when you simply mean 'in my opinion'. Vision implies a long-term plan.

entry_json.definition: connected with seeing or with things you can see
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Visual material helps some learners far more than written explanation does.
example_sentences: The presentation relies heavily on visual aids.
Visual impairment affects around two million people in the country.

contexts.text: Visual material helps some learners far more than written explanation does.
I'm quite a visual learner, so diagrams help me much more than text.
Visual cues improved recall significantly across all age groups.

confusables.difference: Visible means able to be seen. Visual means relating to sight or presented as an image.
minimal_pair: The mountain is visible from here.
The report includes visual data.

confusables.difference: Optical concerns lenses and light physically; visual concerns perception and images.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the results are visual' when you mean they can be seen. That is 'visible'.

entry_json.definition: absolutely necessary; essential for success or for life
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Access to clean water is vital, and yet it is still treated as a local rather than a global problem.
example_sentences: It is vital that applicants meet the deadline.
Bees play a vital role in food production.

contexts.text: Access to clean water is vital, and yet it is still treated as a local rather than a global problem.
Sleep is absolutely vital for me — I'm useless without it.
Early diagnosis is vital in reducing long-term treatment costs.

confusables.difference: Important allows degrees. Vital means without it the thing fails completely, so it is much stronger.
minimal_pair: The meeting is important.
Water is vital to life.

confusables.difference: Essential and vital are close synonyms. Vital carries a slightly stronger sense of life or death.

entry_json.avoid: Vital is absolute, so avoid 'very vital'. After 'it is vital that', use the base form: 'it is vital that he be informed'.

entry_json.definition: a natural substance found in food that the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern countries during the winter months.
example_sentences: Oranges are a good source of vitamin C.
The doctor recommended a daily vitamin supplement.

contexts.text: Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern countries during the winter months.
I take a vitamin supplement in winter because I never see the sun.
Vitamin deficiency remains a significant public health problem in some regions.

confusables.difference: Minerals are elements such as iron and calcium. Vitamins are organic compounds. Both are needed in small amounts.
minimal_pair: The water is rich in minerals.
The fruit is rich in vitamins.

confusables.difference: A supplement is the pill you take; the vitamin is the substance inside it.

entry_json.avoid: In British English the first syllable is /ˈvɪt/, like 'vit', not /ˈvaɪt/ as in American English.

entry_json.definition: the amount of something, especially a large amount; or how loud a sound is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The sheer volume of applications means most are read for less than a minute.
example_sentences: Traffic volume on the bridge has doubled since it opened.
Could you turn the volume down a little?

contexts.text: The sheer volume of applications means most are read for less than a minute.
I always turn the volume right down when I take a call in public.
The volume of freight carried by rail fell by a third over the period.

confusables.difference: Amount is the general word for uncountable quantity. Volume is used for large flows such as traffic, trade and data.
minimal_pair: A small amount of milk.
A huge volume of traffic.

confusables.difference: Quantity is neutral and countable-friendly. Volume emphasises scale.

entry_json.avoid: 'A volume' also means one book in a set. Context must make clear which sense you mean.

entry_json.definition: a person who offers to do something without being paid or forced
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Food banks in most British towns are run almost entirely by volunteers.
example_sentences: The charity is looking for volunteers to help at the weekend.
Over two hundred volunteers took part in the clean-up.

contexts.text: Food banks in most British towns are run almost entirely by volunteers.
I worked as a volunteer at a local library for two years.
Volunteers delivered the majority of frontline support during the emergency.

confusables.difference: An employee is paid. A volunteer is not, though the work may be identical.
minimal_pair: The shop has two employees.
The shop has twelve volunteers.

confusables.difference: A participant takes part in a study or event; a volunteer offers unpaid labour.

entry_json.avoid: Stress the last syllable: /ˌvɒlənˈtɪə(r)/. Many learners stress the first.

entry_json.definition: to choose a person or a course of action formally, in an election or a meeting
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Younger citizens vote far less often than older ones, and policy reflects that.
example_sentences: Members voted to accept the pay offer.
I voted for the first time at eighteen.

contexts.text: Younger citizens vote far less often than older ones, and policy reflects that.
I always vote, even in local elections that nobody talks about.
Turnout among 18- to 24-year-olds who voted rose by nine points in 2017.

confusables.difference: You vote for a person; the group elects them. Vote is what the individual does, elect is the result.
minimal_pair: I voted for her.
They elected her chair.

confusables.difference: Choose is any personal decision. Vote is a formal decision made by a group process.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'vote for a candidate' and 'vote on a proposal'. The prepositions are not interchangeable.

entry_json.definition: the money paid regularly to an employee, usually weekly and for hourly work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Real wages have barely risen since 2008 in several developed economies.
example_sentences: The minimum wage was raised again in April.
Low wages in the care sector make recruitment extremely difficult.

contexts.text: Real wages have barely risen since 2008 in several developed economies.
My first job paid the minimum wage and I still remember the exact figure.
Wage growth lagged behind inflation throughout the period shown.

confusables.difference: A salary is an annual amount paid monthly, usually for professional work. A wage is often hourly or weekly.
minimal_pair: She earns a good salary.
He is paid an hourly wage.

confusables.difference: Income is everything you receive, including benefits and investments. A wage is only what work pays.

entry_json.avoid: 'The minimum wage' always takes 'the'. Do not write 'minimum wage is £11'.

entry_json.definition: to tell someone about a possible danger or problem so that they can avoid it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Scientists warned for decades that the ice was thinning faster than the models predicted.
example_sentences: The label warns against using the product near heat.
I warned him that the road would be closed.

contexts.text: Scientists warned for decades that the ice was thinning faster than the models predicted.
My neighbour warned me about the parking rules before I got a ticket.
The report warns that current targets will not be met without additional funding.

confusables.difference: Warn is helpful: you tell someone about a danger. Threaten is hostile: you say you will cause the harm yourself.
minimal_pair: She warned him about the ice.
She threatened to report him.

confusables.difference: Advise suggests the best action. Warn points out a danger.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'warn someone about something' or 'warn someone that'. Not 'warn to someone'.

entry_json.definition: a statement telling someone about a possible danger or problem
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A weather warning issued a day in advance saves more lives than any rescue service.
example_sentences: The council issued a flood warning on Thursday evening.
He was given a written warning for repeated lateness.

contexts.text: A weather warning issued a day in advance saves more lives than any rescue service.
We got a text warning about the storm the night before it hit.
Early warning systems have reduced deaths from cyclones by an order of magnitude.

confusables.difference: A notice is any announcement, often routine. A warning specifically concerns danger or consequences.
minimal_pair: There is a notice on the door.
There is a warning on the packet.

confusables.difference: An alert is urgent and immediate; a warning may be about a longer-term risk.

entry_json.avoid: You 'issue' or 'give' a warning. Do not write 'make a warning'.

entry_json.definition: materials that are thrown away because they are no longer needed; or the wrong use of time or money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Household waste per person has fallen slightly since 2010, while packaging has not.
example_sentences: The city sends less than half its waste to landfill.
Meetings without an agenda are a waste of everyone's time.

contexts.text: Household waste per person has fallen slightly since 2010, while packaging has not.
I think fast fashion is a complete waste of money and materials.
Food waste accounts for roughly a tenth of global greenhouse gas emissions.

confusables.difference: Rubbish is the everyday British word for what you throw away at home. Waste is the technical term used in policy and data.
minimal_pair: Put the rubbish out.
Industrial waste is regulated separately.

confusables.difference: Litter is rubbish dropped in a public place; waste is the whole category.

entry_json.avoid: Waste is uncountable as material: 'less waste', not 'fewer wastes'.

entry_json.definition: a fault or a lack of strength in a person, plan or system
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main weakness of the study is that it relies entirely on what people say they eat.
example_sentences: Candidates are usually asked to describe their greatest weakness.
The report identifies several weaknesses in the current system.

contexts.text: The main weakness of the study is that it relies entirely on what people say they eat.
My biggest weakness at work is that I take on too much.
A key weakness of the methodology is the absence of a control group.

confusables.difference: A fault is a specific defect that can often be fixed. A weakness is a general lack of strength or a limitation.
minimal_pair: There is a fault in the wiring.
The plan has one serious weakness.

confusables.difference: A disadvantage is a drawback compared with alternatives; a weakness is an internal flaw.

entry_json.avoid: 'A weakness for chocolate' means you cannot resist it. That is a different, informal sense.

entry_json.definition: a large amount of money and property owned by a person or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wealth is distributed far more unequally than income in almost every country studied.
example_sentences: The country's wealth comes largely from oil.
Much of the family's wealth was inherited rather than earned.

contexts.text: Wealth is distributed far more unequally than income in almost every country studied.
There's a huge gap in wealth between the two sides of my city.
The top one per cent hold a disproportionate share of national wealth.

confusables.difference: Income is money coming in each month or year. Wealth is what you already own. A person can have high income and no wealth.
minimal_pair: Her income rose last year.
Her wealth is mostly in property.

confusables.difference: Money is the everyday word. Wealth is the accumulated total of assets and is the term used in economics.

entry_json.avoid: Wealth is uncountable. Write 'great wealth', never 'a wealth' unless you mean 'a wealth of experience'.

entry_json.definition: having a lot of money and property; rich
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wealthy households cut their energy use least when prices rise, because the bill matters less.
example_sentences: The area attracts wealthy buyers from overseas.
Wealthy countries produce far more waste per person.

contexts.text: Wealthy households cut their energy use least when prices rise, because the bill matters less.
The part of town I grew up in was never wealthy, but it was safe.
Wealthy nations account for a disproportionate share of historical emissions.

confusables.difference: Rich is the everyday word and is fine in speech. Wealthy sounds more measured and is preferred in formal writing.
minimal_pair: He is very rich.
The wealthy nations of the north.

confusables.difference: Affluent usually describes areas and societies rather than individuals, and suggests comfortable rather than enormous wealth.

entry_json.avoid: 'Rich' also describes food and colour. In an essay about money, 'wealthy' is less ambiguous.

entry_json.definition: an object used for fighting or attacking, such as a gun or a knife
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Countries that restrict access to weapons report far lower rates of fatal assault.
example_sentences: Police found no weapon at the scene.
Carrying a weapon in public is illegal in most European countries.

contexts.text: Countries that restrict access to weapons report far lower rates of fatal assault.
Where I'm from, almost nobody carries a weapon of any kind.
Legislation restricting the sale of weapons was introduced in 1996.

confusables.difference: Arms is used for military equipment and international trade. Weapon is the ordinary word for an individual object.
minimal_pair: The arms trade is worth billions.
He was carrying a weapon.

confusables.difference: A tool is for work; a weapon is for fighting, though a tool can be used as one.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: /ˈwepən/, with a short e. The 'ea' is not /iː/.

entry_json.definition: to have a particular weight; or to measure how heavy something is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Airlines weigh hand luggage more strictly than they used to, which changes how people pack.
example_sentences: The parcel weighs just under two kilograms.
Weigh the flour before you add the water.

contexts.text: Airlines weigh hand luggage more strictly than they used to, which changes how people pack.
I weigh my suitcase at home now because of the charges.
Samples were weighed before and after drying.

confusables.difference: Weigh is the verb; weight is the noun. "What is your weight?" and "How much do you weigh?" are both correct.
minimal_pair: How much does it weigh?
What is its weight?

confusables.difference: Weigh and way sound identical. Only weigh has the gh.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'it weights two kilos'. The verb is weigh.

entry_json.definition: in or from the west of a country or region; or connected with Europe and North America
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Western diets are unusually high in processed food, and the health effects are now well documented.
example_sentences: The western coast receives most of the rainfall.
Western companies were slow to enter the market.

contexts.text: Western diets are unusually high in processed food, and the health effects are now well documented.
I live in the western part of the city, near the river.
Western consumption patterns are increasingly replicated in emerging economies.

confusables.difference: West is the noun and direction. Western is the adjective describing an area or a culture.
minimal_pair: We drove west.
We stayed in western Ireland.

confusables.difference: Capitalise Western when it means the culture of Europe and North America; lower case for compass direction.

entry_json.avoid: 'The West' as a cultural bloc is a broad generalisation. In Task 2, name specific countries where you can.

entry_json.definition: at any time that; every time that
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Whenever fuel prices rise, public transport use increases within a few weeks.
example_sentences: Come and see me whenever you have a question.
Whenever I try to book, the site crashes.

contexts.text: Whenever fuel prices rise, public transport use increases within a few weeks.
I walk to work whenever the weather allows.
Data were collected whenever a new cohort entered the programme.

confusables.difference: When refers to one particular time. Whenever means every time, or at any time you like.
minimal_pair: Call me when you arrive.
Call me whenever you need help.

confusables.difference: Whenever is about time; wherever is about place.

entry_json.avoid: After whenever, use the present tense for future meaning: 'whenever he arrives', not 'whenever he will arrive'.

entry_json.definition: used to compare two facts that contrast with each other
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Spending on health rose steadily, whereas spending on housing fell in every year shown.
example_sentences: The north of the country is industrial, whereas the south is largely agricultural.
Men in the survey cited pay, whereas women cited flexibility.

contexts.text: Spending on health rose steadily, whereas spending on housing fell in every year shown.
I like cooking, whereas my brother eats out almost every night.
Urban participation rose, whereas rural participation remained flat.

confusables.difference: While can mean the same, but it also means 'during the time that', so it is ambiguous. Whereas only ever signals contrast.
minimal_pair: Sales rose, whereas costs fell.
He read while she cooked.

confusables.difference: However starts a new sentence. Whereas joins two clauses inside one sentence.

entry_json.avoid: Whereas is a conjunction, not a linking adverb. Do not start a new sentence with it in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: in or to any place that; in every place that
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wherever public transport is cheap and frequent, car ownership falls.
example_sentences: Sit wherever you like.
Wherever the disease appeared, the same pattern of spread was observed.

contexts.text: Wherever public transport is cheap and frequent, car ownership falls.
I take my laptop wherever I go, which is probably unhealthy.
Wherever data were unavailable, national estimates were substituted.

confusables.difference: Where refers to one particular place. Wherever means any or every place.
minimal_pair: This is where I work.
I can work wherever there is wifi.

confusables.difference: Wherever is about place; whenever is about time.

entry_json.avoid: 'Wherever possible' is a useful formal phrase. Do not write 'in wherever possible'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce two or more possibilities, or to report a yes-or-no question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The real question is whether cities can grow without generating still more traffic.
example_sentences: I am not sure whether the office is open on Saturdays.
The decision depends on whether funding is renewed.

contexts.text: The real question is whether cities can grow without generating still more traffic.
I can't decide whether to stay another year or move back home.
The study examines whether class size affects attainment.

confusables.difference: If and whether are interchangeable in many reported questions, but only whether can follow a preposition or come before 'to'.
minimal_pair: It depends on whether he comes.
I do not know if he is coming.

confusables.difference: Whether and weather sound identical. Weather is rain and sun; whether introduces alternatives.

entry_json.avoid: After a preposition, always use whether: 'the question of whether', never 'the question of if'.

entry_json.definition: to speak very quietly so that only the person near you can hear
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Librarians spend less time asking people to whisper than they did before headphones.
example_sentences: She whispered something to the person beside her.
He whispered that the meeting had already started.

contexts.text: Librarians spend less time asking people to whisper than they did before headphones.
My friend whispered the answer to me and we both got caught.
Participants were asked to whisper rather than speak aloud during the test.

confusables.difference: Murmur is a low continuous sound and can be many voices together. Whisper is deliberately quiet speech to one person.
minimal_pair: A murmur ran through the hall.
She whispered a warning.

confusables.difference: Mutter suggests complaint spoken unclearly; whisper is simply quiet.

entry_json.avoid: Whisper takes 'to' before the listener: whisper to someone, not whisper someone.

entry_json.definition: the object form of 'who', used in formal English and after prepositions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report does not say to whom the recommendations were addressed.
example_sentences: The candidate whom the panel selected withdrew a week later.
To whom should I send the completed form?

contexts.text: The report does not say to whom the recommendations were addressed.
The person whom I spoke to was extremely helpful, actually.
Participants, most of whom were graduates, completed the survey online.

confusables.difference: Who is the subject: who wrote this? Whom is the object: to whom did you write? In speech, who is normal in both roles.
minimal_pair: Who called you?
Whom did you call?

confusables.difference: That can replace whom in defining relative clauses and is far more natural in speech.

entry_json.avoid: Whom sounds stiff in Speaking. Use it in Writing after a preposition, and after quantifiers such as 'many of whom'.

entry_json.definition: by or among many people; over a large area
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is widely accepted that early intervention is cheaper than later treatment.
example_sentences: The technique is now widely used in hospitals across Europe.
Opinions vary widely on how the money should be spent.

contexts.text: It is widely accepted that early intervention is cheaper than later treatment.
That app is widely used among students here, apparently.
The findings have been widely replicated in subsequent studies.

confusables.difference: Broadly means in general terms, without detail. Widely means among many people or across a large area.
minimal_pair: Broadly speaking, the trend is upward.
The method is widely used.

confusables.difference: Wide is the adjective for physical breadth; widely is the adverb for extent of use or spread.

contexts.text: I take a couple of online courses alongside my degree.
We stayed a couple of nights in a hostel to keep the cost down.
Sales fell for a couple of years before recovering in 2015.

confusables.difference: 'A couple of' means two, or very nearly two. 'A few' is vaguer - roughly three to five.

entry_json.avoid: Fairly informal. If the chart gives you the figure, write 'two' rather than 'a couple of'.

entry_json.definition: one or two days; a deliberately vague short period used when you do not want to promise an exact time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The manager said the decision would take a day or two.
example_sentences: I felt tired for a day or two after the flight, and then I was fine.

I felt tired for a day or two after the flight, and then I was fine.
People expect a reply within a day or two now, which adds real pressure at work.

confusables.difference: The same length of time, a different attitude. 'A couple of days' states it; 'a day or two' leaves room to be wrong.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is fixed: 'a day or two', never 'one or two day'.

entry_json.definition: a fall in how many students there are; a fixed academic collocation built on decline in + plural noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a decline in student numbers at rural schools between 2005 and 2020.
example_sentences: A decline in student numbers forces small universities either to merge or to close.
A decline in student numbers is not always bad news if class sizes improve.
collocations: a sharp decline in student numbers
a steady decline in student numbers

contexts.text: The graph shows a decline in student numbers at rural schools between 2005 and 2020.
A decline in student numbers forces small universities either to merge or to close.
A decline in student numbers is not always bad news if class sizes improve.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in most sentences, but 'decline' suggests a longer and more worrying trend, while 'decrease' is purely numerical.
The preposition is fixed: a decline IN something, never a decline OF it.

entry_json.avoid: Write 'a decline in student numbers', never 'a decline of student numbers'.

entry_json.definition: something wonderful that you had hoped for without really expecting; it works as a noun phrase after the verb 'be'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Playing in that stadium was a dream come true for him.

collocations: a dream come true for sb

contexts.text: Playing in that stadium was a dream come true for him.
Studying abroad was a dream come true, although the first term was hard.
For most people a job they genuinely enjoy is a dream come true rather than a plan.

confusables.difference: The fixed phrase keeps the bare form: 'It was a dream come true'. 'My dream came true' is a full sentence, not this phrase.

entry_json.avoid: Heavily overused in Speaking Part 2. Once is fine; it is not band-8 vocabulary by itself.

entry_json.definition: a small number of countable things, usually three to five; the tone is positive - it says there are some

contexts.text: I have a few friends who are taking the test in the same month.
A few countries have banned the advertising of sugary drinks to children.
Only a few employers offer proper training, and that is the real problem.

confusables.difference: 'A few' means some. 'Few' without the article means almost none and sounds negative: 'Few students attended' is a complaint.
'A few' counts separate things; 'a little' measures something uncountable.

entry_json.avoid: Dropping 'a' reverses the meaning, so check which one you mean before you write it.

entry_json.definition: a short period of several minutes; the standard way to describe a brief wait or a quick task
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You get a few minutes to plan before you start speaking in Part 2.
example_sentences: The train was only a few minutes late, so it did not really matter.
Even a few minutes of walking each hour reduces the harm of sitting all day.

contexts.text: You get a few minutes to plan before you start speaking in Part 2.
The train was only a few minutes late, so it did not really matter.
Even a few minutes of walking each hour reduces the harm of sitting all day.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'A few minutes' can stretch to five or six; 'a couple of minutes' really means two.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a few minute'. 'A few' always takes a plural noun.

entry_json.definition: on several separate occasions, usually three to five; a vague statement of frequency

Students who retake the exam a few times usually improve their planning, not their English.

contexts.text: I have been to Singapore a few times for work.
I go swimming a few times a month, usually when the pool is quiet.
Students who retake the exam a few times usually improve their planning, not their English.

confusables.difference: 'Several times' is slightly more and sounds more formal. In writing prefer 'on several occasions'.

entry_json.avoid: Too vague for Task 1. If the chart gives a number, use the number.

entry_json.definition: a period of roughly three to five years; very common when describing change over time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in this city for a few years now.
example_sentences: Rents were stable for a few years and then rose sharply after 2016.
A few years ago most people carried a camera; now the phone has replaced it.

contexts.text: I have lived in this city for a few years now.
Rents were stable for a few years and then rose sharply after 2016.
A few years ago most people carried a camera; now the phone has replaced it.

confusables.term: in a few years / for a few years
confusables.difference: 'In a few years' points forward to a moment; 'for a few years' measures a stretch of time. They are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: 'A few years ago' needs the past simple: 'I moved here a few years ago', not 'I have moved'.

entry_json.definition: a sensible plan or suggestion; it usually follows 'it is' or the verb 'think'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a good idea to walk part of the journey if you sit down all day.
example_sentences: I think studying with other people is a good idea, at least some of the time.

think it is a good idea

contexts.text: It is a good idea to walk part of the journey if you sit down all day.
I think studying with other people is a good idea, at least some of the time.
Charging for plastic bags seemed a good idea, and the figures suggest it worked.

confusables.difference: 'A nice idea' often carries an unspoken 'but it will not work'. 'A good idea' is genuine approval.

entry_json.avoid: Weak on its own in Task 2. Say why it is a good idea, or write 'an effective measure'.

entry_json.definition: a lot; it works as an adverb after a verb - 'it has changed a great deal' - or before a comparative

Family life has changed a great deal in a single generation.

contexts.text: Car ownership rose a great deal between 1990 and 2010.
Teaching methods have changed a great deal in the last ten years.
Family life has changed a great deal in a single generation.

confusables.difference: The same meaning in a different register. 'A lot' is spoken; 'a great deal' is its written equivalent and lifts an essay sentence.

entry_json.avoid: It modifies verbs and comparatives, not plain adjectives. Not 'a great deal expensive'.

entry_json.definition: much better; 'a great deal' here strengthens a comparative adjective or adverb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air quality in the city is a great deal better than it was a decade ago.
example_sentences: Students do a great deal better when they are taught in small groups.
Rail punctuality was a great deal better in the second half of the period.
collocations: a great deal better than sth

contexts.text: Air quality in the city is a great deal better than it was a decade ago.
Students do a great deal better when they are taught in small groups.
Rail punctuality was a great deal better in the second half of the period.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning. 'A great deal better' is heavier and more formal, so do not use it twice in one paragraph.

entry_json.avoid: Only with comparatives. 'A great deal good' is wrong; it has to be 'better'.

entry_json.definition: a large amount of something uncountable; the pattern is a great deal of + uncountable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Commuting consumes a great deal of time that could be spent with family.
example_sentences: The study required a great deal of data collected over twenty years.
Buying a home takes a great deal of money that young people simply do not have.

contexts.text: Commuting consumes a great deal of time that could be spent with family.
The study required a great deal of data collected over twenty years.
Buying a home takes a great deal of money that young people simply do not have.

confusables.difference: 'A great deal of' goes with uncountables; 'a great many' goes with countable plurals - a great many students.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a great deal of people'. People are countable, so use 'a great many people'.

entry_json.definition: employment that lasts a whole career with one employer; it usually appears in the past or the negative, because the idea has largely disappeared
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandfather had a job for life; my generation changes employer every three years.
example_sentences: Nobody expects a job for life any more, and some people actually prefer it that way.

collocations: the end of a job for life
no longer a job for life

contexts.text: My grandfather had a job for life; my generation changes employer every three years.
Nobody expects a job for life any more, and some people actually prefer it that way.
The end of a job for life has turned retraining into a lifelong task.

confusables.difference: 'A permanent job' is a contract type you can hold today. 'A job for life' is a whole-career idea and is nearly always used to say it no longer exists.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a contract with no end date - that is 'a permanent position'.

entry_json.definition: a type of something; in speech it also hedges, meaning 'roughly' or 'something like'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a kind of festival that only happens in the north of the country.
