contexts.text: It is a kind of festival that only happens in the north of the country.
Social media has become a kind of public square, for better or worse.
My role is a kind of bridge between the engineers and the clients.

confusables.difference: Without the article, 'kind of' is an adverb - 'I was kind of nervous' - and is very informal. 'A kind of' introduces a noun.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a kind of a festival'. Use one article only: 'a kind of festival'.

entry_json.definition: many; it takes a countable plural noun, and the verb that follows is normally plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A large number of people move to the capital every year in search of work.
example_sentences: A large number of respondents said that they preferred online lectures.
A large number of illnesses could be prevented by better diet alone.
collocations: attract a large number of sth

contexts.text: A large number of people move to the capital every year in search of work.
A large number of respondents said that they preferred online lectures.
A large number of illnesses could be prevented by better diet alone.

confusables.difference: 'Number' counts - a large number of cars. 'Amount' measures - a large amount of traffic. Mixing them is one of the commonest Task 2 errors.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a large number of information'. Uncountable nouns need 'a large amount of'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of something uncountable, or 'slightly' before an adjective or adverb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I speak a little Spanish, enough to order food and ask directions.
example_sentences: Unemployment fell a little in the final quarter of the year.
Sleeping a little longer each night makes a measurable difference to concentration.

contexts.text: I speak a little Spanish, enough to order food and ask directions.
Unemployment fell a little in the final quarter of the year.
Sleeping a little longer each night makes a measurable difference to concentration.

confusables.difference: 'A little' means some. 'Little' on its own means almost none and is negative: 'There is little evidence' says the evidence is missing.
'A little' measures uncountables - a little water. 'A few' counts - a few bottles.

entry_json.avoid: Dropping 'a' reverses the meaning, so decide whether you mean 'some' or 'hardly any'.

entry_json.definition: slightly; a spoken softener before an adjective, or a very small quantity of something uncountable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was a little bit worried about the listening section.
example_sentences: Add a little bit of salt at the end rather than at the start.
Most people would be a little bit happier with one day less in the office.

contexts.text: I was a little bit worried about the listening section.
Add a little bit of salt at the end rather than at the start.
Most people would be a little bit happier with one day less in the office.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'a little bit' is gentler still. Both belong to speech.
'Slightly' is the written equivalent and is what an essay needs.

entry_json.avoid: Too informal for writing. In an essay use 'slightly'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of assistance; 'help' is uncountable here, so it takes 'a little' and never a plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: With a little help from my tutor I managed to finish the essay on time.
example_sentences: A little help at the right moment stops a new employee from giving up.
Older relatives often need a little help rather than full-time care.

contexts.text: With a little help from my tutor I managed to finish the essay on time.
A little help at the right moment stops a new employee from giving up.
Older relatives often need a little help rather than full-time care.

confusables.difference: 'Help' has no plural in this sense, so if you need something countable use 'a few tips' or 'a few suggestions'.

entry_json.avoid: Never make 'help' plural. 'A few helps' is not English.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of money; the tone is positive, because it says you have some
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to put a little money aside at the end of every month.
example_sentences: A little money spent on prevention saves a great deal on treatment later.
We had saved a little money, so we travelled by train instead of flying.

contexts.text: I try to put a little money aside at the end of every month.
A little money spent on prevention saves a great deal on treatment later.
We had saved a little money, so we travelled by train instead of flying.

confusables.difference: 'A little money' means you have some. 'Little money' means almost none: 'Little money was available for repairs'.

entry_json.avoid: Money is uncountable. Not 'a few moneys' - say 'a little money' or 'a few coins'.

entry_json.definition: slightly more; used before a comparative or before an uncountable noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students need a little more time to adapt than most timetables allow.
example_sentences: If people walked a little more, the health service would spend a great deal less.
Households spent a little more on housing and a little less on food.

contexts.text: Students need a little more time to adapt than most timetables allow.
If people walked a little more, the health service would spend a great deal less.
Households spent a little more on housing and a little less on food.

confusables.difference: A question of size. 'A little more' matches 'slightly' in a Task 1 description, not 'sharply'.

entry_json.avoid: With countable plurals use 'a few more': 'a few more students', not 'a little more students'.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of sugar; sugar is uncountable, so it takes 'a little' and stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take my tea with a little sugar and no milk.
example_sentences: A little sugar in a home-cooked meal is not the problem; processed food is.
My grandmother added a little sugar to almost everything she cooked.

contexts.text: I take my tea with a little sugar and no milk.
A little sugar in a home-cooked meal is not the problem; processed food is.
My grandmother added a little sugar to almost everything she cooked.

confusables.difference: 'Two sugars' is spoken shorthand for spoonfuls in a hot drink. The substance itself stays uncountable: 'a little sugar'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a little sugars'. Keep the noun singular.

entry_json.definition: an extended period; it follows 'for' or works as the object of verbs such as 'take' and 'spend'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in the same neighbourhood for a long time.
example_sentences: Waiting a long time for treatment is what patients complain about most.
It takes a long time to build the trust a good team depends on.

contexts.text: I have lived in the same neighbourhood for a long time.
Waiting a long time for treatment is what patients complain about most.
It takes a long time to build the trust a good team depends on.

confusables.difference: Modern English needs the article: 'for a long time', not 'for long time'. 'Long time no see' is a fixed joke, not a model.

entry_json.avoid: With a present perfect it means the situation continues: 'I have known her for a long time' - she is still a friend.

entry_json.definition: far back in the past; because it fixes a finished point in time it forces the past simple
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandparents moved to the city a long time ago, before the motorway was built.
example_sentences: The festival began a long time ago as a celebration of the harvest.
Handwriting stopped being essential a long time ago, yet schools still test it.
collocations: that was a long time ago

contexts.text: My grandparents moved to the city a long time ago, before the motorway was built.
The festival began a long time ago as a celebration of the harvest.
Handwriting stopped being essential a long time ago, yet schools still test it.

confusables.difference: 'A long time ago' fixes a point in the past. 'For a long time' measures a stretch that may reach the present.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'I have moved here a long time ago'. A finished past time needs the past simple.

entry_json.definition: a great distance; also used figuratively in 'go a long way' (be enough, help a lot) and 'come a long way' (make great progress)
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I live quite a long way from the centre, so I cycle to the station.
example_sentences: The country has come a long way in twenty years, but rural areas still lag behind.
A small salary goes a long way in a town where rents are low.

contexts.text: I live quite a long way from the centre, so I cycle to the station.
The country has come a long way in twenty years, but rural areas still lag behind.
A small salary goes a long way in a town where rents are low.

confusables.difference: In positive statements English prefers 'a long way': 'It is a long way to the airport'. 'Far' is normal in questions and negatives.

entry_json.avoid: 'Go a long way' is about being sufficient, not about distance. Check which sense you mean.

entry_json.definition: very much, or very often; it follows the verb - 'I read a lot' - and is two words, never one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read a lot in the evenings, mostly online.
example_sentences: Traffic in my city has changed a lot in the last five years.
People complain a lot about hospital waiting times, and the figures support them.

contexts.text: I read a lot in the evenings, mostly online.
Traffic in my city has changed a lot in the last five years.
People complain a lot about hospital waiting times, and the figures support them.

confusables.difference: 'A lot' is the spoken form. 'Much' after a verb belongs mainly to negatives and questions: 'I do not read much'.
'A lot' is always two words. 'Alot' does not exist in English.

entry_json.avoid: Two words, always. In an essay replace it with 'considerably' or 'a great deal'.

entry_json.definition: much more; used before a comparative adjective, before a noun, or on its own after a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Eating out costs a lot more than it did five years ago.
example_sentences: Children today have a lot more choice and a lot more pressure.
We would need a lot more evidence before banning something outright.

contexts.text: Eating out costs a lot more than it did five years ago.
Children today have a lot more choice and a lot more pressure.
We would need a lot more evidence before banning something outright.

confusables.difference: Before countable plurals, formal writing prefers 'many more people'; 'a lot more people' is the spoken version.

entry_json.avoid: Informal. In Task 1 write 'considerably more', or simply give the figure.

entry_json.definition: a large quantity of something; unlike 'many' and 'much' it works with both countable plurals and uncountables
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spend a lot of time revising at the weekend.
example_sentences: A lot of people are moving out of the city because of rent.
There is a lot of plastic waste on the beach at the end of summer.

contexts.text: I spend a lot of time revising at the weekend.
A lot of people are moving out of the city because of rent.
There is a lot of plastic waste on the beach at the end of summer.

confusables.difference: 'Lots of' is more informal still. Between the two, 'a lot of' is the safer spoken choice.
In an essay replace 'a lot of' with 'many' before plurals and 'a great deal of' before uncountables.

entry_json.avoid: Acceptable in Speaking, weak in Task 2. Swap it for 'a large number of' or 'a great deal of'.

entry_json.definition: many tasks to complete; note that adding 'with' changes the meaning entirely - 'have a lot to do with sth' means to be closely connected to it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a lot to do that week, so I turned down the invitation.
example_sentences: There is always a lot to do in the final month before exams.
Diet has a lot to do with how well people sleep.
collocations: a lot to do with sth

contexts.text: I had a lot to do that week, so I turned down the invitation.
There is always a lot to do in the final month before exams.
Diet has a lot to do with how well people sleep.

confusables.term: a lot to do with sth
confusables.difference: One preposition changes everything: without 'with' it means workload, with 'with' it means connection.

entry_json.avoid: Decide which meaning you want before you add 'with'.

entry_json.definition: a method people use to exchange information; the noun 'means' keeps its -s in the singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Email is still a means of communication that almost every workplace depends on.
example_sentences: The report treats social media as a means of communication rather than as entertainment.
A letter was once a means of communication everyone used; today almost nobody writes one.

contexts.text: Email is still a means of communication that almost every workplace depends on.
The report treats social media as a means of communication rather than as entertainment.
A letter was once a means of communication everyone used; today almost nobody writes one.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning; 'a means of communication' is the academic form and lifts a Task 2 sentence.
'Means' never loses its -s, even when it is singular.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'a mean of communication'. The word is 'means' in both singular and plural.

entry_json.definition: a method or instrument for achieving something; followed by a noun or an -ing form, and 'means' is the same in singular and plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling should be treated as a means of transport, not just as a form of exercise.
example_sentences: Taxation is a means of redistributing wealth as well as of raising revenue.
Education is a means of escaping poverty, but only where the jobs exist.

contexts.text: Cycling should be treated as a means of transport, not just as a form of exercise.
Taxation is a means of redistributing wealth as well as of raising revenue.
Education is a means of escaping poverty, but only where the jobs exist.

confusables.difference: 'Method' names a procedure you follow step by step; 'means' names anything that gets you there, including a tool or a route.

entry_json.avoid: The -s belongs to the word itself: 'a means', 'two means'. Never 'a mean'.

entry_json.definition: a way of travelling or of moving goods, such as a bus, a bicycle or a train
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The survey asked respondents to name a means of transport they had used that week.
example_sentences: A means of transport that most people can afford does more for a city than a fast one that few can use.
The metro is a means of transport I rely on every single day.

contexts.text: The survey asked respondents to name a means of transport they had used that week.
A means of transport that most people can afford does more for a city than a fast one that few can use.
The metro is a means of transport I rely on every single day.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in Task 1. 'Mode of transport' is slightly more technical and appears constantly in chart questions.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a transport means', and never 'a mean of transport'.

entry_json.definition: a very short time; a polite, deliberately vague way of asking someone to wait
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Give me a moment or two and I will find the file.
example_sentences: Take a moment or two to plan before you start writing.
A moment or two of quiet before a difficult conversation makes a real difference.

contexts.text: Give me a moment or two and I will find the file.
Take a moment or two to plan before you start writing.
A moment or two of quiet before a difficult conversation makes a real difference.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'A moment or two' is shorter and more polite; 'a minute or two' is closer to real measurement.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken. In writing use 'briefly' or 'for a short time'.

entry_json.definition: several; it takes a countable plural noun and, importantly, a plural verb - 'a number of factors are involved'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A number of factors explain why the policy failed in rural areas.
example_sentences: A number of countries recorded a fall in emissions after 2010.
A number of my colleagues have moved to a four-day week.

contexts.text: A number of factors explain why the policy failed in rural areas.
A number of countries recorded a fall in emissions after 2010.
A number of my colleagues have moved to a four-day week.

confusables.difference: 'A number of students were late' means several. 'The number of students was falling' talks about the figure itself and takes a singular verb.

entry_json.avoid: 'A number of' takes a plural verb. Not 'a number of factors explains'.

entry_json.definition: a length of time, usually a defined one; standard in Task 1 for saying what a chart covers
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart covers a period of time stretching from 1990 to 2020.
example_sentences: Habits formed over a period of time are much harder to break.
Learning a language takes a period of time that no app can shorten.

contexts.text: The chart covers a period of time stretching from 1990 to 2020.
Habits formed over a period of time are much harder to break.
Learning a language takes a period of time that no app can shorten.

confusables.difference: Both exist. 'A period of time' is the natural English phrase; 'time period' is more technical and belongs to scientific writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it when you can name the period. 'Between 1990 and 2020' is far stronger in Task 1.

entry_json.definition: a small amount of money, roughly one or two pounds; used to say a difference in price is trivial
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A coffee near the station costs a pound or two more than one at home.
example_sentences: Most people will pay a pound or two extra for something that lasts longer.
The market is cheaper, but only by a pound or two on a weekly shop.

contexts.text: A coffee near the station costs a pound or two more than one at home.
Most people will pay a pound or two extra for something that lasts longer.
The market is cheaper, but only by a pound or two on a weekly shop.

confusables.difference: The same money, a different point. 'A pound or two' stresses how little it is; 'a couple of pounds' simply counts.

entry_json.avoid: British currency and British speech. Keep it for Speaking, not for an essay.

entry_json.definition: a set of different things of the same type; it takes a plural noun and signals variety within limits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Universities now offer a range of courses that can be studied entirely online.
example_sentences: The clinic treats a range of conditions linked to poor diet.
Employers want a range of skills rather than one narrow specialism.

contexts.text: Universities now offer a range of courses that can be studied entirely online.
The clinic treats a range of conditions linked to poor diet.
Employers want a range of skills rather than one narrow specialism.

confusables.difference: 'Range' suggests a planned set with two ends, like a product line or a price band. 'Variety' stresses that the things differ from each other.

entry_json.avoid: It needs a plural noun: 'a range of courses', not 'a range of course'.

entry_json.definition: an increase in how many people visit a place; the standard Task 1 wording for a rising visitor line
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph shows a rise in the number of visitors to the national park after 2010.
example_sentences: A rise in the number of visitors brings money, but it also brings litter and traffic.
A rise in the number of visitors changes a small town very quickly.
collocations: a sharp rise in the number of visitors
a steady rise in the number of visitors

chunk.pattern: a rise in the number of visitors

contexts.text: The graph shows a rise in the number of visitors to the national park after 2010.
contexts.gap_span: a rise in the number of visitors

contexts.text: A rise in the number of visitors brings money, but it also brings litter and traffic.
contexts.gap_span: A rise in the number of visitors

contexts.text: A rise in the number of visitors changes a small town very quickly.
contexts.gap_span: A rise in the number of visitors

confusables.difference: 'Rise' is the noun for an increase. In British English 'a raise' means a pay increase and is mainly American usage.

confusables.term: an increase in the number of visitors
confusables.difference: Interchangeable. 'Rise' suits a line graph; 'increase' is neutral and works anywhere.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'in': a rise in the number of visitors, never 'a rise of visitors'.

entry_json.definition: several different kinds of something; it takes a countable plural noun and normally a plural verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A healthy diet contains a variety of vegetables rather than one so-called superfood.
example_sentences: The data were collected from a variety of sources over five years.
Cities attract people because they offer a variety of ways to live.

contexts.text: A healthy diet contains a variety of vegetables rather than one so-called superfood.
The data were collected from a variety of sources over five years.
Cities attract people because they offer a variety of ways to live.

confusables.difference: 'Variety' emphasises difference; 'range' emphasises the span from one end to the other, as in a range of prices.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a variety of information'. Choose a countable plural, or write 'various kinds of information'.

entry_json.definition: a large number of different things of the same type; one of the most useful noun phrases in Task 2
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools should offer a wide range of subjects so that late developers are not shut out.
example_sentences: The survey covered a wide range of age groups across six regions.
A single phone now replaces a wide range of devices we used to own separately.
collocations: offer a wide range of sth
cover a wide range of sth

contexts.text: Schools should offer a wide range of subjects so that late developers are not shut out.
The survey covered a wide range of age groups across six regions.
A single phone now replaces a wide range of devices we used to own separately.

confusables.difference: Nearly identical. Use 'range' for things that sit on a scale or a list, 'variety' when you want to stress how different they are.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a wide range of choice'. The noun after it must be plural: 'a wide range of choices'.

entry_json.definition: having the skill, the chance or the permission to do something; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After six months I was able to follow lectures without subtitles.
example_sentences: Patients should be able to book an appointment without waiting three weeks.
Only a third of respondents were able to work from home during the period.

contexts.text: After six months I was able to follow lectures without subtitles.
Patients should be able to book an appointment without waiting three weeks.
Only a third of respondents were able to work from home during the period.

confusables.difference: 'Can' has no infinitive and no perfect form, so 'able to' fills the gaps: 'will be able to', 'has been able to'.
'Able to' takes an infinitive; 'capable of' takes -ing. Never 'capable to do'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'able of doing'. The pattern is fixed: able to do.

entry_json.definition: most importantly of all; it singles out the strongest point in a list and usually opens a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Above all, teachers need time to prepare, not more paperwork.
example_sentences: The policy must be affordable, practical and, above all, enforceable.
Above all, people want to feel that the work they do matters.
collocations: above all, it is important to

contexts.text: Above all, teachers need time to prepare, not more paperwork.
The policy must be affordable, practical and, above all, enforceable.
Above all, people want to feel that the work they do matters.

confusables.difference: 'First of all' orders your points; 'above all' ranks them. Only one point can be 'above all'.

entry_json.avoid: Use it once in an essay. If everything is 'above all', nothing is.

entry_json.definition: the chance or the right to use or reach something; the preposition is always 'to' and the noun is uncountable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Access to fast internet now decides which children can study at home.
example_sentences: The report measured access to clean water in twelve rural districts.
Not everyone has access to the same technology, and that gap is widening.

contexts.text: Access to fast internet now decides which children can study at home.
The report measured access to clean water in twelve rural districts.
Not everyone has access to the same technology, and that gap is widening.

confusables.difference: The preposition is 'to', never 'of': access to education.
The adjective takes a different frame: 'education should be accessible to everyone', not 'access to everyone'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'an access'. The noun is uncountable: 'access to healthcare', not 'an access to healthcare'.

entry_json.definition: to form a stated part of a total, or to explain why something happens; in Task 1 it is the standard verb for shares of a whole, and it never splits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing accounted for almost half of all household spending in 2015.
example_sentences: Transport accounts for a growing share of total emissions.
Stress accounts for a lot of the sick days that employers complain about.
collocations: account for a share of sth
account for the majority of sth

contexts.text: Housing accounted for almost half of all household spending in 2015.
Transport accounts for a growing share of total emissions.
Stress accounts for a lot of the sick days that employers complain about.

confusables.difference: Both can mean 'give a reason', but only 'account for' can express a proportion: 'accounts for 40% of the total'.
A different phrase with a different meaning: to consider something when making a decision.

entry_json.avoid: It always keeps 'for' and never separates: 'account for 30%', not 'account 30%'.

entry_json.definition: said to have done something wrong; the pattern is be accused of + noun or -ing, never a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Anyone accused of a crime is entitled to a fair hearing.
example_sentences: Newspapers are often accused of reporting only the most dramatic cases.
Being accused of something in public can ruin a reputation before any trial.

contexts.text: Anyone accused of a crime is entitled to a fair hearing.
Newspapers are often accused of reporting only the most dramatic cases.
Being accused of something in public can ruin a reputation before any trial.

confusables.difference: 'Accused of' can be everyday and social. 'Charged with' is the formal legal step taken by the police.
'Blamed for' points at a result - blamed for the delay. 'Accused of' points at an act - accused of stealing.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'accused to steal'. The pattern is 'accused of stealing'.

entry_json.definition: to perform the function of something without necessarily being it; very common in academic description, and it keeps the article: act as a barrier
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Trees in a city act as a natural filter for polluted air.
example_sentences: The membrane acts as a barrier between the two solutions.
A good manager acts as a shield between the team and the pressure from above.

contexts.text: Trees in a city act as a natural filter for polluted air.
The membrane acts as a barrier between the two solutions.
A good manager acts as a shield between the team and the pressure from above.

confusables.difference: 'Act as' states a function. 'Act like' describes behaviour that resembles something: 'He acts like a child'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'act as a filter', not 'act as filter'.

entry_json.definition: to make something greater, usually a problem, a cost or a feeling; note that it has no object of its own, unlike 'add sth to sth'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: New office towers add to the traffic that the city already cannot handle.
example_sentences: Rising fuel prices added to the cost of every item on the shelf.
Long shifts add to the stress that nurses already carry.

contexts.text: New office towers add to the traffic that the city already cannot handle.
Rising fuel prices added to the cost of every item on the shelf.
Long shifts add to the stress that nurses already carry.

confusables.difference: 'Add to sth' means the subject increases something. 'Add sth to sth' moves one thing into another: 'Add sugar to the mixture'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for physically putting something somewhere - that needs 'add sth to sth'.

entry_json.definition: either 'remember, this is the reason' when you give support the reader half knows, or 'in the end, contrary to expectation' at the end of a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students should be consulted; after all, it is their time that is being spent.
example_sentences: The meeting was cancelled, so I got an early night after all.
Cheap flights are not really cheap after all, once you add the extras.

contexts.text: Students should be consulted; after all, it is their time that is being spent.
The meeting was cancelled, so I got an early night after all.
Cheap flights are not really cheap after all, once you add the extras.

confusables.difference: 'At last' expresses relief after waiting. 'After all' either supplies a reason or reverses an expectation.
'Finally' orders events in a sequence. 'After all' never does.

entry_json.avoid: It does not mean 'finally'. Never use it to introduce the last paragraph of an essay.

entry_json.definition: repeatedly, usually with a note of frustration; it sits after the verb or at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The same mistakes appear again and again in student writing.
example_sentences: I had to explain the system again and again until everyone understood it.
Governments promise action again and again, and emissions keep rising.

contexts.text: The same mistakes appear again and again in student writing.
I had to explain the system again and again until everyone understood it.
Governments promise action again and again, and emissions keep rising.

confusables.difference: The same meaning, slightly more formal and shorter.
Very close, but more spoken, and it usually adds 'again' at the end.

entry_json.avoid: It carries impatience. Do not use it for something you enjoy repeating.

entry_json.definition: to have the same opinion as someone; with a person or an opinion the preposition is 'with', and the two words never separate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I agree with people who say exams measure memory more than ability.
example_sentences: Most researchers agree with the view that screens before bed harm sleep.
My brother and I rarely agree with each other about politics.
collocations: could not agree with sb more

contexts.text: I agree with people who say exams measure memory more than ability.
Most researchers agree with the view that screens before bed harm sleep.
My brother and I rarely agree with each other about politics.

confusables.difference: 'Agree with' is about opinions; 'agree to' is about accepting a proposal: 'They agreed to the plan'.
'Agree on' means two sides reach a shared decision: 'They agreed on a date'.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'I am agree'. 'Agree' is a full verb, so it is simply 'I agree'.

entry_json.definition: to intend to achieve something; it takes a to-infinitive and is the natural verb for stating the purpose of a policy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme aims to cut car journeys in the centre by a third.
example_sentences: The study aimed to measure how students use online libraries.
I aim to finish the report before the end of the week.

contexts.text: The scheme aims to cut car journeys in the centre by a third.
The study aimed to measure how students use online libraries.
I aim to finish the report before the end of the week.

confusables.difference: Both exist. 'Aim to do' takes a person or an organisation as subject; 'aimed at doing' hangs off a noun such as campaign or policy.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'aim to reducing'. After 'aim to' use the bare infinitive.

entry_json.definition: designed to achieve something; a participle phrase that follows a noun such as policy, campaign or measure, and the verb after 'at' must take -ing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A campaign aimed at reducing sugar consumption cut sales within a year.
example_sentences: The programme is aimed at raising literacy among adults who left school early.
Taxes aimed at discouraging plastic packaging work better than appeals to conscience.
collocations: a policy aimed at doing sth
a campaign aimed at doing sth

contexts.text: A campaign aimed at reducing sugar consumption cut sales within a year.
The programme is aimed at raising literacy among adults who left school early.
Taxes aimed at discouraging plastic packaging work better than appeals to conscience.

confusables.difference: 'Aim to do' needs a subject that intends something. 'Aimed at doing' attaches straight to a noun and needs none.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'aimed at reduce'. After the preposition 'at' the verb takes -ing.

entry_json.definition: intended for a particular group of people; used of advertising, courses and policies to name their audience
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertising aimed at children should be restricted during school hours.
example_sentences: The course is aimed at students who have never studied statistics.
Loans aimed at young people often hide the real cost in the small print.

contexts.text: Advertising aimed at children should be restricted during school hours.
The course is aimed at students who have never studied statistics.
Loans aimed at young people often hide the real cost in the small print.

confusables.difference: With a person it names the audience; with an -ing form it names the purpose. Compare 'aimed at children' and 'aimed at protecting children'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Aimed at' takes a target group, not a place. Not 'a course aimed at London'.

entry_json.definition: concerned entirely with something; 'it is all about X' claims that X is what really matters
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For a lot of employers, hiring is all about attitude rather than qualifications.
example_sentences: The course was all about learning to argue, not about learning facts.
Success in sport is all about consistency over years, not one good season.

contexts.text: For a lot of employers, hiring is all about attitude rather than qualifications.
The course was all about learning to argue, not about learning facts.
Success in sport is all about consistency over years, not one good season.

confusables.difference: 'About' simply names the topic. 'All about' insists it is the only thing that counts, which is an opinion, not a description.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken emphasis. In an essay write 'depends primarily on'.

entry_json.definition: two senses: almost or very nearly, before a strong adjective or participle ('all but impossible'), and everyone or everything except, before a noun or number
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Coal has all but disappeared from the country's electricity supply.
example_sentences: All but two of the regions recorded a fall in unemployment.
Paper maps have all but vanished from everyday life.

contexts.text: Coal has all but disappeared from the country's electricity supply.
All but two of the regions recorded a fall in unemployment.
Paper maps have all but vanished from everyday life.

confusables.difference: 'Almost' is neutral and everyday. 'All but' is formal and needs a strong word after it: all but impossible, all but vanished.
'All but two regions' and 'all regions except for two' mean the same thing; 'all but' is tighter and more formal.

entry_json.avoid: In the 'almost' sense it needs a strong word after it. 'All but tired' means nothing.

entry_json.definition: for the whole day; it takes no preposition of its own - 'I worked all day', never 'in all day'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I sat in front of a screen all day and my back paid for it.
example_sentences: Sitting all day is now treated as a health risk in its own right.
At the weekend the children are outside all day if the weather allows.

contexts.text: I sat in front of a screen all day and my back paid for it.
Sitting all day is now treated as a health risk in its own right.
At the weekend the children are outside all day if the weather allows.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable, but 'all day' is the more natural spoken form.
'All day' is one long stretch; 'every day' is a habit that repeats.

entry_json.avoid: No preposition. Not 'during all day' and not 'in all day'.

entry_json.definition: many different types of something; it takes a plural or uncountable noun and stresses variety
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The market sells all kinds of food you cannot find in supermarkets.
example_sentences: Remote work creates all kinds of problems that nobody predicted.
I read all kinds of things, from novels to technical manuals.

contexts.text: The market sells all kinds of food you cannot find in supermarkets.
Remote work creates all kinds of problems that nobody predicted.
I read all kinds of things, from novels to technical manuals.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning; 'all sorts of' is a little more British and more spoken.
That is the written equivalent and is what an essay needs.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken. In Task 2 write 'a wide range of' or 'various'.

entry_json.definition: for the whole night; like 'all day' it takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I stayed up all night before the exam, which was a mistake.
example_sentences: Working all night damages concentration for several days afterwards.
Shops that stay open all night make a city feel safer to some people and worse to others.

contexts.text: I stayed up all night before the exam, which was a mistake.
Working all night damages concentration for several days afterwards.
Shops that stay open all night make a city feel safer to some people and worse to others.

confusables.difference: 'Overnight' often means 'by the next morning' - the change happened overnight. 'All night' is purely about duration.

entry_json.avoid: No preposition: 'all night', not 'during all night'.

entry_json.definition: in every part of the world; it can modify a noun or a whole clause and already contains its own preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students all over the world now sit the same international examinations.
example_sentences: You find versions of this dish all over the world, each one slightly different.
Users all over the world reported the same fault within an hour.

contexts.text: Students all over the world now sit the same international examinations.
You find versions of this dish all over the world, each one slightly different.
Users all over the world reported the same fault within an hour.

confusables.difference: Nearly the same. 'Around the world' can suggest a journey; 'all over the world' stresses that it is everywhere at once.
'In the world' is neutral; 'all over the world' insists on the spread.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in all over the world'. The phrase already carries its preposition.

entry_json.definition: in every part of a named place, or covering a surface; of an event it also means completely finished
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are new blocks of flats going up all over the city.
example_sentences: You see the same coffee chains all over Europe now.
By the time we arrived the match was all over.

contexts.text: There are new blocks of flats going up all over the city.
You see the same coffee chains all over Europe now.
By the time we arrived the match was all over.

confusables.difference: 'Everywhere' stands alone; 'all over' needs a named place after it - all over the city.
A fixed idiom that also means disorganised: 'his notes were all over the place'.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken. In writing prefer 'throughout the city' to 'all over the city'.

entry_json.definition: many different types of something; the British spoken twin of 'all kinds of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In that job I met all sorts of people I would never otherwise have met.
example_sentences: One password leak causes all sorts of problems that take months to fix.
My mother grows all sorts of herbs on the balcony.

contexts.text: In that job I met all sorts of people I would never otherwise have met.
One password leak causes all sorts of problems that take months to fix.
My mother grows all sorts of herbs on the balcony.

confusables.difference: No real difference in meaning; 'sorts' is a little more British and a little more informal.

entry_json.avoid: Informal. Replace it with 'a wide variety of' in an essay.

entry_json.definition: even more, precisely because of the reason given; it goes before an adjective or adverb and expects a because- or since-clause nearby
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The result is all the more impressive because the school has almost no funding.
example_sentences: The findings are all the more worrying since the sample was young and healthy.
That makes recycling all the more important, not less.
collocations: all the more reason to do sth

contexts.text: The result is all the more impressive because the school has almost no funding.
The findings are all the more worrying since the sample was young and healthy.
That makes recycling all the more important, not less.

confusables.difference: 'Even more' simply intensifies. 'All the more' intensifies because of a stated reason, so the reason must be there.

entry_json.avoid: Without its reason the sentence sounds unfinished. Give the because-clause.

entry_json.definition: continuously, or very often; it sits naturally at the end of the clause and often carries mild complaint
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I use my phone for directions all the time now.
example_sentences: News alerts arrive all the time, and the effect on concentration is measurable.
Being available all the time is the real cost of remote work.

contexts.text: I use my phone for directions all the time now.
News alerts arrive all the time, and the effect on concentration is measurable.
Being available all the time is the real cost of remote work.

confusables.difference: 'Always' usually sits before the main verb; 'all the time' sits at the end and can sound like a complaint.
A different phrase entirely: 'at the time' means at that past moment.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'at the time', which points at one moment in the past.

entry_json.definition: the entire distance, or completely; usually with a verb of movement, or with 'from' or 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I walked all the way home because the buses had stopped.
example_sentences: They came all the way from Argentina for a two-day conference.
If you are going to change the system, change it all the way rather than halfway.

contexts.text: I walked all the way home because the buses had stopped.
They came all the way from Argentina for a two-day conference.
If you are going to change the system, change it all the way rather than halfway.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable when you mean distance. Only 'all the way' also carries the sense of 'completely'.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken. In writing give the distance, or use 'entirely'.

entry_json.definition: together with, in addition to; it adds a second item parenthetically, and the main verb still agrees with the first subject only
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Poor diet, along with a lack of exercise, explains much of the rise in obesity.
example_sentences: Rice production fell, along with wheat, in the final five years of the period.
Along with better pay, people want some say over their own hours.

contexts.text: Poor diet, along with a lack of exercise, explains much of the rise in obesity.
Rice production fell, along with wheat, in the final five years of the period.
Along with better pay, people want some say over their own hours.

confusables.difference: Very close. 'Along with' is usually parenthetical and sits between commas; 'as well as' joins the two items more tightly.
Interchangeable in writing, and 'together with' is the most formal of the three.

entry_json.avoid: The verb agrees with the first subject only: 'The teacher, along with the students, was late'.

entry_json.definition: something you can choose instead of something else; the preposition is always 'to', never 'of' or 'for'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling is a realistic alternative to driving only if the roads are safe.
example_sentences: The report examines a cheaper alternative to landfill for household waste.
Apprenticeships are a serious alternative to university for a lot of school leavers.

contexts.text: Cycling is a realistic alternative to driving only if the roads are safe.
The report examines a cheaper alternative to landfill for household waste.
Apprenticeships are a serious alternative to university for a lot of school leavers.

confusables.difference: The preposition is 'to': an alternative to plastic, never an alternative of plastic.
'Alternative' implies a replacement for something that already exists; 'option' is any choice at all.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'alternative for'. The only preposition is 'to'.

entry_json.definition: used at the end of a list to show that it could continue; it stands in for the examples you have not given
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We covered grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and so on.
example_sentences: Employers look at qualifications, experience, communication skills and so on.
Recycling, public transport, insulation and so on all help, but none of them is enough alone.
collocations: and so on and so forth

contexts.text: We covered grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation and so on.
Employers look at qualifications, experience, communication skills and so on.
Recycling, public transport, insulation and so on all help, but none of them is enough alone.

confusables.difference: The same job. 'And so on' belongs in speech and in less formal writing; 'etc.' looks abrupt in an essay.
More formal than 'and so on', and much less common in speech.

entry_json.avoid: Weak in Task 2. An examiner cannot credit examples you did not give, so name one more instead.

entry_json.definition: any other person; 'else' always comes after the pronoun, and the possessive is 'anyone else's'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I did not tell anyone else until the contract was signed.
example_sentences: A witness is under no obligation to discuss the case with anyone else.
A patient should be able to see their own record before anyone else does.

contexts.text: I did not tell anyone else until the contract was signed.
A witness is under no obligation to discuss the case with anyone else.
A patient should be able to see their own record before anyone else does.

confusables.difference: 'Anyone else' fits questions and negatives; 'someone else' fits positive statements.
Identical in meaning. 'Anybody' is a little more spoken.

entry_json.avoid: The possessive is 'anyone else's', never 'anyone's else'.

entry_json.definition: any other thing; standard in questions and negatives, and in the shop-counter question 'Anything else?'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The assistant asked whether I wanted anything else before she closed the till.
example_sentences: Sleep affects concentration more than anything else a student can control.
People use their phones for messaging more than for anything else.

contexts.text: The assistant asked whether I wanted anything else before she closed the till.
Sleep affects concentration more than anything else a student can control.
People use their phones for messaging more than for anything else.

confusables.difference: 'Anything else' suits questions and negatives; 'something else' suits positive statements: 'I want something else'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Else' follows the pronoun. Never 'else anything'.

entry_json.definition: except for, or in addition to; whether it excludes or adds depends on whether the rest of the sentence is negative
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Apart from the cost, online courses have very few disadvantages.
example_sentences: Apart from one wet afternoon, the whole trip went perfectly.
Apart from 2008, the figure rose in every year of the period.

contexts.text: Apart from the cost, online courses have very few disadvantages.
Apart from one wet afternoon, the whole trip went perfectly.
Apart from 2008, the figure rose in every year of the period.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable when you mean 'not including'. Only 'apart from' also means 'as well as': 'Apart from English, she speaks Arabic'.
The American equivalent; British writing prefers 'apart from'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'apart of'. That is a different phrase, 'a part of', and it needs the article.

entry_json.definition: to attract or interest someone; the preposition is 'to' for the person attracted, and the phrase does not separate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Advertising that appeals to fear works quickly and wears off just as fast.
example_sentences: The museum now appeals to a much younger audience than it did in 2005.
Traditional music appeals to me far more now than it did when I was a teenager.
collocations: appeal to sb's sense of fairness

contexts.text: Advertising that appeals to fear works quickly and wears off just as fast.
The museum now appeals to a much younger audience than it did in 2005.
Traditional music appeals to me far more now than it did when I was a teenager.

confusables.difference: 'Attract' can be physical - a magnet attracts iron. 'Appeal to' is about taste and interest.
In law you appeal against a decision, which is an entirely different use of the word.

entry_json.avoid: For people the preposition is 'to'. Not 'it appeals for me'.

entry_json.definition: to make a formal request for something you want to be given - a job, a place, a visa, a grant
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I applied for the job on the Friday and heard back on the Monday.
example_sentences: Students who apply for financial support should not have to prove hardship twice.
You have to apply for a visa several weeks before you travel.

contexts.text: I applied for the job on the Friday and heard back on the Monday.
Students who apply for financial support should not have to prove hardship twice.
You have to apply for a visa several weeks before you travel.

confusables.difference: 'Apply for' names the thing you want; 'apply to' names the institution you write to. You apply to a university for a place.
With an object it means to put something onto a surface, or to make a rule operate.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'apply a job'. The preposition 'for' is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: to be relevant to or affect a person, group or situation; it is also the verb for writing to an institution
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The same rule should apply to everyone, whatever they earn.
example_sentences: The findings apply to urban schools only and cannot be generalised.
Rules written for factories do not really apply to people working from home.

contexts.text: The same rule should apply to everyone, whatever they earn.
The findings apply to urban schools only and cannot be generalised.
Rules written for factories do not really apply to people working from home.

confusables.difference: 'Apply to' takes the institution or the group affected; 'apply for' takes the thing you want.
The passive means somebody actively enforces or uses it: 'the rule was applied to all staff'.

entry_json.own_context_sentence: Exposure to traffic pollution is highest among the people least likely to own a car.
example_sentences: Early exposure to a second language improved pronunciation more than later study did.
Constant exposure to bad news changes how safe people think their city is.

contexts.text: Exposure to traffic pollution is highest among the people least likely to own a car.
Early exposure to a second language improved pronunciation more than later study did.
Constant exposure to bad news changes how safe people think their city is.

confusables.difference: 'Exposure to' is passive - it happens to you. 'Experience of' suggests you lived through it actively.
'Exposure of' means revealing something: 'the exposure of the scandal'.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable and takes 'to': 'exposure to noise', never 'an exposure of noise'.

entry_json.definition: not to do something that was expected or required; a formal negative that takes a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme failed to reach the households it was designed for.
example_sentences: A third of applicants failed to complete the second stage.
Governments that fail to act now will pay far more later.
collocations: fail to take account of sth

contexts.text: The scheme failed to reach the households it was designed for.
A third of applicants failed to complete the second stage.
Governments that fail to act now will pay far more later.

confusables.difference: 'Failed to arrive' and 'did not arrive' describe the same event, but 'fail to' adds that it was expected.
With a direct object it means not to pass: 'she failed the exam'.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'fail to reaching'. It takes a to-infinitive.

entry_json.definition: to start sleeping, usually without meaning to; 'asleep' is an adjective that can never stand before a noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I fall asleep within minutes if I read rather than look at a screen.
example_sentences: Adults who take more than half an hour to fall asleep are often described as insomniac.
People fall asleep on long coach journeys and miss the only interesting part.

contexts.text: I fall asleep within minutes if I read rather than look at a screen.
Adults who take more than half an hour to fall asleep are often described as insomniac.
People fall asleep on long coach journeys and miss the only interesting part.

confusables.difference: 'Go to sleep' can be deliberate; 'fall asleep' happens to you.
'Asleep' is the state; 'sleepy' is wanting to sleep. And 'an asleep child' is wrong - write 'a sleeping child'.

entry_json.avoid: 'Asleep' never goes before a noun. Not 'an asleep passenger'.

entry_json.definition: to begin to love somebody; the verb is 'fall' because the change is sudden rather than gradual
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandparents fell in love during a summer job and married that winter.
example_sentences: Almost every popular song is about people who fall in love or stop being in love.
You can fall in love with a city in three days and regret moving there in three months.
collocations: fall in love at first sight

contexts.text: My grandparents fell in love during a summer job and married that winter.
Almost every popular song is about people who fall in love or stop being in love.
You can fall in love with a city in three days and regret moving there in three months.

confusables.difference: 'Be in love' is the state; 'fall in love' is the moment it begins.
'Love' can grow slowly; 'fall in love' marks a sudden start.

entry_json.avoid: No article: 'fall in love', never 'fall in the love'.

entry_json.definition: to begin to love a particular person; the person always follows 'with', and the same pattern works for places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She fell in love with someone she met on the first day of the course.
example_sentences: I fell in love with Lisbon before I had even left the airport bus.
Films in which two strangers fall in love with each other are the oldest formula there is.
collocations: fall in love with a place
fall in love with each other
fall madly in love with sb

contexts.text: She fell in love with someone she met on the first day of the course.
I fell in love with Lisbon before I had even left the airport bus.
Films in which two strangers fall in love with each other are the oldest formula there is.

confusables.difference: Without 'with' you simply do not name the person.
'Love' states the feeling; 'fall in love with' marks the beginning of it.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'with', never 'to' or 'in': 'fall in love with her'.

entry_json.definition: to drop from a surface you were on, or of a number or a level, to decrease; the second sense is common in Task 1
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Demand fell off sharply after the subsidy was withdrawn.
example_sentences: I fell off my bicycle twice in the first week of commuting.
Visitor numbers fall off in the autumn, and half the businesses close.

contexts.text: Demand fell off sharply after the subsidy was withdrawn.
I fell off my bicycle twice in the first week of commuting.
Visitor numbers fall off in the autumn, and half the businesses close.

confusables.difference: 'Fall down' is from an upright position to the ground; 'fall off' is from something you were on.
As a noun the phrase is hyphenated: 'a falling-off in demand'.

entry_json.avoid: In the decrease sense it stays intransitive: 'demand fell off', not 'they fell off demand'.

entry_json.definition: to become separated from the thing you were attached to or resting on, and drop to the ground. The object follows 'off' and the phrase never splits: fall off the shelf, not fall the shelf off.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Half the tiles fell off the roof in the storm, and the landlord took a month to replace them.
example_sentences: My phone fell off the table and the screen cracked straight down the middle.
Cyclists are far more likely to fall off in wet weather, which is why helmets should be compulsory.
collocations: fall off the back of sth

contexts.text: I fell off my bike twice in the first week and decided to take proper lessons.
contexts.note: Everyday spoken narrative, Part 2 story.

contexts.text: Without the object, 'fall off' can also mean to decrease: attendance fell off sharply after the fees rose.
contexts.note: Second sense, useful for describing a graph.

contexts.text: Numbers fell off in the second half of the year, though they never returned to the 2010 low.

confusables.difference: You fall off something you were on top of or attached to. You fall down when you were standing and end up on the ground, with no surface named.
minimal_pair: He fell off the ladder.
He fell down in the street.

entry_json.avoid: Do not split it: 'fall the bike off' is not English, and the object always comes after 'off'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The two words link: fall-off, with the stress on OFF.

entry_json.definition: a person who belongs to your family: a parent, child, sibling, or wider relative. Countable, so it needs a or the in the singular: a family member, three family members.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my country it is normal for an older family member to live with the children rather than move into a home.
example_sentences: A close family member helped me pay for my first year of university.
Many patients rely on a family member for transport to hospital appointments.

contexts.text: The person I admire most is actually a family member, my aunt.
contexts.note: Very common opening for the Part 2 'describe a person' card.

contexts.text: Care for the elderly is still provided largely by family members rather than by the state.
contexts.note: Plural, no article, for a general statement.

contexts.text: I am writing to ask whether a family member may visit outside normal hours.

confusables.difference: A relative is usually someone outside the household: cousins, uncles, in-laws. A family member covers everyone, including the parents and children you live with.
minimal_pair: My family members were all at the wedding.
My relatives came from three different countries.

confusables.difference: Family is the whole group, family member is one person in it. You cannot say 'a family' when you mean one person.
minimal_pair: My family is large.
One family member is a doctor.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a familiar member'. And in the singular it must have an article: 'family member helped me' is missing 'a'.

entry_json.definition: a long distance from here, or from the place being talked about. It works as an adverb after the verb, and before a noun it is hyphenated: a far-away village.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My university was far away from home, so I only went back twice a year.
example_sentences: The nearest hospital is forty kilometres away, which is far too far away in an emergency.
Working from home means it no longer matters how far away the office is.

contexts.text: Is your flat far away from the city centre? No, it is about ten minutes on foot.
contexts.note: Part 1 question about where you live.

contexts.text: Rural patients living far away from specialist centres wait significantly longer for treatment.
In questions and negatives we normally drop 'away': How far is the station? It is not far.
contexts.note: Pattern note: 'far' alone is more natural in questions and negatives.

confusables.difference: In positive statements native speakers prefer 'a long way': It is a long way from here. 'Far away' is more natural with 'too', 'not' or 'how'.
minimal_pair: It is a long way from here.
It is not far away from here.

entry_json.avoid: In a plain positive sentence 'It is far from here' sounds odd to a British ear; say 'It is a long way from here'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The r in 'far' is pronounced because 'away' begins with a vowel: fa-ra-way.

entry_json.definition: used to say that the opposite is true, or that something is nowhere near finished. After 'from' you must use the -ing form: far from solving the problem, not far from solve.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Far from solving congestion, the new ring road simply moved the traffic to a different set of streets.
example_sentences: Far from being a waste of time, learning a second language changes how you think.
The government is far from meeting its own target of halving emissions by 2030.

contexts.text: Far from reducing inequality, free university places have mainly benefited middle-class families.
contexts.note: Fronted, with a comma: a strong Task 2 counter-argument opener.

contexts.text: We are far from knowing what the long-term effects of these apps on teenagers will be.
contexts.note: Mid-sentence use after 'be'.

contexts.text: Honestly, I am far from being an expert, but I do read a lot about it.
contexts.note: A useful hedge in Part 3.

confusables.difference: 'Instead of' names the alternative you chose. 'Far from' denies the expected result and usually introduces the opposite one.
minimal_pair: Instead of solving congestion, they built houses.
Far from solving congestion, the road made it worse.

entry_json.avoid: Never follow it with an infinitive: 'far from solve the problem' is wrong; it must be 'far from solving'.

entry_json.definition: a long way from a place, or, with an adjective or noun, the opposite of it: far from perfect means not perfect at all.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The results were far from clear, so the study had to be repeated with a larger sample.
example_sentences: Our house is quite far from the nearest station, which is why we still need a car.
The system is far from ideal, but replacing it would cost more than the city can afford.

contexts.text: I live quite far from the centre, so my commute is about an hour each way.
contexts.note: Literal distance.

contexts.text: The evidence for a link between screen time and poor sleep is far from conclusive.
contexts.note: Figurative: a strong, formal way of saying 'not at all'.

contexts.text: That explanation is far from the truth, as the committee later admitted.

confusables.difference: 'Far from clear' is much stronger than 'not very clear'. It means there is no clarity at all, not just a little.
minimal_pair: The results were not very clear.
The results were far from clear.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a small shortfall. 'Far from' claims the opposite, so it overstates if the thing is only slightly imperfect.

entry_json.definition: much more. 'Far' is an intensifier used only with comparatives, so it goes before more, less, better, worse and never before a plain adjective.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities in the north receive far more rainfall than the coastal south, which explains the difference in farming.
example_sentences: Online courses reach far more students than a lecture hall ever could.
I enjoy reading far more than watching television, though I do both.

contexts.text: I spend far more time on my phone than I would like to admit.
The chart shows that far more households owned a car in 2020 than in 1990.
contexts.note: A cleaner alternative to 'a lot more' in Task 1.

contexts.text: Young people are far more likely to rent than to buy.

confusables.difference: 'Very' cannot go with a comparative. Use 'far more' or 'much more', never 'very more'.
minimal_pair: It is far more expensive.
It is very expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'far many more people' and never 'very more'. With countable nouns say 'far more people'.

entry_json.definition: much more important. A ready-made comparison used to rank two things, normally followed by 'than' or by 'to do sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my view, teaching children how to cook is far more important than teaching them a second language at primary level.
example_sentences: Practical experience is far more important than a long list of qualifications in this industry.
What is far more important is that the water supply stays clean.
collocations: far more important to do sth

chunk.pattern: X is far more important than Y

contexts.text: For me, sleep is far more important than a long gym session.
contexts.note: Part 3 opinion, comparing two options.

contexts.text: Reducing industrial emissions is far more important than asking individuals to recycle.
contexts.note: Task 2 thesis: it ranks one solution above another.

contexts.text: The cost mattered, but reliability was far more important to us.

confusables.difference: 'Far more important' compares two things. 'The most important' picks one out of all of them and needs 'the'.
minimal_pair: Health is far more important than money.
Health is the most important thing of all.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'far more importanter' or 'more far important'. The order is fixed: far + more + adjective.

entry_json.definition: many more chances to do something. A high-frequency Task 2 and Part 3 partnership, usually completed by 'to do sth', 'for sb' or 'than'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living in a capital city gives young people far more opportunities to find work in their own field.
example_sentences: Students who speak English have far more opportunities to study abroad.
Remote working offers far more opportunities for parents with young children.
collocations: far more opportunities to do sth

chunk.pattern: give / offer / have + far more opportunities + to do sth

contexts.text: There are far more opportunities here than in the town I grew up in.
Urban migration continues because cities offer far more opportunities for skilled work.
contexts.note: Standard Task 2 reason for rural-to-urban migration.

contexts.text: The scholarship gave me far more opportunities than I had expected.

confusables.difference: In this pattern 'opportunity' is countable and plural: far more opportunities. 'Much opportunity' is uncountable and sounds odd here.
minimal_pair: far more opportunities
a great deal of opportunity

entry_json.avoid: Not 'far more opportunity of studying'. The natural follow-on is 'to study' or 'for study'.
entry_json.audio_hint: British 'opportunities' has a y-sound in the middle: op-uh-TYOO-nuh-teez.

entry_json.definition: much more than is acceptable or necessary. It goes before an adjective or adverb, or before much and many: far too expensive, far too many cars.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents in the capital are far too high for anyone on an average salary.
example_sentences: The city has far too few green spaces for the number of people living there.
I think teenagers spend far too long staring at a screen.

contexts.text: It was far too crowded, so we left after about ten minutes.
Far too little attention has been paid to what happens to these devices once they are thrown away.
contexts.note: Works with 'little' and 'few' as well as 'much' and 'many'.

contexts.text: The instructions were far too complicated for a first-time user.

confusables.difference: 'Very' just measures. 'Far too' judges: it says the amount is beyond what is acceptable. Very expensive may still be worth buying; far too expensive is not.
minimal_pair: The flat is very expensive.
The flat is far too expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a noun straight after it. Say 'far too many cars', not 'far too cars'.

entry_json.definition: a great deal more homework than a student can reasonably do. Homework is uncountable, so it takes 'much' and never a plural s.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children in my country are given far too much homework, and it leaves them no time for sport or family.
example_sentences: Teachers set far too much homework in the final year, which is one reason students burn out.
Parents often complain that primary pupils are given far too much homework.
collocations: be given far too much homework
far too much homework to do

chunk.pattern: give / set + sb + far too much homework

contexts.text: We had far too much homework at secondary school, honestly about three hours a night.
contexts.note: Part 1 school question.

contexts.text: Setting far too much homework can reduce motivation rather than improve results.
contexts.note: Common Task 2 topic: should homework be reduced?

contexts.text: I am writing because my son is being given far too much homework this term.
contexts.note: A complaint letter, General Training Task 1.

confusables.difference: Homework never takes a plural or 'many'. If you need to count, say 'far too many homework assignments'.
minimal_pair: far too much homework
far too many assignments

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'homeworks'. The word has no plural in English, however many exercises there are.

entry_json.definition: annoyed and bored with a situation that has gone on too long. It follows a linking verb (be, get, feel) and takes 'with' before the cause: fed up with the noise.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got fed up with commuting three hours a day, so I looked for a job closer to home.
example_sentences: A lot of residents are fed up with the constant roadworks on the high street.
I was getting fed up with my old phone freezing every time I opened the camera.

chunk.pattern: be / get fed up with + noun / -ing

contexts.text: To be honest, I was fed up with the weather by the end of February.
contexts.note: Natural in Speaking, informal.

contexts.text: In an essay, write 'residents are increasingly frustrated with the delays' rather than 'fed up'.
contexts.note: Register warning: fed up is too informal for Task 2.

contexts.text: She finally got fed up with waiting and cancelled the order.

confusables.difference: Bored means there is nothing interesting happening. Fed up adds irritation: you have had enough of something that keeps happening.
minimal_pair: I was bored during the lecture.
I was fed up with the lecturer always arriving late.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken only. Using 'fed up' in Task 2 lowers your lexical score; use 'frustrated' or 'dissatisfied' there. Also, the preposition is 'with', not 'of' or 'about'.

entry_json.definition: to be happy, healthy or satisfied. 'Feel' is a linking verb here, so it takes the adjective good, not the adverb well in this sense.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Half an hour of exercise in the morning makes me feel good for the rest of the day.
example_sentences: It feels good to finish a piece of work you have put real effort into.
Volunteering makes people feel good about themselves, which is why so many keep doing it.
collocations: it feels good to do sth

chunk.pattern: make sb feel good / feel good about sth

contexts.text: Swimming is the one sport that always makes me feel good afterwards.
Time spent outdoors makes people feel good, and there is now solid evidence behind that impression.
I did not feel well enough to go in, so I worked from home.
contexts.note: Contrast: health uses 'feel well', mood uses 'feel good'.

confusables.difference: Feel well is about physical health only, and is mostly used in questions and negatives. Feel good covers mood, confidence and satisfaction.
minimal_pair: I do not feel well, I think I have a cold.
I feel good about the interview.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'I feel goodly'. After a linking verb like feel you need the adjective, not an adverb.

entry_json.definition: to want something, or to seem like something. When it means 'want', the next verb takes -ing: I feel like going out. It also introduces a comparison: it feels like winter.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After a long week I never feel like cooking, which is why we order food far too often.
example_sentences: I do not feel like studying this evening, so I will start early tomorrow instead.
The exam felt like a marathon rather than a test of knowledge.

contexts.text: At the weekend I usually feel like doing nothing at all, and I think that is healthy.
contexts.note: The 'want' sense: informal, Speaking only.

contexts.text: Standing in that square, it felt like stepping back two hundred years.
contexts.note: The 'seem like' sense, good for a Part 2 description.

contexts.text: For many commuters the journey feels like a second working day.
contexts.note: The comparison sense is acceptable in writing; the 'want' sense is not.

confusables.difference: Would like is a polite request or offer and takes 'to' plus the infinitive. Feel like is a casual mood and takes -ing.
minimal_pair: I would like to go out tonight.
I feel like going out tonight.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'I feel like to go'. After 'feel like' use the -ing form or a noun.

entry_json.definition: to work out the answer to something, or come to understand a person, after some thought. It is separable: figure out the problem or figure the problem out, but with a pronoun it must split: figure it out.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a whole afternoon to figure out how the referencing software actually worked.
example_sentences: I could not figure out why the bill was so high until I checked the heating settings.
Once you figure the timetable out, getting around the city is straightforward.
collocations: figure out how to do sth

contexts.text: I am still trying to figure out how to use half the features on my new phone.
With a pronoun the phrase always splits: I gave her the map and she figured it out in seconds.
contexts.note: Pattern: never 'figured out it'.

contexts.text: In formal writing prefer 'determine' or 'establish': researchers have yet to establish why the effect disappears.
contexts.note: Register warning: figure out is informal.

confusables.difference: You find out a fact by asking or looking it up. You figure something out by thinking it through yourself.
minimal_pair: I found out the price by ringing the office.
I figured out the price from the table in the brochure.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'figure out it'. A pronoun object goes in the middle: figure it out.
entry_json.audio_hint: The r links into out: FIG-ger-OWT.

entry_json.definition: to write the required information in the spaces on a form or document. It is separable: fill in the form, fill the form in, fill it in.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You have to fill in an online application form and upload two references before the deadline.
example_sentences: Please fill in the registration form and bring it to reception on your first day.
I filled it in twice because the website timed out the first time.

contexts.text: It only takes five minutes to fill the form in if you have your passport with you.
Applicants must fill in section three before the interview.
contexts.note: Formal letter, instructions.

contexts.text: Americans usually say fill out a form; British English prefers fill in.
contexts.note: Variety note: both are correct, fill in is the British norm.

confusables.difference: Fill up means make a container full: fill up the tank. Fill in means write in the blank spaces on a form.
minimal_pair: I filled up the car before the journey.
I filled in the visa form before the journey.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'fill in it'. With a pronoun the phrase must split: fill it in.

lemma: find it difficult to do sth

entry_json.headword: find it difficult to do sth
entry_json.definition: to experience something as hard to do. The 'it' is a dummy subject standing in for the to-infinitive that follows, and it cannot be left out.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many students find it difficult to concentrate when they are studying in a shared flat.
example_sentences: Older workers often find it difficult to retrain for jobs in technology.
I find it difficult to speak English on the phone, even though I am fine face to face.
collocations: find it hard to do sth
find it easy to do sth

chunk.pattern: find + it + adjective + to do sth

contexts.text: I find it difficult to get up early in winter, so I do my studying at night.
Low-income families find it difficult to afford housing near the schools their children attend.
contexts.note: A clean Task 2 way of stating a problem without the word 'problem'.

contexts.text: The same frame works with other adjectives: I find it easy to remember faces but impossible to remember names.

confusables.term: it is difficult for sb to do sth
confusables.difference: Both are correct. 'Find it difficult' reports a personal experience; 'it is difficult for' states a general fact.
minimal_pair: I find it difficult to save money.
It is difficult for young people to save money.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the 'it': 'I find difficult to concentrate' is a very common error and is ungrammatical.

entry_json.definition: to learn a fact for the first time, by asking, reading or being told. It is often followed by a that-clause or a wh-clause in statement word order.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I only found out that the course had a language requirement a week before the deadline.
example_sentences: I rang the college to find out when the results would be published.
Most people find out about local events through social media rather than the newspaper.

contexts.text: How did you find out about this school? A friend of mine recommended it.
The wh-clause keeps statement order: I want to find out how much it costs, not how much does it cost.
contexts.gap_span: find out how much it costs
contexts.note: Embedded question pattern.

contexts.text: Researchers set out to find out whether the effect held in colder climates.
contexts.note: Acceptable in writing, though 'determine' is more formal.

confusables.difference: Find out is the moment of learning; know is the state afterwards. You cannot 'know' a fact for the first time.
minimal_pair: I found out yesterday that she had left.
I know that she has left.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use question word order after it: 'I want to find out where is the office' should be 'where the office is'.
