minimal_pair: I will take an umbrella if it rains.
I will take an umbrella in case it rains.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'will' after it: 'in case it will rain' is wrong. And do not confuse it with 'in any case'.

entry_json.definition: having control of, or responsibility for, a person, group or activity. 'Charge' takes no article, and the thing controlled follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was put in charge of a small team in my second year, which taught me a great deal.
example_sentences: Who is in charge of the department while the manager is away?
A single agency should be in charge of flood defences rather than three separate bodies.
collocations: be in charge of a team
put sb in charge of sth

chunk.pattern: be / put + in charge of + sb / sth

contexts.text: At home I am in charge of the cooking and my brother does everything else.
Local councils should be in charge of planning decisions rather than central government.
'The person in charge' can stand alone with no 'of': I would like to speak to the person in charge.

confusables.difference: Almost the same, but 'in charge of' stresses authority and control, while 'responsible for' stresses duty and blame.
minimal_pair: She is in charge of the team.
She is responsible for any mistakes.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the charge of', which means in somebody else's care and reverses the direction.

entry_json.definition: during a lesson. No article, because it names the activity of being taught rather than a particular room or group.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We do most of the speaking practice in class and the writing at home.
example_sentences: Students who ask questions in class tend to remember more of the material.
He was told off for using his phone in class.

contexts.text: I never used to speak in class, and that is exactly why my English took so long to improve.
Discussion in class is more effective than lecturing for developing critical thinking.
With an article it means a particular group: there are thirty students in the class.
contexts.note: Activity versus group.

confusables.difference: In class means during the lesson. In the classroom refers to the physical room, and is also used figuratively for teaching practice generally.
minimal_pair: She never speaks in class.
There is no projector in the classroom.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the class' when you mean during a lesson, and not 'at class'.

entry_json.definition: together with somebody or something, so that the two work as one. It is formal, and is used both for organisations working together and for measures used in combination.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Congestion charging works best in conjunction with a genuinely reliable bus network.
example_sentences: The research was carried out in conjunction with two European universities.
The drug should be used in conjunction with changes to diet and exercise.

contexts.text: Recycling schemes only reduce waste significantly when used in conjunction with limits on packaging.
contexts.note: A precise way of saying one measure alone is not enough.

contexts.text: The exhibition was organised in conjunction with the city museum.
In speech say 'together with' or 'alongside': it works alongside the bus service.
contexts.note: Register warning: this phrase is written English.

confusables.difference: In conjunction with means working together. In connection with means related to, or concerning. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: The study was done in conjunction with the hospital.
He was questioned in connection with the theft.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in conjunction to'. The preposition is 'with', and the phrase is too formal for Speaking.

entry_json.definition: concerning, or related to. It is formal, and is especially common in news reports and official letters.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am writing in connection with the advertisement that appeared in Saturday's paper.
example_sentences: Two people have been arrested in connection with the fire.
The department has published new guidance in connection with data storage.

contexts.text: I am writing in connection with the room advertised on your website.
contexts.note: A formal opening line for a General Training letter.

contexts.text: Police are questioning a man in connection with the incident.
contexts.note: News style: it avoids saying the person is guilty.

contexts.text: In speech say 'about': I am calling about the advertisement.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: The meaning is the same. 'About' is normal in speech; 'in connection with' is formal written English and would sound strange in conversation.
minimal_pair: I am calling about the job.
I am writing in connection with the post advertised.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Speaking. It sounds like a police statement rather than a conversation.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce something that is strikingly different from what was just said. It stands alone before a clause and takes a comma; for a noun you need 'in contrast to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rail use rose steadily over the period. In contrast, the number of bus journeys fell every single year.
example_sentences: Sales in the north grew by a fifth. In contrast, the southern region saw almost no change.
In contrast, older respondents said they preferred to shop in person.

contexts.text: Cycling increased by 40 per cent. In contrast, car use remained flat throughout the decade.
contexts.note: The standard Task 1 device for opposing two trends.

contexts.text: 'By contrast' means the same and is equally acceptable in academic writing.
The two things contrasted must be genuinely comparable, or the linker misleads the reader.
contexts.note: Logic warning.

confusables.difference: 'In contrast' stands alone before a clause. 'In contrast to' introduces a noun. Using the wrong one leaves a fragment or a double subject.
minimal_pair: In contrast, prices fell.
In contrast to prices, wages fell.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a noun straight after it: 'in contrast the north' is wrong; write 'in contrast to the north'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The noun is stressed on the first syllable: CON-trast. The verb is con-TRAST.

entry_json.definition: very different from somebody or something named. It introduces a noun phrase, and the contrast that follows is usually the surprising one.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In contrast to the previous decade, growth in the 2010s was concentrated in a handful of cities.
example_sentences: In contrast to her sister, she has no interest in living abroad.
Wind generation rose sharply, in contrast to coal, which almost disappeared.

contexts.text: In contrast to the capital, rents in the north remained broadly stable.
contexts.note: Comparing two regions in Task 1.

contexts.text: 'In stark contrast to' is the emphatic version, used when the difference is dramatic.
After 'to' a verb takes -ing: in contrast to walking, cycling covers four times the distance.
contexts.note: 'To' is a preposition here.

confusables.difference: 'Compared to' notes any difference or similarity. 'In contrast to' insists the two are opposite, so it is stronger.
minimal_pair: Compared to last year, sales are slightly up.
In contrast to last year, sales collapsed.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in contrast with' in most academic writing, and never follow 'to' with a full clause.

entry_json.definition: likely to be harmed, or at risk of something bad happening. No article, and the risk itself follows 'of' plus a noun or -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several coastal villages are now in danger of being lost to erosion within twenty years.
example_sentences: The species is in danger of extinction across most of its former range.
Nobody was in danger, but the building had to be evacuated.

contexts.text: Without stronger protection, these forests are in danger of disappearing altogether.
contexts.note: -ing after 'of', not an infinitive.

contexts.text: Cyclists are in danger every time they share a narrow road with lorries.
The adjective is different: cycling on that road is dangerous.
contexts.note: Noun phrase versus adjective.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'At risk' is more common in formal and statistical writing; 'in danger' is stronger and more immediate.
minimal_pair: Children are at risk of obesity.
The building is in danger of collapse.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the danger'. And after 'in danger of' use -ing, not 'to': not 'in danger to disappear'.

entry_json.definition: used to say what the real result of something is, even if it is not officially described that way. It also means that a rule is currently operating.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Charging for the car park is, in effect, a tax on anyone who cannot walk to work.
example_sentences: The subsidy is in effect a payment to landlords rather than to tenants.
The new regulations have been in effect since January.

contexts.text: Free tuition funded by general taxation is, in effect, a transfer from non-graduates to graduates.
contexts.note: A sophisticated Task 2 move: restating what a policy really does.

contexts.text: The ban comes into effect at the end of the month.
contexts.note: The 'operating' sense uses 'come into effect' or 'be in effect'.

contexts.text: Do not confuse the noun 'effect' with the verb 'affect': the ban affected sales; the effect was immediate.
contexts.note: Spelling trap.

confusables.difference: 'In fact' corrects or strengthens a statement. 'In effect' restates something in terms of its real result, often differently from its official name.
minimal_pair: In fact, the tax was never introduced.
The charge is, in effect, a tax.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in affect'. 'Affect' is the verb; the noun in this phrase is 'effect'.

entry_json.definition: used to correct what has just been said, or to add a stronger and often surprising detail. It usually sits at the start of the sentence or after the verb 'be'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People assume the city is expensive. In fact, rents outside the centre are lower than in most of the region.
example_sentences: The journey looks long on the map. In fact, it takes less than an hour.
She is not just a colleague; in fact, we studied together.

contexts.text: Many people believe recycling solves the problem. In fact, reducing consumption matters far more.
contexts.note: Correcting a common assumption: a strong Task 2 move.

contexts.text: I thought it would be difficult, but in fact it was quite straightforward.
It can strengthen rather than correct: the course was good, in fact excellent.
contexts.note: Second function: intensifying.

confusables.difference: Very close in meaning. 'Actually' is more conversational and often softens a correction; 'in fact' is more emphatic and works in writing.
minimal_pair: Actually, it is quite cheap.
In fact, it is cheaper than the alternative.

entry_json.avoid: It needs something to correct or strengthen. Do not use it as a general opener when nothing has been claimed yet.

entry_json.definition: supporting a proposal or person, or choosing one option instead of another. British spelling keeps the u: favour.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am strongly in favour of making public transport free for under-eighteens.
example_sentences: Two thirds of residents voted in favour of the new cycle lanes.
The committee rejected the original design in favour of a cheaper alternative.

contexts.text: There are strong arguments in favour of raising the school leaving age.
contexts.note: The Task 2 discussion frame: arguments in favour of, arguments against.

contexts.text: Are you in favour of the new rules? On balance, yes.
The 'instead of' sense: the plan was dropped in favour of a smaller scheme.
contexts.note: Second meaning: replacing one thing with another.

confusables.difference: 'In favour with' means somebody approves of you, which is a completely different idea. Support takes 'of'.
minimal_pair: I am in favour of the plan.
The proposal found favour with the committee.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in favour to' and not 'in the favour of'. In British writing keep the u in favour.

entry_json.definition: in the position directly before something, on the side that faces forward. It also means in somebody's presence: do not say that in front of the children.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a small park in front of the station where people wait for their buses.
example_sentences: A tall building has gone up in front of our window and blocked most of the light.
He was too shy to speak in front of the whole class.
collocations: sit in front of a screen

contexts.text: The bus stop is right in front of my building, which is very convenient.
Adults now spend around six hours a day in front of a screen.
contexts.note: Fixed collocation with screens.

contexts.text: The presence sense: I did not want to say anything in front of her colleagues.

confusables.difference: In front of means on the forward-facing side, close by. Opposite means facing it from across a road or space.
minimal_pair: The car is parked in front of the house.
The bakery is opposite the house.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the front of' unless you mean inside, near the front of something, as in 'in the front of the car'.

entry_json.definition: completely, with nothing left out or unpaid. It goes after the verb or its object: pay the amount in full.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The deposit will be refunded in full provided the room is left in good condition.
example_sentences: Please write your name in full, including any middle names.
The loan must be repaid in full within five years.

contexts.text: I would be grateful if the amount could be refunded in full.
contexts.note: Letter of complaint: the standard way to request a complete refund.

contexts.text: The findings were published in full on the department's website.
It contrasts with 'in part': the costs were met in part by the council and in full by no one.

confusables.difference: 'Fully' modifies an adjective or participle: fully aware, fully funded. 'In full' follows a verb and is used mostly with payment, publication and writing things out.
minimal_pair: The project is fully funded.
The invoice was paid in full.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the full'. And do not use it where you need 'fully': 'in full aware' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: usually, or considering something as a whole rather than in detail. It can open a sentence with a comma or follow the noun it qualifies: people in general.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In general, students who attend every seminar do better, though there are always exceptions.
example_sentences: Public transport in this city is, in general, reliable and reasonably priced.
In general, the older the building, the more expensive it is to heat.

contexts.text: In general, wealthier countries produce more waste per person.
contexts.note: A hedge: it protects a general claim from obvious exceptions.

contexts.text: In general I prefer cooking at home, but I do eat out at the weekend.
After a noun it means 'as a whole': attitudes to work in general have changed.
contexts.note: Different position, slightly different job.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'Generally' is a single adverb and can sit before the verb; 'in general' is a phrase and usually opens the sentence.
minimal_pair: Generally, people work longer hours now.
In general, people work longer hours now.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the general' and not 'in generally'.

entry_json.definition: at any time in the recorded past. It takes no article and very often follows a superlative: the hottest year in history.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was the largest peaceful demonstration in the country's history.
example_sentences: This was the wettest winter in recorded history for the region.
Few decisions in history have had such far-reaching consequences.

contexts.text: 2023 was the warmest year in recorded history.
contexts.note: Very common in environmental writing.

contexts.text: With a possessive the article stays away: the biggest change in the city's history.
As a school subject it also takes no article: I was never any good at history.

confusables.difference: 'In the past' means before now, at some unspecified time. 'In history' compares across the whole record and usually follows a superlative.
minimal_pair: In the past, people walked more.
It was the hottest summer in history.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the history' without a possessive. Say 'in history' or 'in the country's history'.

entry_json.definition: receiving treatment as a patient. British English drops the article when the meaning is the purpose of the place; American English says 'in the hospital'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother was in hospital for a fortnight after the operation.
example_sentences: He spent three nights in hospital and was discharged on the Friday.
The number of days patients spend in hospital has fallen steadily since 2000.

contexts.text: She was in hospital for a week, and the staff were excellent.
contexts.note: British usage, which the IELTS examiner voices use.

contexts.text: Average time spent in hospital fell from nine days to four over the period.
With an article you are visiting, not a patient: I was at the hospital to see a friend.
contexts.note: Patient versus visitor, exactly like 'at school'.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' you are a patient. With 'the' you are simply inside the building, perhaps working or visiting. American English uses 'the' for both.
minimal_pair: He is in hospital.
I met her in the hospital car park.

entry_json.avoid: In an IELTS answer about being ill, use the British form 'in hospital' with no article.

entry_json.definition: taking new information or events into account. It introduces the reason for reconsidering something, and is formal.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In light of the latest figures, the council has agreed to review the parking charges.
example_sentences: The policy was revised in light of the consultation responses.
In light of what we now know about air quality, the case for the ban is far stronger.

contexts.text: In light of the evidence linking pollution to asthma, stricter limits are justified.
contexts.note: A strong way to introduce evidence-based reasoning in Task 2.

contexts.text: The variant 'in the light of' is equally correct in British English.
contexts.note: Both forms are standard; British writing often keeps 'the'.

contexts.text: I would like to reconsider my application in light of my recent results.

confusables.difference: 'Because of' gives a plain cause. 'In light of' means new information has changed how something should be judged, which is a more analytical claim.
minimal_pair: The trip was cancelled because of the weather.
The plan was revised in light of the new forecast.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in light with' and not 'under the light of'. It takes 'of' plus a noun, never a clause.

entry_json.definition: matching or consistent with something else, such as a rule, a forecast or a trend. It is the standard phrase for saying a result was as expected.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wages have not risen in line with the cost of living, which is why so many households feel poorer.
example_sentences: The results were broadly in line with what the model predicted.
Fees will increase in line with inflation each September.
collocations: bring sth into line with sth

contexts.text: The increase in car ownership was in line with the growth in average income.
contexts.note: Task 1: linking two trends that move together.

contexts.text: The policy brings this country into line with the rest of Europe.
contexts.note: The change-of-state version uses 'into'.

contexts.text: The negative is very common: pay has not kept in line with prices.

confusables.difference: 'In accordance with' means obeying a rule. 'In line with' means matching a pattern, forecast or level, and does not imply obedience.
minimal_pair: built in accordance with the regulations
rising in line with inflation

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in line to'. And do not use it for obeying rules; that needs 'in accordance with'.

entry_json.definition: feeling a strong romantic attachment. No article, and it follows a linking verb: be in love, fall in love.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They met at university, fell in love and have been together ever since.
example_sentences: The film is about two people who fall in love in the middle of a war.
They were very much in love, but they lived on different continents.

contexts.text: My parents fell in love at a wedding and were married within a year.
The novel asks whether people who are in love make good decisions.
It is also used loosely about places: I fell in love with the city on the first day.
contexts.note: Extended, non-romantic use.

confusables.difference: 'Love' as a verb covers family and friends as well. 'In love' is specifically romantic, and 'fall in love' names the moment it began.
minimal_pair: I love my sister.
He is in love with her.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the love'. And 'fall in love' is the event, so do not say 'I am falling in love with my parents'.

entry_json.definition: romantically attached to a particular person. The person follows 'with', never 'to' or 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She was clearly in love with him long before either of them admitted it.
example_sentences: He fell in love with a woman he met on an exchange programme.
Being in love with someone who lives abroad is harder than films suggest.

contexts.text: They fell in love with each other over a very long correspondence.
The preposition never changes: in love with her, not in love to her.
contexts.note: The error nearly every learner makes once.

contexts.text: It extends to things and places: he is in love with the idea of moving abroad.
contexts.note: Figurative use.

confusables.difference: 'In love' with no object describes the state; add 'with sb' when you name the person.
minimal_pair: They are in love.
He is in love with her.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in love to' or 'in love of'. The preposition is 'with'.

entry_json.definition: used to signal that what follows is your personal view. It usually opens the sentence with a comma, and 'opinion' takes the possessive, never an article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my opinion, the money would achieve far more if it were spent on teacher training.
example_sentences: In my opinion, the advantages of remote working outweigh the drawbacks.
The design is, in my opinion, far better than the original.

contexts.text: In my opinion, schools should teach basic financial skills.
contexts.note: Fine in Task 2 when the question asks for your view, but use it once, not in every paragraph.

contexts.text: For variety try 'I would argue that' or 'to my mind'.
contexts.note: Repetition of one opinion phrase costs marks.

contexts.text: In my opinion the second option is better, though I can see the argument for the first.

confusables.difference: 'According to' is used for other sources, never for yourself. 'According to me' is a clear error that examiners notice immediately.
minimal_pair: In my opinion, it is too expensive.
According to the report, it is too expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'according to me' or 'in my point of view'. The correct forms are 'in my opinion', 'in my view' and 'from my point of view'.

entry_json.definition: arranged according to a stated principle, such as size, importance or date. 'Order' takes no article in this phrase.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The candidates are listed in order of preference rather than alphabetically.
example_sentences: The countries are shown in order of population, from largest to smallest.
Please list your qualifications in order of date, starting with the most recent.

contexts.text: The table lists the five cities in order of average rainfall.
contexts.note: Useful when describing how a Task 1 table is organised.

contexts.text: I would rank the causes in order of importance, with cost first.
Some fixed versions drop 'of': in alphabetical order, in chronological order.
contexts.note: With an adjective, no 'of' is needed.

confusables.difference: Completely different. 'In order of' arranges things; 'in order to' states a purpose.
minimal_pair: listed in order of size
built in order to reduce traffic

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the order of' unless you mean approximately, as in 'in the order of 5,000', which is a different phrase.

entry_json.definition: with the purpose of doing something. It is the formal version of purpose 'to', and the negative is 'in order not to', which cannot be shortened.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In order to reduce congestion, several cities have made the centre car-free.
example_sentences: Many students take a part-time job in order to cover their living costs.
He left an hour early in order not to miss the connection.
collocations: in order not to do sth

contexts.text: In order to meet the target, emissions would have to fall by 7 per cent every year.
contexts.note: A clear Task 2 purpose clause; fronted, with a comma.

contexts.text: The negative is 'in order not to': she wrote it down in order not to forget.
contexts.note: You cannot say 'not in order to'.

contexts.text: 'So that' takes a full clause instead: they built the bypass so that lorries could avoid the village.
contexts.note: Alternative structure with a subject and verb.

confusables.difference: 'In order to' takes an infinitive and needs the same subject. 'So that' takes a full clause and allows a different subject.
minimal_pair: She left early in order to catch the train.
She left early so that the others could use the room.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in order for reduce' and not 'in order of reducing'. It is always 'in order to' plus the base verb.

entry_json.definition: used to restate something more simply or more directly. It signals that what follows means the same thing, not something new.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme costs more per passenger than a taxi would. In other words, it is not a serious transport policy.
example_sentences: The proposal doubles the fee for everyone outside the zone. In other words, the poorest residents pay most.
Emissions must peak before 2030; in other words, action cannot wait for the next decade.

contexts.text: Only a fifth of applicants were successful. In other words, four out of five were turned away.
contexts.note: Restating a statistic in a way that makes its meaning land.

contexts.text: It is a long way from anywhere, or in other words, you need a car.
It must not introduce new information; if it does, use 'furthermore' instead.
contexts.note: The rule learners break most often with this linker.

confusables.difference: The same job. 'That is to say' is more formal and slightly more precise; 'in other words' is the everyday choice.
minimal_pair: In other words, it is too expensive.
That is to say, the cost exceeds the budget.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to add a new point. It only reformulates what you have already said.

entry_json.definition: partly, but not completely. It is a careful way of naming one cause among several, and is common in academic writing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fall in high street sales can be explained in part by the rise of online shopping.
example_sentences: The delay was in part the result of a shortage of materials.
Her success is due in part to the support she received early on.

chunk.pattern: in part (+ because of / due to)

contexts.text: The improvement is due in part to cleaner vehicles and in part to the closure of the power station.
contexts.note: Splitting a cause between two factors, which is more honest than claiming one.

contexts.text: It is a hedge: it protects a claim you cannot fully prove.
contexts.note: Why it scores well in Task 2.

contexts.text: The everyday spoken version is 'partly': it was partly my fault.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning. 'Partly' is a single adverb and is more common in speech; 'in part' is the formal written variant.
minimal_pair: It was partly due to the weather.
It was due in part to the weather.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the part'. And do not use it where you mean 'in some places', which is 'in parts'.

entry_json.definition: especially, or more than the others. It normally comes straight after the noun it singles out, or at the start of a sentence with a comma.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young families in particular have been priced out of the areas near the centre.
example_sentences: Older residents, in particular, rely on the bus service.
In particular, the report criticises the lack of consultation.

contexts.text: Coastal cities in particular will have to invest heavily in flood defences.
contexts.note: Placed after the noun it picks out: precise and unmistakable.

contexts.text: Were you looking for anything in particular? Just browsing, thank you.
contexts.note: Fixed question form.

contexts.text: 'Particularly' is the adverb and goes before the word it modifies: particularly expensive.
contexts.note: Different position, same idea.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable, but 'especially' goes before the item and 'in particular' after it. Both single one thing out of a group.
minimal_pair: especially older residents
older residents in particular

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in particularly' and not 'in the particular'.

entry_json.definition: existing and ready to operate, of a system, rule or arrangement. It also means in the correct position. No article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flood defences are now in place along the whole of the eastern bank.
example_sentences: The new safety procedures have been in place since April.
Once the funding is in place, work can begin on the second phase.

contexts.text: Strict recycling targets are already in place in several European countries.
contexts.note: A compact way of saying a policy exists and is operating.

contexts.text: The council should put proper cycle lanes in place before encouraging people to cycle.
contexts.note: 'Put sth in place' is the active version.

contexts.text: 'In place of' is a different phrase meaning instead of: tea in place of coffee.
contexts.note: Adding 'of' changes the meaning completely.

confusables.difference: 'In place' means operating. 'In place of' means instead of. One word changes the sense entirely.
minimal_pair: The system is in place.
They used gas in place of coal.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the place' when you mean operating. That would mean physically inside a location.

entry_json.definition: in the real situation, as opposed to what was intended or expected. It almost always sets up a contrast with theory or with an official rule.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In theory anyone can appeal the decision; in practice the process is so slow that almost nobody does.
example_sentences: The law bans it, but in practice it is rarely enforced.
In practice, most people take the shortest route regardless of the signs.

contexts.text: In theory the scheme is open to everyone; in practice, only those with a car can reach it.
contexts.note: The theory-versus-practice pairing is a strong Task 2 structure.

contexts.text: It sounds sensible, but in practice it would be very hard to enforce.
The British spelling of the verb is 'practise' with an s; the noun keeps the c.
contexts.note: Spelling trap in British English.

confusables.difference: 'In fact' corrects a statement. 'In practice' contrasts what actually happens with what was supposed to happen.
minimal_pair: In fact, the law was repealed.
In practice, the law is ignored.

entry_json.avoid: In British English the noun is spelled 'practice' with a c. 'In practise' is wrong.

minimal_pair: despite the cost
in the face of fierce opposition

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a neutral circumstance. It needs something being resisted or endured.

entry_json.definition: at the very beginning, before everything that followed. It usually appears at the end of a sentence and questions why something was started at all. It can also mean firstly, when listing points.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The real question is why the building was allowed so close to the river in the first place.
example_sentences: If the road had been maintained properly, the accident would not have happened in the first place.
In the first place, the cost is prohibitive; in the second, nobody has asked for it.
collocations: why sth happened in the first place
should not have done sth in the first place

contexts.text: Preventing waste in the first place is far cheaper than recycling it afterwards.
contexts.note: A sharp Task 2 move: attacking the origin of a problem rather than its symptoms.

contexts.text: I do not know why I agreed to it in the first place.
contexts.note: Regret, sentence-final.

contexts.text: The listing sense sits at the front: in the first place, the scheme is too expensive.
contexts.note: Different position, different function.

confusables.difference: 'Firstly' only lists points. 'In the first place' can also mean 'at the outset, before any of this happened', which 'firstly' cannot.
minimal_pair: Firstly, the cost is high.
It should never have been built in the first place.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in first place', which means winning a competition, and not 'at the first place'.

entry_json.definition: having the particular shape, type or appearance named. It is used to specify how something is delivered, and often introduces a concrete example of an abstract idea.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of the support arrives in the form of loans rather than grants, which is why debt keeps rising.
example_sentences: Help came in the form of a small grant from the local council.
The information is presented in the form of a bar chart.
collocations: in the form of a grant
in the form of a chart

contexts.text: The data are presented in the form of two pie charts.
contexts.note: Useful in a Task 1 introduction, though only if you do not simply copy the rubric.

contexts.text: Subsidies in the form of cheap fuel mainly benefit those who already drive.
The verb version is 'take the form of': support took the form of free childcare.

confusables.difference: 'As' is shorter and often better: help came as a grant. Use 'in the form of' when you want to stress the particular shape the thing took.
minimal_pair: It came as a grant.
It came in the form of a grant.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in form of' and not 'under the form of'. The article is required.

entry_json.definition: at some time after now. It takes 'the', and it goes with will, may, is likely to and other future forms.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the future, most short journeys in cities will probably be made on foot or by bike.
example_sentences: I would like to work abroad in the future, though not immediately.
Water may well become a more serious source of conflict in the future than oil.
collocations: at some point in the future

contexts.text: What would you like to do in the future? I am hoping to train as a physiotherapist.
contexts.note: Extremely common Part 1 question.

contexts.text: Cities will need far more green space in the future than they have today.
'In future' without 'the' means from now on, and is a warning: in future, please give more notice.
contexts.note: British English distinguishes the two.

confusables.difference: 'In the future' means at some later time. 'In future' means from now on, and often carries a note of complaint.
minimal_pair: I may study abroad in the future.
In future, please arrive on time.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'the' when you mean at some later time. And do not follow it with a past tense.

entry_json.definition: under the control or in the care of a particular person or group. 'Hands' is always plural, and it often carries a judgement about whether that control is a good thing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Too much of the country's media is in the hands of a very small number of owners.
example_sentences: The decision is now in the hands of the planning committee.
In the hands of a good teacher, even a dull subject becomes interesting.
collocations: in the hands of a few
leave sth in the hands of sb
fall into the hands of sb

chunk.pattern: in the hands of + person / group

contexts.text: When water supply is in the hands of private companies, prices tend to rise faster than wages.
contexts.note: A compact way of making an argument about control and ownership.

contexts.text: Once I had sent the application, it was out of my hands.
contexts.note: The opposite phrase: no longer under my control.

contexts.text: The plural is fixed: not 'in the hand of'.
contexts.note: Form note.

confusables.difference: The same meaning with a possessive instead of 'of': the decision is in her hands. Both are correct; choose whichever reads better.
minimal_pair: in the hands of the committee
in the committee's hands

entry_json.avoid: Never singular: 'in the hand of' is wrong in this idiom.

entry_json.definition: taking new information into account when judging something. This is the British form, with 'the'; American English usually drops it and writes 'in light of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the light of the new figures, the council has agreed to reconsider the closure.
example_sentences: The guidance was rewritten in the light of the inquiry's findings.
In the light of what has happened since, the original decision looks unwise.
collocations: in the light of recent research
in the light of these findings
reconsider sth in the light of sth

contexts.text: In the light of recent research, the recommended limit has been reduced.
contexts.note: British academic form; the examiner voices are British.

contexts.text: The shorter 'in light of' is equally acceptable and increasingly common.
contexts.note: Both variants are correct; be consistent within one essay.

contexts.text: It must be followed by a noun, so a clause needs 'the fact that': in the light of the fact that costs have risen.
contexts.gap_span: in the light of the fact that

confusables.difference: Nearly identical. 'In view of' emphasises an existing circumstance; 'in the light of' emphasises new information that changes the judgement.
minimal_pair: in view of the cost
in the light of new evidence

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a full clause, and do not write 'under the light of'.

entry_json.definition: during the period between now and a future event that has already been mentioned. It needs that later event to have been named first.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new hospital will open in 2028. In the meantime, patients will continue to travel forty kilometres for treatment.
example_sentences: The results come out in August. In the meantime, try not to think about it.
A permanent solution will take years; in the meantime, temporary barriers have been installed.

chunk.pattern: future event named + In the meantime, + clause

contexts.text: Electric lorries are still years away. In the meantime, rail freight offers the quickest reduction in emissions.
contexts.note: Excellent for a Task 2 solutions paragraph that separates short and long term.

contexts.text: I start the new job in September; in the meantime I am doing some temporary work.
'Meanwhile' is the one-word equivalent and can also mean 'at the same time, elsewhere'.

confusables.difference: 'In the meantime' always looks forward to a named event. 'Meanwhile' can also simply mean 'at the same time, in another place'.
minimal_pair: The report is due in June; in the meantime, work continues.
Meanwhile, in the north, snow was falling.

entry_json.avoid: It cannot open a paragraph with nothing before it: the later event must already have been mentioned.

entry_json.definition: in the central part of a space, or halfway through a period. It takes 'the', and the surrounding thing follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a long table in the middle and smaller desks around the edges.
example_sentences: The photograph shows a fountain in the middle, with benches on either side.
I woke up in the middle of the night and could not get back to sleep.
collocations: in the middle of the night

contexts.text: The kitchen is in the middle, which means every room leads off it.
The diagram shows the reservoir in the middle and the treatment works to the north.
contexts.note: Task 1 diagram description.

contexts.text: The idiom 'in the middle of nowhere' means very remote.
contexts.note: Spoken only.

confusables.difference: 'In the centre' is the standard term for the central district of a town and for an exact midpoint. 'In the middle' is more general and more common in speech.
minimal_pair: a fountain in the middle of the square
an office in the centre of town

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in middle'. And when you name the surrounding thing, 'of' is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: in the central part of a named place, or partway through an activity or period. With an activity it means you are busy and cannot stop.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The village sits in the middle of a valley that floods every few winters.
example_sentences: I was in the middle of cooking when the power went off.
The station is right in the middle of the city, which makes it very convenient.
collocations: in the middle of the night
in the middle of a meeting
in the middle of doing sth

contexts.text: Sorry, I was in the middle of something when you rang.
contexts.note: The 'busy' sense, always with -ing or a noun.

contexts.text: The new development lies in the middle of what was farmland twenty years ago.
The verb after 'of' must be -ing: in the middle of writing, not in the middle of write.

confusables.difference: 'During' simply says when. 'In the middle of' places you partway through and often implies an interruption.
minimal_pair: The phone rang during the meal.
The phone rang in the middle of the meal.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before a noun, and never use an infinitive after it.

entry_json.definition: in the middle of a situation, especially a difficult or dramatic one. It is formal and literary, and is used far more with events than with physical places.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The reforms were introduced in the midst of the worst recession in a generation.
example_sentences: The city was rebuilt in the midst of severe shortages of both money and materials.
In the midst of all the criticism, one point was consistently overlooked.
collocations: in the midst of a crisis
in the midst of all this

contexts.text: In the midst of a housing crisis, building luxury flats seems a strange priority.
contexts.note: Formal, and it signals that the situation is serious.

contexts.text: The noun after it is usually an event or condition, not a place.
contexts.note: Collocational restriction.

contexts.text: In speech use 'in the middle of' instead; 'midst' sounds literary in conversation.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: 'In the middle of' covers places, times and activities. 'In the midst of' is restricted to situations, usually difficult ones, and is more formal.
minimal_pair: in the middle of the room
in the midst of a crisis

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for physical position: 'in the midst of the room' sounds archaic.

entry_json.definition: during the hours between waking and midday. It can also mean tomorrow morning when the context is clear: I will call you in the morning.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do my best work in the morning, so I try to protect that time for writing.
example_sentences: The post arrives at about ten in the morning.
Traffic is heaviest in the morning, between seven and nine.

contexts.text: Are you a morning person? Yes, I get far more done in the morning than at night.
Electricity demand rises sharply in the morning and again in the early evening.
contexts.note: Describing a daily-usage graph.

contexts.text: With a named day the preposition changes: on Sunday morning, not in Sunday morning.

confusables.difference: Morning, afternoon and evening take 'in the'; night alone takes 'at' with no article.
minimal_pair: in the morning
at night

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in morning' and not 'at the morning'.

entry_json.definition: soon, within the next months or few years. It is slightly formal and pairs with will, is likely to and is expected to.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The technology is unlikely to become affordable in the near future, whatever the manufacturers claim.
example_sentences: The company plans to open two more sites in the near future.
Any significant fall in prices in the near future seems improbable.
collocations: at some point in the near future

chunk.pattern: in the near future + future form

contexts.text: Electric vehicles are likely to become cheaper than petrol cars in the near future.
contexts.note: Hedged prediction, which Task 2 rewards more than a flat claim.

contexts.text: I hope to visit again in the near future.
contexts.note: Common closing line in a friendly formal letter.

contexts.text: The opposite is 'in the distant future', or 'in the long term'.

confusables.difference: 'Soon' is short and works in speech. 'In the near future' is the formal written equivalent and is common in reports.
minimal_pair: It will change soon.
Change is expected in the near future.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in near future'. The article is required.

entry_json.definition: in the northern part of a country or area. Compass points take 'the' after 'in', and the wider area follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wages in the north of the country are on average a fifth lower than in the capital.
example_sentences: Most of the rainfall occurs in the north, where the mountains are.
The city is in the north of the region, close to the border.
collocations: in the north of the country

contexts.text: The map shows woodland in the north and open farmland in the south.
contexts.note: Task 1 map vocabulary.

contexts.text: I come from a small town in the north of the country.
'To the north of' places something outside the area: the airport lies to the north of the city.
contexts.note: Inside versus beyond.

confusables.difference: 'In the north' is a noun phrase; 'northern' is the adjective and goes before a noun: the northern half.
minimal_pair: in the north of England
northern England

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in north' and not 'at the north' for location within an area.

entry_json.definition: at some time before now. With the past simple it means the period is over; with the present perfect it means at some point up to now.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the past, most people worked within walking distance of their homes.
example_sentences: The building has been used as a school in the past.
In the past, families were much larger than they are today.

chunk.pattern: In the past, + past simple / present perfect

contexts.text: In the past, people rarely moved far from the town where they were born.
contexts.note: The standard Task 2 device for setting up a then-and-now contrast.

contexts.text: I have tried to give up coffee in the past, without much success.
contexts.note: Present perfect: at some point before now.

contexts.text: It contrasts naturally with 'these days' or 'nowadays' in the next sentence.
contexts.note: Pair them for a clean contrast.

confusables.difference: 'In the past' is open and can mean centuries ago. 'In the last few years' is a defined recent window and requires the present perfect.
minimal_pair: In the past, people wrote letters.
In the last few years, letter writing has almost disappeared.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in past'. And do not use it with a present tense: 'in the past people write letters' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: while a particular person is there. It is formal, and often signals that the person's being there changes how people behave.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children behave quite differently in the presence of their parents than they do among friends.
example_sentences: The document must be signed in the presence of a witness.
He was careful never to raise the subject in the presence of his colleagues.
collocations: in the presence of a witness

contexts.text: Interviews with children are conducted in the presence of a responsible adult.
contexts.note: Formal, procedural writing.

contexts.text: The possessive version is shorter: he said nothing in her presence.
In speech say 'in front of' or 'when she was there'.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: 'In front of' is the everyday phrase and can also mean physical position. 'In the presence of' is formal and only about being present.
minimal_pair: Do not say that in front of the children.
signed in the presence of a solicitor

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in presence of'. The article is compulsory, and the phrase is too formal for casual speech.

entry_json.definition: when a particular substance or condition is there. This is the scientific use: a reaction that happens in the presence of oxygen happens only when oxygen is present.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The material corrodes rapidly in the presence of salt water, which limits its use on the coast.
example_sentences: Photosynthesis takes place in the presence of light.
The bacteria multiply quickly in the presence of moisture.
collocations: only in the presence of sth

chunk.pattern: in the presence of + substance / condition

contexts.text: The process only works in the presence of a catalyst.
contexts.note: Describing a process diagram in Task 1.

contexts.text: The negative form is 'in the absence of': the reaction stops in the absence of light.
contexts.note: The two phrases work as a pair.

contexts.text: With people it means while they are there: signed in the presence of a witness.
contexts.note: Same phrase, human sense.

confusables.difference: 'With' is neutral and everyday. 'In the presence of' is the scientific formula, and states a condition the process depends on.
minimal_pair: Mix it with water.
The compound dissolves in the presence of water.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it where plain 'with' or 'when there is' would do; it belongs in technical description.

entry_json.definition: using the same method, or, as a linker, introducing a parallel case. When comparing it is often followed by 'as' plus a noun or clause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities cannot be planned in the same way as they were fifty years ago, because the traffic is different.
example_sentences: The second sample was prepared in exactly the same way as the first.
Children learn grammar without being taught it. In the same way, they pick up accents from those around them.
collocations: in the same way as sth

chunk.pattern: in the same way (as + noun / clause)

contexts.text: Both samples were treated in exactly the same way, so the difference cannot be explained by handling.
contexts.note: Method description.

contexts.text: Smoking was once normal indoors. In the same way, driving into city centres may soon seem unacceptable.
contexts.note: Using a parallel case as an argument, a sophisticated Task 2 move.

contexts.text: The comparison word is 'as', not 'like': in the same way as her mother did.
contexts.note: Preposition note.

confusables.difference: 'Similarly' is a single adverb linker. 'In the same way' can also describe an actual method, which 'similarly' cannot.
minimal_pair: Similarly, prices rose in the south.
It was cooked in the same way as before.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the same way like'. The comparison takes 'as'.

entry_json.definition: in the southern part of a country or area. Compass directions take 'the' after 'in', and the surrounding area follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost all the country's vineyards are in the south, where the summers are hot and dry.
example_sentences: Temperatures are consistently higher in the south than in the north.
The new airport is in the south of the region, about an hour from the capital.
collocations: in the south of the country

contexts.text: Rainfall was heaviest in the north and lightest in the south throughout the period.
contexts.note: Comparing regions in Task 1.

contexts.text: I grew up in the south, so I still find northern winters hard.
'To the south of' means beyond it: the mountains lie to the south of the border.

confusables.difference: 'In the south' is a noun phrase used after a verb. 'Southern' is an adjective and goes before a noun: southern Italy.
minimal_pair: in the south of Italy
southern Italy

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in south' and not 'on the south'.

entry_json.definition: outside on a road in a town, among the buildings. British English says 'in the street'; American English says 'on the street'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There were people selling food in the street outside the station until well after midnight.
example_sentences: Children used to play in the street before there was so much traffic.
I bumped into an old colleague in the street last week.

contexts.text: When I was young we played in the street; now nobody does because of the cars.
contexts.note: A frequent Part 3 point about how childhood has changed.

contexts.text: Americans say 'on the street', which is also heard in British English now.
contexts.note: Variety note.

contexts.text: With a street name use 'in' or 'on' plus the name and no 'the': she lives in Baker Street.
contexts.note: Named streets take no article.

confusables.difference: 'On the road' means travelling, or refers to a road between towns. 'In the street' is the urban space between buildings.
minimal_pair: We were on the road for six hours.
There was a market in the street.

entry_json.avoid: With a named street do not add 'the': not 'in the Oxford Street'.

entry_json.definition: during the summer, either as a general rule or in one particular year. With a year or a possessive it points at one specific summer.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the summer of 2022 the reservoir dropped to its lowest level since records began.
example_sentences: We usually visit my grandparents in the summer.
In the summer the whole coast is booked out months ahead.

contexts.text: In the summer I cycle to work; in the winter I take the bus.
contexts.note: General habit; British speakers use 'the' freely here.

contexts.text: In the summer of 2018 there were fires across the whole region.
contexts.note: One specific summer: the article is required.

contexts.text: Without 'the' the meaning is purely general: it is hotter in summer.
contexts.note: Both forms are correct; only the specific one needs 'the'.

confusables.difference: Both are correct for a general statement. Only 'in the summer' can point at one particular summer, as in 'in the summer of 1976'.
minimal_pair: It rains less in summer.
In the summer of 1976 it barely rained at all.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'at the summer' or 'on the summer'.

entry_json.definition: in the central shopping and business area of a town. It is the British term, and the equivalent for a larger place is 'the city centre'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is very little parking in the town centre, which is part of the reason the shops are struggling.
example_sentences: The library and the market are both in the town centre.
A new pedestrian area was created in the town centre three years ago.

contexts.text: Everything I need is in the town centre, so I hardly ever use the car.
The map shows a new supermarket in the town centre, where the old bus station used to be.
contexts.note: Task 1 maps very often show changes to a town centre.

contexts.text: I am writing to suggest more seating in the town centre for elderly residents.

confusables.difference: 'Downtown' is the American equivalent and takes no article or preposition: I work downtown. British English uses 'in the town centre'.
minimal_pair: in the town centre
downtown

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in town centre' and not 'in the centre town'.

entry_json.definition: following something, and as a result of it. It is formal and almost always used after a major or damaging event.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the wake of the flooding, insurance premiums along the whole river doubled.
example_sentences: Several new safety rules were introduced in the wake of the accident.
In the wake of the pandemic, many companies abandoned their offices altogether.
collocations: in the wake of the crisis
in the wake of the disaster
follow in the wake of sth

contexts.text: In the wake of the financial crisis, house building fell to its lowest level in decades.
contexts.note: Formal, and it packs 'after' and 'because of' into one phrase.

contexts.text: The event named after 'of' should be significant; 'in the wake of lunch' is absurd.
contexts.note: Collocational restriction.

contexts.text: In speech say 'after' or 'following': after the storm, the council cleared the roads.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: 'Following' just means after. 'In the wake of' also implies the event caused what came next, and that the event was serious.
minimal_pair: Following the meeting, a report was issued.
In the wake of the disaster, the law was changed.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the wake of' for trivial events, and not 'in wake of'.

entry_json.definition: in the manner that. It introduces a clause describing how something is done, and 'that' can be left out.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The subject is not taught in the way it was when I was at school.
example_sentences: He explained it in the way a good teacher would, starting from what we already knew.
The city has not developed in the way the planners intended.
collocations: in the way that sb does sth
in the way it was intended
not in the way sb expected

contexts.text: Technology has not changed education in the way that many people predicted.
contexts.note: Useful for challenging a common assumption.

contexts.text: 'That' is optional: it did not work in the way we expected.
Do not confuse it with 'in the way', meaning blocking: the van was in the way.
contexts.note: Same words, entirely different meaning.

confusables.difference: 'In the way that' refers to a specific known manner, often one already mentioned. 'In a way that' introduces a new manner or result.
minimal_pair: taught in the way it was in 1950
designed in a way that saves energy

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'how' after 'the way': 'in the way how it works' is wrong. Use 'the way it works' or 'how it works', never both.

entry_json.definition: in the western part of a country or area. With a capital letter, 'the West' can also mean Europe and North America as a political bloc.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of the country's rainfall falls in the west, on the side facing the ocean.
example_sentences: The oldest part of the town is in the west, near the river.
Industry was concentrated in the west until the 1970s.
collocations: in the west of the country

contexts.text: The diagram shows housing in the west and light industry in the east.
contexts.note: Task 1 map language.

contexts.text: Rainfall is heaviest in the west because of the prevailing winds.
Capitalised, it means a group of countries: attitudes to work differ between the West and East Asia.
contexts.note: Different sense, marked by the capital letter.

confusables.difference: In the west means within the area. To the west means outside it, in that direction.
minimal_pair: The hills are in the west of the county.
The sea lies to the west of the county.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in west' and not 'at the west'.

entry_json.definition: during the winter, either as a general habit or in one particular year. With a year or possessive it identifies a specific winter.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the winter it gets dark at four here, which takes some getting used to.
example_sentences: Heating costs roughly double in the winter.
In the winter of 2010 the whole rail network stopped for a week.

contexts.text: In the winter I hardly go out in the evening at all.
Energy consumption peaks in the winter and falls to its lowest point in July.
Without 'the' it is purely general: nights are longer in winter.
contexts.note: Both are correct.

confusables.difference: Both work for general statements. Only 'in the winter' can identify one particular winter, as in 'in the winter of 1963'.
minimal_pair: It snows in winter.
In the winter of 1963 the sea froze.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'at the winter' or 'on winter'.

entry_json.definition: as far as this particular example or situation is concerned. It points back to something already identified, so it cannot open a text.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most rivers in the study recovered within five years. In this case, however, pollution levels were still rising a decade later.
example_sentences: The rule normally applies to everyone, but in this case an exception was made.
In this case the cheaper option is also the better one.

contexts.text: Higher taxes usually reduce consumption. In this case, however, demand barely changed.
contexts.note: Marking an exception to a general rule.

contexts.text: 'In that case' responds to what somebody has just said: The shop is shut. In that case we will go tomorrow.
contexts.note: Conversational variant.

contexts.text: 'In which case' joins it to the previous clause: the train may be late, in which case we will wait.
contexts.note: Relative version.

confusables.difference: 'In case' introduces a precaution about the future. 'In this case' identifies one situation you have already mentioned. They are unrelated.
minimal_pair: Take a coat in case it rains.
In this case, no coat was needed.

entry_json.avoid: It refers backwards, so do not open a paragraph with it before the case has been described.

entry_json.definition: by the method just described. It links back to a method or mechanism you have already explained, and often introduces its result.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rainwater is collected on the roof and filtered before use. In this way, the building meets most of its own needs.
example_sentences: The heat is recycled rather than released. In this way, energy use is cut by around a third.
Students mark each other's work. In this way, they learn the criteria as well as the content.
collocations: in this way it is possible to do sth

contexts.text: The waste heat is used to warm nearby homes. In this way, nothing is wasted.
contexts.note: Process description: the method comes first, the result second.

contexts.text: It must follow an explanation. If the reader does not yet know the method, the linker fails.
contexts.note: Cohesion rule.

contexts.text: Cities could reduce car use in this way without spending anything on new roads.

confusables.difference: 'In this way' refers to a method. 'In this case' refers to a particular example or situation.
minimal_pair: In this way, costs are reduced.
In this case, costs actually rose.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it when you have not described a method. It points back to how something is done.

entry_json.definition: early enough for something, with a margin to spare. It can also mean eventually, after a long period: in time, attitudes changed.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We got to the airport just in time, but only because the traffic cleared at the last minute.
example_sentences: The repairs were finished in time, though only by a day.
In time, people stopped noticing the new building at all.

contexts.text: We arrived just in time to see the beginning.
In time, the river recovered and the fish returned.
contexts.note: The 'eventually' sense, sentence-initial with a comma.

contexts.text: It is not the same as 'on time', which means at the scheduled moment.
contexts.note: The distinction that matters most here.

confusables.difference: 'On time' means exactly at the arranged time. 'In time' means early enough, with something to spare. A train is on time; you arrive in time to catch it.
minimal_pair: The train left on time.
I arrived in time to catch it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'on time'. Saying 'the bus was in time' when you mean punctual is a clear error.

entry_json.definition: early enough for a named event. The event follows 'for' as a noun; if you want a verb, use 'in time to do sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new platform should be finished in time for the summer timetable.
example_sentences: I got home in time for dinner, which does not happen often.
The report was published in time for the committee meeting.

contexts.text: We arrived in time for the second half, having missed the first completely.
I would be grateful if the repairs could be completed in time for the inspection.
For a verb switch to 'to': in time to see the start.
contexts.note: Pattern contrast.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a noun, 'to' takes a verb. The meaning is the same; only the grammar differs.
minimal_pair: in time for the film
in time to watch the film

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a bare verb after 'for': 'in time for start' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: early enough to be able to do something. It takes the infinitive, and is often preceded by 'just' when the margin was very small.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I looked up just in time to see the train pulling out of the platform.
example_sentences: She got there in time to hear the closing speeches.
We left in time to avoid the worst of the rush hour.
collocations: just in time to do sth

contexts.text: I arrived just in time to catch the last bus home.
contexts.note: A neat detail for a Part 2 narrative.

contexts.text: The flood defences were completed in time to prevent serious damage that winter.
With a noun switch to 'for': in time for the last bus.

confusables.difference: 'To' takes a verb, 'for' takes a noun. Both mean early enough.
minimal_pair: in time to catch the bus
in time for the bus

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in time for catch the bus'. Choose one pattern and complete it properly.

entry_json.definition: in contact with somebody by phone, message or letter. 'Touch' takes no article, and the phrase is completed by verbs such as get, keep, stay or be.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We have stayed in touch since university, mostly through a group message.
example_sentences: Are you still in touch with anyone from your old job?
Do keep in touch and let me know how it goes.

chunk.pattern: be / keep / stay / get + in touch

contexts.text: We were in touch almost every day when we were both studying abroad.
I will be in touch as soon as I have the confirmation.
contexts.note: Standard closing line of a business email.

contexts.text: The opposite is 'out of touch', which can also mean out of date with current thinking.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'In contact' is a little more formal and is used in official contexts such as tracing; 'in touch' is the everyday phrase.
minimal_pair: We keep in touch.
Anyone who was in contact with the patient should be tested.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the touch'.

entry_json.definition: in contact with a particular person. The person follows 'with', and the phrase works with be, keep, stay, get and put.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am still in touch with two teachers from my old school, which surprises me.
example_sentences: Are you in touch with anyone from that course?
The agency put me in touch with a landlord who accepted students.
collocations: put sb in touch with sb

contexts.text: Do you keep in touch with your school friends? A few of them, yes.
contexts.note: Frequent Part 1 friendship question.

contexts.text: Social media makes it far easier to stay in touch with people who move abroad.
The opposite verb is 'lose touch with', with no 'in': we lost touch after he moved.
contexts.note: Note the missing 'in' in the negative version.

confusables.difference: The positive phrases keep 'in': be in touch, keep in touch. The negative drops it: lose touch, not lose in touch.
minimal_pair: We keep in touch.
We lost touch.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'lose in touch' and not 'in touch to somebody'. The preposition is 'with'.

entry_json.definition: in the central part of the town where you live, or, of a person, visiting the town rather than away. No article when it refers to your own town.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am in town this afternoon anyway, so I can pick it up for you.
example_sentences: Is there anywhere in town that repairs shoes?
She is in town for a conference and leaves again on Thursday.

contexts.text: I usually go into town on Saturday morning, before it gets busy.
contexts.note: Movement takes 'into', position takes 'in'.

contexts.text: It is the cheapest place in town for fruit and vegetables.
For a town that is not yours, use the name or an article: I was in the town where she grew up.
contexts.note: Article rule.

confusables.difference: 'In town' means your own town, treated as familiar. 'In the town' identifies a specific town you have named or described.
minimal_pair: I will be in town later.
We stopped in the town where my mother was born.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'go in town' for movement; use 'go into town'.

entry_json.definition: as a result of what has just been described, in a chain of effects. It also means one after another, each taking a turn.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Higher rents push workers further out, which in turn lengthens journeys and increases congestion.
example_sentences: Warmer seas produce stronger storms, which in turn cause more coastal erosion.
Each member of the group spoke in turn.

contexts.text: Deforestation reduces rainfall, which in turn makes farming harder in the surrounding area.
contexts.note: The cleanest way to show a chain of consequences in Task 2.

contexts.text: The candidates were interviewed in turn, in alphabetical order.
contexts.note: The 'one after another' sense.

contexts.text: It usually sits between the subject and the verb: this in turn reduces costs.
contexts.note: Position note.

confusables.difference: 'As a result' starts a new sentence about one effect. 'In turn' continues a chain, showing that an effect became a cause in its turn.
minimal_pair: As a result, prices rose.
Prices rose, which in turn reduced demand.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the turn'. And keep it for chains of two or more linked effects.

entry_json.definition: during the winter season, as a general rule. With no article it makes a statement about winters in general rather than one particular winter.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In winter the roads over the pass are often closed for days at a time.
example_sentences: Demand for electricity is highest in winter in this part of Europe.
Many of the coastal hotels close completely in winter.

contexts.text: It rarely snows here, but it rains almost every day in winter.
Gas consumption is roughly three times higher in winter than in summer.
contexts.note: Comparing seasons in Task 1.

contexts.text: 'In the winter' is equally correct, and is needed when you name a particular year.

confusables.difference: Seasons take 'in'. 'At' is used for clock times and a small set of fixed phrases such as 'at night' and 'at Christmas'.
minimal_pair: in winter
at Christmas

entry_json.avoid: Never 'at winter' or 'on winter'.

entry_json.definition: in the place of something else. It is followed by a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form, never by a plain infinitive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I now cycle to work instead of driving, which saves about eighty pounds a month.
example_sentences: Instead of building a new road, the money could be spent on buses.
She had tea instead of coffee because it was late.

contexts.text: Instead of banning cars altogether, cities could simply make them expensive to park.
contexts.note: -ing after 'of' is compulsory.

contexts.text: Without 'of', 'instead' stands alone at the end of a clause: I did not drive; I cycled instead.
contexts.note: The single word needs no object.

contexts.text: In an essay 'rather than' is often smoother: rather than banning cars, cities could tax them.

confusables.difference: 'Instead of' takes an object; 'instead' alone does not and usually ends the sentence. Mixing them produces 'I went instead of' with nothing after it.
minimal_pair: I had tea instead of coffee.
I did not want coffee, so I had tea instead.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'instead of to drive'. After 'of' use -ing or a noun.

entry_json.definition: money put into something in order to improve it or make a profit. The thing invested in follows 'in'; the amount follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sustained investment in public transport would do more for air quality than any single ban.
example_sentences: Investment in renewable energy has risen sharply since 2015.
The region has suffered from decades of under-investment in housing.

contexts.text: Greater investment in education tends to pay for itself within a generation.
contexts.note: A high-value Task 2 noun phrase; it lets you avoid repeating 'the government should spend'.

contexts.text: Use 'of' for the sum: an investment of two million pounds in new equipment.
contexts.note: Two prepositions, two jobs.

contexts.text: The verb takes the same preposition: the council invested in cycle lanes.

confusables.difference: 'On' is not used with investment. The fixed preposition is 'in', matching the verb 'invest in'.
minimal_pair: investment in housing
spending on housing

entry_json.avoid: Not 'investment on' and not 'investment to'. Note that 'spending' takes 'on' while 'investment' takes 'in'.

entry_json.definition: the fact of taking part in an activity or being connected with it. The activity follows 'in', and the word is often used about crime, politics or community life.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parental involvement in schooling has a measurable effect on how well children do.
example_sentences: He denied any involvement in the decision.
Community involvement in planning decisions is often limited to a single consultation.

contexts.text: Greater involvement in local decision-making tends to increase trust in institutions.
The company denied any involvement in the pollution of the river.
'Involvement with' is used for people and organisations: her involvement with the charity.
contexts.note: Preposition depends on what follows.

confusables.difference: 'In' introduces an activity or event; 'with' introduces a person or organisation.
minimal_pair: involvement in the project
involvement with the union

entry_json.avoid: Not 'involvement to'. And the adjective takes a different preposition again: involved in a project.

entry_json.definition: used to say that the answer varies according to the circumstances. It is more emphatic than 'it depends', and is normally followed by 'on' or a wh-clause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It all depends on how much time you have; if you only have a day, stay in the centre.
example_sentences: Whether it is worth buying depends on how long you plan to stay. It all depends.
It all depends what you mean by success.

contexts.text: Is studying abroad worth it? It all depends on what you want from it.
contexts.note: A legitimate Part 3 opener, provided you then give a real answer.

contexts.text: The wh-clause keeps statement order: it all depends how much it costs.
In writing use 'depends largely on' or 'varies according to'.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'all' adds emphasis and suggests the answer changes completely with the circumstances.
minimal_pair: It depends.
It all depends.

entry_json.avoid: Do not stop there. An examiner will hear 'it all depends' alone as an evasion, so follow it with what it depends on.

entry_json.definition: used to say the answer is not fixed but changes with the situation. The factor follows 'on', and in speech 'on' is often dropped before a wh-word.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Do I prefer working from home? It depends on the week, honestly.
example_sentences: It depends on the weather; if it is dry we will walk.
How long does it take? It depends whether you go by bus or by train.

contexts.text: Do you watch a lot of television? It depends on how busy I am that week.
contexts.note: A natural Part 1 answer that then needs a detail.

contexts.text: The preposition is compulsory before a noun: it depends on the cost, not it depends the cost.
contexts.note: The commonest error with this verb.

contexts.text: In writing prefer 'this depends largely on' or 'the outcome depends on'.

confusables.difference: 'Depending on' is a participle phrase inside a sentence: the price varies depending on the season. 'It depends' is a complete reply.
minimal_pair: It depends on the season.
Prices vary depending on the season.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'it depends of'. The preposition is 'on', and it cannot be dropped before a noun.

lemma: it is difficult for sb to do sth

entry_json.headword: it is difficult for sb to do sth
entry_json.definition: used to say that a particular group finds something hard. 'It' is a dummy subject standing for the to-infinitive, and 'for' introduces the person affected.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is difficult for young people to save for a deposit while paying market rents.
example_sentences: It is difficult for parents to monitor everything their children see online.
It was difficult for me to concentrate with building work going on next door.
collocations: it is difficult for sb to do sth
it is easy for sb to do sth
it is impossible for sb to do sth

chunk.pattern: It is + adjective + for + sb + to + infinitive

contexts.text: It is difficult for rural residents to reach a hospital without a car.
contexts.note: A clean Task 2 way of stating a problem for a specific group.

contexts.text: The same frame works with other adjectives: it is essential for governments to act.
contexts.note: Highly productive pattern.

contexts.text: Compare 'find it difficult to', which reports personal experience.

confusables.term: find it difficult to do sth
confusables.difference: 'It is difficult for X' states a general fact about a group. 'X finds it difficult' reports their experience of it.
minimal_pair: It is difficult for students to find housing.
Students find it difficult to find housing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'it': 'is difficult for students to find housing' has no subject. And do not use 'to' before the person: not 'difficult to young people'.

lemma: it is important to do sth

entry_json.headword: it is important to do sth
entry_json.definition: used to state that an action matters. The dummy subject 'it' stands for the infinitive that follows, and a person can be added with 'for'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is important to distinguish between the cost of building the line and the cost of running it.
example_sentences: It is important to read the terms before signing anything.
It is important for children to learn how to handle failure.
collocations: it is important to remember that…
it is important to note that…
it is important for sb to do sth

contexts.text: It is important to note that the figures cover only urban areas.
contexts.gap_span: It is important to note that
contexts.note: A useful way of adding a qualification in Task 1 or Task 2.

contexts.text: It is important to me that the work is useful, not just well paid.
contexts.note: 'To me' for personal value, 'for me' for effect.

contexts.text: Do not overuse it. Two of these frames in one paragraph reads as padding.
