The report considers the change from an economic point of view only.
collocations: from an economic point of view

contexts.text: From an environmental point of view, the cheapest option is rarely the best one.
I can see the argument from the students' point of view as well as the university's.

confusables.difference: 'In my opinion' takes 'in'; 'point of view' takes 'from'. Mixing them produces the common error 'in my point of view'.
minimal_pair: From my point of view, it is unfair.
In my point of view, it is unfair.

confusables.difference: A more formal synonym: 'from a legal standpoint'. Useful for variety in Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'in my point of view' or 'according to my point of view'. The preposition is 'from'.

entry_json.definition: tell somebody a fact they seem not to have noticed, or show them where something is; it is separable and can be followed by 'that' plus a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report points out that most of the growth came from a single sector.
example_sentences: She pointed out the error before the figures went to print.
It is worth pointing out that the survey covered only city residents.

contexts.text: The report points out that most of the growth came from a single sector.
She pointed out the error before the figures went to print.
He pointed out the building where his grandmother was born.

confusables.difference: 'Mention' is neutral, simply saying something. 'Point out' implies correcting a gap in the listener's knowledge.
minimal_pair: She mentioned the cost.
She pointed out that the cost had doubled.

confusables.difference: 'Indicate' fits data: 'The graph indicates a rise.' 'Point out' fits people making a remark.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for your own opinion. 'Point out' claims the statement is a fact, so 'I would like to point out that this is wrong' sounds combative.

entry_json.definition: introduce a fact you want the reader to notice, using a full clause after 'that'; the 'that' can be dropped in speech but is normally kept in academic writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The authors point out that the sample contained no one under the age of thirty.
example_sentences: Critics point out that the scheme benefits the districts that already have good transport.
It should be pointed out that these figures exclude part-time workers.
collocations: it should be pointed out that...

contexts.text: The authors point out that the sample contained no one under the age of thirty.
Critics point out that the scheme benefits districts that already have good transport.

confusables.difference: With a noun object the phrase splits around it: 'point the error out'. With a clause it does not: 'point out that the figures are wrong'.
minimal_pair: She pointed the error out.
She pointed out that the figures were wrong.

confusables.difference: 'Argue that' presents a contested claim; 'point out that' presents something the writer treats as established fact.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to launch your own opinion in Task 2. It signals fact, so save it for evidence, and use 'I would argue that' for a view.

entry_json.definition: show or identify a particular thing to somebody; separable, so a pronoun must sit in the middle: 'point it out', never 'point out it'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The guide pointed the old city wall out to us from the top of the hill.
example_sentences: Somebody should have pointed the mistake out before it was printed.
Could you point it out on the map?

contexts.text: Somebody should have pointed the mistake out before it was printed.
Could you point it out on the map?

confusables.difference: Use the unsplit version with a clause and the split version with a noun or pronoun object.
minimal_pair: Point out the error.
Point out that there is an error.

confusables.difference: 'Show' is neutral and usually involves demonstrating. 'Point out' is about drawing attention to something already present.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always goes inside: 'point it out', never 'point out it'.

entry_json.definition: a member of the police force; the neutral term that replaced 'policeman' and 'policewoman' in official use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A police officer was standing at the entrance directing people away from the road.
example_sentences: The city plans to recruit two hundred more police officers over the next three years.
She has worked as a police officer for eleven years.

contexts.text: The city plans to recruit two hundred more police officers over the next three years.
A police officer was standing at the entrance directing people away from the road.

confusables.difference: Still understood, but 'police officer' is the standard neutral term and the safer choice in an exam.
minimal_pair: a police officer
a policeman

confusables.difference: 'Police' is always plural as a group noun: 'The police are investigating', not 'is'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a police' for one person. One person is 'a police officer'; 'the police' is the whole force and takes a plural verb.

entry_json.definition: the local office of the police, where crimes are reported; used with 'at' for location and 'to' for movement
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had to go to the police station to report the stolen bicycle.
example_sentences: The nearest police station is open only during the day now.
He was questioned at the police station for several hours.

contexts.text: I had to go to the police station to report the stolen bicycle.
The nearest police station is open only during the day now.

confusables.difference: Not English for the building. The compound is 'police station'.
minimal_pair: the police station
the police office

confusables.difference: 'At the police station' is the usual phrase for being there on business; 'in' focuses on being physically inside.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'police' singular in the compound: 'police station', not 'polices station'.

entry_json.definition: a place where you can send letters and parcels and often pay bills; usually written as two words, and capitalised when it names the national organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The village post office closed last year and the nearest one is now six miles away.
example_sentences: I need to go to the post office to send this parcel before five.
Rural post offices often serve as the only shop for miles.

contexts.text: The village post office closed last year and the nearest one is now six miles away.
I need to go to the post office to send this parcel before five.

confusables.difference: Not English. The compound is 'post office'.
minimal_pair: the post office
the postal office

confusables.difference: British English says 'post' for letters and 'post office' for the building; American English says 'mail'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not join it into one word. 'Postoffice' is not standard spelling.

entry_json.definition: the possibility that something may develop or happen; the preposition is 'for' with a noun, and 'to' with a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rooftop solar has enormous potential for reducing household bills in sunny regions.
example_sentences: The site has considerable potential for redevelopment.
There is real potential for conflict when two departments share a budget.

contexts.text: Rooftop solar has enormous potential for reducing household bills in sunny regions.
The site has considerable potential for redevelopment.

confusables.difference: Use 'to' plus an infinitive when the potential belongs to the subject: 'the potential to grow'. Use 'for' plus a noun or gerund otherwise.
minimal_pair: potential for growth
the potential to grow

confusables.difference: 'Possibility of' is about whether something might happen; 'potential for' suggests unused capacity that could be developed.

entry_json.avoid: After 'for' use a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive: 'potential for reducing costs', not 'potential for reduce costs'.

entry_json.definition: willing to do something, especially something demanding; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive, and it is about willingness rather than readiness
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few people are prepared to give up their car unless the alternative is genuinely faster.
example_sentences: The company said it was prepared to negotiate on pay but not on hours.
I would be prepared to move abroad for the right job.

contexts.text: Few people are prepared to give up their car unless the alternative is genuinely faster.
I would be prepared to move abroad for the right job.

confusables.difference: 'Prepared for' plus a noun means ready in advance: 'prepared for the exam'. 'Prepared to' plus a verb means willing.
minimal_pair: I am prepared for the interview.
I am prepared to travel.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'Prepared to' hints that the person has thought about the cost and accepts it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two patterns. 'Prepared to the exam' is wrong; write 'prepared for the exam'.

entry_json.definition: quite good, better than average but not excellent; 'pretty' here is an adverb of degree and is informal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My listening is pretty good, but reading under time pressure still worries me.
example_sentences: The food at the canteen is pretty good for the price.
She's pretty good at explaining difficult ideas simply.

contexts.text: My listening is pretty good, but reading under time pressure still worries me.
The food at the canteen is pretty good for the price.

confusables.difference: Similar level, but British 'quite good' can sound faintly disappointed, while 'pretty good' sounds positive.
minimal_pair: It was quite good.
It was pretty good.

confusables.difference: 'Very good' is a clear compliment; 'pretty good' holds something back.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'pretty' as a degree adverb in Task 1 or Task 2. Write 'relatively good' or 'fairly strong'.

entry_json.definition: almost completely, or more or less; it goes before the word it softens, and it is informal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The town centre is pretty much empty after seven in the evening.
example_sentences: I've pretty much finished the first draft.
Everyone in my year had pretty much the same timetable.

contexts.text: The town centre is pretty much empty after seven in the evening.
I've pretty much finished the first draft.

confusables.difference: Same job, slightly more neutral, and acceptable in semi-formal writing.
minimal_pair: pretty much identical
more or less identical

confusables.difference: 'Almost' is the formal single word and is safe in Task 1: 'almost entirely residential'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write it in the exam essay. Use 'almost', 'largely' or 'more or less' instead.

entry_json.ipa: ˈpraɪsɪz ˈreɪndʒɪŋ frəm ˈtwenti faɪv ˈjʊərəʊz tə ˈsɪksti ˈjʊərəʊz
entry_json.definition: a model phrase for describing a spread of prices; the pattern is 'prices ranging from + lower figure + to + higher figure', with the participle replacing 'which range'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The hotels near the station offer rooms at prices ranging from €25 to €60 a night.
example_sentences: Tickets were sold at prices ranging from €25 to €60, depending on how early they were booked.
The market sells everything from second-hand books to furniture, at prices ranging from a few euros to several hundred.

contexts.text: The hotels near the station offer rooms at prices ranging from €25 to €60 a night.
Tickets were sold at prices ranging from €25 to €60, depending on how early they were booked.

confusables.difference: 'Range from ... to ...' is the standard pair. 'Between ... and ...' also works, but do not mix them into 'ranging from X and Y'.
minimal_pair: ranging from €25 to €60
ranging between €25 and €60

confusables.difference: The full clause version: 'Prices range from €25 to €60.' The -ing form is a reduced relative clause and attaches to a noun.
minimal_pair: Prices range from €25 to €60.
rooms at prices ranging from €25 to €60

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'ranging from €25 until €60'. The pair is 'from ... to ...'.

entry_json.definition: a school for children aged roughly five to eleven in Britain; used without an article when you mean attending it, as in 'at primary school'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I learned to swim at primary school, in a pool the council later closed.
example_sentences: Class sizes in primary schools have risen in most urban areas.
She teaches at a primary school just outside the city.

entry_json.definition: before; a formal preposition that takes a noun or a gerund, never a clause

contexts.text: Prior to the opening of the bypass, all freight traffic passed through the village.
Applicants must submit references prior to the interview.

confusables.difference: Identical meaning. 'Before' can take a clause: 'before the bypass opened'. 'Prior to' cannot.
minimal_pair: prior to the opening
before the bypass opened

confusables.difference: 'Previously' is an adverb and stands alone: 'The road was previously the only route.' 'Prior to' needs an object.

entry_json.definition: turn out to be something once there is evidence; the subject is the thing being judged, and the pattern is 'prove to be' plus adjective or noun

contexts.text: The new timetable proved to be far more popular than the council expected.
The early results proved to be misleading once the full sample was analysed.

confusables.difference: The everyday equivalent, common in speech: 'It turned out to be fine.' 'Prove to be' is more formal.
minimal_pair: It turned out to be harder.
It proved to be harder.

confusables.difference: With a direct object it means to demonstrate: 'The study proves the link.' With 'to be' it means to turn out.
minimal_pair: The study proved the link.
The link proved to be weak.

entry_json.avoid: 'To be' can be dropped before an adjective, giving 'proved effective'. Do not drop it before a noun: 'proved to be a mistake'.

entry_json.definition: buses, trains, trams and other shared services open to everyone; uncountable in British English, so it takes no article and no plural

contexts.text: Investment in public transport is usually cheaper per passenger than building new roads.
I use public transport every day because parking near the office is impossible.
The chart compares public transport use in four European cities.

confusables.difference: The American form. British English, and most IELTS questions, use 'public transport'.

public transportation

confusables.difference: 'Transport' is uncountable in this sense and has no plural.
minimal_pair: public transport is cheap
public transports are cheap

As one resident put it, the new flats were built for investors rather than for families.
How can I put it? The course was useful but far too long.

To put it simply, it failed.

entry_json.definition: suggest a plan, an idea or a name for others to consider; separable, and the object is usually an abstract noun such as proposal, argument or theory

She put her name forward for the position.

contexts.text: The committee put forward three options, only one of which had been costed.
Several scientists have put forward alternative explanations for the pattern.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb and often the tighter choice in Task 2: 'The report proposes three options.'
minimal_pair: They put forward a plan.
They proposed a plan.

confusables.difference: A different phrasal verb meaning postpone. Same verb, opposite kind of meaning.
minimal_pair: He put forward the meeting date.
He put off the meeting.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object must go in the middle: 'put it forward', never 'put forward it'.

entry_json.definition: dress yourself in a piece of clothing, switch on a device, or start a recording; separable, and a pronoun must sit in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Put a coat on, because it is colder than it looks outside.
example_sentences: I put the heating on for an hour in the morning and that is enough.
She put on her glasses and read the notice again.

contexts.text: Put a coat on, because it is colder than it looks outside.
I put the heating on for an hour in the morning and that is enough.

confusables.difference: 'Put on' is the action of dressing; 'wear' is the state of having something on.
minimal_pair: He put on a coat.
He was wearing a coat.

confusables.difference: For machines both work, though 'turn on' is more usual for switches and 'put on' for heating, lights and music.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'put on it'. With a pronoun the phrase splits: 'put it on'.

entry_json.definition: assemble the parts of something, or create something from separate pieces of work; separable, and a pronoun goes in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took a weekend to put the report together from four different sets of figures.
example_sentences: The furniture arrives flat and you put it together yourself.
She put together a short presentation the night before the interview.

contexts.text: It took a weekend to put the report together from four different sets of figures.
The furniture arrives flat and you put it together yourself.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, better in a technical description: 'The components are assembled on site.'
minimal_pair: We put the kit together.
The kit is assembled on site.

confusables.difference: In the phrase 'more than all the others put together', it means added up as a total, not assembled.
minimal_pair: She put the desk together.
He earns more than the rest put together.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always splits the phrase: 'put it together', never 'put together it'.

entry_json.definition: build or erect something, fix it to a wall, or raise a price or level; separable, with a pronoun in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council put up a fence around the site before any building began.
example_sentences: The landlord put the rent up by eight per cent in a single year.
They put up a notice explaining that the pool would be closed.
collocations: put sb up for the night

contexts.text: The council put up a fence around the site before any building began.
The landlord put the rent up by eight per cent in a single year.

confusables.difference: A three-word phrasal verb with a completely different meaning: tolerate. 'I can't put up with the noise.'
minimal_pair: They put up a fence.
They put up with the noise.

confusables.difference: 'Raise prices' is the formal written choice; 'put prices up' is the everyday spoken one.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'put up with'. Dropping 'with' changes tolerating into building.

entry_json.definition: how good or comfortable a person's life is, judged by health, time, environment and relationships rather than by income alone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Shorter commuting times do more for quality of life than a small pay rise.
example_sentences: The survey ranks cities by quality of life rather than by economic output.
Air pollution has a direct effect on quality of life in the city centre.

contexts.text: Shorter commuting times do more for quality of life than a small pay rise.
The survey ranks cities by quality of life rather than by economic output.
Moving out of the city improved our quality of life more than I expected.

confusables.difference: 'Standard of living' is measured in money and goods. 'Quality of life' includes health, time, safety and environment. An essay that swaps them loses precision.
minimal_pair: Their standard of living rose.
Their quality of life improved.

confusables.difference: 'Lifestyle' is the way somebody chooses to live; 'quality of life' is how good that life is.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it as a synonym for wealth. The whole point of the phrase is that it measures what money does not.

entry_json.definition: a model of the 'quite a + adjective + noun' pattern; note the unusual word order, with 'quite' coming before the article, not after it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He is quite a good player, though he has never trained seriously.
example_sentences: She turned out to be quite a good player after only a year of lessons.
For someone who started at thirty, he is quite a good player.

contexts.text: He is quite a good player, though he has never trained seriously.
She turned out to be quite a good player after only a year of lessons.

confusables.difference: The order is fixed: 'quite' goes before 'a'. 'A quite good player' sounds wrong to a British ear.
minimal_pair: quite a good player
a quite good player

confusables.difference: 'Very' goes after the article: 'a very good player'. Only 'quite', 'such' and 'rather' jump in front of it.
minimal_pair: quite a good player
a very good player

entry_json.avoid: In British English 'quite good' can sound like faint praise, closer to 'not bad' than to 'very good'. Be careful when complimenting somebody.

entry_json.definition: a fairly long period, without saying exactly how long; the same 'quite a + adjective + noun' pattern used with a time expression
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I lived in that flat for quite a long time before I noticed how noisy the street was.
example_sentences: It took quite a long time to get used to studying in a second language.
We waited quite a long time for the results.

contexts.text: I lived in that flat for quite a long time before I noticed how noisy the street was.
It took quite a long time to get used to studying in a second language.

confusables.difference: Shorter and just as natural in speech, with the same vagueness.
minimal_pair: for quite a long time
for quite a while

confusables.difference: Without 'quite' the claim is stronger. 'Quite' softens it to 'fairly'.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 give the actual period. 'Quite a long time' tells an examiner nothing measurable.

entry_json.definition: a fairly large amount or number, or fairly often; it can stand alone after a verb, without a noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read quite a lot, mostly on the train to and from work.
example_sentences: 'Do you travel much?' 'Quite a lot, yes, three or four times a year.'

contexts.text: I read quite a lot, mostly on the train to and from work.
'Do you travel much?' 'Quite a lot, yes, three or four times a year.'

confusables.difference: Add 'of' plus a noun when you name what there is a lot of: 'quite a lot of homework'.
minimal_pair: I read quite a lot.
I have quite a lot of work.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in speech, though 'a bit' suits uncountable amounts better than large numbers.

entry_json.avoid: Too vague for writing. In Task 1 write 'approximately 40 per cent', not 'quite a lot'.

entry_json.definition: a fairly large amount of something; 'of' introduces the noun, which can be countable plural or uncountable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is quite a lot of pressure on students to choose a subject at sixteen.
example_sentences: Quite a lot of people in my class had never taken a formal exam before.
We wasted quite a lot of time looking for parking.

contexts.text: There is quite a lot of pressure on students to choose a subject at sixteen.
Quite a lot of people in my class had never taken a formal exam before.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, used with uncountable nouns: 'a great deal of evidence'.
minimal_pair: quite a lot of evidence
a great deal of evidence

confusables.difference: In positive statements 'much' sounds formal or odd in speech; 'quite a lot of' is what people actually say.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before the noun: 'quite a lot of people', never 'quite a lot people'.

entry_json.definition: the frame 'quite a' plus an adjective and a noun, or plus a noun alone for emphasis; 'quite' goes before the article, which is the point of the pattern
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That was quite a journey, three trains and a two-hour delay.
example_sentences: It is quite a small town, so everybody knows everybody.
Finishing the course while working full time was quite an achievement.

contexts.text: That was quite a journey, three trains and a two-hour delay.
It is quite a small town, so everybody knows everybody.

confusables.difference: 'Quite the' plus a noun is emphatic and slightly ironic: 'quite the expert'. Use 'quite a' for the neutral meaning.
minimal_pair: quite a change
quite the expert

confusables.difference: A fixed quantifier meaning a fairly large number, despite containing 'few'.
minimal_pair: quite a few people came
few people came

entry_json.avoid: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: 'quite an achievement', not 'quite a achievement'.

entry_json.definition: collect money for a purpose, usually from many people or from investors; 'raise' takes an object, unlike 'rise'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The school raised money for new sports equipment by running a summer fair.
example_sentences: Charities find it harder to raise money during a recession.
The company raised money by selling part of the business.

contexts.text: The school raised money for new sports equipment by running a summer fair.
Charities find it harder to raise money during a recession.

confusables.difference: 'Raise' needs an object and is regular: raise, raised. 'Rise' takes no object and is irregular: rise, rose, risen. Money rises in value; people raise money.
minimal_pair: They raised money.
Prices rose sharply.

confusables.difference: 'Collect' is the physical act of gathering; 'raise' covers the whole effort, including events and appeals.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'raise' with 'rise'. Writing 'the school rised money' is a basic error that costs marks.

entry_json.definition: collect money for a stated cause or purpose; 'for' introduces what the money is intended to pay for
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They ran a half marathon to raise money for the local hospice.
example_sentences: The campaign raised money for flood defences in three villages.
Students raise money for charity every year during rag week.
collocations: raise money for a good cause

contexts.text: They ran a half marathon to raise money for the local hospice.
The campaign raised money for flood defences in three villages.

confusables.difference: 'From' names who gives the money; 'for' names what it is spent on. Both can appear: 'raised money from local firms for the new wing'.
minimal_pair: raised money for the hospice
raised money from local firms

confusables.difference: 'Donate' is what an individual giver does; 'raise money for' is what the organiser does.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'to' for the purpose. It is 'raise money for research', not 'raise money to research', unless a verb follows: 'to fund research'.

entry_json.definition: used after a noun to show the extremes of a set; it is a reduced relative clause standing for 'which range from', and it must be followed by 'to'

example_sentences: The museum holds objects ranging from Roman coins to modern photography.
Temperatures ranging from minus five to thirty degrees were recorded during the year.

contexts.text: The centre runs courses ranging from basic literacy to postgraduate research methods.
Temperatures ranging from minus five to thirty degrees were recorded during the year.

confusables.difference: The full verb version needs a subject: 'Prices range from £5 to £50.' The -ing form attaches to a noun instead.
minimal_pair: Prices range from £5 to £50.
items ranging from £5 to £50

confusables.difference: Similar, but 'varying' stresses change while 'ranging' stresses the spread between two limits.

entry_json.avoid: Always complete the pair. 'Courses ranging from basic literacy' with no 'to' leaves the sentence unfinished.

entry_json.definition: instead of; it joins two items of the same grammatical type, and after a to-infinitive the second verb usually appears bare

example_sentences: The problem is one of distribution rather than of supply.
Most students revise in short sessions rather than in one long block.

contexts.text: The council chose to widen the road rather than improve the bus service.
The problem is one of distribution rather than of supply.
I'd take the train rather than fly for a journey that short.

confusables.difference: 'Instead of' takes a noun or an -ing form: 'instead of driving'. 'Rather than' is more flexible and can join adjectives, nouns or verbs.
minimal_pair: instead of driving
rather than drive

confusables.difference: A different structure about preference, followed by a bare infinitive: 'I would rather stay.'
minimal_pair: I would rather stay.
I stayed rather than went out.

entry_json.avoid: Keep both sides parallel: 'rather than improve', not 'rather than improving', when the first half is 'to widen'.

entry_json.definition: what somebody says, feels or does because of something that has happened; the trigger follows 'to', not 'of' or 'for'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The public reaction to the congestion charge was far more positive than politicians expected.
example_sentences: Her first reaction to the news was disbelief.
The chart shows consumer reaction to the price increase over six months.

contexts.text: The public reaction to the congestion charge was far more positive than politicians expected.
The chart shows consumer reaction to the price increase over six months.
My first reaction to the result was relief rather than joy.

confusables.difference: 'Of' names who reacted; 'to' names what they reacted to. Both can appear: 'the reaction of parents to the new rules'.
minimal_pair: the reaction of parents
the reaction to the rules

confusables.difference: 'Response' suggests a considered reply; 'reaction' suggests something immediate and often emotional.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'reaction for'. The dependent preposition is 'to'.

entry_json.definition: like an activity very much; 'enjoy' must be followed by a noun or an -ing form, never by a to-infinitive

example_sentences: I really enjoyed the trip, even though the weather was terrible.
She really enjoys teaching younger students.

contexts.text: I really enjoy cooking at the weekend, mostly because it is the opposite of my job.
I really enjoyed the trip, even though the weather was terrible.

confusables.difference: Not English. 'Enjoy' takes the -ing form: 'enjoy swimming', never 'enjoy to swim'.
minimal_pair: I enjoy swimming.
I enjoy to swim.

confusables.difference: The more formal intensifier, useful in a semi-formal letter: 'I thoroughly enjoyed the course.'

entry_json.avoid: 'Enjoy' always needs an object. 'I really enjoyed' on its own is incomplete; say 'I really enjoyed it'.

entry_json.definition: very good; the most common spoken intensifier, and one that examiners hear so often it adds nothing to your score
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The teacher was really good at explaining things without making anyone feel stupid.
example_sentences: It was a really good film, one of the best I saw last year.
The transport in that city is really good compared with where I live.

contexts.text: The teacher was really good at explaining things without making anyone feel stupid.
The transport in that city is really good compared with where I live.

confusables.difference: A stronger single word that shows range. In Speaking Part 2, swapping one 'really good' for 'excellent' or 'first-rate' is worth more than three more sentences.
minimal_pair: It was really good.
It was excellent.

confusables.difference: Slightly more formal than 'really good', but just as overused.

entry_json.avoid: Do not build a whole answer on it. Repeating 'really good' signals a limited range of vocabulary, which is exactly what the band descriptors measure.

entry_json.definition: enjoy or approve of something a lot; 'like' can be followed by an -ing form or a to-infinitive, with a slight difference in meaning
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I really like living near the sea, even in winter.
example_sentences: I really like the way the new library is organised.
She really likes her new colleagues.

contexts.text: I really like living near the sea, even in winter.
I really like the way the new library is organised.

confusables.difference: 'I really like coffee' is a general preference. 'I would really like a coffee' is a request for one now.
minimal_pair: I really like coffee.
I would really like a coffee.

confusables.difference: 'Love' is stronger and equally natural in speech: 'I love living here.'

entry_json.avoid: Reach past it in the exam. 'I'm very keen on', 'I'm particularly fond of' and 'I get a lot out of' all show more range.

entry_json.definition: the explanations for something; 'why' introduces the clause that follows, and it can be left out
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are several reasons why young people are leaving rural areas.
example_sentences: One of the main reasons why the scheme failed was poor communication.
The report lists three reasons for the delay.

contexts.text: There are several reasons why young people are leaving rural areas.
One of the main reasons why the scheme failed was poor communication.
There are a few reasons why I chose this course.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a noun: 'reasons for the delay'. 'Why' takes a clause: 'reasons why it was delayed'.
minimal_pair: reasons for the delay
reasons why it was delayed

confusables.difference: 'That' can replace 'why' but sounds heavier. Leaving both out is often cleanest: 'the reason people leave'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'reasons why because'. The 'why' already carries the meaning; 'The reason why it failed is because' should be 'The reason it failed is that'.

entry_json.definition: mention somebody or something, or look at a source for information; the preposition 'to' is compulsory and the phrase never splits
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph refers to households rather than to individuals, which changes the interpretation.
example_sentences: Candidates may refer to their notes during the presentation.
The author refers to three earlier studies but discusses none of them.

contexts.text: The graph refers to households rather than to individuals, which changes the interpretation.
The author refers to three earlier studies but discusses none of them.
He kept referring to a book I hadn't read.

confusables.difference: 'Mention' takes a direct object with no preposition: 'She mentioned the cost.' 'Refer to' always needs 'to'.
minimal_pair: She mentioned the report.
She referred to the report.

confusables.difference: With two objects it means to send somebody to a source or a specialist: 'The doctor referred her to a consultant.'
minimal_pair: He referred to the specialist.
The doctor referred her to a specialist.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling change: refer, referring, referred, with a doubled r. 'Refering' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: call somebody or something by a particular name or description; the pattern needs both 'to' and 'as', and the description follows 'as'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economists often refer to this period as the lost decade.
example_sentences: The document refers to the participants as clients rather than patients.
What most people refer to as the city centre is actually two separate districts.

contexts.text: Economists often refer to this period as the lost decade.
The document refers to the participants as clients rather than patients.

confusables.difference: Without 'as' it just means mention. With 'as' it names or labels.
minimal_pair: He referred to the report.
He referred to it as a failure.

confusables.difference: 'Call' needs no prepositions: 'They call it the old town.' 'Refer to ... as' is the formal written version.
minimal_pair: They call it the old town.
They refer to it as the old town.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop either preposition. 'Referred as the lost decade' is wrong; it must be 'referred to as'.

entry_json.definition: considered to be something, in the view of other people; almost always passive, and the description follows 'as'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is widely regarded as the finest example of the architect's later work.
example_sentences: He is regarded as one of the leading researchers in the field.
Cycling was once regarded as a poor person's transport and is now a status symbol.

contexts.text: The library is widely regarded as the finest example of the architect's later work.
Cycling was once regarded as a poor person's transport and is now a status symbol.

confusables.difference: 'Considered' takes 'as' only sometimes, and standard usage prefers it bare: 'considered the best', 'regarded as the best'.
minimal_pair: regarded as the best
considered the best

confusables.difference: The active form needs a subject who holds the view: 'Historians regard him as a reformer.'
minimal_pair: He is regarded as a reformer.
Historians regard him as a reformer.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'as': 'regarded the best' is wrong. And do not write 'regarded as to be'.

entry_json.definition: be connected with something, or understand and sympathise with somebody; the preposition is always 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The second question relates to the cost of the scheme rather than to its design.
example_sentences: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than to the quality of care.
Younger readers relate to the main character because her problems are recognisable.

contexts.text: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than to the quality of care.
Younger readers relate to the main character because her problems are recognisable.
I can really relate to students who work while they study.

confusables.difference: With a direct object it means to connect two things: 'The study relates diet to sleep quality.'
minimal_pair: Diet relates to sleep quality.
The study relates diet to sleep quality.

confusables.difference: The passive-looking adjective form describes a fixed connection: 'The two problems are related.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'relate with'. The dependent preposition is 'to'.

entry_json.definition: connected with something, or belonging to the same family; it works as an adjective after 'be' or directly after a noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Costs related to heating rose faster than any other item in the household budget.
example_sentences: Illnesses related to poor air quality are concentrated in the busiest districts.
We are related, though only distantly.

contexts.text: Costs related to heating rose faster than any other item in the household budget.
Illnesses related to poor air quality are concentrated in the busiest districts.
We're related, though only distantly.

confusables.difference: 'Relating to' is the active participle and reads slightly more formal; after a noun the two are almost interchangeable.
minimal_pair: costs related to heating
costs relating to heating

confusables.difference: 'Relative' is the noun for a family member: 'a close relative'. 'Related' is the adjective: 'we are related'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'related with'. It is always 'related to'.

entry_json.definition: concerning or connected with; a participle phrase that follows a noun and replaces 'which relates to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: All documents relating to the sale must be kept for six years.
example_sentences: Questions relating to funding were referred to the finance committee.
The chapter covers issues relating to water supply in dry regions.

contexts.text: All documents relating to the sale must be kept for six years.
The chapter covers issues relating to water supply in dry regions.

confusables.difference: 'Related to' suggests a connection that already exists; 'relating to' suggests the topic something is about. In practice they overlap.
minimal_pair: problems related to noise
regulations relating to noise

confusables.difference: 'About' is the plain everyday word. 'Relating to' is the formal register for reports and legal writing.

entry_json.avoid: It cannot start a sentence as a linker. Write 'With regard to funding, ...', not 'Relating to funding, ...'.

entry_json.definition: closely connected with the subject under discussion, or useful for a particular person; the preposition is 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The examiner is looking for examples that are relevant to the question, not simply interesting.
example_sentences: Only two of the studies were relevant to the age group being examined.
The course content should be relevant to the jobs students actually apply for.

contexts.text: The examiner is looking for examples that are relevant to the question, not simply interesting.
Only two of the studies were relevant to the age group being examined.

confusables.difference: 'Related to' means connected in some way. 'Relevant to' means useful for the matter in hand. A fact can be related but not relevant.
minimal_pair: The data is related to housing.
The data is relevant to our question.

confusables.difference: 'For' is possible when you mean useful to a person, but 'to' is the safer standard choice.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the spelling: relevant, with three e-sounds and no 'a' in the middle. 'Relevent' and 'revelant' are both common misspellings.

entry_json.definition: depend on somebody or something to work or to help you; the preposition is 'on', and it is often followed by an -ing form or 'to' plus a verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rural communities rely on a bus service that runs three times a day.
example_sentences: The system relies on users updating their details, which many never do.
You cannot rely on the weather in April.
collocations: rely on sb to do sth

contexts.text: Rural communities rely on a bus service that runs three times a day.
The system relies on users updating their details, which many never do.
I rely on my phone far more than I would like to admit.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'Rely on' suggests trust that something will work; 'depend on' can also mean 'be determined by': 'It depends on the weather.'
minimal_pair: I rely on the bus.
It depends on the weather.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. It is always 'on', or 'upon' in formal writing.

entry_json.avoid: After 'rely on' use a noun or an -ing form: 'rely on receiving help', not 'rely on receive help'.

entry_json.definition: give an account of something you have investigated; the subject examined follows 'on', and the same pattern works for the noun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The committee will report on the results of the trial in the spring.
example_sentences: Journalists who report on conflict face particular risks.
The document is a report on air quality in six European cities.

contexts.text: The committee will report on the results of the trial in the spring.
Journalists who report on conflict face particular risks.

confusables.difference: Without 'on' it means to state a fact or an incident: 'She reported the theft.' With 'on' it means to study and describe a subject.
minimal_pair: She reported the theft.
She reported on crime rates.

confusables.difference: 'To' names the person or body you answer to: 'She reports to the head of department.'
minimal_pair: He reports on safety.
He reports to the manager.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'report on' with 'report to'. One names the subject, the other names your boss.

entry_json.definition: admiration for somebody, or careful attention to something such as a rule or an environment; the preposition is 'for'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Respect for the environment has to be taught early, not added later as a school subject.
example_sentences: There is enormous respect for teachers in her country.
The company showed little respect for local planning rules.

contexts.text: Respect for the environment has to be taught early, not added later as a school subject.
There is enormous respect for teachers in her country.

confusables.difference: 'Respect to' only appears in the fixed linker 'with respect to', meaning 'concerning'. For admiration it is 'respect for'.
minimal_pair: respect for the law
with respect to the law

confusables.difference: The plural is a fixed formal phrase: 'pay your respects', meaning to attend a funeral or greet someone formally.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'respect of' for admiration. 'In respect of' is legal English meaning 'concerning', which is a different thing entirely.

entry_json.definition: answer, or act because of something that has happened; the preposition is 'to', and it also works for reacting to treatment or to a signal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council responded to the complaints by extending the consultation period.
example_sentences: Only 12 per cent of those contacted responded to the survey.
Patients who respond well to the first treatment rarely need the second.

contexts.text: The council responded to the complaints by extending the consultation period.
Only 12 per cent of those contacted responded to the survey.
She responded to my email within an hour.

confusables.difference: 'Answer' takes a direct object with no preposition: 'answer the question'. 'Respond' needs 'to'.
minimal_pair: He answered the question.
He responded to the question.

confusables.difference: 'React' is more immediate and often emotional; 'respond' suggests a considered reply.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'respond the question'. The preposition 'to' is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: cause something to happen; the cause is the subject and the effect follows 'in', which is the opposite arrangement to 'result from'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heavy rainfall in March resulted in flooding across the low-lying districts.
example_sentences: Cutting the bus service resulted in a sharp rise in car journeys.
The reform resulted in longer waiting lists rather than shorter ones.

contexts.text: Heavy rainfall in March resulted in flooding across the low-lying districts.
Cutting the bus service resulted in a sharp rise in car journeys.

confusables.difference: The arrow points the other way. 'A resulted in B' means A caused B; 'A resulted from B' means B caused A.
minimal_pair: The rain resulted in flooding.
The flooding resulted from the rain.

confusables.difference: 'Cause' takes a direct object: 'The rain caused flooding.' 'Result in' needs the preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with a noun, not a clause: 'resulted in flooding', not 'resulted in the area flooded'.

entry_json.definition: at this exact moment, or immediately; it strengthens 'now' and normally sits at the end of the clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am living with my parents right now while I save for a deposit.
example_sentences: I can't talk right now; can I call you back in ten minutes?
Right now the priority is finishing the first draft.

contexts.text: I am living with my parents right now while I save for a deposit.
I can't talk right now; can I call you back in ten minutes?

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the right choice in Task 1: 'At present, 40 per cent of homes have solar panels.'
minimal_pair: Right now, prices are falling.
At present, prices are falling.

confusables.difference: In British English 'just now' can mean a moment ago, in the past. 'Right now' is always the present.
minimal_pair: I saw him just now.
He is here right now.

entry_json.avoid: Keep it out of formal writing. Task 1 and Task 2 want 'currently', 'at present' or 'at the time of writing'.

entry_json.definition: an increase in something; as a noun it takes 'in' before the thing that increased, and 'of' before the size of the increase
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows a steady rise in electricity use across all four countries.
example_sentences: There has been a sharp rise in the number of people working from home.
A rise of twelve per cent was recorded in the final quarter.

contexts.text: The chart shows a steady rise in electricity use across all four countries.
There has been a sharp rise in the number of people working from home.

confusables.difference: 'In' names what rose; 'of' names by how much. 'A rise in prices of 5 per cent' uses both correctly.
minimal_pair: a rise in prices
a rise of 5 per cent

confusables.difference: 'Raise' is a verb needing an object and, in American English, a noun meaning a pay increase. The British noun is 'rise'.
minimal_pair: a rise in wages
They raised wages.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a rise on prices' or 'a rise for prices'. Task 1 examiners see this error constantly; the preposition is 'in'.

entry_json.definition: be used up so that none is left; the thing that is finished is the subject, and no object follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had been walking for four hours when the water ran out.
example_sentences: My phone battery ran out halfway through the journey.
Time ran out before the final question could be answered.

contexts.text: We had been walking for four hours when the water ran out.
Time ran out before the final question could be answered.

confusables.difference: 'Run out' has no object: 'The milk ran out.' 'Run out of' takes one: 'We ran out of milk.' The subject swaps.
minimal_pair: The milk ran out.
We ran out of milk.

confusables.difference: Not a possible pattern. Either use 'run out' alone or add 'of'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put the person first without 'of'. 'I ran out water' is wrong; write 'I ran out of water' or 'The water ran out'.

entry_json.definition: have no more of something left; the person or group is the subject and the supply follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I ran out of time in the reading section and guessed the last five answers.
example_sentences: The hospital ran out of beds during the winter peak.
We have run out of milk again.

contexts.text: I ran out of time in the reading section and guessed the last five answers.
The hospital ran out of beds during the winter peak.

confusables.difference: Without 'of' the supply becomes the subject: 'The beds ran out.'
minimal_pair: We ran out of beds.
The beds ran out.

confusables.difference: 'We're out of milk' describes the state; 'we ran out of milk' describes the moment it happened.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. 'I ran out money' is a common slip; the preposition is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: keep money instead of spending it, or spend less than you would otherwise; there is no article before 'money'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cycling to work saves money and takes about the same time as the bus.
example_sentences: Insulating the roof saved us nearly two hundred pounds a year.
Young people find it harder to save money when rents take half their income.

contexts.text: Cycling to work saves money and takes about the same time as the bus.
Young people find it harder to save money when rents take half their income.

confusables.difference: 'Save up' means to collect money over time for a particular purchase: 'saving up for a car'. 'Save money' can also just mean spending less.
minimal_pair: I'm saving up for a car.
Buying in bulk saves money.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, useful for variety: 'Households have had to economise.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'save money', not 'save the money', unless you mean a specific sum already mentioned.

entry_json.definition: stories set in an imagined future or in space, usually built around science and technology; uncountable, so it takes no article and no plural
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read a lot of science fiction as a teenager and it is probably why I studied physics.
example_sentences: Science fiction has predicted several technologies that later became ordinary.
The film is science fiction, but the science in it is surprisingly careful.

contexts.text: I read a lot of science fiction as a teenager and it is probably why I studied physics.
Science fiction has predicted several technologies that later became ordinary.

confusables.difference: The informal abbreviation, fine in Speaking, weaker in Task 2 where the full term reads better.
minimal_pair: I like sci-fi.
The genre of science fiction...

confusables.difference: Fantasy uses magic and invented worlds; science fiction works from science and technology. The two are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'science fictions'. It is uncountable; for one book say 'a science fiction novel'.

entry_json.definition: a program that finds pages on the internet from words you type; a compound noun in which 'search' stays singular
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most people never look past the first page of results a search engine gives them.
example_sentences: Search engines rank pages by rules that are not published in full.
I use a different search engine at work because it stores less data.

contexts.text: Most people never look past the first page of results a search engine gives them.
I use a different search engine at work because it stores less data.

confusables.difference: A browser is the program you open to view pages; a search engine is the service that finds them. They are not the same thing.
minimal_pair: Open your browser.
Type it into a search engine.

confusables.difference: A search engine is one kind of website, but most websites are not search engines.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'search' singular in the compound: 'search engines', not 'searches engines'.

entry_json.definition: look carefully in order to find something or somebody; 'for' introduces what you want, while 'search' with a direct object means to examine a place or a person
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rescue teams searched for survivors for three days after the earthquake.
example_sentences: I spent an hour searching for a document that was on my desk the whole time.
Students search for sources online before they ever open a library catalogue.

contexts.text: Rescue teams searched for survivors for three days after the earthquake.
Students search for sources online before they ever open a library catalogue.

confusables.difference: Without 'for' the object is the place being examined: 'Police searched the building.' With 'for' it is the thing wanted.
minimal_pair: They searched the building.
They searched for the keys.

confusables.difference: The everyday equivalent. 'Search for' suggests a more systematic or urgent effort.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse the two patterns. 'They searched the survivors' means they examined the survivors' pockets, not that they looked for them.

entry_json.definition: a school for pupils aged roughly eleven to sixteen or eighteen in Britain; used without an article when you mean the stage of education
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I only started studying English seriously at secondary school.
example_sentences: Class sizes in secondary schools have grown faster than in primary schools.
The town has two secondary schools and four primary schools.

contexts.text: Class sizes in secondary schools have grown faster than in primary schools.
I only started studying English seriously at secondary school.

confusables.difference: The American term, also used in some other countries. British English, and most IELTS material, says 'secondary school'.
minimal_pair: at secondary school
in high school

confusables.difference: The stage before, for roughly ages five to eleven.

entry_json.avoid: Drop the article for the stage: 'at secondary school', not 'at the secondary school', unless you mean one specific building.

entry_json.definition: try to do something, especially over a long period or in an official way; it takes a to-infinitive and belongs to formal writing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The policy seeks to reduce car use without making life harder for people outside the city.
example_sentences: This essay seeks to explain why the two studies reached opposite conclusions.
Governments have long sought to encourage saving through tax relief.

contexts.text: The policy seeks to reduce car use without making life harder for people outside the city.
This essay seeks to explain why the two studies reached opposite conclusions.

confusables.difference: 'Try' is the everyday word and fits Speaking. 'Seek to' is formal and would sound stilted in conversation.
minimal_pair: The council is trying to cut traffic.
The policy seeks to cut traffic.

confusables.difference: With a noun object it means to look for or ask for: 'seek advice', 'seek asylum'.
minimal_pair: She sought advice.
She sought to explain.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: seek, sought, sought. 'Seeked' is not a word.

entry_json.definition: begin a journey, or explain something clearly in writing; with 'to' plus a verb it means to start with a particular aim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report sets out three options for reducing waste in the county.
example_sentences: We set out early to avoid the traffic on the coast road.
She set out to prove that the original figures were wrong.

contexts.text: The report sets out three options for reducing waste in the county.
We set out early to avoid the traffic on the coast road.

confusables.difference: The explaining sense is separable: 'set the options out'. The journey sense takes no object at all.
minimal_pair: He set out the options.
He set out at dawn.

confusables.difference: For journeys, 'set off' is more common in speech: 'We set off at six.' 'Set out' is slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: The verb does not change in the past: set, set, set. 'Setted out' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: start an organisation, arrange an event, or install equipment ready to use; separable, so a pronoun goes in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She set up a small business selling repaired bicycles two years after graduating.
example_sentences: The university set up a committee to review the marking system.
It took twenty minutes to set the projector up before the talk.

contexts.text: She set up a small business selling repaired bicycles two years after graduating.
The university set up a committee to review the marking system.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, better in Task 2: 'The charity was established in 1998.'
minimal_pair: They set up the charity in 1998.
The charity was established in 1998.

confusables.difference: 'Set out' explains or begins a journey; 'set up' creates or installs. Different phrasal verbs entirely.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object must split the phrase: 'set it up', never 'set up it'.

entry_json.definition: likely or expected to do something very soon; it follows 'be' and is common in news writing and in predictions
entry_json.own_context_sentence: House prices are set to fall for the first time in a decade.
example_sentences: The new line is set to open in 2027 if funding is approved.
Temperatures are set to rise above thirty degrees by the weekend.

contexts.text: House prices are set to fall for the first time in a decade.
The new line is set to open in 2027 if funding is approved.

confusables.difference: 'Due to' means scheduled for a particular time. 'Set to' means expected, with a little more uncertainty.
minimal_pair: The train is due to arrive at six.
Prices are set to rise.

confusables.difference: 'About to' means within minutes; 'set to' can cover months or years.

entry_json.avoid: It needs 'be' in front. Write 'prices are set to rise', not 'prices set to rise', outside a newspaper headline.

entry_json.definition: not having enough of something, or less than a stated figure; it follows 'be' or 'run', and the thing lacking follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The hospital is short of nurses, not of equipment.
example_sentences: We were short of time, so the last section of the report was rushed.
Attendance fell just short of the target set in January.

contexts.text: The hospital is short of nurses, not of equipment.
Attendance fell just short of the target set in January.
I was short of money that year, so I lived at home.

confusables.difference: 'Out of' means none at all is left; 'short of' means some remains but not enough.
minimal_pair: We are out of milk.
We are short of milk.

confusables.difference: The noun version: 'a shortage of nurses'. Use it where the sentence needs a noun phrase.
minimal_pair: The hospital is short of nurses.
There is a shortage of nurses.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. 'Short staff' means something different: a compound describing staff who are not tall.

entry_json.definition: move from standing to a sitting position; it takes no object, and 'down' cannot be separated from it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone had to sit down on the floor because the hall was full.
example_sentences: Please sit down and we will start in a moment.
He sat down beside me and explained what had gone wrong.

contexts.text: Please sit down and we will start in a moment.
Everyone had to sit down on the floor because the hall was full.

confusables.difference: 'Sit' can describe the state as well as the action: 'He sits at the front.' 'Sit down' is the movement into the chair.
minimal_pair: He sits at the front.
He sat down at the front.

confusables.difference: 'Seat' is transitive and formal: 'The usher seated us.' 'Sit down' is what you do yourself.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'sit down' with an object. 'Sit down the baby' should be 'sit the baby down' or 'put the baby down'.

entry_json.definition: move or happen more slowly, or make something do so; it works with or without an object, and with an object it is separable
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economic growth slowed down sharply in the second half of the year.
example_sentences: Traffic slows down at the roundabout, which is why queues form there.
Higher fuel prices slowed the recovery down.

contexts.text: Economic growth slowed down sharply in the second half of the year.
Traffic slows down at the roundabout, which is why queues form there.
I've had to slow down a bit since I started working nights.

confusables.difference: As a verb, 'slow' alone is more formal and common in writing: 'Growth slowed in March.' 'Slow down' is the everyday phrasal version.
minimal_pair: Growth slowed.
Growth slowed down.

confusables.difference: One word as a noun: 'a slowdown in growth'. Two words as the verb.
minimal_pair: Growth slowed down.
There was a slowdown in growth.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 the single verb is tighter: 'growth slowed' uses fewer words than 'growth slowed down' and reads more academic.

entry_json.definition: in order to do something; a formal purpose linker taking a to-infinitive, and its negative is 'so as not to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bus lanes were widened so as to reduce delays at peak times.
example_sentences: She left early so as to avoid the rush hour.
The samples were stored in the dark so as not to affect the results.
collocations: so as not to do sth
with a view to doing sth

contexts.text: The bus lanes were widened so as to reduce delays at peak times.
The samples were stored in the dark so as not to affect the results.

confusables.difference: 'So that' takes a full clause with its own subject: 'so that drivers could pass'. 'So as to' takes only an infinitive and shares the subject.
minimal_pair: so as to reduce delays
so that delays would be reduced

confusables.difference: The same meaning and slightly more common. 'So as to' is especially useful in the negative, where 'in order not to' also works.

entry_json.avoid: The subject must be the same in both halves. 'The lanes were widened so as to drivers save time' is wrong; use 'so that' there.

entry_json.definition: up to the present moment; it pairs naturally with the present perfect because the period is still open
entry_json.own_context_sentence: So far this year the city has recorded its lowest rainfall since records began.
example_sentences: Only three of the twelve councils have responded so far.
So far, so good, though the hardest section is still to come.

contexts.text: So far this year the city has recorded its lowest rainfall since records began.
Only three of the twelve councils have responded so far.
So far I've found the course much easier than I expected.

confusables.difference: A different phrase about extent or distance: 'as far as I know', 'as far as the bridge'. Not about time.
minimal_pair: So far, nothing has changed.
As far as I know, nothing has changed.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, common in reports: 'Sales to date total £2 million.'

entry_json.avoid: Use it with the present perfect, not the past simple: 'has responded so far', not 'responded so far'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce a purpose or a result, followed by a full clause with its own subject and verb, often with 'can', 'could' or 'would'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library extended its opening hours so that students could work later in the evening.
example_sentences: Bins were placed every fifty metres so that visitors would not drop litter.
Write clearly so that the examiner does not have to guess.
collocations: so that sb can do sth
so that sb could do sth

contexts.text: The library extended its opening hours so that students could work later in the evening.
Bins were placed every fifty metres so that visitors would not drop litter.
I set two alarms so that I don't miss the early train.

confusables.difference: 'So that' allows a different subject in the second half; 'so as to' does not.
minimal_pair: so that students could work
so as to help students

confusables.difference: 'So' alone introduces a result, not a purpose: 'It rained, so we stayed in.' 'So that' introduces intention.
minimal_pair: It rained, so we stayed in.
We stayed in so that we could work.

entry_json.avoid: 'That' can be dropped in speech but keep it in writing. Also do not follow it with an infinitive: not 'so that to help'.

entry_json.definition: a way of solving a problem; the problem follows 'to', which is the preposition most candidates get wrong
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no single solution to traffic congestion in a city built before cars existed.
example_sentences: The report proposes a practical solution to the shortage of student housing.
Recycling is only part of the solution to plastic waste.

contexts.text: There is no single solution to traffic congestion in a city built before cars existed.
The report proposes a practical solution to the shortage of student housing.

confusables.difference: 'For' is possible when you mean a product designed for a market, but with problems the standard preposition is 'to'.
minimal_pair: a solution to the problem
a solution for the problem

confusables.difference: 'Answer' also takes 'to'. Both are correct, but 'solution' suits a problem while 'answer' suits a question.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'solution of the problem' in an essay. 'Solution of' belongs to chemistry, where it means a liquid mixture.

entry_json.definition: a thing of a type you cannot name exactly; it takes a singular noun after 'of', usually without an article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There should be some kind of support for students who are the first in their family to go to university.
example_sentences: The machine made some kind of clicking noise before it stopped.
They want some kind of guarantee before they sign.

contexts.text: There should be some kind of support for students who are the first in their family to go to university.
The machine made some kind of clicking noise before it stopped.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in British English; 'sort' is very slightly more informal.
minimal_pair: some kind of delay
some sort of delay

confusables.difference: 'A kind of' points at one example of a category: 'a kind of bread'. 'Some kind of' admits you do not know which.

entry_json.avoid: It signals vagueness, which costs marks in writing. In Task 2 name the thing: 'financial support', not 'some kind of support'.

entry_json.definition: a different person from the one already mentioned; 'else' always follows the pronoun, and the possessive is 'someone else's'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I cannot make the meeting, someone else from the team will attend.
example_sentences: The flat had already been let to someone else by the time I called.
It is easy to spend someone else's money.

contexts.text: If I cannot make the meeting, someone else from the team will attend.
The flat had already been let to someone else by the time I called.

confusables.difference: The order is fixed. 'Else' comes second: 'someone else', 'something else', 'somewhere else'.
minimal_pair: someone else
else someone

confusables.difference: The neutral written alternative; 'someone else' is more natural in speech and in letters.

entry_json.avoid: The apostrophe goes on 'else', not on 'someone': 'someone else's car', never 'someone's else car'.

entry_json.definition: a different thing from the one mentioned; 'else' follows the pronoun and cannot come before it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If the first plan fails, we will have to try something else.
example_sentences: I meant to say one thing and something else came out.
There is something else you should know before you decide.

contexts.text: If the first plan fails, we will have to try something else.
There is something else you should know before you decide.

confusables.difference: Not used alone. English says 'something else', or 'some other thing' with a noun.
minimal_pair: something else
something other

confusables.difference: Use 'anything else' in questions and negatives: 'Is there anything else?' 'Something else' is for statements.
minimal_pair: There is something else.
Is there anything else?

entry_json.avoid: Adjectives also follow the pronoun: 'something useful', 'something else useful'. Never 'useful something'.

entry_json.definition: approximately, before a number, or similar to, before a noun; the meaning depends on what follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Something like forty per cent of the students in my class were international.
example_sentences: The journey costs something like fifteen pounds each way.
I want a job something like the one my sister has.

contexts.text: Something like forty per cent of the students in my class were international.
The journey costs something like fifteen pounds each way.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the one Task 1 needs: 'approximately 40 per cent'.
minimal_pair: something like 40 per cent
approximately 40 per cent

confusables.difference: A vagueness tag added at the end of a list: 'a sandwich or a salad, something like that.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it with figures in Task 1. Examiners want 'approximately', 'just over' or 'around'.

entry_json.definition: a type or category of something, or, as a hedge before an adjective, 'partly'; the noun after 'of' is usually singular with no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That sort of question comes up in every Part 3 discussion.
example_sentences: What sort of music do you listen to when you are working?
I was sort of relieved when the interview was cancelled.

contexts.text: What sort of music do you listen to when you are working?
That sort of question comes up in every Part 3 discussion.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in British English. 'Sort of' is slightly more common in speech in Britain.
minimal_pair: what sort of book
what kind of book

confusables.difference: 'Type' is the most formal of the three and the safest in writing: 'this type of housing'.

entry_json.avoid: The hedging use, 'I was sort of tired', is spoken only, and repeated too often it makes an answer sound uncertain.

entry_json.definition: deal with a problem or organise something that is in a mess; separable, and with a pronoun the split is compulsory
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need to sort out my accommodation before the term starts.
example_sentences: The bank sorted the problem out within a day, to my surprise.
Give me an hour to sort myself out and I will meet you there.

contexts.text: I need to sort out my accommodation before the term starts.
The bank sorted the problem out within a day, to my surprise.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb for writing: 'The dispute was resolved.' 'Sort out' is conversational.
minimal_pair: They sorted it out.
The matter was resolved.

confusables.difference: Without 'out', 'sort' means to arrange into groups: 'sort the papers by date'. With 'out' it means to fix.
minimal_pair: Sort the papers by date.
Sort the problem out.

entry_json.avoid: Too informal for Task 2. Use 'resolve', 'address' or 'deal with' in an essay.

entry_json.definition: seem, from what you have heard, to be a particular thing; it can also mean to have a similar sound, and it takes a noun or a clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That sounds like a good compromise, provided everyone has time to read it first.
example_sentences: It sounds like the flight has been delayed again.
Her accent sounds like my grandmother's.

contexts.text: That sounds like a good compromise, provided everyone has time to read it first.
It sounds like the flight has been delayed again.

confusables.difference: 'As if' plus a clause is the careful written form: 'It sounds as if the flight is delayed.' 'Sound like' plus a clause is common in speech.
minimal_pair: It sounds as if he is unwell.
It sounds like he is unwell.

confusables.difference: With an adjective there is no 'like': 'That sounds good', not 'That sounds like good'.
minimal_pair: That sounds good.
That sounds like a good idea.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'like' before an adjective. 'It sounds like interesting' is wrong; say 'It sounds interesting'.

entry_json.definition: have a conversation with somebody, often about something specific; British English prefers 'to' where American English often uses 'with'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I need to speak to my tutor about changing the deadline.
example_sentences: Could I speak to the manager, please?
She spoke to the whole department about the changes.

contexts.text: I need to speak to my tutor about changing the deadline.
Applicants should speak to a member of staff before submitting the form.

confusables.difference: Standard in American English and increasingly common elsewhere. British IELTS material uses 'speak to'.
minimal_pair: speak to the manager
speak with the manager

confusables.difference: 'Talk to' suggests a longer, more informal conversation; 'speak to' can be a brief or official exchange.

entry_json.avoid: Do not omit the preposition. 'Speak the manager' is wrong; 'speak English' is a different pattern, where the object is a language.

entry_json.definition: use a period of time doing something; 'spend' takes time or money as its object, and no preposition follows it directly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spend more time commuting than I do cooking, which says something about the city.
example_sentences: Children now spend less time outdoors than any previous generation.
We spent three days in the capital and the rest on the coast.

contexts.text: Children now spend less time outdoors than any previous generation.
I spend more time commuting than I do cooking, which says something about the city.

confusables.difference: 'Pass the time' means to fill time while waiting; 'spend time' is neutral about how you use it.
minimal_pair: I read to pass the time.
I spend time reading.

confusables.difference: 'It takes time' is about how long something needs; 'spend time' is about what a person chooses to do.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: spend, spent, spent. 'Spended' is not a word.

entry_json.definition: use a period of time on an activity; the verb after 'time' is always the -ing form, with no preposition in between
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most candidates spend too much time on the first task and rush the second.
example_sentences: I spend about an hour a day listening to podcasts in English.
Teenagers spend a great deal of time comparing themselves with people they will never meet.

contexts.text: I spend about an hour a day listening to podcasts in English.
Teenagers spend a great deal of time comparing themselves with people they will never meet.

confusables.difference: With a noun you need 'on': 'spend time on homework'. With a verb you need the -ing form and no preposition.
minimal_pair: spend time on homework
spend time doing homework

confusables.difference: Not English. The infinitive does not work here.
minimal_pair: spend time studying
spend time to study

entry_json.avoid: Never use a to-infinitive: 'spend time to study' is wrong. Use 'spend time studying'.

entry_json.definition: be in somebody's company for a period; the person follows 'with', and this is one of the most useful phrases in Speaking Part 1
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to spend time with my family at least one weekend a month.
example_sentences: Working long hours means less time spent with the people who matter.
She spends most of her free time with friends from her old school.

contexts.text: I try to spend time with my family at least one weekend a month.
Working long hours means less time spent with the people who matter.

confusables.difference: Not the natural phrase for company. 'Spend time on' suits tasks: 'spend time on the report'.
minimal_pair: spend time with my family
spend time on the report

confusables.difference: Not idiomatic. English says 'spend time with'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'spend time to my family'. The preposition is 'with'.

entry_json.definition: rise from sitting to standing; it takes no object, and with 'for' it means to defend somebody or a principle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Everyone stood up when the results were announced.
example_sentences: I have to stand up every half hour because sitting hurts my back.
She stood up for a colleague who was being blamed unfairly.

contexts.text: I have to stand up every half hour because sitting hurts my back.
Everyone stood up when the results were announced.

confusables.difference: 'Stand' alone can be the state: 'He stands at the door.' 'Stand up' is the movement out of a chair.
minimal_pair: He was standing by the door.
He stood up.

confusables.difference: Adding 'for' changes it to defending somebody: 'She stood up for her colleague.'
minimal_pair: She stood up.
She stood up for her colleague.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: stand, stood, stood. 'Standed' is not a word.

entry_json.definition: begin with a particular person or thing; the phrase 'to start with' is also a fixed linker meaning 'firstly' or 'at first'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: To start with, the essay needs a clear position in the introduction.
example_sentences: The presentation starts with a short summary of the method.
We started with twelve volunteers and finished with seven.

contexts.text: To start with, the essay needs a clear position in the introduction.
We started with twelve volunteers and finished with seven.

confusables.difference: 'Begin' is slightly more formal but identical in meaning: 'The report begins with a summary.'
minimal_pair: It starts with a summary.
It begins with a summary.

confusables.difference: 'Start by' takes an -ing form and names the action: 'Start by reading the question.'
minimal_pair: Start with the question.
Start by reading the question.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'to start with' as a linker with the verb. As a linker it opens a sentence and needs a comma.

entry_json.definition: remain at home rather than going out, especially in the evening; it takes no object
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We stayed in on Friday and cooked instead of going to a restaurant.
example_sentences: I would rather stay in than queue in the rain for a table.
