Most students stay in during the last week before exams.

contexts.text: We stayed in on Friday and cooked instead of going to a restaurant.
I would rather stay in than queue in the rain for a table.

confusables.difference: The same idea in a neutral form that works in writing too. 'Stay in' is more conversational.
minimal_pair: We stayed in.
We stayed at home.

confusables.difference: With an object it means to remain inside a place or a job: 'stay in the room', 'stay in education'. Different pattern.
minimal_pair: We stayed in.
She stayed in education until she was 22.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Task 2 for people remaining at home. Write 'remain at home' or 'stay indoors'.

entry_json.definition: spend one or more nights in a hotel; British English uses 'in' or 'at' for hotels, and 'stay' rather than 'live', because the visit is temporary
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We stayed in a small hotel near the station for three nights.
example_sentences: Business travellers usually stay in hotels close to the airport.
It is often cheaper to rent a flat than to stay in a hotel for a week.

contexts.text: We stayed in a small hotel near the station for three nights.
It is often cheaper to rent a flat than to stay in a hotel for a week.

confusables.difference: 'Live' suggests a permanent home. For a holiday or a trip, English uses 'stay'.
minimal_pair: We stayed in a hotel for a week.
He lives in a hotel.

confusables.difference: 'At' focuses on the hotel as a location or a booking; 'in' focuses on being inside it. Both are correct.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'stay in hotel'. The article is needed: 'in a hotel' or 'in the hotel'.

entry_json.definition: remain in bed rather than getting up; 'bed' takes no article here, because the phrase is about the activity of sleeping or resting
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The doctor told him to stay in bed for two days and drink plenty of fluids.
example_sentences: At the weekend I stay in bed far longer than I should.
Children who stay in bed later at weekends often sleep badly on Sunday night.

contexts.text: The doctor told him to stay in bed for two days and drink plenty of fluids.
At the weekend I stay in bed far longer than I should.

confusables.difference: With 'the' it points at one particular piece of furniture, which is rarely the meaning you want.
minimal_pair: Stay in bed.
Don't sit on the bed.

confusables.difference: The British informal noun for staying in bed late by choice: 'I had a lie-in on Sunday.'

entry_json.avoid: Drop the article in the fixed phrases: 'in bed', 'to bed', 'out of bed'. Use 'the' only when you mean a specific bed as an object.

entry_json.definition: continue with something and not change to anything else; the thing you keep to follows 'to', and it is often a plan, a rule or a topic
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Candidates who stick to the question score better than those who write everything they know.
example_sentences: It is easier to stick to a budget when the bills are paid automatically.
The committee stuck to its original decision despite the objections.

contexts.text: Candidates who stick to the question score better than those who write everything they know.
It is easier to stick to a budget when the bills are paid automatically.

confusables.difference: Very close. 'Stick with' suggests staying loyal to a choice; 'stick to' suggests not deviating from a rule or a plan.
minimal_pair: Stick to the plan.
Stick with the same supplier.

confusables.difference: The literal sense with glue takes an object: 'Stick the label to the box.'
minimal_pair: Stick to the rules.
Stick the label to the box.

entry_json.avoid: Note the irregular past: stick, stuck, stuck. 'Sticked' is not a word.

entry_json.definition: likely to be affected by something, or depending on something before it can happen; it follows a noun or 'be', and belongs to formal written English
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The plan is subject to approval by the planning committee in October.
example_sentences: Coastal areas are subject to flooding during winter storms.
All prices are subject to change without notice.

contexts.text: The plan is subject to approval by the planning committee in October.
Coastal areas are subject to flooding during winter storms.

confusables.difference: The verb form, with '-ed', means to be forced to undergo something unpleasant: 'They were subjected to long interviews.'
minimal_pair: Prices are subject to change.
They were subjected to questioning.

confusables.difference: The plainer everyday alternative for the conditional sense: 'depending on approval'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'subject to' with 'subjected to'. The first is a condition, the second is something done to somebody.

entry_json.definition: manage to do something difficult; 'in' is followed by the -ing form, never by a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only a few countries have succeeded in cutting emissions while growing their economies.
example_sentences: She succeeded in persuading the committee to fund a second year.
The campaign succeeded in raising awareness but not in changing behaviour.

contexts.text: Only a few countries have succeeded in cutting emissions while growing their economies.
She succeeded in persuading the committee to fund a second year.

confusables.difference: Not English. The pattern is 'succeed in doing'.
minimal_pair: succeeded in reducing costs
succeeded to reduce costs

confusables.difference: 'Manage' takes the infinitive and is more common in speech: 'She managed to persuade them.'
minimal_pair: She managed to persuade them.
She succeeded in persuading them.

entry_json.avoid: The most common error with this verb is the infinitive. Always use 'in' plus -ing.

entry_json.definition: a model of the 'such a + adjective + noun' pattern used for emphasis; 'such' comes before the article, and the phrase often leads to a result clause with 'that'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving the market to the square was such a good idea that three other towns copied it.
example_sentences: It is such a good idea that I am surprised nobody tried it earlier.
Cycle hire was such a good idea for short journeys across the centre.

contexts.text: Moving the market to the square was such a good idea that three other towns copied it.
It is such a good idea that I am surprised nobody tried it earlier.

confusables.difference: Grammatically possible but very formal and rare. 'Such a good idea' is the natural form.
minimal_pair: such a good idea
so good an idea

confusables.difference: 'So' goes with an adjective alone: 'It was so good.' 'Such' goes with an adjective plus a noun: 'such a good idea'.
minimal_pair: It was so good.
It was such a good idea.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'a such good idea'. 'Such' always comes before the article.

entry_json.definition: the frame 'such + a/an + adjective + singular noun', used for emphasis and often followed by 'that' plus a result; drop the article with plural or uncountable nouns
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was such an expensive city that most graduates moved out within two years.
example_sentences: There was such a long queue that we gave up and went home.
Such heavy rain had not been recorded since 1954.

contexts.text: It was such an expensive city that most graduates moved out within two years.
There was such a long queue that we gave up and went home.

confusables.difference: 'So' takes a bare adjective: 'so expensive'. 'Such' takes an article and a noun: 'such an expensive city'.
minimal_pair: It was so expensive.
It was such an expensive city.

confusables.difference: With plurals and uncountables there is no article: 'such problems', 'such heavy rain'.
minimal_pair: such a problem
such problems

entry_json.avoid: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: 'such an important issue', not 'such a important issue'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce one or more examples of the group just named; it takes nouns, not clauses, and no comma is needed when the examples are essential
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Renewable sources such as wind and solar now supply almost a third of the country's electricity.
example_sentences: Subjects such as history and geography are being dropped by smaller schools.
Facilities such as libraries and sports halls are often the first to be cut.

contexts.text: Renewable sources such as wind and solar now supply almost a third of the country's electricity.
Subjects such as history and geography are being dropped by smaller schools.

confusables.difference: 'For example' can introduce a whole sentence and takes a comma: 'For example, wind power has grown.' 'Such as' attaches examples to a noun.
minimal_pair: sources such as wind
For example, wind power has grown.

confusables.difference: 'Like' does the same job in speech but is considered less formal in academic writing.
minimal_pair: subjects such as history
subjects like history

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a clause. 'Such as people use the bus' is wrong; write 'such as bus users'.

entry_json.definition: have an illness or a long-term problem; 'from' introduces the condition, and the phrase works for places and systems as well as people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Around one in six adults suffers from a long-term health condition.
example_sentences: The city suffers from severe congestion at both ends of the day.
She has suffered from asthma since childhood.
collocations: suffer from a lack of sth

contexts.text: Around one in six adults suffers from a long-term health condition.
The city suffers from severe congestion at both ends of the day.

confusables.difference: Without 'from' the object is a single event or a loss: 'The team suffered a defeat.'
minimal_pair: He suffers from back pain.
The team suffered a defeat.

confusables.difference: Heard in informal British speech, but 'suffer from' is the standard form for writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a temporary feeling. 'I suffer from tiredness today' is wrong; say 'I am tired today'.

entry_json.definition: state the main points of something briefly; separable, so the object can sit in the middle, and with a pronoun it must
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One sentence sums the whole argument up better than the three pages before it.
example_sentences: Could you sum the findings up in a paragraph for the front page?
That photograph sums it up: an empty high street on a Saturday afternoon.

contexts.text: Could you sum the findings up in a paragraph for the front page?
That photograph sums it up: an empty high street on a Saturday afternoon.

confusables.difference: Without an object the phrase stays together and often opens a conclusion: 'To sum up, the evidence is mixed.'
minimal_pair: To sum up, the evidence is mixed.
She summed the evidence up.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb, and the better choice in academic writing: 'The table summarises the results.'

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object must go in the middle: 'sum it up', never 'sum up it'.

entry_json.definition: give a short statement of the main points at the end; used without an object, especially in the fixed linker 'to sum up'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: To sum up, the benefits of the scheme fall to the city while the costs fall to the villages around it.
example_sentences: Before we finish, let me sum up the three main points.
To sum up, neither approach works on its own.

contexts.text: To sum up, the benefits of the scheme fall to the city while the costs fall to the villages around it.
Before we finish, let me sum up the three main points.

confusables.difference: Both close an essay. 'In conclusion' is the more formal of the two and is the safer choice in Task 2.
minimal_pair: To sum up, ...
In conclusion, ...

confusables.difference: With an object the phrase splits: 'sum the argument up'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add new arguments after it. A summary that introduces fresh material confuses the reader and weakens the conclusion.

entry_json.definition: certain to happen or to do something, in the speaker's judgement; it follows 'be' and takes a to-infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Anyone who leaves revision to the last week is sure to run out of time.
example_sentences: Prices are sure to rise once the subsidy ends.
Be sure to keep a copy of the receipt.

contexts.text: Anyone who leaves revision to the last week is sure to run out of time.
Be sure to keep a copy of the receipt.

confusables.difference: 'Sure of' plus a noun is about your own confidence: 'I am sure of the answer.' 'Sure to' plus a verb predicts an event.
minimal_pair: I am sure of the answer.
It is sure to happen.

confusables.difference: Stronger, and often used for something unwelcome: 'Delays are bound to happen.'

entry_json.avoid: It expresses your prediction, not proof. In Task 2 prefer 'is likely to' unless you can support the certainty.

entry_json.definition: a large structure filled with water for swimming; a compound noun in which 'swimming' works as a modifier
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The town's only swimming pool closed for repairs and never reopened.
example_sentences: Many hotels advertise a swimming pool that turns out to be the size of a bath.
There is an outdoor swimming pool that opens for six weeks in summer.

contexts.text: The town's only swimming pool closed for repairs and never reopened.
Many hotels advertise a swimming pool that turns out to be the size of a bath.

confusables.difference: Once the context is clear, 'pool' alone is natural: 'I go to the pool twice a week.'
minimal_pair: a swimming pool
the pool

confusables.difference: An older British term, still seen on Victorian buildings, but 'swimming pool' is the modern word.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'swimming' as the modifier: 'a swimming pool', not 'a swim pool' or 'a pool of swimming'.

entry_json.definition: make good use of an opportunity, or, with a person as object, treat somebody unfairly for your own benefit; the meaning depends on what follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Few students take advantage of the free language support the university offers.
example_sentences: We took advantage of the cheap fares and booked six months early.
Employers who take advantage of workers with no contract are rarely prosecuted.

contexts.text: Few students take advantage of the free language support the university offers.
We took advantage of the cheap fares and booked six months early.
Employers who take advantage of workers with no contract are rarely prosecuted.

confusables.difference: Only the positive meaning, with no risk of sounding like exploitation.
minimal_pair: Take advantage of the offer.
Make the most of the offer.

confusables.difference: With a person the meaning turns negative: exploiting them. Be careful which one you mean.
minimal_pair: She took advantage of the discount.
He took advantage of his staff.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of'. 'Take advantage the offer' is wrong, and 'take an advantage of' is not English either.

entry_json.definition: look after somebody or something, or deal with a task; the person or job follows 'of', and the phrase does not split
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Somebody has to take care of elderly relatives, and it usually falls to one member of the family.
example_sentences: I will take care of the booking if you sort out the tickets.
Take care of yourself during exam season; sleep matters more than one extra hour of revision.

contexts.text: Somebody has to take care of elderly relatives, and it usually falls to one member of the family.
I will take care of the booking if you sort out the tickets.

confusables.difference: The everyday British equivalent for people and possessions. 'Take care of' also covers tasks: 'take care of the paperwork'.
minimal_pair: She looks after her mother.
She takes care of the paperwork.

confusables.difference: 'Care about' is emotional concern; 'take care of' is practical responsibility.
minimal_pair: I care about the environment.
I take care of the garden.

entry_json.avoid: The phrase never splits. 'Take him care of' is wrong; write 'take care of him'.

entry_json.definition: leave the ground at the start of a flight, or, figuratively, suddenly become successful; used without an object in both senses
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The plane took off nearly two hours late because of a technical problem.
example_sentences: Online grocery shopping really took off during the pandemic.
We were told to fasten our seatbelts ten minutes before the aircraft took off.

contexts.text: The plane took off nearly two hours late because of a technical problem.
Online grocery shopping really took off during the pandemic.

confusables.difference: With an object it means to remove: 'take your coat off'. Without an object it is about aircraft or sudden success.
minimal_pair: The plane took off.
He took his coat off.

confusables.difference: The opposite for aircraft: 'The plane landed at six.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an object to this sense. 'The pilot took off the plane' means something else entirely.

entry_json.definition: gain control of something, or begin doing a job somebody else was doing; it works with or without an object
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A larger firm took over the company and closed two of its three factories.
example_sentences: When the manager left, her deputy took over.
Machines have taken over many of the routine tasks in warehouses.

contexts.text: A larger firm took over the company and closed two of its three factories.
Machines have taken over many of the routine tasks in warehouses.

confusables.difference: One word as a noun: 'a hostile takeover'. Two words as the verb.
minimal_pair: They took over the firm.
It was a hostile takeover.

confusables.difference: Add 'from' to name the person you replace: 'She took over from the previous head.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for simply buying something small. 'Take over' implies control of an organisation or a role.

entry_json.definition: start doing a job or a role that another person was doing; the person being replaced follows 'from'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She took over from the previous head of department halfway through the year.
example_sentences: Electric buses are gradually taking over from diesel ones on city routes.
Who will take over from him when he retires?

contexts.text: She took over from the previous head of department halfway through the year.
Electric buses are gradually taking over from diesel ones on city routes.

confusables.difference: With a direct object it means to gain control of a thing: 'take over the company'. With 'from' it means to succeed a person.
minimal_pair: They took over the company.
She took over from the manager.

confusables.difference: 'Replace' is the single formal verb: 'She replaced the previous head.' 'Take over from' focuses on continuing the work.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'take over of'. The preposition is 'from' for the person, and nothing at all for the thing.

entry_json.definition: be one of the people doing an activity; there is no article before 'part', and it takes no object without 'in'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Over four hundred people took part, which was double the number expected.
example_sentences: Only a third of those invited actually took part.
I would like to take part, but the sessions clash with my classes.

contexts.text: Over four hundred people took part, which was double the number expected.
I would like to take part, but the sessions clash with my classes.

confusables.difference: A completely different phrase. 'Take part' means to join in; 'take place' means to happen.
minimal_pair: Four hundred people took part.
The event took place in June.

confusables.difference: Add 'in' plus a noun to name the activity: 'take part in the study'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an article: 'take part', not 'take a part'. 'Take a part' suggests acting a role in a play.

entry_json.definition: join in an activity or event with other people; the activity follows 'in', and the phrase does not split
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who take part in sport report lower levels of stress during exam terms.
example_sentences: Around two thousand people took part in the survey.
She took part in a debate on the future of the town centre.
collocations: take an active part in sth

contexts.text: Students who take part in sport report lower levels of stress during exam terms.
Around two thousand people took part in the survey.
I took part in a language exchange last summer.

confusables.difference: The formal equivalent. 'Take part in' is fine everywhere; 'participate in' suits Task 2 better.
minimal_pair: take part in the study
participate in the study

confusables.difference: 'Attend' only means being present; 'take part in' means actively joining in.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'take part of'. 'Take part of' means to take a portion of something, which is a different meaning.

entry_json.definition: happen, especially of an arranged event; it never takes an object and it has no passive form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The ceremony takes place in the main hall on the last Friday of term.
example_sentences: The changes described in the diagram took place over about forty years.
Negotiations are taking place behind closed doors.

contexts.text: The changes described in the diagram took place over about forty years.
The ceremony takes place in the main hall on the last Friday of term.

confusables.difference: 'Be held' is passive and needs an organiser behind it: 'The meeting was held in June.' 'Take place' is active and neutral.
minimal_pair: The meeting was held in June.
The meeting took place in June.

confusables.difference: 'Happen' suits accidents and unplanned events; 'take place' suits arranged ones.
minimal_pair: An accident happened.
The wedding took place.

entry_json.avoid: It has no passive. 'The event was taken place' is wrong; write 'The event took place'.

entry_json.definition: employ somebody, or accept a job or a responsibility; separable, with a pronoun going in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The firm took on twelve apprentices, more than it had for a decade.
example_sentences: I took on too much work last term and my marks suffered.
She has taken on the role of course representative.

contexts.text: The firm took on twelve apprentices, more than it had for a decade.
I took on too much work last term and my marks suffered.

confusables.difference: 'Take up' means to start a new activity or hobby. 'Take on' means to accept a burden or hire somebody.
minimal_pair: She took up running.
She took on extra work.

confusables.difference: The formal single verb: 'The firm employs 300 people.' 'Take on' focuses on the moment of hiring.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object must split the phrase: 'take them on', never 'take on them'.

entry_json.definition: consider something when making a decision or a judgement; the object usually sits in the middle, though a long object can follow 'account'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Any comparison of the two cities must take the difference in population into account.
example_sentences: The figures do not take inflation into account.
Planners took into account the number of vehicles expected in twenty years' time.

contexts.text: Any comparison of the two cities must take the difference in population into account.
The figures do not take inflation into account.

confusables.difference: A shorter formal variant with the same meaning: 'The report takes account of new data.'
minimal_pair: take the cost into account
take account of the cost

confusables.difference: Slightly less formal and more about remembering than about calculating.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'take in account' or 'take into consideration of'. The two correct forms are 'take X into account' and 'take account of X'.

entry_json.definition: remove a piece of clothing or something attached, or subtract an amount; separable, and a pronoun must go in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please take your shoes off before you go into the hall.
example_sentences: She took off her coat and hung it by the door.
The shop took ten per cent off the marked price.

contexts.text: Please take your shoes off before you go into the hall.
The shop took ten per cent off the marked price.

confusables.difference: The opposite for clothing: 'put your coat on', 'take your coat off'.
minimal_pair: Put your coat on.
Take your coat off.

confusables.difference: Without an object it is about aircraft leaving the ground or about sudden success.
minimal_pair: He took his coat off.
The plane took off.

entry_json.avoid: A pronoun object always splits the phrase: 'take it off', never 'take off it'.

entry_json.definition: start a new activity or hobby, or occupy space or time; separable, and with a pronoun the object goes in the middle
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I took photography up during a long winter and it became a serious hobby.
example_sentences: The sofa takes too much space up in a room this size.
She took up running after her doctor suggested more exercise.

contexts.text: I took photography up during a long winter and it became a serious hobby.
The sofa takes too much space up in a room this size.

confusables.difference: With a full noun object either order works. With a pronoun only the split version is possible.
minimal_pair: take up photography
take it up

confusables.difference: 'Take on' is about accepting work or responsibility; 'take up' is about starting a hobby or filling space.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'take up it'. Pronouns sit between the verb and 'up'.

entry_json.definition: start playing golf as a new hobby; a model of the pattern 'take up + activity', where the activity takes no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My father took up golf when he retired and now plays three times a week.
example_sentences: She took up golf at university because the club had free lessons.
People often take up golf later in life, when other sports become harder.

contexts.text: My father took up golf when he retired and now plays three times a week.
People often take up golf later in life, when other sports become harder.

confusables.difference: 'Play golf' describes what you do; 'take up golf' describes starting the hobby for the first time.
minimal_pair: He plays golf.
He took up golf last year.

confusables.difference: The opposite: stopping an activity you used to do.

entry_json.avoid: Sports and activities take no article after 'take up': 'take up golf', not 'take up the golf'.

entry_json.definition: the unsplit order of the same phrasal verb, used when the object is a full noun rather than a pronoun; it means to start an activity or to occupy space or time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Older people who take up a new skill report better memory and mood.
example_sentences: Storage takes up almost a quarter of the floor space in the building.
He decided to take up a language after twenty years away from study.

contexts.text: Older people who take up a new skill report better memory and mood.
Storage takes up almost a quarter of the floor space in the building.

confusables.difference: The split order, compulsory with pronouns: 'take it up'.
minimal_pair: take up the offer
take it up

confusables.difference: The formal single verb for the space sense: 'Storage occupies a quarter of the floor space.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use this unsplit order with a pronoun. 'Take up it' is always wrong.

entry_json.definition: occupy more space than is reasonable; 'room' here is uncountable and means space, so it takes no article
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The old desk takes up too much room in a bedroom this small.
example_sentences: Bins on the pavement take up too much room for wheelchairs to pass.
I got rid of the printer because it took up too much room.

contexts.text: The old desk takes up too much room in a bedroom this small.
Bins on the pavement take up too much room for wheelchairs to pass.

confusables.difference: Countable 'a room' is a part of a building. Uncountable 'room' means space, and takes no article.
minimal_pair: There is no room left.
There is a room free.

confusables.difference: 'Space' is the neutral word and works in writing; 'room' in this sense is more conversational.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'take up too many rooms' when you mean space. With this meaning 'room' has no plural.

entry_json.definition: discuss somebody or something in conversation; the topic follows 'about', and the phrase does not split
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nobody in my family talked about money when I was growing up.
example_sentences: The article talks about the effect of screen time on sleep.
We talked about the plan for an hour and decided nothing.

contexts.text: Nobody in my family talked about money when I was growing up.
The article talks about the effect of screen time on sleep.

confusables.difference: 'Discuss' takes a direct object with no preposition: 'discuss the problem'. Adding 'about' is a very common error.
minimal_pair: We discussed the problem.
We talked about the problem.

confusables.difference: 'To' names the person you speak with; 'about' names the topic. Both can appear: 'talk to my tutor about the deadline'.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'discuss about'. If you want 'about', the verb must be 'talk' or 'speak'.

entry_json.definition: have a conversation by telephone; the article before 'phone' is kept, and the person you speak to follows 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother would rather talk on the phone than send a message.
example_sentences: We talked on the phone for an hour, which we had not done in years.
Talking on the phone while driving is illegal in most countries.
collocations: talk on the phone to sb

contexts.text: My grandmother would rather talk on the phone than send a message.
Talking on the phone while driving is illegal in most countries.

confusables.difference: 'By phone' names the method in a formal notice: 'Bookings can be made by phone.' 'On the phone' describes the conversation itself.
minimal_pair: Talk to her on the phone.
Bookings can be made by phone.

confusables.difference: Wrong preposition. It is 'on the phone'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'on the phone', not 'on phone'.

entry_json.definition: say what is true; 'the' is fixed here, and 'to tell the truth' also works as a phrase meaning 'to be honest'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children are more likely to tell the truth when they are not afraid of the punishment.
example_sentences: To tell the truth, I found the second task easier than the first.
He did not tell the truth about how long the work would take.

contexts.text: Children are more likely to tell the truth when they are not afraid of the punishment.
To tell the truth, I found the second task easier than the first.

confusables.difference: Not English. The verb is 'tell': 'tell the truth', 'tell a lie', 'tell a story'.
minimal_pair: tell the truth
say the truth

confusables.difference: Possible but literary or dramatic. 'Tell the truth' is the everyday phrase.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article. 'Tell truth' is wrong; it is always 'tell the truth'.

entry_json.definition: usually be a particular way, without being so in every case; a hedge that protects a general claim from being disproved by one exception
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities with good public transport tend to be less polluted than those built around the car.
example_sentences: Older houses tend to be more expensive to heat.
Candidates who read the question twice tend to be more accurate.
collocations: have a tendency to do sth

contexts.text: Cities with good public transport tend to be less polluted than those built around the car.
Older houses tend to be more expensive to heat.

confusables.difference: Almost the same, though 'tend to be' sounds more careful and more academic in an essay.
minimal_pair: They are usually cheaper.
They tend to be cheaper.

confusables.difference: Same structure with an action verb: 'tend to rise', 'tend to leave'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a second hedge. 'Tend to usually be' is redundant; one hedge is enough.

entry_json.definition: do something regularly or usually; it takes a to-infinitive and is the most useful hedging verb in Task 2
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Younger workers tend to change jobs more often than their parents did.
example_sentences: Prices tend to rise in the weeks before a holiday.
People tend to underestimate how long a piece of writing will take.

contexts.text: Younger workers tend to change jobs more often than their parents did.
Prices tend to rise in the weeks before a holiday.
I tend to study better in the morning.

confusables.difference: With 'towards' plus a noun it means to move in a direction: 'The figures tend towards a plateau.'
minimal_pair: Prices tend to rise.
The line tends towards a plateau.

confusables.difference: 'Used to' is a past habit that has stopped. 'Tend to' is a present tendency.
minimal_pair: I used to walk to work.
I tend to walk to work.

entry_json.avoid: The negative is 'tend not to do sth', which is more natural than 'do not tend to do sth' in writing.

entry_json.definition: the standard way of expressing gratitude; two words as a phrase, hyphenated only when it works as a noun, as in 'a thank-you note'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thank you for taking the time to look at my application.
example_sentences: Thank you, that is exactly what I needed.
I would like to say thank you to everyone who helped with the move.

contexts.text: Thank you for taking the time to look at my application.
Thank you, that is exactly what I needed.

confusables.difference: 'Thanks' is the informal short form, fine with friends and colleagues, weaker in a formal letter.
minimal_pair: Thanks!
Thank you very much indeed.

confusables.difference: After 'for' use the -ing form: 'thank you for helping', not 'thank you for help me'.
minimal_pair: Thank you for helping.
Thank you for your help.

entry_json.avoid: In a formal letter do not end with just 'thanks'. Write 'Thank you for your time' followed by 'Yours sincerely'.

entry_json.definition: a stronger, more formal expression of thanks; 'very much' comes at the end, never between 'thank' and 'you'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thank you very much for arranging the extension at such short notice.
example_sentences: Thank you very much indeed for all your help this term.
'Here's your change.' 'Thank you very much.'

contexts.text: Thank you very much for arranging the extension at such short notice.
'Here's your change.' 'Thank you very much.'

confusables.difference: Warmer and more personal; 'very much' is slightly more formal and more common in writing.
minimal_pair: Thank you so much!
Thank you very much.

confusables.difference: A brief, semi-formal ending for an email, less formal than 'thank you very much'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not split it: 'Thank you very much', never 'Thank very much you'.

entry_json.definition: because of somebody or something, when the result is good; using it for a bad result sounds sarcastic
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thanks to the new cycle lanes, journeys across the centre are faster than by car.
example_sentences: Thanks to a scholarship, she was able to finish the degree.
The harvest was saved thanks to two weeks of unexpected rain.

contexts.text: Thanks to the new cycle lanes, journeys across the centre are faster than by car.
Thanks to a scholarship, she was able to finish the degree.

confusables.difference: Neutral about whether the result is good or bad. 'Thanks to' implies gratitude.
minimal_pair: Thanks to the rain, the crops survived.
Because of the rain, the match was cancelled.

confusables.difference: Formal, and traditionally follows a noun or 'be': 'The delay was due to snow.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a bad outcome unless you intend sarcasm. 'Thanks to the strike, I missed my exam' reads as bitter, not neutral.

entry_json.definition: on the particular day already mentioned; it is the reported-speech version of 'today', and it takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The letter arrived on a Friday, and that day everything changed.
example_sentences: She said she would call, but no call came that day.
We had planned to walk, but it rained all that day.

contexts.text: She said she would call, but no call came that day.
We had planned to walk, but it rained all that day.

confusables.difference: 'Today' is the day you are speaking. 'That day' is a day in the story you are telling.
minimal_pair: I'm busy today.
He was busy that day.

confusables.difference: Adding 'on' is possible for emphasis, but the bare form is more usual: 'that day'.

entry_json.avoid: In reported speech, 'today' becomes 'that day': 'He said he was leaving that day', not 'leaving today'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce a clearer or more exact restatement of what you have just said; it is followed by a comma in careful writing and often abbreviated to 'i.e.'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The survey covered only adults of working age, that is, those between 18 and 65.
example_sentences: Attendance rose in the second half, that is, after the fee was removed.
The results apply to one city only, that is, they cannot be generalised.

contexts.text: The survey covered only adults of working age, that is, those between 18 and 65.
Attendance rose in the second half, that is, after the fee was removed.

confusables.difference: The longer version, identical in meaning and slightly more formal.
minimal_pair: that is, adults over 18
that is to say, adults over 18

confusables.difference: 'For example' gives one case out of many; 'that is' restates the whole thing more precisely.
minimal_pair: fruit, for example apples
citrus fruit, that is, oranges and lemons

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to introduce an example. 'That is' means the same thing said again; 'for example' means one of several.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is finished, that nothing more will follow, or that somebody has got something right
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That's it, we've covered everything on the list.
example_sentences: 'So you turn left at the lights?' 'That's it, then straight on.'
One more paragraph and that's it, the essay is done.

contexts.text: That's it, we've covered everything on the list.
'So you turn left at the lights?' 'That's it, then straight on.'

confusables.difference: 'That's all' means nothing more remains. 'That's it' can also mean 'exactly right'.
minimal_pair: That's all, thank you.
That's it, you've got it.

confusables.difference: The full form is rare in speech and sounds emphatic or annoyed: 'That is it, I'm leaving.'

entry_json.avoid: Never use it in writing. In an essay conclusion write 'In conclusion' or 'To sum up'.

entry_json.definition: the years from 1801 to 1900; centuries take 'the' and an ordinal number, and the preposition before them is 'in'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of the terraced housing in the city was built in the 19th century.
example_sentences: Railways transformed travel in the 19th century more than any invention since.
The population of London tripled during the 19th century.

contexts.text: Most of the terraced housing in the city was built in the 19th century.
Railways transformed travel in the 19th century more than any invention since.

confusables.difference: The article is compulsory: 'in the 19th century', never 'in 19th century'.
minimal_pair: in the 19th century
in 19th century

confusables.difference: Used before a noun it is hyphenated and drops 'the': '19th-century architecture'.
minimal_pair: built in the 19th century
19th-century architecture

entry_json.avoid: Remember the century number is one higher than the years: the 19th century means the 1800s.

entry_json.definition: the years from 1901 to 2000; used with 'in' for the period and with 'of' after 'the first half'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Life expectancy rose by more than thirty years over the course of the 20th century.
example_sentences: Two world wars shaped the first half of the 20th century.
Car ownership became normal in the second half of the 20th century.

contexts.text: Life expectancy rose by more than thirty years over the course of the 20th century.
Car ownership became normal in the second half of the 20th century.

confusables.difference: 'The 1900s' usually means the decade 1900 to 1909, so it is not a safe substitute for the century.
minimal_pair: in the 20th century
in the 1900s

confusables.difference: 'Last century' is relative to now and can confuse a reader in a hundred years. Name the century in academic writing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article. It is 'in the 20th century', never 'in 20th century'.

entry_json.definition: the years from 2001 to 2100; the ordinal is 'twenty-first', and the phrase takes 'in' or 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main environmental challenge of the 21st century is not producing energy but storing it.
example_sentences: Skills that mattered in the 20th century are not always the skills of the 21st century.
Cities in the 21st century are growing faster than at any point in history.

contexts.text: The main environmental challenge of the 21st century is not producing energy but storing it.
Cities in the 21st century are growing faster than at any point in history.

confusables.difference: The article is required: 'in the 21st century'.
minimal_pair: in the 21st century
in 21st century

confusables.difference: Shorter and clear in speech, but 'the 21st century' is precise and better in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Write the ordinal correctly: 21st, not 21th. The pattern is 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 21st, 22nd, 23rd.

entry_json.definition: the disadvantages of something; the topic follows 'about', and this is the plain spoken version of 'the drawbacks'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the bad things about living in the centre is that nothing is ever quiet.
example_sentences: The bad things about working from home only appeared after a few months.
There are good things and bad things about studying in a second language.

contexts.text: One of the bad things about living in the centre is that nothing is ever quiet.
The bad things about working from home only appeared after a few months.

confusables.difference: The formal written equivalent, and the one Task 2 wants: 'the drawbacks of remote working'.
minimal_pair: the bad things about it
the drawbacks of it

confusables.difference: Note the preposition changes: 'things about', but 'disadvantages of'.
minimal_pair: the bad things about cars
the disadvantages of cars

entry_json.avoid: Keep it out of Task 2. Examiners reward 'drawbacks', 'disadvantages' or 'negative consequences' over 'bad things'.

entry_json.definition: the most enjoyable or most useful aspect of something; often followed by 'about' plus the topic, or by a relative clause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The best thing about the course was meeting people from other departments.
example_sentences: The best thing I ever bought was a second-hand bicycle.
For me the best thing is being able to walk to work.

contexts.text: The best thing about the course was meeting people from other departments.
For me the best thing is being able to walk to work.

confusables.difference: Adding 'to do' turns it into advice about action: 'The best thing to do is wait.'
minimal_pair: The best thing is the location.
The best thing to do is wait.

confusables.difference: The formal written version for Task 2.

entry_json.avoid: It takes 'about', not 'of': 'the best thing about the course', never 'the best thing of the course'.

entry_json.definition: the most sensible course of action; it is usually followed by 'is' plus a bare infinitive, without 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The best thing to do is book the ticket early and accept that plans might change.
example_sentences: When you cannot answer a question, the best thing to do is move on and come back.
The best thing to do would be to speak to your tutor directly.
collocations: the best thing to do is...

contexts.text: When you cannot answer a question, the best thing to do is move on and come back.
The best thing to do would be to speak to your tutor directly.

confusables.difference: Without 'to do' it names a feature, not an action.
minimal_pair: The best thing is the price.
The best thing to do is wait.

confusables.term: it is best to do sth
confusables.difference: The tighter written form: 'It is best to book early.'

entry_json.avoid: After 'is', the bare infinitive is normal: 'the best thing to do is book', not 'is to book' in speech, though both are accepted.

entry_json.definition: a superlative frame: 'the best' plus a noun, then 'in' plus the area compared; superlatives take 'in' with places, not 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The library is said to be the best collection of maps in the country.
example_sentences: It is the best hospital in the country for that particular operation.
She was the best player in the league that season.

contexts.text: It is the best hospital in the country for that particular operation.
She was the best player in the league that season.

confusables.difference: Superlatives take 'in' with places and groups: 'the best in the world', 'the tallest in the class'.
minimal_pair: the best in the country
the best of the country

confusables.difference: Safer than a bare superlative, because it is much harder to disprove.
minimal_pair: the best hospital in the country
one of the best hospitals in the country

entry_json.avoid: A bare superlative is a strong claim. In Task 2 hedge it: 'one of the best' or 'among the best'.

entry_json.definition: the true situation; used in fixed patterns such as 'this is the case', 'if that is the case' and 'as is the case with'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This is often the case in cities where housing has been treated as an investment.
example_sentences: If that is the case, the figures in the second table must be wrong.
As is the case with most surveys, the response rate was low.
collocations: as is the case with sth

contexts.text: This is often the case in cities where housing has been treated as an investment.
As is the case with most surveys, the response rate was low.
If that's the case, I'd rather take the train.

confusables.difference: A completely different phrase meaning as a precaution: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains.'
minimal_pair: If that is the case, we should act.
Take a coat in case it rains.

confusables.difference: Means 'anyway' and introduces a further point: 'In any case, the deadline has passed.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse 'if that is the case' with 'in case'. The first refers back to a fact, the second prepares for a possibility.

entry_json.definition: how far or how much something is true; a formal frame taking a full clause after 'which', and often the opening of a Task 2 response
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The essay examines the extent to which car use can be reduced without new taxes.
example_sentences: Opinion differs on the extent to which schools should teach values.
The extent to which the results can be generalised is unclear.

contexts.text: The essay examines the extent to which car use can be reduced without new taxes.
The extent to which the results can be generalised is unclear.

confusables.difference: The question form, which is how many Task 2 prompts are written: 'To what extent do you agree?'
minimal_pair: To what extent do you agree?
the extent to which I agree

confusables.difference: The plain everyday version. 'The extent to which' is the academic register.

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with a full clause, not a noun: 'the extent to which prices rose', not 'the extent to which of prices'.

entry_json.definition: used to turn a whole clause into a noun phrase so it can be the subject or object of a sentence; the clause after 'that' keeps its normal word order
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fact that the scheme was never evaluated makes it impossible to judge.
example_sentences: Nobody disputes the fact that the population is ageing.
The fact that she had no formal training did not stop her.

contexts.text: The fact that the scheme was never evaluated makes it impossible to judge.
Nobody disputes the fact that the population is ageing.

confusables.difference: A long way of saying 'because'. Examiners see it constantly; the shorter word is usually better.
minimal_pair: due to the fact that it rained
because it rained

confusables.difference: The correct way to follow 'despite' with a clause, since 'despite' itself needs a noun.
minimal_pair: despite the rain
despite the fact that it rained

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it just to add words. 'Due to the fact that' should almost always be 'because'.

entry_json.definition: the thing that comes before all others in time or importance; often followed by a relative clause with no relative pronoun
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first thing you notice about the city is how quiet the centre is.
example_sentences: The first thing to check is whether the form has been signed.
The first thing I look for in a flat is natural light.

contexts.text: The first thing you notice about the city is how quiet the centre is.
The first thing to check is whether the form has been signed.

confusables.difference: 'First of all' is a linker opening a list of points. 'The first thing' is a noun phrase and needs a verb after it.
minimal_pair: First of all, consider the cost.
The first thing to consider is the cost.

confusables.difference: 'At first' means in the beginning, before things changed: 'At first I found it hard.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it as a linker on its own. 'The first thing, the cost is high' is not a sentence; you need 'is'.

entry_json.definition: a narrative opener naming your first action in a story; the relative pronoun is left out, and 'was' is followed by a bare infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first thing I did when I arrived was find somewhere to live.
example_sentences: The first thing I did after the exam was sleep for ten hours.
The first thing I did was call my parents to tell them the news.
collocations: the first thing I did was...

contexts.text: The first thing I did when I arrived was find somewhere to live.
The first thing I did after the exam was sleep for ten hours.

confusables.term: the first thing I did was to...
confusables.difference: Both 'was find' and 'was to find' are correct. The bare infinitive is more natural in speech.
minimal_pair: The first thing I did was find a flat.
The first thing I did was to find a flat.

confusables.difference: 'Firstly' organises an argument; 'the first thing I did' tells a story. Part 2 needs the second.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the past tense throughout: 'The first thing I did was call', not 'was to calling' or 'was called'.

entry_json.definition: used to mark an event that has never happened before; usually preceded by 'for' and paired with the present perfect
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For the first time in history, more people live in cities than in the countryside.
example_sentences: For the first time in history, the majority of new cars sold were electric.
It was the first time in history that the tournament had been cancelled.
collocations: for the first time in history

contexts.text: For the first time in history, more people live in cities than in the countryside.
For the first time in history, the majority of new cars sold were electric.

confusables.difference: Without 'in history' the claim is much smaller and safer: 'for the first time since 2010'.
minimal_pair: for the first time in history
for the first time since 2010

confusables.difference: The single formal adjective: 'an unprecedented rise'. Useful when you want the idea without the long phrase.

entry_json.avoid: It is a very strong claim. Use it only where you are sure; otherwise write 'for the first time in decades'.

entry_json.definition: the day after the one being described; the written narrative equivalent of 'tomorrow' in reported speech
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The storm passed overnight and the following day the roads were clear again.
example_sentences: She submitted the application on Monday and heard back the following day.
The results were published the following day.

contexts.text: The storm passed overnight and the following day the roads were clear again.
She submitted the application on Monday and heard back the following day.

confusables.difference: Almost identical. 'The following day' is slightly more formal and more common in written narrative.
minimal_pair: the next day
the following day

confusables.difference: 'Tomorrow' is relative to now. In a story about the past, use 'the following day'.
minimal_pair: I'll go tomorrow.
He went the following day.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix 'tomorrow' into a past narrative. Once you are in the past, it must be 'the following day'.

entry_json.definition: used before a noun to introduce a list or an item that comes next in the text; it can also stand alone before a colon
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The following factors were considered: cost, location and travel time.
example_sentences: Applicants must provide the following documents before the interview.
The following table shows the results for each of the four cities.

contexts.text: The following factors were considered: cost, location and travel time.
Applicants must provide the following documents before the interview.

confusables.difference: 'As follows' comes after the verb and before a colon: 'The reasons are as follows:'. 'The following' comes before a noun.
minimal_pair: The following reasons apply:
The reasons are as follows:

confusables.difference: The time meaning, about the next day, is a separate use of the same word.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'the followings'. 'Following' is an adjective here and never takes a plural s.

entry_json.definition: the advantages of something; the topic follows 'about', and this is the everyday spoken version of 'the benefits'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of the good things about a small town is that you know your neighbours.
example_sentences: The good things about the job outweigh the long hours.
There are good things about both systems.

contexts.text: One of the good things about a small town is that you know your neighbours.
The good things about the job outweigh the long hours.

confusables.difference: The written equivalent, and note the preposition changes to 'of': 'the benefits of exercise'.
minimal_pair: the good things about exercise
the benefits of exercise

confusables.difference: Also takes 'of'. This is the phrase Task 2 questions themselves use.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 2 write 'the benefits' or 'the advantages'. 'Good things' reads as A2 vocabulary in a B2 essay.

entry_json.definition: the aspect that matters most; usually followed by 'is' plus a clause or an infinitive, and used to focus attention
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The important thing is that the data was collected the same way in both years.
example_sentences: The important thing is not to panic when you cannot hear a word.
The important thing about the diagram is the direction of the arrows.

contexts.text: The important thing is that the data was collected the same way in both years.
The important thing is not to panic when you cannot hear a word.

confusables.difference: The superlative claims there is only one. 'The important thing' is softer and easier to defend.
minimal_pair: The important thing is preparation.
The most important thing is preparation.

confusables.difference: A neater cleft alternative that shows more range: 'What matters is consistency.'

entry_json.avoid: Follow it with 'is'. 'The important thing, preparation' is not a sentence.

entry_json.definition: the most recent occasion; it introduces a clause with no preposition and normally takes the past simple
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The last time I took a test like this I ran out of time on the final section.
example_sentences: The last time the river flooded was in 2007.
When was the last time you read a book for pleasure?

contexts.text: The last time the river flooded was in 2007.
When was the last time you read a book for pleasure?

confusables.difference: Without 'the' it works as an adverb: 'Last time I was late.' With 'the' it is a noun phrase: 'the last time I was late'.
minimal_pair: Last time I was late.
The last time I was late was in March.

confusables.difference: A separate phrase meaning finally, after a long wait.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a preposition: 'the last time I went', not 'in the last time I went'.

entry_json.definition: the single thing that matters more than all others; a superlative frame followed by 'is' plus a clause or an infinitive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most important thing in the writing paper is answering the question that was actually asked.
example_sentences: For most families the most important thing is a school within walking distance.
The most important thing to remember is that the graph shows percentages, not totals.

contexts.text: The most important thing in the writing paper is answering the question that was actually asked.
For most families the most important thing is a school within walking distance.

confusables.difference: Without 'most' the claim is softer and safer.
minimal_pair: The important thing is cost.
The most important thing is cost.

confusables.difference: A tighter linker with the same emphasis: 'Above all, the essay must answer the question.'

entry_json.avoid: Use it once at most in an essay. Two things cannot both be the most important, and a marker will notice.

entry_json.definition: the day after the one in the story; used in past narrative, and it takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We arrived late at night and the next day walked the whole length of the old town.
example_sentences: He promised to send the file and it arrived the next day.
The next day everything looked more manageable.

contexts.text: We arrived late at night and the next day walked the whole length of the old town.
He promised to send the file and it arrived the next day.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' it appears mainly in fixed phrases like 'next-day delivery'.
minimal_pair: It arrived the next day.
next-day delivery

confusables.difference: 'Tomorrow' looks forward from now; 'the next day' looks forward from a point in the past.
minimal_pair: I'll call tomorrow.
He called the next day.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'tomorrow' inside a past-tense story. Once the narrative is in the past, use 'the next day'.

entry_json.definition: the opposite side of a named thing, or, figuratively, the opposing view; the noun follows 'of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The industrial estate is on the other side of the railway from the housing.
example_sentences: There is a footbridge to the other side of the motorway.
It is worth hearing the other side of the argument before deciding.
collocations: the other side of the road
the other side of the argument

contexts.text: The industrial estate is on the other side of the railway from the housing.
It is worth hearing the other side of the argument before deciding.

confusables.difference: Almost identical and slightly more formal, useful in Task 1 map descriptions.
minimal_pair: the other side of the road
the opposite side of the road

confusables.difference: The linker for contrasting ideas. 'The other side of the argument' is a noun phrase; 'on the other hand' is a connector.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before the noun: 'the other side of the road', not 'the other side the road'.

lemma: the other side of the world

entry_json.headword: the other side of the world
entry_json.ipa: ði ˌʌðə saɪd əv ðə ˈwɜːld
entry_json.definition: a place very far away, often another continent; used loosely rather than geographically, and usually with 'on' or 'to'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My sister lives on the other side of the world and we speak more now than when she lived here.
example_sentences: Fruit is flown from the other side of the world so that it can be sold out of season.
Moving to the other side of the world at nineteen was harder than I expected.
collocations: on the other side of the world
from the other side of the world

chunk.pattern: the other side of the world

contexts.text: Fruit is flown from the other side of the world so that it can be sold out of season.
contexts.gap_span: the other side of the world

contexts.text: My sister lives on the other side of the world and we speak more now than when she lived here.
contexts.gap_span: the other side of the world

confusables.difference: 'Abroad' just means another country. 'The other side of the world' stresses enormous distance.
minimal_pair: She works abroad.
She works on the other side of the world.

confusables.difference: The neutral formal word, better in Task 2: 'overseas suppliers'.

entry_json.avoid: It is figurative, so avoid it in Task 1 where you should give the actual region or country.

entry_json.definition: the part that remains; the verb agrees with what follows 'of', so 'the rest of the group are' but 'the rest of the money is'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first section takes half the time; the rest of the paper has to fit into what is left.
example_sentences: The rest of the students had already gone home.
I spent the rest of the afternoon rewriting the introduction.
collocations: for the rest of my life

contexts.text: The first section takes half the time; the rest of the paper has to fit into what is left.
The rest of the students had already gone home.

confusables.difference: 'The others' stands alone and means the remaining people or things: 'The others had left.'
minimal_pair: The rest of the group left.
The others left.

confusables.difference: The verb 'rest' means to relax. The noun 'the rest' means the remainder. Same spelling, unrelated meanings.

entry_json.avoid: Make the verb agree with the noun after 'of': 'the rest of the students were', 'the rest of the money was'.

entry_json.definition: all the other countries apart from the one being discussed; it takes a singular verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The country produces more solar power per person than the rest of the world combined.
example_sentences: What happens to that region's water supply matters to the rest of the world.
The pandemic showed how quickly one place can affect the rest of the world.
collocations: compared with the rest of the world

contexts.text: The country produces more solar power per person than the rest of the world combined.
What happens to that region's water supply matters to the rest of the world.

confusables.difference: 'The whole world' includes the country you are talking about; 'the rest of the world' excludes it.
minimal_pair: the rest of the world
the whole world

confusables.difference: An adverb or adjective, useful for compressing: 'sales worldwide'.

entry_json.avoid: Treat it as singular: 'the rest of the world is', not 'are'.

entry_json.definition: almost all of a group; the verb agrees with the noun after 'of', so a plural noun takes a plural verb
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The vast majority of journeys under two miles are still made by car.
example_sentences: The vast majority of respondents said they would use the service again.
The vast majority of the world's population now lives within reach of a mobile signal.

contexts.text: The vast majority of journeys under two miles are still made by car.
The vast majority of respondents said they would use the service again.

confusables.difference: 'The majority' means more than half. 'The vast majority' means almost all. Do not use the stronger phrase for a narrow margin.
minimal_pair: the majority of voters
the vast majority of voters

confusables.difference: Shorter and just as accurate. In Task 1, 'most' often reads better than 'the vast majority'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a figure near fifty per cent. If the number is 55 per cent, write 'a small majority' or 'just over half'.

entry_json.definition: used to say that plural things exist or are present; 'there' is an empty subject and the verb agrees with the noun that follows
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are three main reasons why people move to the capital.
example_sentences: There are far more cyclists on the roads than there were ten years ago.
In the second diagram there are two entrances instead of one.

contexts.text: There are three main reasons why people move to the capital.
In the second diagram there are two entrances instead of one.

confusables.difference: 'There is' takes a singular noun, 'there are' a plural one. The verb looks forward to the noun, not back at 'there'.
minimal_pair: There is one entrance.
There are two entrances.

confusables.difference: 'They are' refers to people or things already mentioned. 'There are' introduces them for the first time.
minimal_pair: There are two options.
They are both expensive.

entry_json.avoid: With a list, the verb agrees with the first item: 'There is a bank, two shops and a cafe' is standard, though many writers prefer to reorder.

entry_json.definition: used to say that one thing or an uncountable amount exists or is present; the verb is singular because the noun after it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a strong case for investing in rail rather than in new roads.
example_sentences: There is little evidence that longer school days improve results.
There is a small park at the north end of the site.
collocations: there is a need for sth

contexts.text: There is a strong case for investing in rail rather than in new roads.
There is a small park at the north end of the site.
There's a market near my flat every Saturday.

confusables.difference: 'It is' refers to something already known; 'there is' introduces something new.
minimal_pair: There is a problem.
It is a serious problem.

confusables.difference: Not a possible pair in this pattern. The present perfect is 'there has been': 'There has been a rise.'

entry_json.avoid: Do not start too many sentences with it in Task 2. 'There is' delays the real subject and weakens the sentence.

entry_json.definition: the past form used for one thing or an uncountable amount that existed at a time in the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a sharp drop in visitor numbers in the final year shown.
example_sentences: There was no mention of cost anywhere in the proposal.
There was a bakery on the corner when I was a child.

contexts.text: There was a sharp drop in visitor numbers in the final year shown.
There was a bakery on the corner when I was a child.

confusables.difference: Singular noun takes 'was', plural takes 'were'. 'There was two shops' is a basic agreement error.
minimal_pair: There was one shop.
There were two shops.

confusables.difference: 'It was' points back at something known; 'there was' introduces something new into the story.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1 this pattern is useful for change: 'There was a steady rise between 1990 and 2000.' Do not overuse it in a single paragraph.

entry_json.definition: the past form used for plural things that existed or were present at a time in the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There were almost twice as many bus routes in 1980 as there are today.
example_sentences: There were several factors behind the decline.
There were no lifts in the original building.

contexts.text: There were almost twice as many bus routes in 1980 as there are today.
There were several factors behind the decline.

confusables.difference: Match the verb to the noun after it: 'there was one factor', 'there were several factors'.
minimal_pair: There was one factor.
There were several factors.

confusables.difference: 'They were' refers back to a known group; 'there were' introduces them.

entry_json.avoid: Agreement is the whole point of this phrase. 'There were a lot of traffic' should be 'There was a lot of traffic', because 'traffic' is uncountable.

entry_json.definition: at the present time, in contrast with the past; it takes no preposition and normally pairs with the present simple
entry_json.own_context_sentence: These days most people book their travel without ever speaking to anyone.
example_sentences: Students these days face far higher fees than their parents did.
These days I read far less than I used to.

contexts.text: These days most people book their travel without ever speaking to anyone.
These days I read far less than I used to.

confusables.difference: The same meaning and the same slightly informal feel. Both are acceptable in Task 2, but neither should open every paragraph.
minimal_pair: These days people work longer.
Nowadays people work longer.

confusables.difference: Not used for the present period. 'To this day' means up until now and is a different phrase.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a preposition: 'these days', never 'in these days'.

entry_json.definition: used to report a general belief without naming who holds it; 'they' refers to people in general, and it belongs to conversation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They say the winters here are milder than they used to be, and the records agree.
example_sentences: They say it takes about three weeks to form a habit.
They say the new line will open next year, but nobody has seen a date.

contexts.text: They say the winters here are milder than they used to be, and the records agree.
They say it takes about three weeks to form a habit.

confusables.difference: The formal passive version for writing: 'It is said that the practice began in the 1800s.'
minimal_pair: They say it began in the 1800s.
It is said that it began in the 1800s.

confusables.difference: What Task 2 actually needs. Vague attribution to 'they' is worth nothing as evidence.
minimal_pair: They say sugar is harmful.
Research suggests that sugar is harmful.

entry_json.avoid: Never use it as evidence in an essay. An unnamed 'they' is exactly the vague attribution examiners penalise.

entry_json.definition: consider something carefully, or have something in your mind; 'about' introduces the subject of your thinking, often over a period
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have been thinking about applying for the course in September.
example_sentences: Planners rarely think about how a street feels to somebody walking down it.
I think about my old school more than I expected to.

contexts.text: I have been thinking about applying for the course in September.
Planners rarely think about how a street feels to somebody walking down it.

confusables.difference: 'Think of' is usually a quick act of recall or invention: 'I can't think of the word.' 'Think about' is sustained consideration.
minimal_pair: I can't think of his name.
I'm thinking about my future.

confusables.difference: After 'about' use the -ing form: 'think about applying', not 'think about to apply'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow 'about' with an infinitive. It is a preposition, so it takes a noun or an -ing form.

entry_json.definition: bring somebody or something to mind, invent an idea, or have an opinion; with an opinion it usually appears in a question with 'what'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cannot think of a single reason why the meeting needs to be an hour long.
example_sentences: What do you think of the new library building?
She thought of a way to cut the process from three steps to one.

contexts.text: I cannot think of a single reason why the meeting needs to be an hour long.
What do you think of the new library building?

confusables.difference: 'Think about' is extended consideration; 'think of' is a single moment of recall or invention.
minimal_pair: I thought about it all week.
I thought of a solution.

confusables.difference: Adding 'as' means to regard in a particular way: 'I think of him as a friend rather than a colleague.'

entry_json.avoid: For opinions, English uses 'What do you think of...?' or 'What do you think about...?', never 'How do you think about...?'.

entry_json.definition: during the afternoon of today; it takes no preposition, and the tense shows whether the afternoon has already passed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have a seminar this afternoon, so I will not be free until five.
example_sentences: It rained heavily this afternoon and the match was called off.
Could we meet this afternoon rather than tomorrow?

contexts.text: I have a seminar this afternoon, so I will not be free until five.
It rained heavily this afternoon and the match was called off.

confusables.difference: 'In the afternoon' is a general habit: 'I study in the afternoon.' 'This afternoon' is one particular one.
minimal_pair: I study in the afternoon.
I am studying this afternoon.

confusables.difference: Never with a preposition. 'This afternoon' stands alone.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in this afternoon' or 'on this afternoon'. Phrases with 'this' take no preposition.

entry_json.definition: during the evening of today; it takes no preposition and is normally used with a future or a present form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am meeting friends this evening after work.
example_sentences: The results will be announced this evening.
Is there anything on television this evening?

contexts.text: I am meeting friends this evening after work.
The results will be announced this evening.

confusables.difference: 'Tonight' covers the evening and the night. 'This evening' is more specific and slightly more formal.
minimal_pair: I'm going out tonight.
I'm going out this evening.

confusables.difference: The general habit rather than one particular evening.

entry_json.avoid: No preposition is needed: 'this evening', not 'in this evening'.

entry_json.definition: of the type just described; it takes a singular noun without an article, and the plural version is 'these kinds of'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This kind of housing was built quickly and cheaply, and it is now the hardest to heat.
example_sentences: This kind of question comes up in almost every listening section.
These kinds of scheme work only where the bus service is already reliable.

contexts.text: This kind of housing was built quickly and cheaply, and it is now the hardest to heat.
This kind of question comes up in almost every listening section.

confusables.difference: The article is wrong here. It is 'this kind of house', never 'this kind of a house'.
minimal_pair: this kind of house
this kind of a house

confusables.difference: A very common error. Match the demonstrative to 'kind': 'this kind of' or 'these kinds of'.
minimal_pair: these kinds of houses
these kind of houses

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'these kind of'. Either both singular or both plural.

entry_json.definition: during the morning of today; it takes no preposition, and the tense depends on whether the morning is over
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I finished the whole first draft this morning before anyone else arrived.
example_sentences: This morning the trains were delayed by ice on the line.
I have already had three meetings this morning.

contexts.text: This morning the trains were delayed by ice on the line.
I have already had three meetings this morning.

confusables.difference: The general habit: 'I work best in the morning.' 'This morning' is one particular morning.
minimal_pair: I work best in the morning.
I worked well this morning.

confusables.difference: If the morning is still going on, the present perfect is natural: 'I have had three meetings this morning.' Once it is over, use the past simple.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a preposition. 'In this morning' is a common error; the phrase stands alone.

entry_json.definition: during the summer of this year, either the one coming or the one just past; no preposition is used
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am planning to work at a summer camp this summer to improve my English.
example_sentences: This summer was the hottest since records began in that region.
The library will be closed for refurbishment this summer.

contexts.text: I am planning to work at a summer camp this summer to improve my English.
This summer was the hottest since records began in that region.

confusables.difference: General or habitual: 'It is busy in the summer.' 'This summer' points at one specific season.
minimal_pair: It is busy in the summer.
It was busy this summer.

confusables.difference: Never with a preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Let the verb tense do the work. 'This summer I will travel' looks forward; 'This summer was hot' looks back.

entry_json.definition: on this particular occasion, in contrast with previous ones; also used in 'this time last year' to fix a point in the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This time I am going to plan the essay before I start writing it.
example_sentences: This time last year the same street was completely flooded.
The result was different this time.

contexts.text: This time I am going to plan the essay before I start writing it.
This time last year the same street was completely flooded.

confusables.difference: 'At this time' means at this moment or period and is formal: 'We cannot comment at this time.'
minimal_pair: This time I'll be ready.
We cannot comment at this time.

confusables.difference: Points forward to the following occasion; 'this time' is the current one.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'in this time'. That would mean within this period, which is a different idea.

entry_json.definition: during the coming or the most recent weekend; British English says 'at the weekend' in general, but 'this weekend' takes no preposition
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am going to see my family this weekend for the first time since March.
example_sentences: This weekend the museum is free for local residents.
We did nothing at all this weekend, which was exactly what I needed.

contexts.text: I am going to see my family this weekend for the first time since March.
This weekend the museum is free for local residents.

confusables.difference: British English uses 'at the weekend' for the general habit; American English uses 'on the weekend'. 'This weekend' needs neither.
minimal_pair: I relax at the weekend.
I'm busy this weekend.

confusables.difference: Never with a preposition.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in this weekend' or 'on this weekend'. The phrase stands alone.

entry_json.definition: during the current year; it takes no preposition, and it pairs with the present perfect while the year is still running
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Applications have risen by almost a fifth this year.
example_sentences: This year I finally started swimming regularly.
The figures for this year are not yet complete.

contexts.text: Applications have risen by almost a fifth this year.
This year I finally started swimming regularly.

confusables.difference: No preposition is used with 'this'. 'In 2019' takes 'in'; 'this year' does not.
minimal_pair: this year

confusables.difference: 'The year' needs something to identify it: 'the year I left school'.

entry_json.avoid: While the year is still going, use the present perfect: 'have risen this year', not 'rose this year'.

entry_json.definition: the people who; a formal way of referring to a group defined by what they do, and it always takes a plural verb
